questions.stem: Your support agent's harness receives a response with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` containing two tool_use blocks — `get_customer` and `lookup_order`. The loop executes only the first block, appends that single result, and re-invokes Claude, which then re-requests the ignored lookup, adding an extra round-trip to most multi-tool turns. How should the loop handle these responses?
questions.why: The loop structure is: extract the tool_use content blocks, execute each tool, append tool_result blocks, then call Claude again — a multi-tool response is handled in one iteration, not one tool at a time.
ww: Forcing a specific tool locks every turn to that one tool and cannot express requests that legitimately need two lookups — it misuses a routing control as a loop fix.
Relying on Claude to re-request dropped tools rationalizes the defect — each ignored block costs a full extra API round-trip, which is exactly the observed waste.
Loop decisions come from structured stop_reason values and tool_use blocks, never from parsing reply prose for tool names.

questions.stem: The same harness assumes every response includes a tool call. When a customer opens with a greeting or sends a thank-you, Claude replies with plain text and `stop_reason: "end_turn"`, and the harness throws an exception and drops the conversation. `tool_choice` is left at its default. What should the harness do instead?
questions.why: With tool_choice at its default auto, Claude decides whether a tool is needed; a correct harness handles both response shapes — executing tools on tool_use and returning the text reply on end_turn.
ww: "any" forces at least one tool call even on greetings where none is appropriate, producing spurious tool invocations to paper over a harness defect.
A prompt rule is probabilistic and, like forcing "any", manufactures pointless tool calls instead of fixing the harness's missing end_turn path.
Response handling belongs on the structured stop_reason field, not on string-matching marker text in the reply.

questions.stem: Designing the support agent's MCP server, the team must expose three things: refund and escalation actions the agent performs, a return-policy document set the agent only ever reads, and a reusable escalation-summary template. They are deciding which MCP primitive should carry each. Which assignment matches the protocol's capability categories?
questions.why: The three MCP primitives map by capability: tools are actions Claude calls, resources are read-only data Claude can access, and prompts are pre-built reusable templates.
ww: Wrapping read-only reference data as tools adds a tool-call round-trip for what should simply be readable data, collapsing the protocol's action/data distinction.
It swaps the last two categories: prompts are reusable instruction templates, not document storage, and resources are the read-only data primitive.
Resources are read-only by definition — refund and escalation actions change state and must be tools.

questions.stem: Your `process_refund` tool returns a bare `isError: true` whenever a final-sale item is ineligible for refund under written policy. The agent treats these as outages — apologizing for technical difficulties and promising to retry later — and the ops dashboard counts them as tool failures, inflating error rates. How should the tool represent this outcome?
questions.why: A business-rule denial is not a failure of the tool — it is a valid answer that the action is disallowed. Structuring it as retriable: false with a customer-friendly explanation stops pointless retries and lets the agent state the policy accurately.
ww: Marking a policy outcome retryable wastes attempts on a result no retry can change — those are the transient category's semantics, not a business rule's.
Returning success with embedded error metadata masks failures and corrupts agent decision-making — the corpus rules this pattern out explicitly.
Escalating every failure floods humans with self-explanatory policy outcomes; a structured category lets the agent explain the denial directly.

questions.stem: On multi-issue cases, the coordinator runs billing, returns, and delivery subagents in parallel. Today, any subagent hitting a transient database timeout reports a failure upward, and the coordinator aborts the entire case — discarding the other subagents' completed work — before a human restarts it from scratch. Where should this error handling live instead?
questions.why: Transient failures belong at the subagent level — local retry with backoff — and only errors the subagent cannot resolve escalate, carrying context and partial progress; one subagent's failure must never terminate the whole workflow.
ww: Never terminate the entire workflow for one subagent failure — the other issues' completed investigations are valid work the coordinator should keep.
Catching errors and silently returning success is explicitly prohibited — it hides failures from the coordinator's recovery logic.
Transient errors are retryable locally; escalating all of them to humans discards the transient/permanent distinction that drives recovery decisions.

questions.stem: Telemetry shows the agent calls `lookup_order`, waits a full turn, then calls `check_return_eligibility` with the same order identifier on nearly every return case — two round-trips where one would do. An engineer has already sketched a combined `lookup_order_with_eligibility` tool and asks you to review the design. What should you recommend?
questions.why: The corpus prefers prompting the agent to bundle habitually-paired tool requests into one turn — the model can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously — over creating a composite tool.
ww: A composite tool hides the composition; bundling-by-prompt is the documented preferred approach for habitually-paired calls.
Hooks validate, block, or transform tool interactions — reaching for hook infrastructure to inject extra calls is a disproportionate mechanism where a bundling instruction suffices.
Both calls take the same order identifier the customer supplied — nothing structural forces sequencing; the extra turn is habit, not dependency.

questions.stem: Privacy rules require verifying identity via `get_customer` before the agent discloses any order detail. After two rounds of system-prompt strengthening, violations fell from 12% to 3% of conversations, then stopped improving — audits still find disclosures to unverified callers every week. The team asks how to reach zero. What should you advise?
questions.why: For security-critical sequencing, enforce at the code level: a precondition that blocks the downstream call until verification succeeds is deterministic, where prompt compliance is probabilistic.
ww: Prompt instructions can reduce violations but never guarantee zero — the plateau at 3% is the expected behavior of a probabilistic control, not a sign one more revision will finish the job.
Few-shot examples of the correct sequence are still probabilistic guidance — the corpus rejects them for mandatory sequencing.
After-the-fact detection does not prevent the disclosure; the requirement is to make the violating call impossible, not to review it later.

questions.stem: To speed up eligibility checks, an engineer gave the returns subagent a general `run_report_query` tool accepting free-form queries against the support database. Logs now show it querying unrelated customer-PII tables mid-case for extra context. A prompt line restricting it to return tables cut the misuse roughly in half. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Least privilege is enforced at the tool interface: replacing the broad query capability with a scoped, validating tool fixes the root cause deterministically — the documented pattern for an over-broad tool being misused.
ww: Prompt instructions against misusing a tool are probabilistic — the corpus's fetch_url pattern rejects exactly this fix; halving misuse is not eliminating it.
Routing a simple, high-frequency check through the coordinator adds a full extra loop per case and still leaves the over-broad capability in place.
Adding subagents is separation theater — the mechanism for separation of responsibilities is tool restriction, and the broad query interface would survive the split.

questions.stem: Mid-conversation, the agent offers a policy-compliant store credit for a damaged item. The customer replies: 'No — I want to talk to a person.' Following its three-attempts-before-escalation instruction, the agent offers a replacement instead, and the customer repeats the demand, now angrier. What behavior should the escalation design enforce here?
questions.why: An explicit request for a human triggers immediate escalation — the agent must not attempt to solve first, and no attempt counter overrides that structural signal.
ww: A minimum-attempts rule violates the immediate-escalation requirement for explicit human requests — the documented trap of never escalating until N attempts have been made.
Acknowledge-then-offer applies to expressions of frustration without a human request; 'I want to talk to a person' is explicit, so offering alternatives misapplies that pattern.
Self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and irrelevant here — the structural signal, an explicit request, has already fired.

questions.stem: A customer reports a package missing. Confirming the claim needs a warehouse-scan lookup, but that system has returned errors for two hours. The agent has silently retried nine times while the customer waits, and no policy covers proceeding without the scan record. What should the agent do now?
questions.why: When repeated attempts cannot make progress, escalation is the defined trigger — and the handoff should carry what was attempted plus the context gathered so far.
ww: Indefinite retries after repeated failures is exactly the 'unable to make progress' condition escalation exists for — waiting hours holds the customer hostage to an outage.
Abandoning the case pushes the burden back onto the customer; the escalation path, not closure, handles blocked-but-valid claims.
Nothing in policy authorizes refunds without the required verification — the agent must not invent policy to resolve its own blockage.

questions.stem: A quarterly audit of escalation routing finds the human queue dominated by routine warranty lookups the agent was authorized to resolve, while two goodwill-credit edge cases the agent settled autonomously were later reversed on appeal. No written guidance defines which cases route where. Which change most effectively fixes this calibration?
questions.why: The root cause is undefined decision boundaries: explicit escalate-when / resolve-when criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing the two is the documented fix for mis-calibrated routing.
ww: Model self-rated confidence is uncalibrated — confidently wrong cases sail through, as the reversed goodwill decisions show.
A separate classifier model is overkill that adds infrastructure without addressing the missing decision boundaries in the prompt.
Customer mood does not correlate with case complexity — sentiment-triggered escalation floods the queue with resolvable-but-angry cases.

questions.stem: Escalations currently arrive with a one-line note, and human agents keep re-asking customers for details the agent already gathered. An engineer proposes wiring the human console to display the full conversation transcript at handoff so nothing is lost. How should you evaluate this proposal?
questions.why: The handoff mechanism is a complete, self-contained structured summary carrying the named fields; human agents lack transcript access by design, and a summary beats forcing them to re-read an entire conversation.
ww: Completeness is not the bottleneck — a raw transcript forces re-reading the whole conversation to find what matters; the corpus explicitly rejects transcript access as the fix.
Re-running the agent's tools duplicates work already done and slows resolution — the information exists; it was just never packaged.
Escalating earlier does not fix the information loss and degrades the autonomous resolution rate.

questions.stem: The agent's system prompt requires restating the confirmed order ID whenever any monetary amount is quoted. In long multi-issue conversations this holds for roughly eight turns, then stops — affected sessions measure only about 2,700 tokens, and no summarization or trimming is configured. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: Behavioral drift at a few thousand tokens is attention dilution: each accumulated assistant response weighs against the system prompt's authority, degrading rule-following long before any capacity limit matters.
ww: Context-window overflow is impossible at roughly 2,700 tokens — the window is orders of magnitude larger.
False — the system prompt is included with every request; it never expires after turn one.
No summarization or trimming exists in this design, so nothing was evicted — the rule is still present in context, just increasingly outweighed.

questions.stem: A nightly support-ops job runs `claude -p` to triage the day's unresolved tickets and flag handling errors. Every night it flags the documented under-$5 automatic goodwill credit as an unauthorized refund, because the job receives only the ticket dump and a two-line prompt. What change would most reduce this recurring false positive?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude project context — conventions and review criteria — which is exactly what eliminates false positives on documented, deliberate behavior.
ww: Re-pasting the manual into every job's prompt duplicates content that belongs in version-controlled project context, must be maintained per job, and bloats each invocation.
-p is the documented way to run Claude Code in a pipeline; reverting to interactive mode abandons the automation rather than informing it.
A keyword filter suppresses the symptom and would also hide a genuinely unauthorized credit — the fix is missing context, not censored output.

questions.stem: A named Claude Code session spent three days tracing a recurring refund miscalculation through the support tooling. Overnight, teammates rewrote only the tax-and-fees configuration module; everything else the session analyzed is untouched. The team wants to continue this morning without stale conclusions or needless re-analysis. What is the most effective way to continue?
questions.why: When most prior context is still valid, resume the named session and tell the agent exactly which files changed so it performs targeted re-analysis of just those files.
ww: Resuming as-is leaves the session reasoning over stale tool results for the rewritten module as if they were current.
Re-analyzing everything discards three days of still-valid context — wasteful when only one module changed.
fork_session is for comparing divergent approaches from a shared baseline, not for refreshing stale results — neither branch would reflect the rewritten module.

questions.stem: An engineer's Claude Code sessions in the demand-forecasting module reliably flagged missing changelog entries on every commit for weeks. After setting up a new laptop and restoring their project checkout, the same convention never fires again, even on files it used to catch. Rather than investigate, the engineer starts appending 'remember the changelog rule' to every prompt. What is the most effective first step instead?
questions.why: `/memory` shows exactly which memory files are loaded in the current session — the documented first diagnostic step whenever a previously reliable rule stops firing, turning a guess into a fact before anything is changed.
ww: Repeating the rule louder in the prompt treats the symptom, not the root cause — the corpus explicitly rejects this in favor of checking what's actually loaded.
Nothing in the documented CLAUDE.md/memory mechanism involves installation corruption; the far more likely cause is a configuration file the new machine simply never picked up.
Memory-file discovery is static configuration, not a behavior that re-establishes itself with use — waiting doesn't change which files are loaded.

questions.stem: The inventory-forecasting service is growing: demand-forecasting's Python files need a strict type-hints convention, supplier-sync's Go files need a specific retry-wrapping pattern, and test files scattered across both modules need one shared testing convention. The team wants each convention applied automatically based on which files Claude Code is actually touching, with no engineer needing to remember to mention it. What configuration best achieves this?
questions.why: `.claude/rules/` with glob-pattern frontmatter loads automatically only when Claude works on matching file paths — deterministic, path-based application across both modules and the scattered test files.
ww: Headed sections in one CLAUDE.md rely on model inference to pick the right section, not deterministic file-path matching.
Per-directory CLAUDE.md files don't work well when relevant files — like the scattered test files — are spread across many directories, not confined to one.
Skills are invoked on demand for workflow-specific guidance; conventions that should apply automatically based on file type belong in path-scoped rules, not a manually-triggered skill.

questions.stem: The team wires a semantic, embedding-backed code-search tool into Claude Code, expecting it to replace ad-hoc text search for finding conceptually related code across the reporting module. Sessions keep calling `Grep` instead, missing renamed or refactored call sites the semantic tool would have caught. The new tool's description reads only 'Searches code.' What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions; spelling out the unique capability a tool provides over the familiar built-in is the documented fix when an agent defaults to `Grep` over a more capable alternative.
ww: Removing `Grep` breaks legitimate literal-search cases; the root cause is an under-specified description, not the built-in's continued existence.
A blunt "always prefer" rule is keyword-sensitive and misroutes cases where `Grep` genuinely is the right tool.
A larger context window doesn't fix tool selection driven by a vague description — it just makes the wrong tool's manual search less costly.

questions.stem: The team's `/backfill-supplier` skill needs a supplier-region code as its argument to scope which records it touches. Nothing in the slash-command menu signals that an argument is required, so engineers regularly invoke it bare, and the skill silently backfills every region at once. Which SKILL.md frontmatter key most directly fixes this?
questions.why: `argument-hint` is displayed when the command is invoked, prompting for required arguments — the frontmatter key that directly closes the gap between engineers not knowing an argument is expected and the menu.
ww: `context: fork` isolates output into a subagent context; it does nothing to signal that an argument is required.
`allowed-tools` scopes which tools the skill may use, not whether it knows which region to scope its writes to — a legitimate Write call still touches every region.
A skill's description appears in the slash-command menu's summary line, not as an argument prompt shown at invocation the way `argument-hint` is.

questions.stem: Claude Code implements a rate limiter for the reporting module's export endpoint, reasons through concurrent-request edge cases in its own response, and concludes the sliding-window logic is correct. Asked in the same conversation to review its own change before merge, it reports no issues. Days later, a burst of concurrent requests reveals the window can double-count under specific timing. What most directly addresses why the same-session check missed this?
questions.why: A second independent instance, without the generator's reasoning context, mirrors human peer review and catches what the author rationalized away — the documented fix for same-session confirmation bias.
ww: Extended thinking on the generation stage doesn't fix the self-check limitation — it's still the same session reasoning from the same starting conclusion.
A self-review instruction on the same instance carries the same confirmation bias as the unprompted self-check that already missed the bug.
Tests for edge cases the session already considered won't surface a timing interaction it never reasoned about in the first place.

questions.stem: A legacy `/rollback-migration` command was written before the team adopted Skills, as a plain file at `.claude/commands/rollback-migration.md` that reads the typed target version as `$ARGUMENTS`. A new hire argues it will stop working soon and must be converted into a `.claude/skills/` folder with a SKILL.md. Is the new hire correct?
questions.why: `.claude/commands/` is legacy but still supported and unified with `.claude/skills/` — both create `/name` commands, and `$ARGUMENTS` continues to hold the typed text with no conversion required.
ww: Legacy commands are explicitly documented as still supported, not deprecated or non-functional — this claim is false.
No such partial-migration requirement exists for `$ARGUMENTS` — the mechanism works unchanged in the legacy file location.
Duplicating the command into both locations isn't a documented requirement and would just create two copies to keep in sync for no benefit.

questions.stem: A developer wants to skip the slow style pass inside the shared `/lint-check` skill during their own iterative work, without changing what the other six teammates run after pulling the same repo. They are deciding where to put a modified version. Where should they create it, and why does it take effect automatically?
questions.why: A personal skill at the same name, in user scope, automatically overrides the project skill of that name — no edit to the shared file, and nothing teammates see after pulling.
ww: A different name creates a new, separate `/lint-check-fast` command instead of overriding `/lint-check` — the documented trap for exactly this intention.
Editing the shared file directly, even temporarily, risks affecting teammates mid-change and depends on manual discipline to revert — not the documented mechanism.
Override resolution is by matching name and scope, not by a prompted preference note — a differently-named skill is simply a different command.

questions.stem: The reporting module needs a new `region_code` field added to the export-request struct, three call sites already identified, and the exact type and default value already agreed in the design doc. Before starting, an engineer opens planning mode so Claude Code can explore the module's structure first. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: Direct execution is for a task with clear scope, a defined approach, and routine changes — exactly this case; planning mode's exploration adds overhead with no ambiguity left to resolve.
ww: Planning mode's value is investigating undefined scope or design decisions; approving a plan for an already fully-specified change is process for its own sake.
Splitting one small, already-scoped change across both modes doesn't match either mode's intended use — the whole task is routine.
Re-deriving a type and default value already settled in the design doc is redundant exploration of a question that isn't actually open.

questions.stem: A debugging session tracing an intermittent supplier-sync failure reaches 55,000 tokens. It holds the exact error code that reproduces the bug, the specific config flag that was ruled out, several dead-end theories chased and abandoned, and the last few exchanges narrowing down the actual cause. The team needs to cut tokens while keeping the session useful going forward. Which strategy is most effective?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — extract critical structured data verbatim, summarize lower-density discussion, keep recent exchanges verbatim — preserves exactly the precision this session needs while compressing the rest.
ww: Pure summarization risks turning the precise error code and config flag into vague paraphrase, losing exactly the detail needed to avoid re-diagnosing them.
Keeping only the most recent tokens drops the error code and ruled-out flag if either was established earlier in the session.
A bigger token budget doesn't decide which content matters; it delays the same problem at higher cost.

questions.stem: A prompt asks Claude Code to convert raw supplier invoices into a normalized export format, described only in prose. Successive runs disagree on how to represent invoice status — one emits `pending`, another `PENDING` — and unit prices sometimes appear as decimals, sometimes as integer minor units. Rewriting the prose with more detail each time hasn't converged the output. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: Concrete input/output example pairs unambiguously show the target format and decision logic; the model generalizes the pattern to new invoices instead of guessing from prose.
ww: A larger context window doesn't resolve ambiguity in what the instructions actually specify.
A longer checklist is still prose description — the corpus rejects lengthening prose as a fix for output that's already inconsistent.
Inferring format from downstream consumption is indirect and unreliable compared to showing the exact expected shape directly.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude Code to both flag issues in a changed module and generate fixes for each one it finds, currently handled in a single combined prompt. Output quality is inconsistent — some genuine issues go unflagged, and some generated fixes address problems the pass never explicitly called out. What restructuring would most likely improve both stages?
questions.why: Prompt chaining breaks a complex task into sequential focused prompts where each step's output feeds the next — identify, then fix — producing more focused, consistent results at each stage.
ww: Lengthening a single combined prompt still asks one pass to do two competing jobs at once.
Requesting the list first within the same response doesn't separate the two into distinct steps — the fix stage still doesn't consume the flagging stage's actual output as its input.
A bigger token budget for one stage doesn't address the two tasks competing for attention within one pass.

questions.stem: The reporting module's CLAUDE.md covers formatting conventions every session must follow, plus a lengthy quarterly data-reconciliation procedure and an equally long incident-postmortem template, each invoked only a few times a year. An engineer proposes moving just the reconciliation procedure into a Skill and leaving the postmortem template inline to limit the change's scope. How should the team evaluate this proposal?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md content loads in every session while Skills are invoked on demand; universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md, but both occasional-use procedures belong in Skills — a half-move still clutters every session for no benefit.
ww: "Most of the token savings" rationalizes leaving one clutter-causing procedure in place — it still loads every session for content only a few sessions need, the exact defect the proposal was meant to fix.
Moving universal formatting conventions into Skills too means they'd need explicit invocation every session — the corpus explicitly rejects moving everything to Skills.
Splitting into more CLAUDE.md files keeps both procedures loading in every session regardless of file count — it doesn't move them on-demand.

questions.stem: The team is retiring a deprecated pagination helper referenced somewhere across the reporting module's roughly 120 files. Mapping every call site and how each one uses the helper produces a long, detailed inventory — and running that mapping in the main session leaves little room for the follow-up conversation about the replacement interface. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: An Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns a concise summary, preserving the main session's context for the design and implementation phases that follow.
ww: Running the mapping directly in the main session is exactly the failure mode described — it consumes the room the interface discussion needs.
`/compact` mid-task loses precision the interface discussion may still need — not the documented fix for this discovery-then-design sequence.
Splitting across sessions joined with `--continue` adds coordination overhead and consistency risk instead of isolating the verbose output.

questions.stem: A named Claude Code session spent two days investigating recurring timeout errors in the supplier-sync module, mapping its retry-and-connection-pooling logic in detail. Before the team resumes this morning, that entire layer is swapped for a different retry library as part of an unrelated migration — nothing the session mapped still describes how retries actually work. What is the most effective way to continue?
questions.why: When tool results are stale because the code has fundamentally changed, it's better to restart with a short summary of prior findings than resume and reason over now-incorrect tool data.
ww: Targeted re-analysis of "just the changed part" fits when most context is still valid — here the entire mechanism the session mapped is gone, not one isolated piece.
`fork_session` branches from a shared, still-valid baseline to compare approaches — it doesn't refresh a session whose baseline is itself now obsolete.
Resuming as-is reasons over stale tool results as though they were still current — exactly the failure a fresh start avoids.

questions.stem: A single long-running Claude Code session is migrating 200 legacy endpoints to a new validation library, one at a time, holding every discovered quirk in conversation history alone. By endpoint 140, its suggestions start referencing generic 'typical' validation patterns instead of the specific quirks it identified for earlier endpoints. What is the most effective way to prevent this?
questions.why: Writing intermediate findings to a scratchpad file, read at the start of each continuation, lets the task survive context limits and counteracts context degradation — the model reaching for generic patterns instead of specifics it discovered earlier.
ww: More aggressive summarization of exact quirks is what blurs them into generic patterns in the first place — it doesn't preserve them.
A larger context window doesn't stop degradation; the documented fix is persisted state, not raw capacity.
Restarting from scratch every 20 endpoints discards findings a scratchpad would have preserved, re-losing exactly the specifics needed.

questions.stem: The coordinator issues three parallel `Task` calls — web-search, filing document-analysis, and internal-report document-analysis — for a packaging-waste compliance review. The web-search subagent returns first, with partial early findings. An engineer wants the coordinator to forward those findings straight to report-generation immediately, without waiting on the other two calls. What should the architecture require instead?
questions.why: The coordinator aggregates results only once every Task call in a delegation round completes — passing a partial subset onward, or letting subagents message each other directly, breaks the hub's role as the single aggregation and information-control point.
ww: Splitting report-generation's input across two deliveries defeats coordinated aggregation and risks it acting on a state the coordinator was still assembling.
Subagents do not communicate directly — information flow between them exists only through the coordinator, which decides what each subagent receives and when.
Cancelling calls and proceeding on a partial subset discards two-thirds of the delegated work and abandons the completion-based aggregation the hub pattern requires.

questions.stem: An engineer evaluating a new citation-checking MCP server for personal use adds it to the project's version-controlled `.mcp.json` so 'everyone can see what I'm testing,' even though no teammate uses it yet and it isn't ready to be a shared dependency. What is the most effective correction?
questions.why: `.mcp.json` is for shared, version-controlled team configuration; personal overrides and experimental servers belong in the user-scoped `~/.claude.json` until the tool is actually adopted team-wide.
ww: Committing an unadopted, personal tool to shared project config makes every teammate's session load a dependency nobody else uses or has vetted.
An environment-variable gate still leaves the server declared in version-controlled project config — the scope itself is the problem, not the absence of a toggle.
A comment is documentation, not configuration — the server still loads for every teammate; the scope itself is the problem, not the absence of a note.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent keeps calling `draft_report_section`, a formatting tool meant only for report-generation, even after its `system_prompt` is rewritten twice to say 'only extract and summarize, never draft report text.' Its `AgentDefinition` still lists `draft_report_section` among its `allowed_tools`, left over from an early prototype. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: `allowed_tools` is the enforcement lever — a subagent that still has a tool granted can still call it regardless of what the system_prompt says; removing the tool from the configuration is the fix that actually removes the capability.
ww: A third prompt revision repeats a fix that already failed twice — system_prompt wording is behavioral guidance, not a capability restriction, and cannot override a tool the AgentDefinition still grants.
A few-shot example is still prompt-level guidance; it does not remove the subagent's actual ability to call draft_report_section.
Detecting the problem after the fact doesn't stop it from recurring — the subagent still has, and will keep using, a tool outside its scope.

questions.stem: The web-search subagent's `extract_key_findings` tool and the document-analysis subagent's `extract_citations` tool are each described only as 'extracts relevant text from a source.' When a request could plausibly involve either a web page or a filing PDF, selection between the two tools is close to a coin flip. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The primary lever for tool selection is the description itself — specifying accepted input formats, examples, and explicit boundary cases is the documented fix for near-identical descriptions, and should be checked before adding any new infrastructure.
ww: A pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure that compensates for an under-specified signal instead of fixing the signal itself.
Merging into one tool loses the semantic precision that lets a subagent scope its own action to its role — the fix is better descriptions, not fewer tools.
Deferring to the other subagent on ambiguity is a probabilistic prompt instruction and does nothing to fix the descriptions actually causing the ambiguity.

questions.stem: The coordinator delegates synthesis by telling the subagent to 'use the compliance-cost findings from the filing-review step,' without including those findings in the prompt itself. The synthesis subagent, whose context holds nothing from that step, writes plausible-sounding cost figures that trace to no actual filing. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Subagents have isolated context and cannot see prior findings by reference — the coordinator must include the complete findings directly in the prompt, in structured form separating content from source metadata, so the subagent has real data instead of fabricating plausible figures.
ww: A findings-on-request pattern still starts from the same gap — nothing guarantees the coordinator supplies the actual data instead of another pointer, and it adds an avoidable round-trip.
Independent re-verification duplicates work the filing-review subagent already did and risks a different, possibly conflicting, set of figures.
A post-hoc citation check catches the symptom after fabricated numbers are already written — it doesn't stop the subagent from lacking real data in the first place.

questions.stem: Mid-batch, the document-analysis subagent finds two credible sources reporting different compliance-cost estimates for the same regulation. Rather than finish analyzing the current filing, it pauses the entire review and messages the coordinator asking which figure to use before it will continue to the next document. What should the design require instead?
questions.why: Subagents should not resolve conflicts autonomously, but they also should not block the pipeline waiting for reconciliation — complete analysis with both conflicting values, annotate the conflict with source attribution, and let the coordinator or a human reconcile later.
ww: Stopping and asking before completing analysis blocks the pipeline unnecessarily — the documented approach is to finish with both values annotated, not halt for a decision that can happen downstream.
Applying a heuristic to pick a value abandons a decision that belongs above the subagent's scope — annotation exists to preserve both values, not resolve between them.
Discarding both figures throws away real, credible findings instead of preserving them with attribution for reconciliation.

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent's `finalize_and_distribute_report` tool accepts a `send_now: boolean` so an internal QA pass can run before external distribution. Logs show it is sometimes called with `send_now=true` on the very first attempt, skipping the QA preview entirely. Which redesign makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible?
questions.why: A boolean parameter on one tool is always bypassable by calling it directly with the unsafe value; splitting into a preview tool that issues a single-use token and an execute tool that requires it makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible, not just discouraged.
ww: A prompt rule is probabilistic guidance — it reduces but cannot guarantee against the exact bypass already observed in logs.
Changing the default behavior still leaves a bypassable parameter in place — nothing stops a caller from explicitly overriding it on the first call, exactly as already happens.
An orchestration-layer dialog requires separate infrastructure outside the tool contract and is not the two-tool guarantee the corpus recommends for mandatory previews.

questions.stem: Investigating packaging-waste compliance costs, the coordinator delegates 'financing and grant mechanisms' to both the web-search subagent and the document-analysis subagent without distinguishing their scopes. Both independently research the same grant programs, and token usage nearly doubles with no added coverage. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The coordinator must explicitly partition the research space — assigning distinct subtopics or source types to each subagent — before delegating; this prevents duplication at the source instead of cleaning it up afterward.
ww: Deduplicating after the fact still pays the token cost of the duplicated research; the fix belongs at partitioning time, before delegation.
Removing the tool eliminates a subagent's ability to contribute to that subtopic at all, rather than simply assigning it a distinct scope.
Merging subagents collapses the specialization that hub-and-spoke depends on, rather than fixing the coordinator's failure to partition the task.

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent has two formatting tools, `render_as_table` and `render_as_narrative`. On some requests it instead writes a plain-text paragraph describing how it would format the data, without calling either tool. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` guarantees the model calls some tool rather than returning conversational text, while still letting it pick whichever of the two formatting tools actually fits — exactly the guarantee needed when a subagent sometimes replies in prose instead of calling a tool.
ww: Forcing one specific tool blocks the other legitimate formatting choice entirely — the fix needs to guarantee a tool call, not dictate which one.
A prompt instruction to always use a tool is exactly the kind of probabilistic guidance `tool_choice: any` exists to replace with a guarantee.
There is no documented mechanism for disabling free-text replies outright — response shape is controlled through `tool_choice`, not by removing that capability.

questions.stem: Investigating packaging-waste compliance costs across several regions, the coordinator's adaptive plan discovers mid-investigation that one region's cost data sits behind a specialized industry-report subscription no assigned source provides. The coordinator revises the remaining subtasks to substitute an accessible regulatory-filing source for that region instead. Which decomposition pattern does this exemplify, and why does it suit this task?
questions.why: Generating and revising subtasks in response to a mid-investigation discovery is dynamic adaptive decomposition — appropriate because the full scope and source landscape weren't known until initial findings came in, unlike a task where every step could be set in advance.
ww: A fixed pipeline's steps are set in advance and don't change based on discoveries — revising the plan mid-stream is the opposite of what a fixed pipeline does.
Substituting a source category is a decomposition-strategy decision, not a tool-access restriction on any subagent.
Reproducibility is the argument for a fixed pipeline on a predictable, template-following task — this task's own source landscape wasn't knowable until research began.

questions.stem: Policy requires that any single citation-purge action affecting more than 25 sources at once route to human sign-off before it runs. Today this rule exists only as a system-prompt instruction. During a high-volume cleanup pass, a purge affecting 60 sources executed without sign-off. What change most reliably closes this gap?
questions.why: Threshold enforcement on a critical operation needs to be deterministic, not probabilistic — a PreToolUse hook fires regardless of what the LLM does, blocking any call above the threshold before it executes and routing it to escalation.
ww: A stronger prompt is still prompt-level compliance — probabilistic by nature, which is exactly what already failed once at 60 sources.
A few-shot example is additional prompt guidance, not a deterministic block — it cannot guarantee the threshold is never crossed again.
After-the-fact logging documents a violation that has already happened; it doesn't prevent the purge from executing in the first place.

questions.stem: To speed up report assembly, the report-generation subagent stops carrying a source mapping for each individual claim through the pipeline, instead appending one consolidated bibliography section listing every source used somewhere in the document. Reviewers can no longer trace any specific claim back to the source that supports it. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Provenance must survive synthesis — requiring structured claim-to-source mappings that downstream agents preserve and merge is what lets a final report attribute every individual claim, which a general end-of-document bibliography cannot do.
ww: A better-sorted bibliography is still a document-level list — it does nothing to restore claim-level traceability.
Re-deriving attributions after the fact by searching again is expensive and error-prone; the mapping should be preserved through the pipeline, not reconstructed later.
Removing citations from the body entirely makes the traceability problem worse, since even the document-level list no longer connects to specific claims.

questions.stem: Frustrated by the round-trip cost of the coordinator's refinement loop, an engineer grants the synthesis subagent its own web-search tool so it can independently fill small gaps it notices while drafting, without reporting back to the coordinator first. What is the most effective response to this change?
questions.why: The coordinator owns gap evaluation and loop termination as part of its aggregation-and-validation responsibility; letting the synthesis subagent search independently breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling instead of routing the gap back through the coordinator's refinement loop.
ww: Scoping the domains still leaves the synthesis subagent doing research work outside its role — the problem is the responsibility boundary, not which sources it can reach.
Removing the refinement loop discards the coordinator's defined mechanism for evaluating coverage and knowing when a report is sufficient.
Logging the independent searches documents the boundary violation after the fact without preventing it from happening again.

questions.stem: The research team runs two workloads through Claude: a live fact-check a researcher waits on mid-call, and a nightly regeneration of source-credibility summaries for that day's newly ingested documents, with no one waiting on the output. Which API approach fits each, and why?
questions.why: The API choice should match the latency requirement: a blocking, live interaction needs the synchronous API's immediate response, while a non-blocking overnight job with no one waiting is exactly the profile the Batches API's 50% savings and up-to-24-hour window suit.
ww: The live fact-check is blocking — a researcher is waiting mid-call, and batch processing carries no latency guarantee, making it unsuitable regardless of cost savings.
Defaulting to synchronous for the nightly job forfeits the cost savings on a workload with no latency pressure at all — exactly the case batch is designed for.
This assignment is inverted — the blocking, live case needs synchronous, and the non-blocking overnight case is what batch actually suits.

questions.stem: Two of five assigned source categories time out entirely; the other three return complete, usable findings. Rather than pass anything forward, the synthesis subagent halts and reports a failure, reasoning the input set is too incomplete to work from. What should the design require instead?
questions.why: When upstream inputs are incomplete, the synthesis agent should complete synthesis with what is available, annotate coverage so readers know which conclusions are well-supported versus where gaps exist, and propagate that uncertainty upward — not refuse to produce output at all.
ww: Treating incomplete input as an unrecoverable error discards three genuinely complete, usable source categories for no reason.
Waiting indefinitely blocks the report on categories that already timed out, with no guarantee they ever return.
Substituting unrelated cached results fabricates coverage rather than honestly annotating the actual gap.

questions.stem: The pipeline extracts equipment-inspection reports into a fixed schema. Source reports write dates as "3/14," "14 March," and "2024-03-14," and technician hours as "3.5 hrs," "3h30m," and "210 min." The schema defines `inspection_date` as ISO-8601 and `labor_hours` as a decimal. Where should normalization guidance for these varied source formats live?
questions.why: The schema constrains the output's shape; normalization rules belong in the prompt to govern how messy source formats map into that shape — the two work together, not as substitutes.
ww: Loosening the schema reintroduces the inconsistency it exists to prevent, and just pushes normalization work downstream instead of handling it at extraction time.
A format-flag field records which style was seen instead of converting it, leaving downstream consumers to still handle three different value shapes.
Retrying treats a formatting-mapping gap as if it were a random model error; nothing about the request has changed, so nothing about the output will either.

questions.stem: A new extraction field asks the model to copy `defect_severity` directly from the report's explicit "Severity:" label into the output — no computation, comparison, or multi-step inference required. An engineer proposes adding "think step by step before extracting this field" to improve accuracy. What is the most effective response?
questions.why: Reasoning cues are for multi-step mathematical reasoning, multi-stage analysis, N-item comparison, or step-wise transformation; a single-step, already-explicit label copy is the documented case where a cue is not needed.
ww: This overgeneralizes a technique that helps multi-step tasks into a blanket rule, contradicting the explicit guidance not to add it for single-step work.
Document length has nothing to do with whether a given field's extraction is single-step or multi-step; the field's own reasoning demands are what matter.
Stacking more prompting techniques onto a task that needs neither doesn't compound a benefit — there is no reasoning gap here for either technique to close.

questions.stem: A pipeline's retry step resubmits a failed document within the same conversation, needing the model to call `resubmit_correction`. The conversation's tool list still includes the original `extract_fields` tool. With `tool_choice` left at `{"type": "any"}`, logs show the model sometimes re-calls `extract_fields` instead of submitting the correction. What configuration most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool guarantees that tool is the one called on this turn; `"any"` only guarantees some tool from the array gets called, and does not exclude an earlier-stage tool still sitting in the same conversation's tool list.
ww: `"any"` is exactly what already explains the failure — it lets the model reach back for `extract_fields`, which remains a valid choice from its perspective.
`"auto"` is even less constrained than `"any"` — it doesn't even guarantee a tool call at all, let alone the correct one for this turn.
Permanently removing the tool breaks the earlier extraction stage for every future document; the fix needs to apply to this turn's decision, not delete the tool from the pipeline.

questions.stem: A `run_document_ocr` tool sometimes fails to produce usable text — for example, on a low-quality scan — and currently returns only `{"isError": true}`. The pipeline's retry-with-feedback step is supposed to resubmit with a corrective instruction, but has nothing specific to change, so it resends the identical request and gets the identical failure. What should the tool's error response include instead?
questions.why: Structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, and any partial results — is what a retry-with-feedback step needs to construct a corrective retry, rather than resending an identical request against an identical failure.
ww: A retryable flag tells the pipeline whether to retry at all, not what to change — without detail, the retry just repeats the identical failing request.
Logging for a human to review the next morning gives an automated, in-session retry-with-feedback step nothing to act on right now.
Retrying internally without surfacing any diagnostic detail just repeats a scan-quality problem the tool itself cannot fix, and still leaves the pipeline with nothing specific if all attempts fail.

questions.stem: Since the parts-replacement pipeline moved to `tool_use` with a strict schema, every response parses cleanly and every field passes its type check. Auditors still occasionally find records where `part_number` holds a value that matches the expected format but was actually copied from an adjacent line item, not the part the record describes. What is the most accurate way to interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate the syntax-error class but do nothing for the semantic class — a value that's the right type in the right field-shape but drawn from the wrong source line is a semantic error requiring its own check.
ww: No amount of type tightening can verify that a syntactically valid value was pulled from the correct source line — that's a cross-referencing problem, not a type problem.
Reverting would reintroduce the syntax-error class tool_use eliminated, stacking it on top of a semantic error that would still be unresolved.
Passing schema validation proves only structural validity; semantic errors sail through it by definition, so treating a schema pass as proof of correctness misses exactly this failure class.

questions.stem: An inspection record's schema requires `inspection_date` and `next_due_date`, both valid ISO-8601 strings — the schema itself has no way to express that `next_due_date` must fall after `inspection_date`. A recent batch shipped several records where the two dates were reversed, undetected until a downstream audit caught them. What should the team add?
questions.why: Pydantic validators encode business logic — like a field-ordering constraint — that no JSON schema can express; this is exactly the semantic-validation layer that should run in code after extraction.
ww: Asking the model to self-report a boolean isn't independent verification — the same model that reversed the dates once could just as easily misjudge its own flag.
Both fields are already valid, correctly-typed ISO-8601 strings; no amount of format tightening can express an ordering relationship between two separate fields.
A prompt reminder is probabilistic guidance, and exactly the kind of rule an already schema-passing, already-reversed batch shows isn't being reliably followed.

questions.stem: The retry-with-feedback loop for defect-code extraction resubmits each failure with the specific validation error, and most retries eventually succeed. The team wants to know, across thousands of retries, which recurring source-document construct — an abbreviation, a merged table cell, a handwritten annotation — drives most first-pass failures, so they can fix the prompt or schema at the source. What should they add?
questions.why: A `detected_pattern` field lets the team group failures by the specific construct that triggered them, turning isolated retries into a systematic signal about which recurring prompt or schema weakness to fix.
ww: Free-text notes are unstructured and don't aggregate — they can't be grouped or counted by cause the way a structured pattern field can.
A raw retry count shows volume but nothing about cause, which is exactly what the team needs to identify the underlying weakness.
Capping retries doesn't diagnose why failures recur; it only reduces how many chances each individual document gets, an unrelated lever.

questions.stem: A parts-replacement record states `total_parts_cost: $340.00`, but a later billing audit finds the four listed part prices actually sum to $310.00 — a $30 discrepancy nobody caught at extraction time. What design change most directly catches this class of error at the moment of extraction, rather than in a later audit?
questions.why: Building the re-derivation into the output schema — a stated value plus an independently re-derived value plus a conflict flag — surfaces the mismatch as machine-readable data at extraction time, not weeks later.
ww: Monthly reconciliation catches the problem only much later, and only for whatever records happen to be sampled — the pattern moves detection to extraction time instead.
Asking the model to "double-check" conversationally is a soft request, not a structural check — self-correction needs to be built into the output schema, not requested as a courtesy.
A full second pass duplicates the cost of the entire extraction rather than adding a lightweight structural re-derivation of just the total.

questions.stem: A batch of three unrelated inspection reports arrives needing extraction, and none depends on another's results. The coordinator currently issues one `Task` call for the first report, waits for its result, then issues the next `Task` call for the second report in a following response, and so on. What most effectively reduces this latency?
questions.why: Parallel execution requires emitting multiple independent `Task` calls within a single coordinator response; issuing them across separate turns runs them sequentially regardless of how independent the underlying work actually is.
ww: Merging unrelated reports into one call reintroduces cross-document interference risk and abandons the clean parallel-and-independent structure the task already has.
Shortening prompts doesn't change the sequential structure — the calls still execute one after another because they're issued across separate turns.
Pre-fetching content doesn't address the root cause; the calls remain sequential because of how and when they're issued, not because of fetch timing.

questions.stem: A nightly batch of 200 inspection-report extractions runs through the Message Batches API. Results return the next morning: 188 succeed, and 12 fail because those particular scans were long enough to exceed a per-request limit. The team needs to fix and reprocess only the 12 failures. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: `custom_id` identifies exactly which requests failed, so only those need reprocessing, and the underlying cause — length exceeding a limit — should be fixed, such as by chunking, before resubmitting, not just retried unchanged.
ww: Resubmitting all 200 re-pays for 188 already-successful extractions and risks duplicate downstream results for those records.
Resubmitting unchanged repeats the same length-limit failure; the cause needs fixing before retrying, not just cost-tolerant repetition.
Waiting for the next scheduled run doesn't fix the underlying cause and needlessly delays reprocessing of failures already identified by `custom_id`.

questions.stem: A nightly `claude -p` step summarizes each night's extraction batch into a compliance ledger, needing exactly three fields every run: `batch_id`, `records_processed`, `flagged_for_review`. On batches with zero flagged records, the step sometimes replies with a sentence like "No records required review" instead of the record, and the ledger parser throws. What is the most reliable fix?
questions.why: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` enforces well-formed, schema-compliant output on every run, including the zero-flag case, where a prompt instruction alone can still be skipped.
ww: A prompt instruction to "respond in JSON" is exactly the unreliable approach already failing on zero-flag runs.
CLAUDE.md documentation doesn't enforce output shape — it's read as behavioral guidance, not parsed by the CLI as a structural contract.
A default-record fallback silently manufactures data the pipeline never actually confirmed, masking the underlying reliability problem instead of fixing it.

questions.stem: The review step for extracted inspection records is instructed only to "flag anything that looks unusual." On a 300-record sample, it flags a technician working a rare but legitimate double-shift and misses a genuinely fabricated-looking part number in a different record. Reviewers say the flagging feels arbitrary. What change would most reliably fix this?
questions.why: Replacing an abstract instruction with explicit, testable criteria — naming exactly what to check and providing examples — is the documented fix for inconsistent flagging driven by vague intent.
ww: "Better judgment" is still an abstract instruction — no more testable or consistent than the wording it replaces.
A blanket volume adjustment doesn't fix which specific things get flagged, and can raise false positives on legitimate outliers as easily as it catches real problems.
A second independent opinion is useful for review quality generally, but doesn't give either instance the concrete criteria the first instance is missing.

questions.stem: A single extraction call processes one lengthy compiled inspection binder — several individual site reports concatenated into one long document. The pipeline reliably captures the binder's cover-sheet summary and its final sign-off section, but a defect noted only in a site report buried in the binder's middle is consistently missed. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Explicit section headings help the model navigate mid-document content, and a key-findings summary at the start places critical information in the most reliably processed position — the documented mitigations for lost-in-the-middle degradation.
ww: Aggressive pre-summarization risks discarding the specific mid-binder defect before extraction even runs.
Rotating position doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern — whichever report ends up in the middle is still at risk, regardless of which one that is.
`max_tokens` controls how much the model can generate in its response, not how well it attends to content buried in the middle of a long input.

questions.stem: The pipeline's `run_document_ocr` tool returns 50+ fields per page — bounding boxes, per-character confidence, font metadata — when only the plain text and an overall page-confidence score matter downstream. On multi-page inspection binders, this bulk accumulates in context, and extraction quality on later pages starts to drift. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook filtering tool results down to the relevant fields before they accumulate in context removes the noise at the source, rather than asking the model to work around tokens that are still consumed.
ww: The irrelevant fields are still consumed as tokens even if the model is told to ignore them — the attention cost remains.
Aggressive summarization treats the symptom while verbose OCR output keeps flooding in on every subsequent page.
A larger context window raises cost and delays the problem without addressing the actual noise accumulating from verbose tool output.

questions.stem: A request for the pipeline reads only "just pull the important stuff out of these inspection files," with no target schema or field list specified. Rather than asking which fields count as "important" before doing anything, what should the pipeline do?
questions.why: Stating a reasonable set of assumptions and proceeding, rather than blocking on a clarifying question or guessing silently, avoids the abandonment that comes with making users answer questions before any work starts.
ww: Even one compound question still demands upfront effort from the user before anything happens, when the documented pattern favors proceeding over asking.
Hidden defaults leave the user unaware of what was actually assumed, unable to tell whether the output matches their intent.
Extracting every available field ignores that "important" was never defined, producing an unfocused dump rather than a stated, correctable assumption.

questions.stem: Your support agent's response sometimes pairs a short acknowledgment — 'Let me check that order for you' — with a `tool_use` block for `lookup_order`. The harness currently checks whether the response contains any text at all; whenever it does, it treats the turn as finished and returns that text to the customer without executing the tool. What should the harness check instead?
questions.why: The loop must branch on the structured `stop_reason` field — `tool_use` means execute the pending block regardless of any accompanying acknowledgment text; only `end_turn` means the response is actually finished.
ww: Text presence is not the stop signal — Claude can emit acknowledgment text alongside a `tool_use` block in the same response; treating any non-empty text as completion causes exactly this dropped-tool-call bug.
Parsing reply text for a natural-language completion phrase is the documented anti-pattern the exam explicitly rejects in favor of checking the structured `stop_reason` field.
Iteration counts are unrelated to whether Claude still has a pending tool call to run; stopping on a counter instead of `stop_reason` can cut a turn off mid-loop.

questions.stem: In one turn, your agent's response contains three `tool_use` blocks — `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, and `check_warranty_status` — all needed before Claude can continue. The harness executes and appends `tool_result` blocks for the first two, then calls Claude again, planning to supply the third result on a later turn. What is wrong with this approach?
questions.why: The application executes each requested tool and appends a `tool_result` content block for it before Claude continues; leaving one `tool_use` block from the same turn unanswered gives Claude an incomplete context to reason from next.
ww: The API is stateless — nothing server-side tracks outstanding tool calls across requests; the messages array the application sends is the only record Claude has of what happened.
`max_tokens` governs response length and produces its own distinct stop reason; it has no bearing on how many `tool_use` blocks a turn contains or whether their results were supplied.
Bundling into a composite tool addresses a different problem — reducing round-trips for tools always called together — not a harness bug that fails to return results for tools it already called.

questions.stem: Your `file_warranty_claim` tool returns a bare `isError: true` whenever a claim is denied because the product is past its warranty window — a written, final policy outcome. The agent treats every denial as an outage: it apologizes for a technical problem and retries, and the ops dashboard now counts these denials as tool failures. How should the tool represent this outcome?
questions.why: Business-rule errors are a distinct category: `retriable: false` signals that re-invoking cannot change the outcome, and a customer-friendly explanation lets the agent communicate the policy result directly instead of treating it as a failure.
ww: Retrying is the correct response only to transient errors like timeouts; a warranty-window denial is a fixed policy outcome that no retry will ever change, so retrying only wastes attempts.
A denial is not an empty result — it is a definite, negative answer the tool determined; masking it as a successful empty lookup hides the actual outcome from the agent's reasoning.
Marking a business-rule denial as retryable is the exact failure mode the exam rejects — it wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change regardless of parameters.

questions.stem: Your `reverse_loyalty_redemption` tool permanently claws back redeemed loyalty points and cannot be undone once it runs. Policy requires the agent to show impact details and get explicit confirmation before every reversal. The team is choosing between four designs to guarantee this ordering. Which design makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible, not just discouraged?
questions.why: The two-tool token-binding pattern makes the sequence architecturally impossible to skip: no confirmation token exists until a preview call generates one, so execute cannot run first — a code-level guarantee, not a hope.
ww: A `dry_run` boolean on a single tool is exactly the design the exam rejects: the agent can call it with `dry_run=false` on the very first attempt, bypassing the preview entirely.
Prompt instructions and few-shot examples are probabilistic — the model may not follow them under load; critical, irreversible sequencing needs a deterministic, code-level guarantee instead.
A server-side timing heuristic is fragile to timing conditions and doesn't actually verify a preview occurred — it can be satisfied by simply waiting, with no preview ever shown.

questions.stem: Your returns-investigation coordinator's prompt is a numbered script: check `lookup_order`, then `check_return_eligibility`, then if eligible call `process_refund`, then done. On a case involving a partial shipment where only some items arrived damaged, the coordinator follows all four steps correctly but never investigates the missing items separately. Which change to the coordinator's prompt is most effective?
questions.why: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures; a goal-oriented prompt lets the coordinator adapt its investigation to whatever a case reveals, instead of locking into a script that breaks on cases it wasn't written to anticipate.
ww: Adding another fixed step deepens the same rigidity that caused the problem — the next case the script doesn't anticipate will surface an identical gap.
More subagents executing the same brittle script does not fix the script; the coordinator's rigid, procedural prompt is the root cause, not a capacity shortage.
A flag for one specific edge case still leaves a fixed, procedural sequence underneath; the underlying problem is the prompt's step-by-step rigidity, not this one missing branch.

questions.stem: Your team ships an `/escalate-case` command so any engineer can type `/escalate-case billing-dispute` to open a pre-formatted escalation with the reason code attached. It must be available to everyone the moment they clone the repository, and the typed reason code must land inside the command's generated note. Where should the command live, and how does it read the typed text?
questions.why: Project-wide commands live in `.claude/commands/` in the repo, so they're version-controlled and available to everyone on clone; the text typed after the command name is available inside the file as `$ARGUMENTS`.
ww: Personal commands in `~/.claude/commands/` aren't shared via version control, so new clones wouldn't get the command; an environment variable also isn't how typed command text is passed in.
Commands and skills can both take the typed text as `$ARGUMENTS`; hardcoding a value defeats the purpose of a reusable command and isn't required.
A personal-scope location isn't shared with the team on clone, and Claude doesn't automatically infer a reason code from conversation history in place of a typed argument.

questions.stem: Your delivery-status subagent's carrier-tracking lookup times out. Instead of reporting the timeout, it silently falls back to a cached status from two days earlier and reports success with no indication the data may be stale. The coordinator presents this to the customer as current. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A subagent must never catch and silently return success; when it falls back to older data, that must be surfaced as structured context — failure type, what was attempted, and the staleness — so the coordinator can decide how to present it, rather than masking the gap.
ww: Retrying indefinitely ignores that a carrier timeout may need a coordinator-level decision — retry, use the fallback with a caveat, or escalate — which the subagent isn't positioned to make alone.
Never terminate the entire workflow for one subagent's failure — re-running the whole case discards other subagents' completed work over a single recoverable timeout.
Removing the fallback doesn't fix the reporting problem; the actual defect is that success was reported without disclosing the fallback, not that a fallback exists at all.

questions.stem: Your team is adding case-escalation ticketing to the support agent's MCP tooling. A well-maintained community MCP server already integrates with your ticketing platform's standard API. An engineer proposes building a custom in-house server instead, arguing it gives the team full control over field mapping. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: For standard integrations, prefer existing community MCP servers; build custom servers only for unique, team-specific workflows no existing server covers — building a custom server here reinvents a maintained standard integration.
ww: Wanting more control alone doesn't justify reinventing a maintained standard integration; custom-build effort belongs on workflows unique to the team, not a well-covered ticketing API.
There's no documented basis for a volume threshold that should trigger replacing a working community integration with a custom one built for the same standard workflow.
Running duplicate servers for the same capability adds maintenance burden and ambiguity about which result to trust, with no benefit over simply choosing the community server.

questions.stem: Telemetry shows your agent calls `get_customer`, waits a full turn, then calls `fetch_loyalty_tier` with the same customer ID on nearly every loyalty-related case — two round-trips where one would do. An engineer has sketched a combined `get_customer_with_loyalty_tier` tool and asks you to review the design. What should you recommend?
questions.why: The preferred approach is prompting the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn, since it can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously — a composite tool hides the composition rather than fixing the sequencing.
ww: Building a composite tool is explicitly not the preferred fix here — it hides two distinct operations behind one interface instead of letting the agent request both naturally in one turn.
A hook auto-firing a second tool call on every `get_customer` invocation forces the pairing even for cases that never needed loyalty data, and hooks aren't the documented fix for this pattern.
Forcing both tools into every response over-applies the fix — plenty of cases legitimately need only one of the two, and a blanket tool_choice constraint removes that flexibility.

questions.stem: A customer disputes a $14,000 wire-transfer-linked charge, claiming it was unauthorized. `get_customer` and `lookup_order` both return clean results, but nothing in the transaction history clearly confirms or refutes the claim, and a wrong call either way carries real financial and legal exposure. What should the agent do?
questions.why: High-stakes ambiguity — where a wrong decision could cause significant harm — is one of the documented escalation triggers; a large disputed charge with genuinely unclear evidence is exactly this case, not one the agent should resolve unilaterally.
ww: Approving without evidence isn't a policy-authorized action; the agent must not invent a resolution favoring one side when the case is genuinely ambiguous and high-stakes.
Denying based on the absence of confirming evidence overstates what an unclear record actually shows, and risks a wrong call on a high-exposure case the agent isn't positioned to close out alone.
Requesting more documentation delays without resolving the actual decision point — the ambiguity here isn't a missing-information gap the customer can fill, it's a high-stakes judgment call.

questions.stem: After an expensive investigation into a customer's disputed multi-order billing history, the team wants to evaluate two candidate resolutions — a partial refund versus a full account credit — starting from that same completed investigation, without either evaluation's reasoning influencing the other. What is the most effective way to continue?
questions.why: `fork_session` creates branches that inherit context up to the branch point, then diverge independently — exactly what's needed to compare two candidate resolutions from one shared, expensive baseline without either contaminating the other.
ww: Evaluating both resolutions sequentially in the same resumed session lets the second evaluation's reasoning be biased by the first's conclusions — the opposite of an independent comparison.
Two brand-new sessions would each have to redo the expensive investigation from scratch, wasting the work already completed and shared by both candidate resolutions.
A single combined recommendation isn't an independent comparison of the two options — it collapses exactly the separation `fork_session` exists to preserve.

questions.stem: Before an escalation summary reaches a human agent, your team routes it through a second Claude Code instance that has no access to the first, drafting instance's reasoning trace, and asks it to independently flag any missing context or unsupported claims before the handoff goes out. Which named architecture pattern does this design exemplify?
questions.why: Evaluator-optimizer names exactly this two-stage design: a generator produces the draft, and an independent critic or reviewer instance evaluates it separately, mirroring human peer review without the drafting instance's confirmation bias.
ww: Coverage annotation describes marking which synthesis conclusions are well-supported versus data-gapped, not a second independent instance reviewing a completed draft for missed context.
Structured error propagation describes how a failing subagent reports failure type, attempted parameters, and partial results — this scenario has no failure being reported.
Context isolation describes what a subagent receives from the coordinator, not a second reviewing instance independently evaluating a completed draft afterward.

questions.stem: Your support agent already extracts precise transactional facts — order ID, agreed credit amount, promised delivery date — into a persistent case-facts block included in every prompt, outside the summarized conversation history. An engineer proposes replacing it with a vector-database retrieval system 'to make fact recall more robust.' How should the team evaluate this proposal?
questions.why: The persistent case-facts block already survives summarization by living outside compressed history; adding external storage and retrieval is unneeded infrastructure for facts that comfortably fit in one small, always-included block — overkill for session-level precision.
ww: Semantic retrieval is suited to recalling specific exchanges across months of history, not to a handful of precise transactional figures a case-facts block already carries reliably in every prompt.
Running both mechanisms for the same figures adds complexity and a second source of truth to keep in sync, with no accuracy gain the case-facts block doesn't already provide.

Raising the summarization threshold only delays compression — the facts still eventually pass into summarized history and lose precision, and it doesn't address a proposal for a block that already avoids that failure mode.

questions.stem: A customer calls in and gives only a phone number to identify themselves. The `get_customer` tool returns three separate accounts sharing that number, since the number is registered to a shared family plan. The agent must proceed on the correct one before discussing any order or billing detail. What should it do?
questions.why: When a lookup returns several matching records, the agent must request additional identifiers — email, order number, another detail — never pick a match by heuristic; this resolves the ambiguity directly.
ww: Picking the account with the most recent activity is exactly the heuristic-selection pattern the exam rejects — it risks acting on the wrong family member's account and discussing the wrong order or billing detail.
Selecting the first result is arbitrary and carries the same misidentification risk as picking by recency; nothing about tool result order indicates which account is actually calling.
Escalating is unnecessary here — the ambiguity is directly resolvable by asking for one more identifier, without involving a human.

questions.stem: Your agent auto-closes cases whenever its per-field confidence on the resolution details is high, and human reviewers only ever look at the low-confidence cases flagged for review. Months later, a reviewer stumbles onto a systematic error affecting a class of auto-closed cases that had never been sampled. What should the oversight design add?
