questions.why: Even high-confidence outputs need regular, stratified auditing — sampling only the flagged low-confidence stream leaves the automated high-confidence path completely unmeasured, letting a novel, systematic error pattern compound undetected exactly as happened here.
ww: Lowering the threshold routes more cases to review generally, but doesn't add the stratified auditing of the high-confidence stream needed to catch a systematic error already living inside cases the model is confident about.

A second score from the same model on the same resolution isn't independent, ground-truth-based measurement — self-reported confidence is exactly what needs calibration and auditing against a validation source, not more of itself.

Customer sentiment about whether a case 'felt' correctly resolved is not the same as verified resolution accuracy and isn't the documented oversight mechanism for catching systematic errors in the automated stream.

questions.stem: A platform team's onboarding agent runs a code-review subagent and a test-generation subagent under one coordinator. To save a round trip, an engineer proposes letting the two subagents message each other directly with extra test scenarios, skipping the coordinator. What is the strongest reason to keep this routed through the coordinator?
questions.why: Hub-and-spoke keeps the coordinator as the single point of visibility, giving it centralized, uniform error handling and control over what context each subagent receives — properties that direct subagent-to-subagent messaging removes.
ww: The corpus treats centralized error handling as the benefit of the hub-and-spoke pattern, not something a coordinator sheds by delegating; decentralized handling is the failure mode, not an efficiency gain.
The pattern's correctness doesn't hinge on how many subagents are involved or whether calls are parallel — the coordinator mediates every inter-agent exchange regardless of scale.
Hub-and-spoke is the correct architecture independent of scale; treating coordinator mediation as overhead to shed for a single exchange misreads why the pattern exists.

questions.stem: After a schema change, an automation must regenerate a config file where nearly every line differs from the previous version. The current script issues a separate targeted-replacement call per changed line, and several calls fail because the old text no longer appears verbatim. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.why: When most of a file's content is changing, a unique-anchor targeted replacement isn't the right tool at all — reading the file, generating the new version, and writing it back is the sanctioned approach for wholesale changes.
ww: Shorter anchor strings are more likely to match multiple locations, not fewer — this makes the ambiguity worse, and it doesn't address the deeper issue that most of the file is changing anyway.

A shell-based find-and-replace bypasses the tool built for reliable file modification; the sanctioned fallback for this case is reading and rewriting the file, not routing around it with a shell command.
Enumerating file paths locates which file to change, but it does nothing about a targeted-replacement call failing because the anchor text isn't unique or the change is too broad for that mechanism.

questions.stem: A monorepo's infra/terraform/ directory requires every modified file to carry a change-justification comment — a rule that applies nowhere else in the repository, regardless of which service's code sits alongside it. Where should this rule live so it loads automatically only when Terraform files are touched, without bloating every other session?
questions.why: Path-scoped rules with YAML frontmatter glob patterns load automatically only when Claude is working on matching files, keeping the Terraform-specific requirement out of every other session.
ww: A CLAUDE.md heading loads into every session regardless of which files are being touched and relies on the model inferring when to apply it, rather than deterministic path matching.
A Skill is workflow-scoped and invoked on demand — it depends on the engineer remembering to run it, which doesn't guarantee the rule applies on every Terraform edit.

Scattering a separate CLAUDE.md per directory is the documented weaker alternative to rules/ glob patterns, especially awkward once the scoped convention needs to apply more precisely than a whole subdirectory.

questions.stem: The `resolve_module_owner` tool description reads only: 'Returns the current owner of a module.' It works only for actively maintained modules — for archived ones it returns stale data with no warning, and engineers now cite that output as authoritative. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A good tool description states what a tool does, what input it needs, and explicitly names its boundary cases — where it should NOT be trusted — which is exactly the gap here.
ww: A clearer name alone doesn't communicate the boundary case; the exam principle is that descriptions, not names, are the primary lever the model reasons from.
Adding a classifier is infrastructure layered on top of an under-specified description — the corpus's rule is to fix the description first, not compensate for it with a new component.
A `dry_run` parameter solves a different problem — guaranteeing a mandatory preview before an action — not a description that fails to flag when a result is unreliable.

questions.stem: The automation's `generate_release_notes` tool must run only after `tag_release` finishes, since notes reference the new tag. This ordering exists only as a step in the system prompt. When a slow CI run delayed `tag_release`, the agent invoked `generate_release_notes` first, producing notes citing a tag that didn't exist yet. What change most reliably prevents this?
questions.why: A programmatic precondition makes the dependency architecturally enforced — the second tool literally cannot run without the first completing — where a prompt-only rule remains probabilistic.
ww: Reordering prose in the system prompt is still a prompt instruction; the model can still deviate from it under load or ambiguity, since nothing enforces the order in code.
Few-shot examples make correct behavior more likely, not guaranteed — for a consistency-critical ordering, that's the same probabilistic reliability the corpus warns against.
A fixed delay is a timing heuristic that assumes a particular latency; it's fragile to slow runs and doesn't actually verify the first step completed.

questions.stem: The `check_deprecated_packages` audit tool returns an empty result list both when a repository genuinely has zero deprecated packages, and when its backend vulnerability index is unreachable — the same signal either way. Engineers now can't tell a clean audit from one that silently didn't run. What should the tool's response distinguish?
questions.why: An empty result is a successful, informative answer — zero deprecated packages — and must be distinguishable from a query that couldn't run at all; conflating the two in either direction corrupts what the agent reports downstream.
ww: Collapsing both cases into the same empty response means the automation can silently report "clean" when the audit never actually ran — exactly the corrupted decision-making the corpus warns an ambiguous empty signal causes.
Flagging every empty result as a failure treats a valid, successful zero-findings answer as an error, causing the agent to needlessly re-work or escalate audits that already succeeded.
A blind retry does nothing to distinguish the two cases going forward — a genuine zero-findings audit gets retried for no reason, and an unreachable index likely fails the same way again.

questions.stem: An engineer assumes the shared `.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md` always wins over any personal skill with the same name, reasoning project config should win since it's what the team agreed on. After the team updates the shared skill's checks, the engineer's `/commit` behavior doesn't change at all. What is going on?
questions.why: Personal skills at `~/.claude/skills/` override project skills of the same name — the engineer's shared-skill update never had a chance to matter because their own personal override is what actually runs.
ww: Renaming to a different command avoids future collisions but doesn't explain the current behavior, and it also loses the familiar `/commit` name for that engineer.
Commands and skills are unified in current Claude Code — the same-name override rule applies to both, not just to commands.
This inverts the actual precedence rule — project configuration does not automatically win; a personal skill of the same name takes precedence, which is exactly what's masking the update.

questions.stem: A mapping subagent and a dependency-audit subagent independently report the same module's line count — 2,340 and 2,510 — because they ran against different commits. Both numbers reach the report-writing subagent as plain sentences, with no timestamp or commit reference attached, and it silently keeps the audit subagent's figure. What should change?
questions.why: Structured metadata carrying each figure's source commit lets the report-writing subagent preserve and attribute both values instead of merging them into a single unsourced number — the corpus's explicit rule for conflicting statistics.
ww: Picking whichever number is larger is an arbitrary rule with no connection to which figure is actually correct for the report's intended commit — it doesn't resolve the underlying attribution loss.
A prompt instruction to double-check is probabilistic and still doesn't give the subagent the structured metadata needed to actually reconcile or attribute the two figures.

Having the report-writing subagent re-run the line-count check duplicates work already done by a specialized subagent and breaks the separation of responsibilities between mapping/audit and reporting roles.

questions.stem: Three internal MCP tools return timestamps in different formats: Unix epoch from one, ISO 8601 from another, a locale-formatted string from a third. None of these tools are ones the team controls. Downstream reporting has started mis-ordering build history because of the mismatch. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook intercepts and normalizes output centrally and deterministically, working even for third-party tools the team cannot modify — the corpus's primary use case for this hook.
ww: Documenting formats in the system prompt relies on the LLM correctly interpreting and converting three different formats every time, which is probabilistic, not guaranteed.
A tool the agent must remember to call after every retrieval adds an extra LLM call and depends on the agent reliably invoking it — hooks avoid that overhead entirely.
Patching source code you don't control creates fragmented, unmaintainable forks of tools the team doesn't own — exactly the alternative the corpus rejects.

questions.stem: A dependency-scanning subagent audits every service's lockfile for outdated packages. One lockfile fails to parse after a tooling upgrade changed its schema, so the subagent silently substitutes last week's cached scan for that service instead of failing. The report lists every service's findings with identical confidence, stale data included. What should the output do instead?
questions.why: Graceful degradation means completing the report from available data while explicitly annotating which parts rest on lower-confidence or stale input, propagating the uncertainty instead of hiding it.
ww: Dropping the service discards recoverable value — the stale data is still informative once flagged, and omission throws away information the corpus says should be annotated, not deleted.
Holding the entire report hostage to one recoverable parsing gap blocks a deliverable that's otherwise complete and correct for every other service.
Returning an error for the whole run treats a partial, still-usable result as a total failure — the corpus's principle is to complete and annotate, not abort.

questions.stem: An engineer unfamiliar with the team's job queue asks Claude Code to add deduplication so a job never runs twice concurrently. The first version misses cross-instance duplication, the second misses a dedup key that changes mid-retry, the third leaves stale locks after a crash — a different gap each time. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: The interview pattern front-loads exactly the domain-specific questions — cross-instance behavior, key changes, crash recovery — that three separate generation attempts each discovered the hard way, replacing several correction cycles with one clarifying turn.
ww: Continuing to patch one newly discovered gap at a time is the slow, reactive pattern the corpus contrasts against front-loaded clarification — each fix risks missing the next gap.
An exhaustive upfront design document isn't the interview pattern — it substitutes broad, generic coverage for a few targeted questions specific to this task's actual unknowns.
The repeated misses trace to unsurfaced requirements, not generation quality — a larger model would face the same unspecified requirements and likely miss them too.

questions.stem: The build-automation subagent has accumulated 18 tools across three MCP servers plus all six built-ins, added as new needs arose. It frequently calls the wrong one among near-duplicate options, even after every description was rewritten to be clearer. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: Reducing the tool count to the 4-5 actually relevant to the role shrinks the decision space the model must discriminate across on every turn — the corpus's documented fix once description quality alone hasn't resolved misrouting.
ww: A pre-filtering classifier is infrastructure added on top of an oversized tool set rather than reducing the set itself — the corpus treats tool count as the root cause here, not a symptom to route around.
The scenario states descriptions were already rewritten and misrouting persisted — the bottleneck is tool count, not description clarity needing more time.
Broadening every subagent's tool set to match spreads the same reliability problem to peers that currently select correctly with a smaller, role-scoped set.

questions.stem: The boilerplate-generation subagent scaffolds new module files from a template — nothing else. Its AgentDefinition includes shell access, added at design time on the reasoning that scaffolding might someday need a shell command. It has since started running git history-rewriting commands on branches other subagents are also working on. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Removing the unneeded shell access entirely closes the capability at the interface level — a scaffolding role that only ever needs to write files has no legitimate use for a shell tool in the first place.
ww: A prompt instruction restricting how a tool is used is probabilistic — it doesn't remove the capability, so the subagent can still deviate from it.
Keeping broad access 'in case it's needed someday' is exactly the anti-pattern least-privilege design rejects — scope to what the role actually requires now.

Blocking only the two specific commands seen so far leaves the underlying broad shell access in place for whatever misuse comes next — the fix belongs at the tool-scope level, not a growing blocklist.

questions.stem: Designing the build-automation agent's MCP server, the team must expose three things: `trigger_rebuild` and `invalidate_cache`, actions the agent performs; a build-configuration reference the agent should only ever read, never edit; and a reusable postmortem template the agent fills in after a failed build. Which MCP primitive should carry each?
questions.why: The three MCP primitives map by capability: tools are actions Claude calls, resources are read-only data Claude can access, and prompts are pre-built reusable templates — matching the rebuild/cache actions, the read-only config reference, and the fill-in-the-blank postmortem template exactly.
ww: Forcing the read-only reference and the reusable template into the tools primitive discards the protocol's distinction between an action Claude invokes and data or a template it merely consumes.

Resources are read-only by design and cannot represent actions like triggering a rebuild or invalidating a cache — auditability is a property of logging the action, not of misclassifying it as a resource.
This swaps the reference and the template's roles: a static reference document the agent reads is a resource, not a prompt, and a reusable fill-in template is a prompt, not a resource.

questions.stem: Code generation and code review run as two separate Claude Code sessions with no shared conversation history — independent on paper. Both, however, were configured with the same few-shot example set, which happens to omit a common null-input edge case. The reviewer approves a generated function that mishandles exactly that case. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: True independence requires the reviewer's inputs, not just its conversation history, to differ from the generator's — sharing the same example set reproduces the same blind spot even without any shared session or transcript.
ww: Extended thinking makes the reviewer reason longer over the same inputs; it doesn't introduce the missing null-input example the shared set never included.
A self-review instruction added to the generator's own prompt keeps the check inside the same instance and the same reasoning that produced the bug — the opposite of independent review.
Merging the two sessions removes even the nominal separation that exists today, which moves further from independent review, not toward a fix.

questions.stem: Your CI coordinator runs three independent analysis subagents on every PR — correctness, style, and dependency-risk — each spawned via a separate `Task` call. Today the coordinator emits one `Task` call, waits for its subagent to finish, then emits the next `Task` call in a following response, tripling wall-clock time versus running all three together. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Multiple Task calls issued together in one coordinator response execute in parallel; spreading them across separate responses forces them to run sequentially, exactly the tripled wall-clock time observed here.
ww: Runner-level parallelism affects other CI jobs, not this coordinator's own sequential Task-calling pattern — the fix has to change how and when the Task calls are emitted.
Merging distinct specialist subagents into one loses the benefit of parallel, independently-scoped delegation and doesn't address the actual sequencing defect.
Shrinking each subagent's scope reduces per-call latency, but the three calls are still emitted across separate turns, so they still run one after another.

questions.stem: After an incident where a `/apply-autofix` skill's Bash access let it run an unintended shell script mid-fix, the team is scoping a new `/format-pr` skill that should only ever read and edit files during PR formatting cleanup — never execute shell commands. Which SKILL.md frontmatter change most directly enforces this?
questions.why: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter is the mechanism for scoping which tools a skill may use during execution — restricting it to `[Read, Edit]` keeps `/format-pr` from ever reaching Bash.
ww: `context: fork` isolates a skill's output/context from the main session; it does not restrict which tools the skill is permitted to call.
`argument-hint` only affects what's displayed when invoking the command — it has no effect on tool access.
`.claude/commands/` and `.claude/skills/` are functionally unified naming locations for the same `/name` mechanism; moving between them doesn't add a tool-scoping restriction.

questions.stem: A new CI step must run Claude Code fully unattended to review each pull request; no one is available to answer interactive prompts. An engineer, unfamiliar with the CLI, sets `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` in the pipeline's environment config, expecting it to suppress interactive prompts. The step still hangs waiting for input on every run. What actually fixes this?
questions.why: `-p`/`--print` is the documented flag for non-interactive Claude Code — it processes the prompt, prints the result, and exits; without it, Claude Code waits for interactive input and a pipeline hangs.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is not a real Claude Code setting — no amount of waiting makes a nonexistent environment variable take effect.
`--batch` is not a documented Claude Code flag.
Redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` is an undocumented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned approach — `-p` is.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's merge gate calls `claude -p` and needs a single verdict object — a `pass_fail` flag plus a list of blocking file paths — to decide whether the queue unblocks a PR. Prose responses vary in wording enough that the gate script's parser fails on roughly one run in twenty. Which configuration most reliably guarantees parseable output?
questions.why: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` forces schema-conformant JSON the gate script can reliably parse — a guarantee prompt-based or CLAUDE.md-based instructions can't provide.
ww: A CLAUDE.md instruction to respond in JSON is not enforced — the model can still return prose, exactly the intermittent failure already being seen.
A prompt-level formatting instruction is compliance the model may or may not follow on any given run — it doesn't remove the underlying variability.
A token-budget increase addresses truncation, not format compliance — the parser is failing on wording variance, not on cut-off responses.

questions.stem: Finance asks your team to move the CI pipeline's pre-merge review — the check a PR cannot merge without, while the author waits on the result — onto the Message Batches API to capture its 50% cost discount. What should the team do?
questions.why: Batch is for non-blocking, latency-tolerant work; a pre-merge check the author is waiting on must match its API to the latency requirement and stay synchronous, since batch carries no latency SLA.
ww: Cost savings don't override the latency mismatch — a blocking check cannot tolerate an up-to-24-hour, no-SLA response time regardless of discount.
Typical fast turnaround in testing doesn't remove the lack of an SLA — the one run that takes the full 24 hours defeats the point of a pre-merge gate.
Splitting into more batch requests doesn't change the API's own processing-window guarantee — each request still carries the same no-SLA risk.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's CLAUDE.md holds three kinds of guidance: formatting conventions every review must follow, a security-review checklist invoked only during periodic audits, and a stricter validation rule that should apply automatically whenever Claude Code touches files under `payments/`. An engineer proposes bundling the checklist and the payments rule into one new Skill, leaving only formatting in CLAUDE.md. How should the team evaluate this?
questions.why: Universal, always-relevant content stays in CLAUDE.md; workflow-specific guidance invoked on demand (the security checklist) belongs in a Skill; conventions that should load automatically based on file location (the `payments/` rule) belong in `.claude/rules/` with a glob — a Skill only loads on explicit invocation, so it can't provide that automatic path-triggered behavior.
ww: The `payments/` rule needs to load automatically whenever matching files are touched; a Skill only runs when explicitly invoked, so bundling it in loses that automatic trigger.
Moving the universal formatting conventions into a Skill means they no longer load by default — every session would need an explicit invocation to get baseline conventions.
Leaving all three in CLAUDE.md loads the security checklist and the payments-specific rule into every session regardless of relevance — the exact 'wall of rules' problem this section addresses.

questions.stem: A named Claude Code session spent a full day mapping how the CI pipeline's retry-and-backoff logic works, ahead of a planned refactor. Before the team picks the work back up, an unrelated migration this week rewrote that retry logic entirely. What is the most effective way to continue?
questions.why: When tool results are stale — here, the entire retry-and-backoff logic the session mapped no longer describes the actual code — starting fresh with a short summary of prior findings beats resuming a session anchored to now-incorrect tool results.
ww: Resuming carries forward the session's stale tool results from before the migration rewrote the retry logic — the session doesn't know its own findings are now wrong.

`fork_session` inherits the same context up to the branch point, so a fork of this session still starts from the same stale mapping; it's for comparing two approaches from a shared valid baseline, not for recovering from staleness.
`/compact` compresses existing context — it doesn't re-execute any exploration or refresh stale tool results with current file contents.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's test-generation step defines a separate test-writing tool per language — `write_python_test`, `write_js_test`, `write_go_test` — each shaped to that framework's assertion style. A PR's diff includes template files whose eventual language isn't determined by file extension alone, and the step must still emit one schema-valid test definition per changed file, never a prose explanation. Which `tool_choice` configuration is most effective?
questions.why: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees a tool call happens on every file — always structured output — while still letting the model choose whichever language-specific tool actually fits, exactly the case where the correct type isn't known ahead of time.
ww: Forcing `write_python_test` specifically guarantees structure only for Python files — it produces a wrong or failing call for every JS or Go file in the diff.
`{"type": "auto"}` leaves the model free to explain in prose instead of calling any tool — no structure guarantee at all.
A prompt instruction to 'always call the matching tool' is probabilistic compliance, not a guarantee — the same class of failure `tool_choice` exists to eliminate.

questions.stem: The team adds few-shot examples teaching the review bot which findings should block a merge outright versus post as a non-blocking comment. The first draft has fifteen examples: ten obvious blocking cases (a hardcoded credential) and five obvious non-blocking ones (a naming nit). The bot still guesses inconsistently on genuinely borderline cases — a caught-but-unhandled edge case, a deprecated-but-functional call. What is the most effective revision?
questions.why: Few-shot examples are most effective when targeted at exactly the ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — a handful of well-chosen borderline examples outperforms many examples of clear-cut cases the model already handles correctly.
ww: More clear-cut examples don't teach the boundary — the bot is already correct on obvious cases; the failure is specifically on borderline ones.
Written instructions are already what's failing to draw a consistent boundary; more prose doesn't fix what examples are better suited to demonstrate.
Model self-rated confidence is a poorly-calibrated proxy for actual difficulty — a confidently-wrong call on a borderline case is exactly the failure mode being reported.

questions.stem: An engineer wants the review bot to respond in a fixed JSON-only format, with no prose preamble, for the life of the CI run. They set an environment variable, RESPONSE_FORMAT=json, in the pipeline's runner config, expecting the harness to relay it to Claude before each call. Responses keep mixing in prose anyway. Where should this constraint actually be defined?
questions.why: The system prompt is the correct location for persistent behavioral rules and response-format requirements that should hold for an entire conversation.
ww: A constraint stated only in the first user message can lose authority as later messages accumulate — it's not the durable, per-request-included instruction the system prompt provides.
A prefilled first assistant message the model 'said' itself doesn't bind later responses — the model can still deviate from its own earlier statement.
Environment variables have no effect on model behavior at all — the API has no mechanism to read pipeline env vars into a request; the constraint has to be an actual message field.

questions.stem: Mid-run, a critical CVE advisory is published for a dependency the pipeline is currently reviewing a PR against. The team wants the review bot's very next response, still in the same run, to factor in this new advisory without waiting for the pipeline's next full invocation. What is the most effective way to inject this?
questions.why: Prefilling isn't limited to assistant-message continuation — prefixing incoming real-time context, like an advisory update, onto the next message is the documented pattern for injecting mid-conversation updates without restarting anything.
ww: Rewriting the system prompt mid-run typically requires rebuilding the session/request setup — a heavier, less direct change than prefixing the update onto the next message.
Sending a separate synthetic user message breaks the natural flow of the review conversation rather than attaching the update to real, ongoing work.
Waiting loses the point of a mid-run update — the goal is factoring in the advisory before this run finishes, not on the next scheduled pass.

questions.stem: The nightly dependency-audit job reviews 30 independent package manifests across the org's services in a single pass. Comments are detailed for the first several manifests, then shrink to one-line 'no issues' notes for the rest — including one manifest with a real license-incompatible dependency the pass missed entirely. What should the team do?
questions.why: Attention dilution across many items in one pass — not context-window size — causes shallow, inconsistent coverage; per-item focused passes plus a separate integration pass restore consistent depth.
ww: A larger context window doesn't fix attention quality — more available tokens doesn't mean consistent attention per manifest.
Shrinking the batch size may help somewhat but doesn't structurally fix the root cause — dilution reappears once the per-run count is large enough again.
A prompt instruction to be equally thorough is exactly the kind of proportionate-sounding fix that doesn't survive contact with many items in one pass — probabilistic guidance, not a structural fix.

questions.stem: The team routes the independent second-instance reviewer's findings automatically: any finding it flags immediately blocks the PR. Some flagged issues are genuinely uncertain edge cases a human would want to weigh in on, while others are clear-cut. What change lets downstream routing distinguish these without adding a third review pass?
questions.why: Confidence-calibrated routing — the reviewing instance self-reporting confidence per finding — lets downstream automation auto-act on high-confidence findings while routing low-confidence ones to a human, without adding another pass.
ww: Escalating everything defeats the purpose of automating the clear-cut cases and doesn't use the distinction the team is asking for.
A single averaged PR-level score loses the per-finding granularity needed to route individual findings differently.
A second pass in the same conversation still carries the first pass's own reasoning in context — it isn't independent scrutiny, and it's the extra pass the team is trying to avoid.

questions.stem: Each commit on an open PR triggers a fresh `claude -p` invocation to re-review the changed files. A developer replies inline on one finding, 'intentional, ignore this,' then pushes a follow-up commit. The next invocation re-flags the identical finding, with no memory of the developer's reply. An engineer proposes adding a `session_id` so the CLI can look up the earlier exchange itself. Is this the correct diagnosis?
questions.why: The API is fully stateless — every call is independent with no server-side memory. Each fresh `-p` invocation only 'remembers' prior context if the harness explicitly includes it, here the developer's reply, in the new request.
ww: No such parameter exists; the API has no session-lookup mechanism — this is the exact fabricated-parameter misconception the corpus documents.
A vector database is for retrieval over long, sprawling histories, not for basic run-to-run memory of one recent reply — a much smaller, simpler problem.
A single developer reply and one follow-up commit is nowhere near a context-window limit — the invocation is stateless from the start, not overflowing.

questions.stem: Over the past year, hundreds of independent CI review sessions have each analyzed a different PR in isolation, with no shared memory between runs. A security lead wants to know whether a specific unsafe-deserialization pattern has ever been flagged before, across any of that history, without manually rereading hundreds of separate review outputs. Which approach most effectively supports this kind of recall?
questions.why: Semantic retrieval over the full archived history retrieves specifically relevant past exchanges on demand — the fix for precise recall from a long, sprawling record that summarization or windowing would compress or discard.
ww: A progressively-summarized digest compresses away exactly the specific pattern-level detail this kind of lookup needs.
A rolling window of only the most recent reviews discards most of the year's history the lead needs to search.
Exact-match keyword tagging misses findings described in different wording, since useful recall here depends on meaning, not literal text.

questions.stem: A recruiting pipeline extracts structured candidate records from resumes and application forms. The schema marks `current_employer` required and non-nullable, reasoning every applicant needs one listed. An audit of 6,000 records finds 14% carry a plausible employer name tracing to no real company — those applicants are recent graduates or first-time job seekers with no prior employer. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: Nullable fields let the model return `null` instead of fabricating a value to satisfy a required field — the correct fix when information may be genuinely absent.
ww: Post-hoc lookup validation doesn't remove the generation-time pressure that produced the fabrication in the first place — it only catches some of it after the fact.
A prompt instruction asking for confidence-gated filling is probabilistic guidance, not a structural guarantee — the model can still fabricate under required-field pressure.
A placeholder string is still a fabricated non-null value forced by the required field — it doesn't solve the underlying problem, just renames it.

questions.stem: The recruiting pipeline's coordinator has `parsing_agent`, `validation_agent`, and `enrichment_agent` subagent types fully described in its system prompt, each with a clearly scoped role. Engineers notice it never delegates any of the three — it attempts every applicant's full parse-validate-enrich cycle itself in one long response. Its `AgentDefinition` lists only `read_document` among `allowed_tools`. What most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: A coordinator's allowedTools must include Task — without that grant, no amount of prompt wording enables spawning subagents; it's a structural, configuration-level gap.
ww: Rewriting the prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds — the prompt cannot compensate for a missing `Task` grant.
The subagent descriptions are already clear and complete; adding more description text doesn't enable spawning when the tool itself is absent.
Token budget has no bearing on whether the coordinator is permitted to call `Task` — this addresses a nonexistent constraint.

questions.stem: Since the pipeline moved to `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema, every extracted record parses cleanly and every field passes its type check. Auditors still occasionally find `years_of_experience` holding a plausible integer that turns out to be the applicant's age, copied from a birthdate line elsewhere in the resume rather than computed from listed job history. What is the most accurate way to interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate malformed JSON and wrong-typed fields, but do nothing for content that is schema-valid yet semantically wrong — that class needs business-rule validation and feedback, not schema tightening.
ww: No schema constraint can verify a number came from the right source sentence — the field is a valid integer either way, so tightening the schema catches nothing here.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the syntax-error class tool_use already eliminated, stacked on top of the still-unsolved semantic error.
A schema validator proves only structural validity; a wrong-but-plausible value passes type checking by definition, so this isn't a syntax failure.

questions.stem: A weekly candidate-shortlist digest concatenates all 40 candidates' extracted profiles into one long prompt so a synthesis pass can highlight standout qualifications. It reliably surfaces details for the first and last several candidates, but consistently omits a rare, relevant certification held by a candidate in the middle — even though that candidate's own record correctly includes it. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Structured, position-independent blocks per candidate reduce reliance on the model's attention pattern across one long undifferentiated input — the corpus's preferred fix alongside key-findings-first framing.
ww: Trimming to the top candidates by an unrelated proxy (resume length) risks dropping genuinely qualified candidates and doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern.
Rotating position doesn't fix the fundamental degraded-attention pattern in the middle of long inputs — it only moves which content lands there.
A larger context window doesn't fix attention quality at a given position — more available tokens don't guarantee more consistent attention across them.

questions.stem: The pipeline's project-root CLAUDE.md defines formatting and normalization conventions every extraction session must follow. A subdirectory-level CLAUDE.md inside the validation module adds stricter numeric-precision rules specific to that module. An engineer assumes the subdirectory file replaces the root file's guidance whenever Claude works inside `validation/`. Is this assumption correct?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md files load as a concatenated set from root down to the working directory — every discovered file contributes; there is no documented override-precedence mechanism between levels.
ww: There is no override-precedence mechanism between CLAUDE.md levels — this states the opposite of how concatenation actually works.
The root file is never dropped; it stays part of the concatenated context alongside every subdirectory file discovered along the path.
File modification time plays no role in CLAUDE.md loading — all discovered files load together regardless of edit history.

questions.stem: The team wants a dedup-and-merge step for duplicate resume submissions. Several valid architectural approaches exist — deduplicating at ingestion, at validation, or as a separate reconciliation pass — and the right fit depends on tradeoffs the team hasn't worked through. An engineer wants to start implementing the ingestion-time approach immediately. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: Multiple viable approaches, real architectural tradeoffs, and no settled decision yet is the textbook case for planning mode — explore and present a plan before any side effects.
ww: Reactive switching from direct execution to planning after hitting difficulty is expensive — plan upfront when the task already shows the signs that call for it.
Building three parallel implementations before evaluating tradeoffs is expensive rework exactly planning mode is meant to avoid.
Naming one approach doesn't resolve the underlying tradeoffs; the choice among ingestion-time, validation-time, and reconciliation-pass still needs the exploration planning mode provides.

questions.stem: Asked to extract 'every credential the candidate holds,' the coordinator decomposes the task into subtasks covering only formal degrees. The parsing, validation, and enrichment subagents all complete their assigned subtasks correctly. The final candidate record never mentions the professional certifications, licenses, or continuing-education units documented elsewhere in the same application packet. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: Every subagent executed correctly on what it was assigned — the gap traces to the coordinator's own partitioning of the task, which never covered the missing credential types in the first place.
ww: The parsing subagent performed correctly on its assigned subtask; it was never asked to look for non-degree credentials at all.
A missing confidence field wouldn't explain complete omission of an entire credential category — the subtask covering it was never created.
Tool selection inside the enrichment subagent is irrelevant when the coordinator never delegated a subtask covering these credentials to begin with.

questions.stem: The pipeline's extraction tool already enforces its JSON schema via `tool_use` — every response is schema-valid. An engineer argues that validating the extracted record again in application code, using a separate Pydantic model, is redundant now that the schema is enforced at generation time. Is this reasoning correct?
questions.why: Tool use enforces shape at generation time; code-side validation catches semantic and business-rule violations the schema has no way to express, plus provides defense-in-depth for downstream consumers.
ww: This restates the misconception directly — schema enforcement and business-rule validation check different things, so the second pass isn't redundant.
The value of code-side validation doesn't depend on which output method produced the JSON — business rules still need checking regardless.
The two serve complementary roles — the tool schema constrains generation, the Pydantic layer validates meaning; replacing one with the other loses the piece it doesn't cover.

questions.stem: Across thousands of retry-with-feedback cycles in the extraction pipeline, the team wants to know which recurring source-document construct — a multi-column resume layout, a non-standard date abbreviation, a scanned image-only PDF — drives most first-pass validation failures, so they can fix the prompt or schema at the source instead of just retrying. What should they add?
questions.why: Tracking which construct triggered each failure in a structured field lets the team aggregate across retries and identify systematic prompt or schema weaknesses, rather than treating each failure as isolated.
ww: Free-text notes filled in by hand don't aggregate — they don't answer which pattern drives most failures at scale the way a structured field does.
Lowering the retry cap doesn't surface which construct is causing failures — it only changes how many attempts each document gets.
Escalating everything after one retry doesn't identify the recurring pattern either — it routes around the diagnostic question instead of answering it.

questions.stem: A recruiter's working session correcting a batch of parsed candidate records reaches 65,000 tokens. It holds a counter-offer salary figure stated verbally, a start date reached after negotiation, tangents comparing compensation benchmarks across unrelated roles, and the last few exchanges finalizing the shortlist. Which strategy cuts tokens while keeping the session useful?
questions.why: The hybrid approach preserves precise transactional facts verbatim in a structured block, compresses lower-density discussion, and keeps recent turns for conversational coherence — pure summarization risks losing exact figures.
ww: Full summarization loses precision on exactly the figures that matter most — a counter-offer was discussed isn't the same as the actual number.
A pure sliding window can drop the salary figure or start date if either was mentioned earlier than the retained window.
A larger window delays the problem without solving it, and doesn't address the precision loss pure summarization would still cause once the window fills again.

questions.stem: The enrichment pass has surfaced a licensing-verification gap on 12 candidate records — the source documents that would resolve it are available and simply weren't queried during the first extraction pass. An engineer suggests shipping the batch now with a 'verification pending' note on those records instead of re-running extraction against the available source. What should the coordinator do instead?
questions.why: The gap is recoverable — the source is available and simply wasn't queried — so the coordinator's refinement loop should re-delegate a targeted query and re-invoke, not settle for a caveat.
ww: Coverage annotation is for gaps that genuinely cannot be resolved, not a substitute for the refinement loop when re-delegation is still available.
Looping indefinitely without a sufficiency criterion is also wrong — the coordinator needs a defined stopping point, not open-ended re-delegation as the answer to every gap.
Having the enrichment subagent independently query sources it wasn't scoped for breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling.

questions.stem: A new schema field, `duplicate_certification_flags`, requires comparing each listed certification against every other one to catch near-duplicates — up to a dozen comparisons per candidate. Prompted with only the field name, the model misses a third of true duplicates once a resume lists more than six certifications. Which prompting addition most reliably improves accuracy?
questions.why: Comparison across N items is one of the documented triggers for a reasoning cue — instructing step-by-step comparison improves accuracy on this kind of multi-item task.
ww: Temperature controls output variability, not the model's ability to systematically compare many items against each other.
Non-duplicate examples don't target the actual failure mode — missed true duplicates — the way a reasoning cue for the comparison task itself would.
Splitting the field doesn't reduce the number of pairwise comparisons the model still needs to reason through correctly.

questions.stem: Each `verify_reference` call in the enrichment step returns 25+ fields — a contact's organizational history, past call logs, other candidates they've referenced — when only `reference_name`, `relationship`, and `confirmation_status` matter for the record. On long multi-candidate sessions this bulk accumulates turn after turn, and the model starts confusing which reference belongs to which candidate. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Trimming tool outputs to relevant fields before they enter context, via a PostToolUse hook, conserves context and prevents the model from being distracted by irrelevant fields turn after turn.
ww: Telling the model to ignore fields in the system prompt doesn't remove the tokens from context — they're still consumed and still available to distract attention.
Aggressive summarization treats the symptom while the verbose results keep flooding in on every subsequent call.
A larger context window raises cost and doesn't address the underlying noise problem — the irrelevant fields are still there, just with more room around them.

questions.stem: A hiring manager submits a request that reads only 'just tell me if this candidate is qualified,' with no target schema or list of criteria specified. Rather than sending back several clarifying questions about which qualifications matter before doing anything, what should the pipeline do?
questions.why: Proceeding with stated, reasonable assumptions and inviting corrections avoids the abandonment heavy upfront questioning causes, while keeping the assumption visible for the requester to correct.
ww: Compounding several questions into one message still demands upfront effort from the requester before any value is delivered.
Hidden defaults leave the requester unaware of what was assumed, so they can't tell whether the answer matches their actual intent.
Blocking entirely on a fully specified schema is the same abandonment-inducing pattern as heavy upfront questioning, just framed as a refusal instead of a question list.

questions.stem: Before a schema migration, the team must survey a large archive of previously processed candidate records to catalog which legacy field-naming conventions are still in use. Running this survey in the coordinator's main session returns thousands of per-record summaries and nearly fills its context before the migration-design conversation starts. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: Isolating verbose discovery in an Explore subagent keeps the bulk out of the main conversation; only a concise summary returns, preserving context for the design phase that follows.
ww: Running /compact mid-survey loses precision the migration design may still need, and doesn't prevent the fill-up — it only reacts to it after the fact.
Splitting across sessions with manual merging adds coordination overhead and consistency risk that subagent isolation avoids entirely.
Sampling risks missing legacy conventions absent from the sample entirely — a different problem, and still doesn't address exhausting context in the main session.

questions.stem: Claude applies your repository's error-handling convention in some sessions and silently ignores it in others, on the same machine and the same checkout. The convention is written down, nobody can predict when it takes effect, and it has cost two rounds of review comments this month. What is the most effective first diagnostic step?
questions.why: `/memory` lists the memory files actually loaded in the current session. Intermittent rule-following is a discovery problem first, so confirm whether the file holding the rule is in the loaded set before changing anything.
ww: Repeating the instruction each session treats the symptom. The corpus names this explicitly as the wrong response to inconsistent rule-following — it hides a discovery failure behind manual effort.
`.claude/rules/` loads only when Claude works on files matching its globs. A convention that must always apply becomes narrower, not more reliable, and the intermittency is not diagnosed.
Skills load on demand when invoked. A universal standard would then require explicit invocation every time, which the corpus rejects for always-applicable content.

questions.stem: Your project `CLAUDE.md` has reached 500-plus lines. Every rule in it genuinely applies to every session — naming, error handling, logging, dependency policy — but maintainers can no longer find or review anything, and edits collide. The team wants the same content to keep loading in full. What is the supported way to reorganize it?
questions.why: `@import` is the complementary modularization path when content must remain part of the concatenated `CLAUDE.md` context. Files stay small and reviewable while every standard still loads every session.
ww: `.claude/rules/` is path-scoped conditional loading. It is the right tool for conventions tied to a file type or directory, but here every rule must apply always — glob-scoping would stop most of them loading.
Skills are invoked on demand. The corpus rejects moving universal standards into Skills precisely because they would then need explicit invocation each time.
Per-subdirectory memory files work poorly when content applies project-wide, and the corpus notes they do not scale when the governed files are spread across many directories.

questions.stem: A library migration will touch 45-plus files and forces decisions about how shared helpers are restructured. Your team's habit is to begin in direct execution and switch into plan mode only once a task turns out to be messy. The last two migrations each needed substantial rework after that switch. What should the team do?
questions.why: Wide scope plus architectural decisions is exactly the plan-mode profile. Planning first, then executing an approved plan, avoids the expensive rework that premature execution causes.
ww: This preserves the actual defect. The corpus names reactive switching as the trap: by the time the task 'turns out messy' the premature work is already done and must be redone.
Periodic summaries report on work already executed. They do not produce the up-front design decision that a 45-file restructuring needs before any file is touched.
Slicing by file does not remove the cross-cutting decisions about shared helpers; it just distributes them, so each slice makes an uninformed local choice.

questions.stem: The assistant produces a set of rule adapters. Its reasoning trace shows it considered, then set aside, a boundary condition on negative amounts. Asked in the same session to check its work thoroughly, it reports nothing. A human finds the defect a week later. What most directly addresses the cause?
questions.why: A session that generated the code retains its own justifications and is anchored to them. Independence means a separate instance receiving only the artifact and the review criteria, which is what catches what the generator rationalized away.
ww: Extended thinking gives the same anchored instance more reasoning, not independent scrutiny. The corpus rejects it for exactly this self-check limitation.
Self-review instructions run inside the same context and inherit the same confirmation bias — the model re-reads the reasoning that dismissed the edge case and reaffirms it.
A second pass in the same conversation is not an independent review. The generation reasoning is still in context, so the model confirms its own prior conclusions.

questions.stem: A generated proration helper mishandles zero-length billing periods, affecting roughly one account in forty. The engineer has re-described the defect in prose three times, most recently as "really handle every zero-day case," and each regeneration fixes one reading while breaking another. Two rounds have now regressed a case that previously passed. What converges fastest?
questions.why: Test-driven iteration makes 'done' machine-checkable and anchors generation to the spec. Every round then feeds Claude concrete failures, so refinement is targeted instead of guesswork.
ww: Prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently. The corpus names re-describing the bug more emphatically as the losing alternative to a concrete failing case.
Selecting among candidates by an existing suite that was itself written after the code just re-tests what is already covered; the missed cases are absent from that suite by construction.
Documentation is still prose. Writing tests after generation is verification, not test-driven iteration — it gives no failure signal to iterate against during generation.

questions.stem: Generated rule adapters must return a fixed result envelope: a status field, a decimal amount, and an array of applied rule identifiers. The prompt already states this requirement in detail, yet roughly one adapter in eight nests the identifiers under an extra object or returns the amount as a string. What most reliably fixes the format?
questions.why: When prose instructions already fail to produce a consistent format, examples showing the exact required shape are the effective technique — they give the model a concrete pattern instead of more description.
ww: The instructions are already failing. Adding more or repeating them does not change the failure mode; the corpus is explicit that more detailed instructions do not fix format inconsistency.
Temperature controls randomness generally, not adherence to a specific output shape. The corpus rejects it as a fix for a named formatting problem.
Rewriting the output afterwards patches the symptom and is fragile as the envelope evolves; it leaves the generation itself as unreliable as before.

questions.stem: Before the team can restructure the rules engine, someone must enumerate every call site of a deprecated evaluator across roughly 200 files. Running that discovery in the working session fills most of the context window with match listings, and the design discussion that follows becomes noticeably vaguer. What is most effective?
questions.why: Subagent context isolation is the documented fit: verbose discovery runs in the subagent, only a concise summary enters the main conversation, and the main session's window stays available for design and implementation.
ww: `/compact` mid-task loses precision the implementation phase still needs — exact identifiers and locations get abstracted away. The corpus rejects it against subagent isolation.
A bigger window does not improve attention quality over the same bulk of low-value listings, and the cost rises while the noise problem remains.
Splitting across sessions adds coordination overhead and consistency risk, and the corpus names it as the weaker alternative to running discovery in an isolated subagent.

questions.stem: Your internal API registry is exposed through an MCP server with a `find_endpoint` tool. Logs show the assistant spends several turns per task guessing endpoint names to work out what the registry even contains before it can ask anything useful. The registry publishes a stable structured index. What is most effective?
questions.why: MCP resources exist to expose content catalogs — they give the agent an immediate map of what data exists as readable context, removing the exploratory calls that guessing requires.
ww: A listing tool adds another LLM call and relies on the agent remembering to invoke it first. A resource supplies the map as context without depending on the agent's choice.
A static dump bloats every request and goes stale. Resources are requested on demand, which is the documented advantage over pasting the catalog into the prompt.
A better description helps the agent choose between similar tools; it does not tell the agent which components actually exist, which is the missing information here.

questions.stem: A refactor session is approaching its context limit. It holds a few decisions the remaining work depends on — a chosen migration order, an agreed compatibility cutoff, one field rename — plus a long abandoned exploration and the last dozen implementation turns. How should the context be reduced?
questions.why: The hybrid approach is the tested one: critical structured values preserved verbatim, lower-density discussion summarized, recent exchanges kept intact for conversational coherence.
ww: Pure summarization loses precision exactly where it matters — an agreed rounding mode becomes 'rounding was discussed'. That imprecision is the reason the hybrid split exists.
A recency window drops the exact values if they were agreed early, which is the documented failure of keeping only the last N tokens.
Delaying compression buys time without changing what compression does to precise values; they are still flattened when it eventually runs.

questions.stem: Your team ships a `/regen-fixtures` skill that rewrites generated test fixtures. A dry run last week left three untracked build artifacts behind, and reviewers now want the skill constrained so that while it runs it cannot reach past file reads and writes into commands that touch the working tree. Where is that constraint configured?
questions.why: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter is the key that scopes tool access during skill execution — for example limiting a skill to file operations to prevent destructive actions.
ww: `.mcp.json` configures MCP servers and their credentials for the project. It is not where a skill's tool scope is declared.
A written rule in `CLAUDE.md` is guidance the model may or may not follow. Tool scoping for a skill lives in frontmatter, not prose.
There is no `config.json` commands array governing per-command tool access; the corpus names this as a misconception about where skill scoping lives.

questions.stem: Your codegen assistant must hold three behaviours for a whole working session: never invent a rule identifier, always state which assumptions it made, and keep explanations to two sentences. These are currently written into the first user message of each session. By the tenth exchange all three have decayed. Where do they belong?
questions.why: Behavioural rules that apply for the entire conversation — tone, response format, standing constraints — belong in the system prompt, which is included in every request rather than sitting as one aging turn.
ww: Prefilling shapes the opening of an individual response. It is the documented tool for suppressing filler phrases, not for carrying three standing constraints across a session.
Environment variables have no effect on model behaviour; the corpus names this explicitly as a wrong location for behavioural constraints.
A first assistant message is content the model can drift away from, exactly as the first user message did. It carries no standing authority.

questions.stem: Each call to your `get_rule_definition` tool returns 40-plus fields — full revision history, approver metadata, localized descriptions — when only the identifier, effective dates, and formula matter. Across a long session those results accumulate turn after turn and later answers start confusing similar rules. What is most effective?
questions.why: Trimming at `PostToolUse` keeps the irrelevant fields out of context in the first place — tokens are never spent, and the model is not distracted by fields that have no bearing on the task.
ww: An instruction to ignore fields still pays for every token and still carries the attention cost. The fields are in context regardless of what the prompt says about them.
Aggressive summarization treats the symptom while verbose results keep flooding in each turn, so the window refills as fast as it is cleared.
A larger window raises cost without removing the noise; the corpus rejects widening as a fix for tool-output bloat.

questions.stem: A maintenance tool your assistant can call rewrites rule definitions in bulk. Policy says any invocation affecting more than 50 definitions must go to a release manager instead of executing. The rule currently lives in the system prompt, and an audit found two bulk rewrites above the threshold that ran anyway. What enforcement is most effective?
questions.why: A `PreToolUse` hook runs deterministically before the tool executes and can block it outright. For safety-critical thresholds the corpus is explicit that hooks, not prompt text, are the enforcement mechanism.
ww: A tool description is still input the model weighs probabilistically. Moving the same sentence to a different prompt surface does not make compliance guaranteed.
Few-shot examples improve judgement on ambiguous cases but remain probabilistic. The corpus reserves them for guidance, not for enforcement that must always hold.
A warning returned after the call is evaluated leaves the decision with the model, and the audit shows the model already proceeds past the stated rule.

questions.stem: An expensive session has finished mapping the rules engine's dependency graph. The team now wants to evaluate two restructuring approaches from that same completed analysis — one extracting a shared evaluator, one keeping evaluation inline — without either exploration influencing the other. What is most effective?
questions.why: `fork_session` is the documented mechanism for exactly this: both branches inherit context up to the fork point, then diverge independently, so one expensive analysis serves two uncontaminated explorations.
ww: Running them sequentially in one session biases the second evaluation with the first's reasoning and conclusions — the contamination the team is trying to avoid.
Fresh sessions discard the shared baseline, so each must redo the expensive dependency analysis before it can start.
A single combined request keeps both explorations in one reasoning context, so the second is shaped by the first exactly as sequential evaluation would be.

questions.stem: A three-week schema migration runs through hundreds of tool calls and is about a third complete. Twice a session has ended unexpectedly mid-run, and both times work restarted from nothing: which tables were already converted, and which were blocked on foreign keys, existed only inside that conversation. What is most effective?
questions.why: A scratchpad file holds intermediate state and findings outside the conversation, so the task survives context limits and session boundaries and each continuation starts by reading what is already known.
ww: There is nothing intact to resume — the sessions ended unexpectedly, and the corpus is explicit that findings held only in conversation do not survive an interruption.
An end-of-session summary is written once, at the end. Work discovered mid-run is already lost when a session ends without warning.
A larger window delays the limit without persisting anything; nothing written only in conversation survives a crash.

questions.stem: Your coordinator delegates from a fixed script: query these four databases in this order, open the top ten results from each, summarise each in 120 words. When a subagent surfaces a promising lead outside those four sources, nothing in the system pursues it. Which change is most effective?
questions.why: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than a procedure. Goal-oriented delegation lets subagents adapt to what they discover; a fixed script breaks whenever reality deviates from it.
ww: One more step deepens the rigidity that caused the problem. The corpus is explicit that adding more detailed step-by-step instruction is the wrong response to checklist-shaped output.
More agents executing a bad script does not fix the script. The corpus names increasing subagent count as the wrong lever for shallow, procedural results.
Relocating the same procedure preserves it. The subagents would still execute predetermined steps instead of adapting their approach to what they find.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent reports that it has nothing to work with, though the web-search and document-analysis subagents both completed successfully and their results sit in the coordinator's own history. This has happened on all nine cycles run so far, and re-running the upstream subagents changes nothing. What is the root cause and correct fix?
questions.why: Subagents receive only what the coordinator explicitly includes in their prompt — they never see the coordinator's conversation history. Passing the completed findings into the synthesis prompt is the documented fix.
ww: Ordering is not the issue: the results exist and are complete. Sequencing changes when synthesis runs, not whether the findings reach it.
Giving synthesis its own retrieval tool widens its privileges beyond its scope and works around the real gap, which is the coordinator failing to pass context it already holds.
Subagents exchanging data through a shared file bypasses the coordinator, which then loses the visibility and uniform error handling hub-and-spoke exists to provide.

questions.stem: Your hand-built coordinator loop executes both tools Claude requested, then sends back a fresh user message describing what each returned. Claude answers as though neither tool had run and requests them both again. The loop has been in production a week and every multi-tool turn ends the same way. What is wrong with the request the loop sends?
questions.why: Results re-enter the conversation as structured `tool_result` content blocks matched to their originating `tool_use` by `id`, appended to the accumulated messages. Prose narration is not the protocol, so the calls remain unanswered.
ww: The loop does resend the conversation; the defect is the form the results take, not a missing task description.
Multiple results are returned together in one request, one `tool_result` block per call — splitting them across requests is not required.
The API is stateless and carries no conversation identifier; state is the `messages` array the application sends each time.

questions.stem: The coordinator has two retrieval tools: `analyze_publication`, held by the document-analysis subagent, and `analyze_source`, held by the web-search subagent. Both descriptions read only "Analyzes a source and returns findings." Requests naming an uploaded PDF go to the web-search subagent's tool 45% of the time. What is most effective?
questions.why: Descriptions are the primary input Claude uses to select a tool, so misrouting between near-identical names is a description defect. Fix the signal — purpose, accepted input, and boundaries — before adding any layer.
ww: A pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure on top of the ambiguity without removing it. The corpus names it as the canonical wrong answer to tool misrouting.
Consolidating loses the semantic precision that lets the model distinguish two genuinely different retrieval paths, trading one ambiguity for a broader one.
Widening every agent's tool set breaks role scoping and enlarges the decision space, which degrades selection reliability rather than improving it.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent now carries nineteen tools accumulated over successive projects — several near-duplicates for fetching, parsing, and citing. It selects the wrong one often enough that reviewers no longer trust its output. The web-search subagent, with five role-scoped tools, selects correctly. What is most effective?
questions.why: Tool count itself degrades selection reliability by enlarging the decision space each turn. The corpus's own comparison is eighteen tools versus four or five role-scoped ones — reduce the decision space first.
ww: Better descriptions help, but the corpus is explicit that with this many overlapping tools the count is the root cause; nineteen well-described near-duplicates still compete every turn.
Few-shot examples target specific ambiguous cases. They do not reduce the number of candidates the model must discriminate between on every call.
Handing over the full catalog is the documented anti-pattern — agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them, and the decision space grows further.

questions.stem: Each subagent returns findings as plain sentences and separately lists the documents it consulted. When the report is assembled, reviewers spot-checking twenty claims find six attributed to a document that does not contain them. Four reports this quarter have come back from the review board for this same reason. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Attribution is lost because content and metadata travel as merged free text. A structured format that separates the claim from its source URL, document name, and location preserves the mapping through aggregation.
ww: An instruction to preserve text cannot restore structure that was never there — the mapping is already ambiguous once several sentences are merged and rewritten.
Re-searching duplicates work already done and can attribute a claim to a different document that happens to support it, which is the wrong-citation failure again.
A bibliography lists what was consulted but leaves individual claims untraceable to specific sources, which is exactly the gap the audit found.

questions.stem: Your literature tool signals a paywalled record, a malformed query string, and a temporarily unreachable index identically: `isError: true` plus one sentence of prose. The coordinator responds to all three the same way and gets it wrong two times out of three. How should the error response be restructured?
questions.why: Structured errors carry a category — transient, validation, business, permission — plus a retryability flag, so the coordinator branches on data rather than inferring intent from prose. A withdrawn record is permanent; a timeout is transient.
ww: Retrying internally is right for transient failures only. Applied to a permanently withdrawn record it loops on an outcome that can never change and never surfaces the decision.
Richer prose still forces the agent to guess from text. The corpus states that an explicit retryable flag beats making the agent infer retryability from an error string.
Returning success with embedded error metadata masks failures — the documented worst option, since downstream steps treat unusable records as retrieved.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent receives roughly 80,000 tokens of combined findings. Reviewers notice it consistently reflects the opening summaries and the closing conclusions, while substantive results sitting in the middle of the input are absent from every draft. Three cycles running, the same mid-input material has gone unmentioned. What is most effective?
questions.why: This is the lost-in-the-middle pattern. Placing critical material in the reliably processed opening position and adding section headings to help the model navigate mid-input content are the documented mitigations.
ww: Rotation moves which content is neglected without changing the underlying attention pattern — some agent's findings still land in the weak middle every run.
Compressing to a fixed budget risks discarding exactly the critical findings the summary is meant to protect; the corpus rejects it for that reason.
Splitting and merging adds a stage and a second merge point without addressing positional attention; each half still has a neglected middle.

questions.stem: Analysing a record always requires both its bibliographic header and its full text, yet the document-analysis subagent requests the header in one turn and the text in the next. That extra round-trip is now on nearly every record in the cycle. What most effectively removes it?
questions.why: The preferred approach is to prompt the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn — Claude can request multiple tools simultaneously, so the round-trip disappears without adding a tool.
ww: A composite tool is the corpus's explicitly not-preferred option: it hides the composition inside a new interface when the agent could simply issue both calls in one turn.
Folding the text into the header response is a composite tool by another name, and it forces the full text into context even when only the header was wanted.
Caching speeds the second call up but the agent still spends a separate turn on it, so the extra round-trip that was the actual complaint remains.

questions.stem: A synthesis draft covers four of the five material properties the brief named explicitly; corrosion behaviour is absent entirely, though the analysis subagent's logs show it processed records that discuss it at length. The coordinator must decide what to do about the missing section before the report ships. What should it do?
questions.why: The coordinator owns gap evaluation and the refinement loop: detect the gap, re-delegate targeted queries to the agents that can gather evidence, then re-invoke synthesis on the enriched findings.
ww: Letting synthesis search breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling — the corpus rejects it as the fix for a coverage gap.
Coverage annotation is for gaps that cannot be recovered. Here re-delegation is available, so shipping with a caveat substitutes for a loop that would have closed the gap.
Re-invoking synthesis on the same findings cannot produce evidence that was never gathered; stronger wording yields more hedging, exactly as observed.

questions.stem: Your team needs the research pipeline to reach a widely used issue tracker and a widely used document store, plus an internal sample-registry service that exists nowhere else. An engineer proposes building all three MCP servers in-house for consistency and control. How should the team evaluate this?
questions.why: The corpus's rule is to prefer existing community MCP servers for standard integrations and to spend custom build effort only on workflows unique to your team — here, the internal sample registry.
ww: Building a custom server for a standard integration reinvents a maintained one. The corpus names building your own for control as the wrong trade.
Resources expose read-only catalogs; the pipeline also needs to act against these systems. Actions are tools, so resources alone cannot replace all three servers.
This spends the most custom effort exactly where community servers already exist, and defers the one integration that genuinely requires a custom build.

questions.stem: On roughly one property in nine, two credible sources report materially different values, and the analysis subagent has no basis for adjudicating between them. Reviewers have flagged three reports this quarter where the discarded value later proved the better one. The team is deciding what the subagent should do on such a disagreement. Which behaviour is correct?
questions.why: Conflicts are not the analysis subagent's to resolve. It completes the work with both values, marks the conflict explicitly with source attribution, and leaves reconciliation to the coordinator or a human.
ww: A credibility ranking is still a heuristic that silently discards a value, abandoning a decision above the subagent's scope — the same defect made systematic.
Blocking the pipeline to ask before completing analysis is unnecessary; the subagent can finish its work and surface the conflict for later reconciliation.
A range hides both original values and their sources, so reviewers still cannot see which body reported what — the very visibility that was lost.

questions.stem: A supplier-datasheet archive the pipeline normally draws on has been unreachable all week, so one of the brief's five evidence streams contributed nothing this cycle. The synthesis subagent returned a complete-looking draft in which no conclusion is marked as resting on thinner evidence than any other. What should its output do instead?
questions.why: Graceful degradation: complete the synthesis using available data, annotate coverage so well-supported conclusions are distinguishable from gaps, and propagate that uncertainty upward.
ww: Returning an error because input is incomplete discards work that is genuinely useful — the corpus rejects it in favour of annotated partial coverage.
Blocking indefinitely on sources that are down for the whole window delivers nothing, and the gap is unrecoverable this cycle regardless of waiting.
Reweighting produces conclusions that look fully supported while the gap stays invisible, which is the uniform-confidence problem restated.

questions.stem: Every field in the extraction schema is mandatory and non-nullable, on the reasoning that aggregation should never receive a partial row. An audit of 2,000 papers finds that in roughly 7% of them the grant identifier the model returned is convincing but simply not present anywhere in the text. Which schema change stops the invention at its source?
questions.why: A required, non-nullable field pressures the model into inventing a value when the source has none. Nullable fields let it return `null` — completeness by extraction rather than by fabrication.
ww: Confidence scores describe an invented value without preventing it. The schema still forbids the honest answer, so the model still supplies something.
