A registry check catches some invented values after the fact and silently accepts plausible ones that happen to match; the schema pressure remains.
A second pass meets the same required, non-nullable field, so it fabricates on exactly the papers where the information is missing.

questions.stem: Extraction across the record set measures 96% accurate on a labelled audit, and the team proposes auto-accepting every high-confidence extraction with no reviewer involvement. Scanned pre-1990 proceedings make up about 4% of volume and were barely represented in that audit. Before reducing review, what should the team do first?
questions.why: An aggregate figure can hide a severe failure rate on one rare segment. Validate accuracy per document type and per field, and keep sampling the automated stream so novel error patterns surface before they compound.
ww: A higher threshold on an aggregate metric still averages away the weak segment — the rare scanned proceedings can fail badly at any threshold set on the overall number.
Reviewing only flagged items leaves the auto-accepted stream unmeasured, which is where undetected novel error patterns accumulate.
Unstratified sampling spends reviewer capacity on easy segments and under-samples the rare, worst-performing ones — the exact segment at issue here.

questions.stem: Your assistant is configured as a coordinator with specialist workers for exploration, scaffolding, and cleanup. In three weeks it has never delegated once — it attempts every chore itself, badly, while the workers sit idle. Its `AgentDefinition` sets `allowed_tools` to Read, Grep, and Glob. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Subagents are spawned through the `Task` tool. A coordinator whose `allowedTools` omits `Task` has no mechanism to delegate, regardless of what its prompt says.
ww: A prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds. The corpus names rewriting the system prompt as the wrong response to a coordinator that never delegates.
Descriptions tell the orchestration layer what an agent type is for; they do not enable spawning. The `Task` tool does.
Better worker descriptions improve selection among specialists once delegation is possible, but here no delegation can occur at all.

questions.stem: An engineer needs every place the legacy `resolveTenant` helper is actually invoked, so she can judge the blast radius of changing it. The monorepo holds roughly 4,000 files and the helper is referenced from several packages. The assistant must choose a built-in tool for the first step. Which should it use, and why?
questions.why: Grep is content search — it looks inside files for patterns such as function names and call sites. Finding all callers of a symbol is the corpus's own example of a Grep task.
ww: Glob matches file paths, not file contents. It would return files *named* after the helper, not the files that call it.
The defining module shows what it exports, not who imports it. Callers live in other files and are invisible from the definition alone.
Enumerating directories is discovery by bulk listing rather than by content, and it still cannot say which files reference the helper.

questions.stem: Every chore the assistant completes must post a structured record to the team's work tracker: chore type, files touched, and outcome. Three recording tools exist, one per chore type. On roughly one chore in twelve the assistant explains what it did in prose and calls nothing, so the tracker gets no record. Which configuration guarantees a record?
questions.why: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees the model calls some tool and never returns conversational text. With several recording tools defined it still picks the best-fitting one, so structure is guaranteed without forcing the wrong tool.
ww: `auto` permits a text response by design, and the prompt instruction is probabilistic — which is exactly the one-in-twelve failure already observed.
Forcing one specific tool guarantees a call but the wrong one whenever the chore is of a different type, producing mis-typed records instead of missing ones.
Reconstructing a record from prose reintroduces the parsing fragility that structured tool calls exist to remove, and it fires only after the failure.

questions.stem: Your monorepo needs three sets of conventions applied automatically: Go services follow one error-wrapping style, TypeScript packages follow an async style, and test files everywhere follow one shared testing convention. Tests sit beside the code they cover rather than in a dedicated tree. What configuration applies each set where it belongs?
questions.why: `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` frontmatter loads a rule set only when Claude works on files matching its globs — deterministic file-path matching, and it handles tests co-located with source.
ww: Headings in the root memory file rely on the model inferring which section applies, rather than on deterministic path matching, and load all three sets every session.
Per-directory memory files work poorly when the governed files are scattered — co-located tests would force the testing convention into every directory.
Skills load on demand when invoked. Conventions that must apply automatically to matching files cannot depend on an engineer remembering to invoke them.

questions.stem: Standardising a logging call, the assistant issues an `Edit` anchored on `log.Printf(`. The call fails: that text appears in nineteen places across a 900-line file, so `Edit` cannot determine which occurrence to change. Two of the nineteen sit inside a vendored block that must be left untouched. What is the sanctioned way to complete the change?
questions.why: `Edit` works by unique text match. When no unique anchor exists the documented fallback is Read, modify the loaded content, then Write the updated version — a reliable full-file modification.
ww: A shorter anchor is *more* likely to be non-unique, not less. The corpus names this explicitly as the wrong instinct after an anchor collision.
Forcing the change through `sed` bypasses the tool designed for the job and rewrites every occurrence indiscriminately, including any that should be left alone.
Writing without reading first means composing the file from memory rather than from its actual contents. The fallback is Read *then* Write for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: An engineer asks the assistant to make a neglected package deployable again. What that will take is unknown at the outset: the first pass finds an unpinned dependency, which exposes a broken build step, which in turn reveals a service call nobody documented. Which decomposition strategy fits?
questions.why: The scope is unknown up front and each step depends on the previous step's discoveries — the defining conditions for dynamic adaptive decomposition. Map structure, prioritise high-impact areas, adapt as dependencies surface.
ww: A predetermined order cannot react to discoveries such as the external-gateway dependency; fixed pipelines suit tasks whose structure is known in advance.
One giant prompt over every module produces attention dilution — deep on some modules, shallow on others — which the corpus rejects for exactly this task shape.
Repeating a fixed per-module pipeline still assumes every module needs the same steps, which is false when coverage and dependencies differ module to module.

questions.stem: The build-cache MCP server is about to roll out to forty engineers. Each authenticates with a personal token that must never enter the repository, but the server's endpoint and arguments should be identical for everyone and visible in code review. Which configuration meets both requirements?
questions.why: `.mcp.json` at the project root is version-controlled and shared, and its `${VAR}` substitution resolves the credential from the environment at runtime — so configuration is reviewable while tokens stay out of the repository.
ww: User-scope configuration gives every engineer their own copy, which is how endpoints drift apart and new joiners arrive with nothing configured at all.
A committed placeholder is a credential-shaped value in version control and leaves each working copy differing from the reviewed file.
A setup script still lands the definition in user scope, so it is neither reviewable nor kept current when the endpoint changes.

questions.stem: The exploration worker was given a general `run_command` tool so it could invoke build helpers while investigating. It has begun using that tool to install packages and rewrite lockfiles mid-investigation, twice leaving the workspace in a state the engineer had to undo by hand. What is most effective?
questions.why: Least privilege: each agent gets only the tools its scope requires. Replacing a general-purpose tool with a constrained alternative enforces the boundary at the interface level rather than relying on behaviour.
ww: A prompt prohibition is probabilistic. The corpus rejects prompt instructions as the fix when a tool's breadth is what enables the scope creep.
Per-call approval puts a human in the loop on every command, which does not narrow the worker's scope and undermines the automation the assistant exists to provide.
Logging makes misuse auditable after the fact; the workspace is still damaged and must still be undone by hand.

questions.stem: Your repository ships a `/preflight` skill that every engineer receives on clone. One engineer needs a stricter local variant under that same command name, with nothing changing for the rest of the team. Her new personal version has produced a second, separate entry in the command menu instead of replacing the original. What is the cause and fix?
questions.why: A personal skill overrides a project skill of the *same name*. A differently-named directory simply defines a different command, which is why the original still runs and a second entry appeared.
ww: Personal skills do override project skills of the same name — that is the documented way to customise without forking the team's version.
Precedence follows the skill's name and location. No override key is involved in resolving a naming collision.
Deleting the repository's copy locally diverges her checkout and removes the command again the moment she pulls.

questions.stem: Your `find_owning_team` tool answers with `{"teams": [], "isError": true}` both when a component genuinely has no registered owner and when the ownership service is down. On outage days the assistant reports components as unowned; on genuinely unowned ones it retries and escalates. How should the tool signal these?
questions.why: An empty result is a successful query with no matches, not an error. Only a query that could not run gets `isError: true` with a category — conflating the two corrupts the agent's decision in both directions.
ww: Flagging a valid empty result as an error still makes the agent treat a correct answer as a failure; a description the agent must interpret is the guessing this design exists to remove.
Returning an empty list when the registry is down is exactly the masking that makes the assistant state a service is unowned when ownership data may well exist.
Internal retry is right for the outage case but wrong for the genuinely-unowned case, where it burns attempts on an answer that is already correct.

questions.stem: An engineer asks the assistant to prepare a service for review: check the dependency licences, regenerate the API client, and summarise open migrations. None of the three depends on the others' results. The coordinator currently issues them one after another, and the wait is now the engineers' main complaint. What is most effective?
questions.why: Multiple `Task` calls in a single coordinator response execute in parallel. Independent subtasks are the documented case for it, and parallel execution is what removes the accumulated wait.
ww: Shorter prompts shave time off each step but leave the work strictly serialised, so the total wait remains the sum of three chores.
One agent doing all three loses the specialisation the workers provide and still performs the chores sequentially within its own turn.
Issuing `Task` calls across separate turns runs them sequentially. Parallel spawning requires the calls to appear in a single response.

questions.stem: The assistant's system prompt sets three standing rules: cite a file path with every claim, never propose a change outside the package under discussion, and keep summaries under five bullets. Engineers report all three hold early and decay by around turn fifteen, though the session is only about 3,000 tokens. What is the root cause?
questions.why: As assistant responses accumulate, the system prompt's authority diminishes relative to the growing body of model-generated content, and the model increasingly pattern-matches its own prior outputs.
ww: Context overflow is impossible at roughly 3,000 tokens. The corpus names this figure precisely to rule the explanation out.
The system prompt is included in every request, not just the first. That it 'applies once' is a named misconception.
The three rules govern different things — citation, scope, and length — and are satisfiable together, so mutual competition does not explain uniform decay.

questions.stem: The assistant has `get_service_metadata`, returning ownership and deployment configuration, and `get_service_dependencies`, returning the dependency graph. Both are called often and an engineer proposes replacing them with one `get_service` tool that returns everything, arguing fewer tools means fewer wrong choices. How should the team evaluate this?
questions.why: Consolidating distinct tools trades away semantic precision. The corpus rejects merging two well-scoped tools into one broad one — the fix for selection problems is clearer descriptions, not fewer distinctions.
ww: Reducing tool count helps when an agent carries far more tools than its role needs. Two well-scoped, frequently-used tools are not that situation.
A section parameter recreates the original distinction inside the tool while hiding it from the description the model actually selects on.
No misrouting has been reported; the proposal would remove a working distinction to solve a problem that has not appeared.

questions.stem: Escalations reach the on-call queue as a chore name plus one free-text sentence. About a quarter are handed straight back asking for detail, the engineers who do act begin by repeating the investigation the assistant already completed, and median time to first human action now exceeds a day. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: The human sees only the handoff payload, so it must be self-contained: actions already taken, the root cause as far as it is known, the reason for escalation, and a recommended action.
ww: Escalating sooner does not fix the information loss and degrades the autonomous resolution rate — the corpus names it as the wrong lever.
A raw transcript forces the engineer to re-read an entire session to reconstruct the state, which is slower than receiving the compiled summary.
Re-running duplicates work the assistant already completed and delays resolution further, which is the complaint restated rather than solved.

questions.stem: Three assistant workloads are under cost review: an interactive dependency query an engineer waits on, an overnight sweep that regenerates API clients for every service, and a weekly licence audit across the monorepo. The team wants the Message Batches API's 50% discount wherever it fits. Which assignment is correct?
questions.why: Batch suits scheduled, latency-tolerant workloads — an overnight regeneration and a weekly audit both qualify. Anything a human is blocking on stays synchronous, because batch offers no latency SLA.
ww: The interactive query does have a deadline: an engineer is waiting. Up to 24 hours is unacceptable for a blocking request.
This inverts the rule — it batches the blocking request and pays full price for the scheduled job that is the best batch candidate.
Batch has no latency SLA, so 'usually fast' is not a property to plan against; the worst case is up to 24 hours regardless of request size.

questions.stem: A new pipeline stage shells out to the Claude Code CLI with the review prompt as its only argument. The stage emits nothing and holds the runner until the job's wall-clock limit kills it. Teammates propose four ways to make it run unattended. Which is the documented approach?
questions.why: `-p` (or `--print`) is the documented non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits. Without it Claude Code waits for interactive input and the pipeline hangs.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is not a real environment variable. The corpus lists it among the plausible-sounding but non-existent options this question is built to catch.
There is no `--batch` flag on the CLI. Batch processing is a separate API, not an invocation mode for Claude Code.
Redirecting stdin is a Unix workaround rather than the documented approach, and it does not make the CLI print and exit the way `-p` does.

questions.stem: A small service turns each review into per-line annotations and needs four fields it can rely on for every finding. Today it splits the model's prose on headings and blank lines; it broke twice last month when the phrasing shifted. What is the most reliable way to get parseable findings?
questions.why: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` enforces the shape at the CLI level, producing well-formed output that downstream tooling can parse reliably instead of regex-matching prose.
ww: A format section in the memory file is guidance the model may or may not follow consistently — the corpus rejects it against schema-enforced CLI output.
A prompt-specified delimiter is still variable compliance. The parser remains at the mercy of wording, which is the failure already occurring.
A conversion pass adds a second model call and a second place for the format to drift, when the first invocation can be constrained directly.

questions.stem: Developers have stopped reading the severity field: a finding marked high on one pull request looks, to them, indistinguishable from one marked low on the next. The only guidance the reviewer has is to assign a severity that fits the issue. What most reliably makes severity consistent?
questions.why: When a vague instruction produces inconsistent output, the fix is to move from abstract to concrete: explicit, testable criteria for each level with examples, rather than an appeal to judgement.
ww: "Be more consistent" is the same abstraction restated. The corpus names replacing vague intent with explicit criteria as the change that works.
A numeric score without defined criteria relocates the same unanchored judgement into a number, so the bands inherit the inconsistency.
A re-rating pass applies the same vague standard a second time, and adds a call without giving the model any clearer definition to apply.

questions.stem: Schema-shaped findings have eliminated every parse failure from the ingestion service. A quarterly audit still turns up findings whose `severity` is a valid enum value but plainly wrong for the defect described, plus a handful naming a file outside the change set. An engineer wants the schema tightened further. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas via tool use eliminate the entire syntax class and do nothing for the semantic class. A structurally valid finding can still name the wrong line — that needs business-rule validation and retry with the specific error.
ww: No schema constraint can know which lines this particular diff changed. An integer range restricts the type, not the semantic relationship to the pull request.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the syntax-error class on top of the semantic one — strictly worse, as the corpus states.
Blaming the diff metadata assumes the extraction is right; the corpus treats a valid-but-wrong value as the defining semantic error, not an input freshness problem.

questions.stem: The finding tool's JSON schema is maintained by hand, and a separate validation class in the ingestion service re-checks the same fields. Twice this quarter a field was added to one and not the other, and malformed findings reached the pull request. An engineer proposes a review checklist item covering both files. How should the team respond?
questions.why: A typed model can generate the JSON Schema used in the tool definition, making the tool contract and the code's validator a single source of truth that cannot drift apart.
ww: A checklist is a process patch for an architecture problem — the corpus names exactly this proposal as the weaker answer.
Tool use enforces structure at generation time only. Code-side validation still carries the semantic and business rules no JSON schema can express.
A drift alarm detects the divergence after it is written rather than making it impossible, and it still requires both definitions to be maintained.

questions.stem: Validation rejects any finding whose `suggested_fix` is empty, and the pipeline retries with the document and the specific error. On roughly 60 findings per week the retries exhaust all three attempts; inspection shows these are findings where the diff genuinely offers no concrete fix — a missing test, an architectural concern. An engineer wants max retries raised to ten. What should the team do instead?
questions.why: Retry-with-feedback fixes only what the model can correct from the context it has. When the information genuinely is not there, retries burn tokens and pressure the model into fabrication — the fix is schema design, not loop tuning.
ww: More attempts against absent information stay absent. Backoff changes the cost curve, not the outcome, and the corpus rejects raising the limit for this case.
No feedback can conjure a fix the diff does not support. Better instructions help format and arithmetic errors, not missing information.
Removing the field discards a genuinely useful value on the majority of findings that do have a concrete fix; nullable preserves it where it exists.

questions.stem: Each review response reports `issues_found` as an integer alongside the findings array. A post-incident review turns up pull requests that merged green because `issues_found` read 0 while the array held three findings the pipeline then skipped. Nothing caught the contradiction. What design change most directly catches it?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern is structural: extract both the claimed value and an independently re-derived one, with a conflict flag, so internal contradictions surface as machine-readable data on every response.
ww: "Double-check" is a vague instruction with no detection mechanism — the corpus names this as the losing alternative to building re-derivation into the output.
Computing the count in code hides the disagreement rather than surfacing it: a response whose own reasoning miscounted still goes unexamined.
Monthly reconciliation detects the problem weeks late. The pattern exists to move detection to the moment the response is produced.

questions.stem: The review job decomposes each pull request into per-language source passes: one for Go files, one for TypeScript. A quarterly audit finds that migration scripts, CI workflow files, and infrastructure manifests have never once been reviewed, though every pass completed successfully and reported no errors. What is the root cause?
questions.why: When every subtask succeeds but the output covers the wrong ground, the fault is the coordinator's decomposition, not subtask performance. It must explicitly partition the whole space before delegating.
ww: Nothing is being filtered — the files are never assigned to a pass at all, so no findings about them are ever produced to filter.
This assumes findings exist and are lost downstream. The passes only cover Go and TypeScript files, so nothing about the missing classes is generated.
Migrations, workflow files, and manifests are a well-known defect surface; treating zero findings as evidence of quality mistakes a coverage gap for a clean result.

questions.stem: A pull request touching 16 files goes through the reviewer in a single pass. Feedback is detailed on three files and cursory on the rest, an off-by-one in a loop bound goes unflagged, and the same nil-check pattern is criticised in one file and approved in another. How should the team restructure the review?
questions.why: Uneven depth, missed obvious bugs, and contradictory verdicts on the same pattern are the signature of attention dilution. Per-file passes restore consistent depth; a separate integration pass covers cross-file data flow.
ww: This pushes the problem onto developers instead of fixing the review architecture, and large changes are sometimes legitimately atomic.
The constraint is attention across many items, not room to write. More output budget does not make per-file attention consistent.
A bigger context window does not fix attention quality — the corpus names this explicitly as the trap on this scenario.

questions.stem: A pipeline tool force-expires every cached build artifact for a service. It cannot be reversed from the pipeline and silently invalidates other teams' builds, so policy requires a human to see the blast radius first. The assistant chooses its own call order. Which design makes skipping the preview impossible?
questions.why: Two-tool token binding makes execution impossible without a prior preview: the token only comes into existence when the preview runs, so the ordering is a code-level guarantee rather than a behavioural hope.
ww: A boolean parameter is bypassable by calling with it set to false — the exact weakness token binding was designed to replace.
Prompt instructions with examples are probabilistic. The requirement here is a guarantee, and prompt compliance cannot provide one.
A timing heuristic is fragile and unrelated to whether a preview actually ran; a slow session passes it without any preview at all.

questions.stem: Engineers keep re-typing the same long prompt to reproduce the CI reviewer's behaviour locally before pushing, and six of them have each built a slightly different local version. The team wants a `/local-review` command everyone gets automatically on clone or pull, with nothing to configure. Where should the command file be created?
questions.why: Project-wide commands live in `.claude/commands/` inside the repository. Being version-controlled is what makes them automatically available to everyone who clones or pulls.
ww: `~/.claude/commands/` is personal and not shared through version control, so each engineer would have to create it themselves.
`.claude/rules/` holds path-scoped conventions that load automatically on matching files. It does not define an invocable slash command.
The CI configuration directory is not a location Claude Code discovers commands from; co-locating it there would leave `/local-review` undefined.

questions.stem: A weekly full-repository audit runs on the Message Batches API for the 50% discount. Its report must be on the platform lead's desk by Monday 09:00. In testing every batch returned within about two hours, so the team schedules submission for Monday 06:00. What is the correct submission planning rule?
questions.why: Batch processing has a window of up to 24 hours and no latency SLA. Submission deadlines must be planned against that worst case — downstream deadline minus 24 hours — not against typical observed times.
ww: A synchronous fallback pays full price for the whole audit precisely when the batch is slow, forfeiting the saving the batch was chosen for.
Batch size does not carry a latency guarantee; smaller batches are still subject to the same 24-hour window with no SLA.
Polling changes how quickly results are noticed, not when they are produced. A batch that takes 23 hours still misses a 09:00 deadline.

questions.stem: Two of the reviewer's six finding categories were added last quarter and are wrong roughly half the time. Since they shipped, the rate at which developers open any finding at all has fallen by two-thirds — including in the four categories they used to trust. The team has one sprint. What is most effective?
questions.why: High-false-positive categories cause developers to dismiss everything, including accurate findings. Surgically disabling the noisy pair stops the trust bleed now while their prompts are repaired.
ww: Showing precision still posts every noisy finding. Developers already skip the stream wholesale, and a number beside it does not restore the habit of opening them.
Uniform strictness reduction damages the four high-precision categories unnecessarily while leaving the new ones proportionally just as noisy.
Improving all six over weeks is too slow — trust keeps eroding throughout, which is the cost the one-sprint deadline exists to avoid.

questions.stem: The test-generation worker reports `status: failed` and nothing more when it cannot build a module. The coordinator therefore responds identically whether the build broke on a missing credential, a compiler error, or a flaky network mount, and the run log preserves none of that difference. What should the worker return instead?
questions.why: A failing subagent must return structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and possible alternatives — because that is what lets the coordinator choose between retry, reroute, partial continuation, and escalation.
ww: Severity ranks failures without saying what went wrong, so the coordinator still cannot tell a retryable mount problem from a permanent compiler error.
A retry count reports effort, not cause. It leaves the coordinator unable to choose between rerouting, continuing with partial results, and escalating.
Returning success with embedded error metadata masks the failure — the corpus names this as the option never to take.

questions.stem: A named session holds an expensive dependency analysis of the monorepo from three weeks ago. A large refactor has since moved roughly a third of the packages, and the engineer estimates that re-running the analysis outright would take most of a day. She wants to continue that investigation today. What is the best way to proceed?
questions.why: When prior tool results are stale, a resumed session reasons over old evidence as if current. A fresh session with an injected structured summary carries the conclusions forward without the outdated evidence.
ww: Resuming as-is is precisely the failure the corpus warns about: the session treats three-week-old tool results for moved packages as accurate.
`/compact` compresses context; it does not distinguish stale results from current ones, so the outdated evidence survives in summarised form.
Re-running the whole analysis discards conclusions that are still valid and repeats an expensive step the summary could have carried forward.

questions.stem: During your agent's rollout, an engineer builds the agentic loop by hand. After each Claude API call the code must decide whether to run the requested tools and call Claude again, or stop and send the reply to the customer. In staging, some sessions never terminate and keep re-invoking Claude after it has clearly finished answering. What should the loop use to decide whether to continue or stop?
questions.why: The orchestrator inspects the structured stop_reason after each call: tool_use means Claude wants a tool run (execute it, append the tool_result, loop again); end_turn means Claude finished (stop and return). This is the documented loop-control mechanism.
ww: Parsing natural-language text for a 'done' phrase is the explicit exam trap: control flow must key off structured stop_reason, not fragile string matching that breaks when phrasing varies.

An iteration cap is a safety backstop, not the stop decision; a hard limit of five would truncate legitimate multi-tool resolutions and still misfires on short ones. stop_reason determines termination.
Tying termination to which tool was called invents a rule the API does not use; many valid resolutions never call process_refund, and the loop would hang. The signal is stop_reason: "end_turn".

questions.stem: Your agent's search_orders MCP tool returns {"results": [], "isError": true} in two very different situations: when a customer genuinely has no orders on file, and when the orders database is unreachable. Logs show that on days the database has brief outages, your agent confidently tells customers "you have no orders," and on legitimately empty accounts it retries and then escalates. How should the tool signal these two outcomes?
questions.why: An empty result is a successful query with zero matches, not a failure; conflating it with an access failure corrupts the agent's decision both ways. Signalling 'ran, no matches' as success (isError false) lets your agent confidently report 'no orders found,' while reserving isError:true for a query that could not run stops it from telling a customer they have no orders when the database was simply down.
ww: Marking a valid empty result as an error and papering over it with retry instructions treats a legitimate answer as a failure; the agent burns retries and escalates a query that worked fine, and prompt-based retry rules are probabilistic rather than fixing the signal.

Returning an empty list in both cases masks the access failure: when the database is down the agent reports 'you have no orders,' a false statement caused by hiding the failure, and latency is an unreliable, fragile proxy for whether the query actually ran.

Flagging every zero-match result as an error forces the agent to treat a valid answer as a failure and retry a query that succeeded, which is exactly the empty-result-as-error anti-pattern the corpus rejects.

questions.stem: The team requires that your agent verify a caller's identity with get_customer before any refund is issued. The rule lives only in your agent's system prompt ("always call get_customer before process_refund"). Audit logs show that in roughly 7% of refunds your agent skipped get_customer and called process_refund directly off a customer-supplied order number, twice refunding the wrong account. What change most reliably guarantees the verification step precedes every refund?
questions.why: When correct sequencing is mandatory—verify identity before a financial action—the enforcement must be programmatic, not prompt-based. A precondition that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified identifier makes the wrong order impossible at the code level, whereas any prompt-level rule is followed only probabilistically.
ww: Strengthening and repositioning the prompt rule is still prompt-level enforcement; instruction compliance is probabilistic, so a stronger sentence reduces but never eliminates the skips that already caused wrong-account refunds.

Few-shot examples make the correct sequence more likely but still leave it to the model's discretion on each turn; for security-critical sequencing the corpus requires code-level preconditions, not example-driven nudges.

A model self-check is the same probabilistic instance making the same judgement it already skips 7% of the time; self-reported compliance provides no deterministic guarantee that verification actually ran before the refund.

questions.stem: The team's four support tools run as an MCP server that six engineers use locally while iterating on your agent. Each engineer authenticates to the backend with their own personal API token. The team wants one shared, version-controlled tool configuration without committing any credentials to the repository. Which configuration approach is most effective?
questions.why: Project-scoped .mcp.json is version-controlled and shared with the team; ${VAR} substitution injects each developer's own token from the environment at runtime, keeping the config shared while credentials stay out of the repo.
ww: Putting the server in each user's ~/.claude.json gives inconsistent, un-shared tooling — the opposite of the version-controlled shared config the team wants; user scope is for personal overrides.
Committing a placeholder token is a security risk and invites accidental real-credential commits; env-var substitution exists precisely so no token, real or placeholder, lives in the repo.

CLAUDE.md is loaded instructional context, not a credential store; putting a token there both leaks it into version control and misuses the memory file. Credentials belong in env vars referenced by .mcp.json.

questions.stem: When your agent escalates mid-conversation, the team's human agents complain they must re-ask customers for details your agent already gathered — the customer ID, the order, what was tried. The human console shows only that escalate_to_human fired with a short free-text note; it has no access to the conversation transcript. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: Human agents lack transcript access by design, so the escalation payload must be a complete, self-contained structured handoff summary — customer ID, root-cause analysis, amount, actions taken, and recommended action — everything the human sees.
ww: Handing over the raw transcript contradicts the design (humans don't get transcript access) and forces re-reading the whole conversation; a structured summary is the documented fix.
Making the human re-run your agent's tools duplicates completed work and slows resolution — exactly the information loss the structured handoff exists to prevent.
Escalating earlier does not fix the information-transfer gap and degrades autonomous resolution; the problem is what gets passed at handoff, not when.

questions.stem: Your agent's process_refund tool starts rejecting some refunds because they fall outside the team's 30-day return window. The tool currently returns a generic {"error": "Operation failed"}, and logs show your agent retries process_refund up to three times on these rejections before finally escalating. How should the tool's error handling be changed?
questions.why: A policy-limit rejection is a business-rule error: a valid answer that the action is disallowed. Return retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation so the agent stops retrying and communicates the policy outcome.
ww: Labeling a policy denial as transient/retryable wastes retries on an outcome that can never change — the exact misclassification the business-error category exists to prevent.

A generic "Operation failed" leaves the agent unable to distinguish policy denial from an outage, so it retries or escalates incorrectly; structured error categories fix this, not blanket first-failure escalation.

A prompt rule capping retries is probabilistic and still leaves your agent guessing the error's nature from opaque text; the deterministic fix is a structured business-error response the tool returns.

questions.stem: To bound cost, your agent keeps only the last 25 message pairs of each conversation verbatim and drops everything older. On long returns cases this backfires: a customer states an accessibility requirement and an agreed store-credit arrangement early on, and 30 turns later your agent contradicts both because those turns have fallen out of the retained window. What is the most effective way to restructure the conversation state?
questions.why: A pure sliding window drops early preferences and commitments that turn out to be critical later. The hybrid approach keeps recent exchanges verbatim for coherence, compresses older discussion into a running summary, and preserves agreed structured facts in a block that is never dropped—so early commitments survive regardless of how long the conversation runs.
ww: Widening the window from 25 to 60 pairs only delays the same failure; any fixed window still eventually discards the early turns, so a sufficiently long case reproduces the contradiction.

A bigger context window is the classic misconception here: it raises cost and merely postpones dropping, and larger inputs also invite lost-in-the-middle attention gaps rather than reliably preserving the early commitment.

Replaying the entire untrimmed history on every request is precisely what makes cost and latency scale with conversation length; the stateless API resends everything each call, so unbounded history is the problem the window was meant to solve, not a fix.

questions.stem: Your agent's lookup_order tool returns 40+ fields per order (warehouse routing, carrier metadata, internal SKUs), but only order_id, status, total, items, and return_eligible matter for support. In long multi-issue sessions the accumulated tool output floods the window and your agent's later answers drift. What is the most effective way to conserve context?
questions.why: Verbose tool results consume tokens disproportionately and persist every turn; a PostToolUse hook filters each result to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context, conserving the window and reducing distraction.
ww: Telling the model to ignore fields still leaves every token in context — the attention and cost burden remains; the tokens must be removed before they enter, not mentally skipped.
More aggressive summarization treats the symptom while verbose tool results keep flooding in each turn; trimming the source is the root-cause fix.
A larger window raises cost and merely delays the same flooding; the noise from 40-field results persists. This is the bigger-context misconception.

questions.stem: In extended billing conversations, a customer says early on "apply the 15% loyalty discount I was promised," but 20+ turns later your agent quotes the wrong amount. Investigation shows the discount detail was compressed by summarization into a vague note like "promotional pricing was discussed." What fix is most effective?
questions.why: Precise transactional facts must be extracted into a persistent case-facts block carried in every prompt outside the summarized history, so they survive context compression verbatim instead of being abstracted away.
ww: Raising the threshold only delays compression; the facts still eventually get summarized into vagueness. It buys time without fixing the precision loss.
Revising the summarization prompt still relies on the summarizer executing perfectly every time; the case-facts block removes that dependency by keeping facts out of summarization entirely.
External storage plus retrieval is overkill for session-level facts; a compact in-prompt case-facts block is the documented, lighter fix.

questions.stem: The team wants to raise your agent's first-contact resolution by having it escalate the genuinely hard cases and resolve the rest. A vendor proposes running sentiment analysis on each message and escalating whenever the customer sounds angry. Your agent's logs show calm messages describing tangled multi-account billing errors and irate messages about trivially fixable typos. How should escalation be triggered instead?
questions.why: Escalation should key off structural signals — explicit human requests, policy silence, missing data, repeated failures — because sentiment does not correlate with case complexity; a calm message can be genuinely complex and an angry one trivially resolvable.
ww: Sentiment is an unreliable complexity proxy: customer mood does not track difficulty, so an anger threshold floods the human queue with resolvable cases and misses calm-but-hard ones.
Model self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and poorly correlated with actual difficulty — the model can be confidently wrong — so a 1-10 self-score is not a reliable escalation trigger.
An automatic complexity classifier is over-engineering that needs training data the team likely lacks; the sanctioned approach is escalating on structural signals, not a bespoke model.

questions.stem: A customer messages: "This is unacceptable, I've been waiting a week!" The team's policy covers this delay with a standard shipping credit that your agent is authorized to issue. Your agent's escalation design must decide what to do with this first expression of frustration. What is the most appropriate behavior?
questions.why: A first expression of dissatisfaction is not a request for a manager: acknowledge the emotion, propose a concrete resolution, and escalate only if the customer reiterates the desire for a human.
ww: Immediate escalation on frustration alone conflates mood with an explicit human request and needlessly hands off a case your agent is authorized and able to resolve.
Resolving silently ignores the acknowledge-emotion step; the pattern is acknowledge, then resolve — skipping acknowledgment degrades the interaction even when the fix is correct.
Interrogating the customer about whether they want a manager before helping inverts the flow; the agent should offer a resolution first and only escalate on a reiterated request.

questions.stem: Your agent calls get_customer and lookup_order in two separate sequential turns even when a request plainly needs both up front ("refund order #1234 on my account"). This adds an extra API loop to most resolutions and inflates latency at holiday volume. What is the most effective way to reduce the number of loops?
questions.why: The preferred fix is to prompt the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn — Claude can naturally emit multiple tool calls simultaneously, removing the extra loop without hiding the composition.
ww: A composite tool works but is not preferred: it hides the composition and adds a bespoke tool where prompting the agent to request both in one turn is the lighter, documented answer.

Forcing tool_choice "any" on every turn guarantees a tool call but does not make your agent batch the two lookups together, and it prevents ever ending the turn with a text reply; it targets the wrong problem.
Raising the loop limit accommodates the extra loops instead of eliminating them; the latency from an unnecessary round-trip remains. Bundling removes the loop.

questions.stem: A customer asks your agent to price-match a competitor's lower price. The team's written policy covers refunds when the team's own price drops after purchase, but says nothing at all about matching other retailers' prices. Your agent has already run get_customer and lookup_order and has all available system data. What should your agent do?
questions.why: A policy gap — where the agent cannot determine the correct action within defined policy — is a valid escalation trigger; the agent must escalate rather than invent policy for a case the rules do not cover.
ww: Stretching the own-site price-drop rule onto a competitor scenario is a wrong policy interpretation the agent is not authorized to make; the correct move is escalation.
Refusing with a flat 'we don't match competitor prices' asserts a rule the policy never states; silence is not a documented denial, so the agent must escalate for interpretation.
Approving at the agent's own discretion invents policy to chase a metric and risks unauthorized concessions; policy-gap ambiguity must go to a human.

questions.stem: Your agent still misroutes borderline messages like "I need help with my recent purchase" between get_customer and lookup_order. An engineer plans to add few-shot examples to the system prompt to fix it and asks how to choose them. Which approach most effectively improves selection?
questions.why: Few-shot examples should target the specific ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — 4-6 examples aimed at the edge cases, each with rationale — not a pile of easy, unambiguous examples.
ww: Ten to fifteen unambiguous examples do not address the ambiguous edge cases that actually cause misrouting; the exam explicitly rejects flooding the prompt with clear-cut examples.
One common-case example per tool covers exactly the requests your agent already handles correctly and ignores the borderline cases; the examples must target the failure region.
More emphatic instructions are the failing approach already — when prose instructions produce inconsistent selection, concrete targeted examples work where more instruction text does not.

questions.stem: The team standardized your agent's operator runbook so every engineer's local Claude Code sessions follow the same review and safety conventions. Three engineers who set this up months ago see the conventions applied; a newly onboarded engineer reports Claude ignores them entirely, though everyone shares the same repository and up-to-date code. What is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.why: When existing members follow a convention a new member doesn't, the guidance is in the original developers' user-scope ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not version-controlled; moving it to project-level config shares it with everyone.
ww: The stem states everyone shares the same repo with up-to-date code, so a stale clone is ruled out; the missing guidance was never in the project file to begin with — it lives in user scope.
A per-user CLAUDE.md cache that must be rebuilt is a fabricated mechanism; the discrepancy comes from user-scope vs project-scope placement, not a cache. Use /memory to see which files loaded.
Re-stating the rule louder each session treats the symptom, not the root cause; the guidance simply isn't in a shared file, so the fix is relocating it to project scope.

questions.stem: A newly onboarded engineer asks Claude Code to find everywhere the legacy `computeSurcharge` routine is actually called, so she can understand the billing flow. Claude Code must decide which built-in tool to reach for first. Telemetry from earlier sessions shows engineers most often want the call sites, not the files whose names resemble the function. Which tool should Claude Code use to locate the call sites?
questions.why: Grep is content search: it looks inside files for patterns like function names, call sites, and imports. 'Find all callers of computeSurcharge' is a content target, so Grep is the correct built-in.
ww: Glob matches file *paths*, not file *contents* — `**/computeSurcharge*` only finds files whose names contain the string and misses every call site inside otherwise-named files. This is the documented Grep-vs-Glob confusion.
Using Bash `find` for a filename match is the same wrong problem as Glob (it matches paths, not contents) and bypasses the tool designed for the job; content discovery is Grep's role.

Reading a directory in full upfront to 'build complete context' is the exam's discovery anti-pattern — it burns the context window on irrelevant files instead of driving discovery from a content search.

questions.stem: The same engineer now wants Claude Code to map how a shipment record flows from ingestion to invoicing across the unfamiliar integration layer. Session logs show that when Claude Code tries to Read every file in the integration package first, it fills the context window before it reaches the invoicing code. What investigation strategy should Claude Code follow?
questions.why: Codebase understanding is built incrementally: Grep to find an entry point, Read it, Grep for usages, Read consumers, and repeat until the picture is complete — discovery is driven by content search plus targeted reads.
ww: Globbing the whole tree and reading every match before searching is explicitly called out as the same anti-pattern as bulk reading — it burns context on files the flow never touches.
Reading every file upfront to 'get full context' is the documented anti-pattern; it exhausts the context window on irrelevant files rather than following the actual flow.
Concatenating every file into one buffer is bulk upfront reading in disguise — it loads the same irrelevant content and defeats incremental, content-driven investigation.

questions.stem: An engineer must rename the legacy `calculateTax` function everywhere it is used. Investigation reveals that `utils/tax.ts` wraps and re-exports it as `getTax`, and `index.ts` re-exports that wrapper again. Claude Code greps only for `calculateTax`, reports the call sites it finds, and the engineer proceeds — but a downstream module that imports `getTax` breaks in production. What should Claude Code have done to find every caller?
questions.why: When a function is re-exported or wrapped, searching only the original name misses callers that use the wrapper's alias. The strategy is to first collect all exported names (original plus every wrapper/re-export), then search for each name across the codebase.
ww: A case-insensitive grep still searches only for `calculateTax` — it never discovers the distinct alias `getTax`, so it misses every consumer that imports the wrapper.
Globbing filenames matches paths, not the names of functions imported inside files; consumers of `getTax` need not live in tax-named files, so this misses call sites.
Bulk-reading the whole repository is the upfront-reading anti-pattern and, worse, still relies on catching the alias by eye rather than systematically enumerating exported names then searching each.

questions.stem: Claude Code is applying a boilerplate change to a large config module and calls Edit with the anchor snippet `return config;`. The Edit fails because that exact text appears in eleven places in the file, so Edit cannot decide which occurrence to modify. What is the correct fallback for a reliable modification?
questions.why: Edit works by unique text matching and fails on non-unique anchors. The sanctioned fallback is Read the full file, modify the content, then Write the updated version — a reliable full-file modification.
ww: A shorter anchor is *more* likely to be non-unique, not less — `config` appears even more often than `return config;`, so this makes the ambiguity worse.
Forcing the change with Bash `sed` bypasses the tool designed for the job; the exam's sanctioned fallback for a non-unique Edit is Read + Write, not shelling out to sed.
Handing the edit back to a human is burden-shifting — a documented distractor mold that pushes the problem onto the user when a reliable Read + Write fallback exists.

questions.stem: The team wires a semantic, index-backed code-search MCP server into Claude Code so engineers can find behavior by meaning, not just literal strings. In production, Claude Code keeps falling back to built-in Grep even for conceptual queries the semantic server handles far better. The MCP tool's description currently reads only "Searches the codebase." What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions; agents fall back to a familiar built-in when an MCP tool's description doesn't make its superior capability explicit. Enhancing the description to highlight the semantic advantage fixes the root cause. This is the fix-the-signal-before-adding-a-layer distinction.
ww: Disabling Grep breaks legitimate literal-content search; the root cause is an under-specified description, not the built-in tool's existence.

A blanket 'always prefer MCP tools' rule is blunt and keyword-sensitive, misrouting cases where the built-in genuinely is the right tool — it patches a symptom rather than fixing the description signal.
A pre-routing classifier adds an infrastructure layer to compensate for a bad signal; the exam's rule is to fix the tool description first before adding a routing layer (Key Distinction #10).

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to split the shipping-integration layer out of the Java monolith into its own service — a change that touches dozens of files and forces decisions about service boundaries and shared data models. The engineer is tempted to let Claude Code start editing immediately. Which execution approach should Claude Code use?
questions.why: Large scope, architectural decisions, and changes across many files call for planning mode: Claude explores and designs with Read/Grep/Glob only, presents a plan before executing, and avoids expensive rework from premature execution.
ww: 'Start direct, switch to planning when it gets hard' is the exact reactive-switching trap the exam rejects — reactive switching is expensive; plan upfront when the task demands it.
Generating a whole architectural extraction in one pass is premature execution on an ill-defined design; it produces exactly the expensive rework planning mode exists to prevent.
Forcing the human to pre-decompose the architectural work is burden-shifting; the boundary decisions are precisely what planning mode is meant to explore and propose.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to generate a boilerplate carrier-integration adapter, described only in prose. After two iterations the generated adapter still shapes its output differently each time — one run nests the tracking fields, another flattens them, and timestamp formats vary. The engineer keeps re-describing the requirements in more detail. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: When natural-language descriptions of a transformation are interpreted inconsistently, 2-3 concrete input/output example pairs unambiguously show the expected format and decision logic, and the model generalizes the pattern — the fastest route to consistent shape.
ww: More prose adjectives leave the transformation ambiguous — the description is already failing, and adding text to a failing instruction doesn't fix inconsistent format.
Temperature controls randomness, not which specific output structure the model chooses; the inconsistency is an underspecified-format problem, not a sampling one.
A post-processing reshaper patches the symptom downstream instead of fixing the root cause (the ambiguous spec); examples fix generation itself.

questions.stem: Claude Code's project CLAUDE.md has grown into a wall of rules. Engineers want the Java files to follow the billing team's exception conventions, the Python routing files to follow async patterns, and the co-located test files to follow one shared testing convention — but only when Claude Code is actually working on files of that kind. The test files are scattered next to the code they cover. What configuration best applies the right conventions automatically?
questions.why: Conventions scoped to a file type or directory belong in `.claude/rules/` with glob patterns; the rules load automatically only when Claude works on matching paths, which handles co-located test files correctly regardless of directory.
ww: Root CLAUDE.md headings rely on model inference to decide which conventions apply, rather than deterministic file-path matching — the exam prefers glob-based rules for path-scoped conventions.
A CLAUDE.md per subdirectory doesn't work well when the relevant files (co-located tests) are spread across many directories; you'd have to duplicate the rule everywhere.
Universal, path-triggered conventions shouldn't require manual invocation each time; skills are for on-demand workflow guidance, not automatic path-scoped rules.

questions.stem: The team builds a `/audit-deps` skill that makes Claude Code do a deep, verbose dependency and coverage scan. Engineers report that after running it mid-task, Claude Code becomes less responsive and loses track of the original task they were working on, because the scan's large output floods the conversation. How should the skill be configured to fix this while keeping full analysis capability?
questions.why: When a skill generates large output or exploration context, `context: fork` runs it in an isolated subagent context so the output does not pollute the main conversation window, while full analysis capability is retained.
ww: A faster model doesn't fix context pollution — the verbose output still floods the main window and displaces the original task.
Compressing the scan to a short summary sacrifices the analysis capability the skill exists to provide; forking isolates the verbose work instead of discarding it.
Splitting into two skills doesn't prevent context leakage — each still dumps its output into the main session; isolation, not smaller chunks, is the fix.

questions.stem: An engineer resumes yesterday's named session that had mapped the entire routing service. Overnight, three files in that service were refactored by another team. The engineer wants to continue the investigation efficiently without trusting stale analysis. What is the best way to continue?
questions.why: If you resume after code modifications, tell the agent exactly which files changed so it performs targeted re-analysis of just those files, rather than trusting stale results or re-exploring the whole codebase.
ww: Resuming as-is makes the agent reason over stale tool results for the changed files — the exam's explicit wrong choice when files have changed.
Always starting from scratch is wasteful when most of the mapping is still valid; only three files changed, so a full re-analysis discards good context.
`/compact` compresses context and risks losing precise details, but does nothing to refresh the stale analysis of the three changed files — it addresses the wrong problem.

questions.stem: After Claude Code completes an expensive analysis of the billing monolith, the team wants to evaluate two competing refactoring strategies — one that introduces a repository layer and one that keeps direct data access — both starting from that same completed analysis, without the two explorations contaminating each other. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: `fork_session` creates divergent branches that inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently — exactly the pattern for comparing two approaches from one shared, expensive analysis baseline without re-analyzing or cross-contaminating.
ww: Running both strategies sequentially in one session biases the second evaluation by the first's reasoning and conclusions — the two must stay independent.
Two brand-new sessions each must redo the shared baseline analysis, wasting the expensive work that forking would reuse.
Compacting between strategies still runs them in one lineage (so the second is contaminated by the first) and risks losing analysis precision — it solves neither independence nor reuse.

questions.stem: The team asks Claude Code to add comprehensive test coverage to the legacy shipping-integration layer, whose full scope no one knows in advance — some modules have no tests, some have partial coverage, and hidden external-API dependencies keep surfacing as work proceeds. Which decomposition strategy should Claude Code use?
questions.why: An open-ended task whose scope is unknown up front, where each step depends on prior discoveries and dependencies emerge during work, calls for dynamic adaptive decomposition: map structure first, prioritize high-impact areas, and adapt the plan as dependencies surface.
ww: A fixed pipeline with predetermined steps can't react to discoveries; the scope and hidden dependencies are unknown up front, so a fixed script breaks when reality deviates.
One giant single-pass prompt over everything causes attention dilution — deep on some modules, shallow on others — and is the documented anti-pattern for large multi-part work.
Reusing a fixed prompt-chaining template is right only for predictable, reproducible workflows; here the structure is unknown, so a fixed chain is the wrong pattern.

questions.stem: Claude Code generates a batch of migration wrappers and, in its own reasoning trace, notes and then dismisses a possible edge case around null carrier IDs; the bug is only caught later when a human reviews the PR. The team wants to catch these self-dismissed issues automatically before human review. Which approach directly addresses the root cause?
questions.why: The self-check limitation is confirmation bias — the generating instance retains its reasoning and rationalizes its own choices. A second independent instance reviewing without the generator's reasoning context mirrors peer review and catches what the author dismissed.
ww: Extended thinking on the generation stage still runs in the same biased instance and does not fix the self-check limitation.
Self-review instructions keep the same instance and the same confirmation bias — it already 'considered' the case and dismissed it, so asking it to re-check itself repeats the failure.
More max_tokens gives room to write more code but does nothing about the biased self-assessment; the problem is who reviews, not output length.

questions.stem: As Claude Code rolls out to the whole engineering org, long automation sessions start exhausting the context window. The culprit is a `get_build_status` MCP tool that returns 40+ fields per call — build logs, timestamps, runner metadata — when only the status, failing step, and commit hash matter, and every bloated result lingers in context for every later turn. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Verbose tool outputs consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance and persist across turns; a PostToolUse hook that filters results to the relevant fields before they accumulate conserves context and reduces noise at the source.
ww: Telling the model to 'ignore irrelevant fields' still consumes the tokens — the attention and context cost remains because the fields are already in context.
More aggressive conversation summarization treats the symptom; verbose tool results keep flooding in every turn, so the root cause is untouched.
A larger context window raises cost and merely delays the same problem — the noise and per-turn accumulation remain.

questions.stem: Across the org, Claude Code reliably picks the right built-in tool for clear requests, but on genuinely ambiguous asks like "help me understand the recent purchase-order changes" it inconsistently chooses between the semantic MCP search and Grep. The team wants to raise selection accuracy on exactly these ambiguous cases. What few-shot strategy is most effective?
questions.why: Few-shot examples should target the specific ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — 4-6 examples aimed at those cases, each with rationale, rather than many examples of clear cases.
ww: 10-15 examples of clear, unambiguous requests don't address the ambiguous edge cases where misrouting actually occurs — the documented wrong move.
A single ambiguous example is too thin to cover the range of ambiguous phrasings; the exam calls for 4-6 targeted examples, not one.
Reverting to longer prose instructions is exactly what fails on ambiguous selection; examples, not more instruction text, give the model the concrete pattern.

questions.stem: The team's first CI job invokes `claude "Review the changed files in this PR for correctness issues"` inside a GitHub Actions step. The job never finishes; the Actions runner eventually times out at the 60-minute limit, and the step logs show Claude Code printed a prompt and then produced no further output. What is the correct way to run Claude Code in this pipeline?
questions.why: Without a non-interactive flag, Claude Code waits for interactive input and the pipeline hangs. `-p`/`--print` is the documented way to process a single prompt, print to stdout, and exit — exactly what a CI step needs.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is a fabricated environment variable; it does not exist and has no effect on Claude Code's interactivity. This is the canonical non-existent-feature trap for CI invocation.
`--batch` is not a real Claude Code CLI flag; batch processing is a Message Batches API concept, not a CLI switch, and would not fix an interactive-input hang. Fabricated flag.
Redirecting from `/dev/null` is an undocumented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned approach; the exam names `-p` as the correct mechanism and treats stdin tricks as a fragile substitute.

questions.stem: With `-p` working, the team's job pipes Claude's review into a script that must open one inline GitHub comment per finding, each carrying a file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix. Claude currently returns prose paragraphs, so the script parses them with brittle regex that breaks whenever wording shifts. What is the most reliable way to get machine-parseable findings?
questions.why: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` guarantees well-formed, schema-conformant output that downstream tooling can parse reliably — the sanctioned mechanism for structured CLI output feeding the GitHub API.
ww: A CLAUDE.md 'Output Format' section is guidance loaded into context, not an enforcement mechanism; compliance is inconsistent, so the parser still breaks. The corpus explicitly rejects this for structured CI output.
A prompt instruction to emit JSON has variable compliance — the model can still return prose preambles or markdown fences. Prompt-based JSON is the exact anti-pattern the schema flag removes.
A JSON-repair library treats the symptom (reconstructing structure after the fact) instead of removing the problem at the source; the schema flag makes repair unnecessary.

questions.stem: The team's findings are now structured, but developers say the suggested-fix field is uneven: some findings give a concrete diff-level change, others say only 'refactor the retry logic' or 'possible null issue.' The team already added the instruction 'always include a specific, concrete fix suggestion,' yet the output stays inconsistent. Which change most reliably produces consistently actionable fixes?
questions.why: When prose instructions produce inconsistent format, few-shot examples showing the exact required shape are the most effective fix — they give the model a concrete pattern to reproduce rather than more text to interpret.
ww: Adding more explicit instructions is the debunked move: the instruction is already failing, and more text does not resolve format inconsistency. Few-shot beats instruction-refinement here.
Temperature controls randomness, not adherence to a specific output structure; lowering it does not make the fix field consistently concrete. Wrong mechanism.
A post-processing rewrite patches the symptom downstream instead of fixing the generation; it cannot invent a concrete fix the model never reasoned about. Symptom-level fix.

questions.stem: The team's reviewer assigns a severity to each finding, but the prompt only says "rate severity appropriately." Analytics show the same class of issue—an unchecked null dereference—is labelled critical on one PR and medium on another, and developers say the levels feel arbitrary. What change most reliably makes severity ratings consistent across PRs?
questions.why: The root cause is an abstract instruction ("rate severity appropriately") that leaves the boundary between levels undefined, so identical issues land in different buckets. Replacing it with explicit, testable criteria for each level, each anchored by a concrete example, gives the model a consistent rubric to apply—moving from vague intent to concrete, example-backed definitions.
ww: Shifting every rating down one level applies a blanket strictness change that damages the accurate levels without fixing the underlying inconsistency; the same issue would still be rated differently across PRs, just uniformly lower.

Bolting self-reported confidence onto severity adds infrastructure without addressing the root cause; uncalibrated model self-confidence is unreliable and does not encode the missing criteria for what makes an issue critical versus medium.

A larger context window does not fix a definitional gap; severity is inconsistent because the levels are undefined, not because the model lacked room to see the PR, so a bigger model changes cost, not consistency.

questions.stem: Adoption analytics show the team's finding categories have very different reliability: correctness findings are dismissed 9% of the time, performance 19%, naming 51%, and documentation 47%. Developer comments say 'half of what it posts is noise, so I skim past all of it.' Trust in the accurate categories is now eroding too. Which approach best restores developer trust while the team improves the noisy categories?
questions.why: High-false-positive categories cause developers to dismiss everything, including accurate findings. Surgically disabling the noisy categories stops the trust bleed immediately while their prompts are fixed, preserving the value of the precise categories.
ww: Displaying confidence scores still surfaces all the noisy findings; developers keep seeing the noise and trust keeps eroding. It does not stop the bleed.
A uniform strictness reduction damages the already-precise correctness category unnecessarily while only partly reducing the noisy ones; the problem is category-specific, not global.
Adding few-shot examples across all categories is slow; trust continues to erode during the weeks it takes, and it wastes effort on categories that are already accurate.

questions.stem: As the team fixes the noisy categories, the team wants to learn which specific code constructs drive the naming false positives rather than guessing. Developers dismiss findings frequently but the team cannot aggregate why. What change most effectively lets them analyze which finding types are noise?
questions.why: A `detected_pattern` field labels which construct triggered each finding, so dismissals can be grouped by pattern to reveal which types drive false positives systematically instead of case by case.
ww: Capturing full reasoning logs bloats storage and still leaves the team reading prose per finding; it does not give the aggregate per-pattern dismissal signal.
Free-text dismissal reasons are unstructured and do not aggregate; the team cannot cleanly group them by pattern, which is exactly the analysis they need.
Classifying each dismissal with a second model adds cost and latency and still produces unstructured, non-aggregated labels; the structured field is the direct mechanism.

questions.stem: The team's CI also generates test cases for changed modules. On a PR adding shipment-status tracking, Claude proposes 11 tests, but reviewers note that 7 of them re-test scenarios the existing suite already covers. The generation prompt and CLAUDE.md are thorough. What change most effectively reduces duplicate test suggestions?
questions.why: Claude can only avoid duplicating tests it can see. Putting the existing test files in context gives it the coverage map, so it generates genuinely new scenarios.
questions.cite: Domain-3_v2 §3.8 (existing test files in context); Domain-4_v2 §4.18
ww: Instructing Claude to avoid existing coverage is useless when it has no visibility into what the suite already contains; the instruction cannot compensate for missing context.
Capping the count assumes the model orders tests by priority and that duplicates fall off the end; it may drop novel tests and keep duplicates. Wrong assumption.
Keyword matching is fragile and misses semantic duplicates worded differently while dropping distinct tests that happen to share names. Symptom-level and unreliable.

questions.stem: When an author pushes follow-up commits to a the team PR, the CI re-runs the review from scratch. Developers complain that each re-run re-posts near-duplicate comments on code that was already addressed, with slightly reworded findings piling up on the same lines. What is the most effective way to keep re-runs consistent and stop the duplicate flood?
questions.why: Including the prior findings in the re-run prompt and asking Claude to report only new or unresolved issues keeps the reviewer consistent across runs and prevents duplicate comments on unchanged code.
ww: After-the-fact text de-duplication is a fragile symptom patch that misses reworded duplicates and cannot tell a genuinely new issue from a reworded old one; feeding prior findings fixes the cause.
A blank-slate re-run re-litigates old findings and floods the PR with duplicates; the corpus explicitly rejects the 'objectivity' rationale for starting fresh each time.
Re-running only the latest-commit files can miss issues introduced by cross-file interactions and still re-posts duplicates within those files; it does not address run-to-run consistency.

questions.stem: The team wants to cut CI cost by moving analyses to the Message Batches API's 50% discount. Three workloads exist: a style check that blocks PR merge until it completes, a nightly test-generation job for changed modules, and a weekly full-codebase security audit. Which assignment correctly matches each workload to an API approach?
questions.why: Batch fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads: the nightly test generation and weekly audit both tolerate the up-to-24h window and gain 50% savings, while the merge-blocking style check must stay synchronous.
ww: Putting the blocking style check on Batch is wrong: developers wait on it to merge and Batch has no latency SLA (up to 24h), which is unacceptable for a blocking check.
Leaving nightly test generation synchronous forgoes an easy 50% saving on a scheduled, non-blocking job whose 24h window is perfectly acceptable.
Keeping all three synchronous captures none of the batch savings on the two workloads that clearly tolerate the window; off-peak scheduling does not reduce per-call cost.

questions.stem: The team batches the weekly security audit across 400 changed files. The batch returns with 388 files analyzed and 12 failed on context-limit errors because those files were unusually large. The team needs the results reconciled and the failures reprocessed with minimal cost. How should they handle the partial failure?
questions.why: `custom_id` identifies exactly which items failed; the fix is to modify the strategy for those items (chunk the oversized files) and re-submit only the failures, avoiding re-paying for the 388 successes.
ww: Batch results can arrive in any order, so matching by submission order silently mis-joins data; `custom_id` is the required join key.
Re-submitting all 400 pays again for 388 successes and can produce duplicate downstream results; selective re-submission by custom_id is the sanctioned approach.
Context-limit errors are not transient — the files are too large; re-submitting unchanged fails again. The cause (size) must be fixed via chunking before retry.

questions.stem: The team wants CI-invoked Claude to generate tests that match the team's fixture conventions, mock the shared HTTP client the same way every time, and use the project's assertion helpers — yet generated tests keep inventing their own fixtures and ad-hoc mocks. The pipeline invokes Claude with only the changed diff and a short prompt. What most reliably makes generated tests follow the team's conventions?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude durable project context — testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria — which improves generation quality and reduces low-value output across every run.
ww: A one-line prompt reminder cannot convey the team's actual fixture and mocking conventions; the model has no way to know the specifics, so it keeps improvising. Guidance without the concrete conventions in context.
max_tokens governs output length, not adherence to conventions; more room does not teach the model the project's patterns. Wrong mechanism.
Plan mode defers execution for architectural decisions; test generation for a scoped diff is routine, and planning does not inject the missing convention knowledge that CLAUDE.md provides.

questions.stem: The team wants a new CI job that adds comprehensive tests to a large legacy module with no existing coverage; the full scope is unknown up front, and each area's needs depend on what earlier exploration reveals (some sub-modules have hidden external-API dependencies). An engineer proposes a fixed pipeline: enumerate every file, then generate tests for each in a predetermined order. Which decomposition strategy fits this task?
