questions.why: The scope is open-ended and each step depends on prior discoveries (e.g., hidden external-API dependencies), which is exactly when dynamic adaptive decomposition applies: map structure first, prioritize by risk, and adapt as dependencies emerge.
ww: A fixed pipeline suits predictable, fully-known structures; here the scope is unknown up front and a rigid script cannot react to discoveries like a newly-found API dependency. Wrong pattern for open-ended work.
A single giant pass over the whole module causes attention dilution — deep on some files, shallow on others — the anti-pattern for large multi-file work.
Running a fixed pipeline twice inherits the same rigidity and cannot adapt to discovered dependencies; it doubles work without adding adaptability.

questions.stem: A the team PR touches 16 files in the routing engine. A single review pass over all files at once gives deep feedback on a few files and shallow feedback on the rest, misses an obvious off-by-one bug, and flags a pattern in one file while approving the identical pattern in another. How should the team restructure the review?
questions.why: The inconsistency is attention dilution across many files at once. Per-file passes give each file full attention for local issues, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file problems — the sanctioned multi-pass structure for large PRs.
ww: Forcing developers to split the PR shifts the burden onto humans instead of fixing the review architecture, and does not address cross-file issues within a legitimately large change.
A bigger context window does not fix attention quality; more available tokens is not the same as consistent attention per token. This is the explicitly debunked 'bigger context' trap.
Consensus voting across two noisy full-PR runs suppresses real single-run findings and still inherits the diluted attention of each pass; it hides signal rather than improving depth.

questions.stem: In the team's review flow, the same Claude session that generates a suggested refactor is then asked, in that same conversation, to 'review your change carefully for bugs before finishing.' Subtle bugs the model reasoned about during generation still reach production — its self-review consistently reaffirms its original approach. What most directly addresses this self-check limitation?
questions.why: A model retains its generation reasoning and is anchored to its own decisions, so same-session self-review inherits the same blind spots. An independent instance with only the artifact and criteria evaluates the code on its merits and catches what the generator rationalized away.
ww: A stronger self-review instruction runs in the same instance with the same confirmation bias; it does not create independence.
More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny; extended thinking does not remove the generator's anchoring to its own choices.

A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context; the model re-reads its own justifications and confirms them. Same-conversation second pass is not independent review.

questions.stem: The team's CI reviewer reads Unix epoch timestamps from a `git_blame` tool, ISO 8601 dates from a `pr_metadata` tool, and numeric CI status codes (1=queued, 2=running, 3=passed) from a third-party build tool it cannot modify. The reviewer keeps misreading these mixed formats when it composes feedback. What is the most maintainable way to normalize the tool outputs?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook is deterministic code that fires after each tool returns, normalizing all outputs centrally regardless of which tool produced them — the maintainable single point of control, including for third-party tools you cannot modify.
ww: Documenting formats in the system prompt relies on the model interpreting mixed formats correctly every time — probabilistic, and it is already failing. Hooks are deterministic.
Modifying owned tools plus separate wrappers fragments the normalization logic across multiple places, which is exactly the maintenance problem the central hook avoids.
A `normalize_data` tool the model must remember to call adds an LLM call each time and relies on probabilistic compliance; the deterministic hook needs no model cooperation.

questions.stem: The team's extraction schema marks every field — including purchase_order_number and tax_id — as required and non-nullable, reasoning that downstream ERP posting needs a complete record. In a 5,000-invoice audit, 11% of outputs carry a plausible-looking PO number that appears nowhere in the source document; those invoices simply had no PO. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: A required, non-nullable field pressures the model to fabricate a value to satisfy the schema when the data is absent. Making the field nullable and non-required lets the model emit null instead of hallucinating — completeness by honest extraction, not by fabrication.
ww: Relying on a prompt instruction against fabrication is probabilistic; the schema constraint (required + non-nullable) still structurally demands a value, and the prompt cannot reliably override that pressure. The fix is the schema, not another instruction.
A downstream reconciliation job is a symptom-level patch that detects fabrications after they are produced rather than preventing them; the model is still forced to invent values at extraction time.

Temperature controls randomness, not the schema-driven pressure to fill a required field; the model fabricates because the contract demands a non-null value, and lowering temperature does not change that requirement.

questions.stem: Incoming documents are a mix of invoices, receipts, and PO confirmations, and the pipeline must ALWAYS hand the ERP schema-valid JSON — never a prose reply. The team defined three extraction tools (one per document type) but sometimes Claude answers a hard-to-classify scan with an explanatory paragraph instead of calling any tool. Which configuration guarantees a structured tool call every time?
questions.why: tool_choice {"type": "any"} guarantees the model will call some tool rather than return conversational text; with multiple extraction schemas it still picks the best-fitting one, so the output is always structured. That is the output guarantee the pipeline needs.
ww: tool_choice "auto" permits a plain-text response instead of a tool call, and a system-prompt instruction to "always return JSON" is probabilistic — exactly the prose-preamble failure being observed. "auto" gives no structure guarantee.

A JSON-repair library treats the symptom (fixing malformed prose after the fact) instead of removing the problem at the source; forcing a tool call eliminates the free-text response entirely rather than patching it.

Forcing extract_invoice specifically guarantees a tool call but the WRONG tool for receipts and PO confirmations — it would run invoice extraction on every document type. "any" lets the model choose the correct schema.

questions.stem: After moving extraction to tool_use with strict JSON schemas, the team's JSON parse failures dropped to zero. But the downstream ERP reconciliation still rejects about 3% of invoices because the extracted total does not equal the sum of the extracted line items. An engineer proposes tightening the schema further to "catch" the mismatches. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate the entire syntax-error class but do nothing for the semantic class — a response can be perfectly schema-valid and still state a total that doesn't match the line items. The remaining failures are semantic and require validation plus retry/self-correction, not a tighter schema.
ww: No JSON Schema constraint can express or verify that numbers sum correctly — arithmetic relationships are business-rule (semantic) checks that live in code (e.g., Pydantic validators), not in the schema shape.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the entire syntax-error class on top of the unchanged semantic class — strictly worse. tool_use is not the cause of the arithmetic mismatch.

A passing schema validator proves only structural validity, not content correctness; assuming the mismatches are all genuinely bad invoices ignores that extraction itself can pick up the wrong number — semantic errors sail through schema validation by definition.

questions.stem: The validate-then-retry loop resubmits a failed extraction with the document, the previous output, and the specific validation error. It works well for format and arithmetic errors. But on 40 documents, purchase_order_number keeps failing validation across all 3 retries; investigation shows those documents never contained a PO number at all. An engineer wants to raise max retries from 3 to 10. What should the team do instead?
questions.why: Retry-with-feedback only fixes errors the model can correct from the provided context (format, structure, arithmetic). When the information is genuinely absent from the source, no number of retries can extract what isn't there — the fix is schema design (nullable, accept null) not loop tuning.
ww: Absent information stays absent regardless of retry count; increasing retries from 3 to 10 burns tokens for nothing and, worse, the repeated pressure to fill a required field invites fabrication.
No feedback message can conjure data that is not in the document; a more forceful demand only increases fabrication pressure on a field that cannot be legitimately filled.

Keeping the field required "for data quality" guarantees fabricated values on documents that lack a PO; routing all 40 to humans mistreats a legitimate "not present" answer as a failure — null is the correct extraction, not a defect.

questions.stem: Weeks after posting, monthly reconciliation keeps surfacing invoices where the extracted total silently disagrees with the line items — sometimes the model grabbed a subtotal, sometimes the source invoice itself was internally inconsistent. The team wants to catch these at extraction time, not weeks later. What extraction design catches this?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern is structural: extract both the value as written (stated_total) and an independently re-derived value (calculated_total), plus a conflict_detected flag. This surfaces arithmetic drift as machine-readable data on every extraction and lets the pipeline route conflicts to review instead of silently trusting either number.
ww: "Be careful with totals" is a vague instruction with no detection mechanism — it cannot surface a mismatch as a signal the pipeline can act on, so silent disagreements still slip through.
Running reconciliation weekly still detects errors after posting rather than at extraction time; the self-correction pattern moves detection to the moment of extraction, which is the stated goal.

Self-correction here is not an optional conversational "are you sure?" follow-up — the exam pattern builds the re-derivation into the output schema so checking happens on every extraction and produces a machine-readable conflict signal.

questions.stem: The team's process_payment_hold tool rejects a hold because the invoice amount exceeds the client's per-invoice auto-hold policy limit. The extraction agent keeps re-calling the tool, treating the rejection like a transient outage, and burns retries. How should the tool's error handling be structured?
questions.why: A business-rule violation (policy limit exceeded) is not a tool failure — it is a valid answer that the action is disallowed. Structure it as retriable: false with a customer-friendly explanation so the agent stops retrying and communicates the policy outcome appropriately.
ww: A generic "Operation failed" leaves the agent unable to distinguish policy denial from a transient outage, so it retries or escalates incorrectly — the error category and its non-retryability must be explicit.
Marking a policy denial as a transient, retryable error wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change — re-invoking the tool cannot make a policy limit disappear.
Returning success with embedded error metadata masks the failure — the agent believes the hold succeeded when it did not, which is exactly the silent-failure anti-pattern.

questions.stem: The team needs to reprocess a 240,000-document monthly archive for a new client, with results due by 9 a.m. the next day — no human is waiting per-document. The team plans to use the Message Batches API for the 50% savings. Before committing all 240,000 documents, what is the most effective way to de-risk the run?
questions.why: Sample-first iteration validates the prompt/schema on a small synchronous sample for fast feedback, then submits the full batch only once the sample passes. This maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying (and waiting up to 24h) to discover a prompt defect replicated across all 240,000 requests.
ww: Submitting the full batch and iterating on the whole thing costs a full batch and up to 24h per iteration — a prompt defect is replicated across every request before it is caught. The point of the sample is to catch defects cheaply first.

Spreading submissions across the day does nothing to validate the prompt; it addresses scheduling, not the risk that a prompt defect ruins all 240,000 extractions. Sample-first is what de-risks the run.

custom_id joins results to inputs and identifies failures, but it cannot fix a systematic prompt defect — skipping sample validation means every document may fail the same way, and custom_id only tells you which (all of them).

questions.stem: One client's onboarding step runs extraction from a nightly CI job that shells out to the Claude Code CLI in --print mode, then posts the parsed fields to the client's ERP via an API call. The job intermittently breaks because the CLI sometimes returns a prose preamble around the JSON, so the parser chokes. What is the most reliable way to get downstream-parseable output?
questions.why: For the Claude Code CLI in print mode, --output-format json combined with --json-schema enforces the schema and guarantees well-formed output that downstream tools can parse reliably — the correct mechanism for structured CLI output feeding an API.
ww: A CLAUDE.md "Output Format" section is not guaranteed to produce consistent output — it is guidance the model may or may not follow, which is exactly the intermittent-preamble failure being seen.

A prompt instruction to return only JSON yields variable compliance; the CLI can still emit a preamble on some runs, so the parser keeps breaking. The flag-level enforcement is deterministic where the instruction is not.

A regex strip is a fragile post-hoc workaround that fails whenever the JSON itself is malformed or the preamble contains a brace; --json-schema removes the problem at the source instead of patching the symptom.

questions.stem: The team's extraction reports 97% overall accuracy on a labeled audit, and the team proposes auto-processing every high-confidence extraction with no human review. A skeptical lead notes that handwritten-receipt scans are a small fraction of volume. Before turning off review, what should the team do first?
questions.why: An aggregate 97% can hide a 40% failure rate on one rare document type — overall metrics average away segment-level failures. Before reducing human review, validate accuracy by document type and field, and add stratified random sampling so every segment independently meets the bar and novel error patterns are caught.
ww: Auto-processing on the aggregate threshold is exactly the masking trap: the 97% average conceals that the rare handwritten-receipt segment may fail 40% of the time, and those failures post as wrong payments.
Raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until calibrated against a labeled validation set; trusting it directly means the threshold itself may be miscalibrated per segment.

Auditing only low-confidence extractions leaves novel error patterns in the high-confidence automated path undetected — stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream is what measures the true error rate of automation.

questions.stem: To route extractions to human review, the team has the model emit a single 1–10 confidence score per document and reviews anything under 8. Reviewers report that many "high-confidence" extractions are still wrong on specific fields, while some flagged documents are perfectly fine. What is the most effective redesign of the confidence signal?
questions.why: The design should output confidence per extracted field (not one score per document) and calibrate the thresholds against a labeled validation set, because raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until calibrated against ground truth. This targets reviewer capacity at the specific fields that are actually uncertain.
ww: Raising the cutoff on an uncalibrated single document score does not fix miscalibration — it floods review with correct documents while still missing per-field errors hidden under a high document-level score.

Averaging two self-ratings from the same model does not calibrate confidence against ground truth; the model can be confidently wrong twice. Calibration requires a labeled validation set, not repeated self-assessment.
A flat unstratified 10% wastes reviewer capacity on easy segments and undersamples the problem fields; calibrated field-level routing directs oversight where accuracy is actually at risk.

questions.stem: Each lookup_vendor call in the team's enrichment step returns 40+ fields (full address history, tax registrations, contact log), but only vendor_id, name, and remit_to matter for extraction. On long multi-invoice sessions, the context fills with these fields turn after turn, and the model starts confusing remit-to addresses. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Verbose tool results consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance and stay in context every subsequent turn. A PostToolUse hook trims the result to only the relevant fields before it enters context, conserving the window and removing the noise that distracts the model.
ww: Instructing the model to ignore fields still leaves the tokens in context — the attention cost and clutter remain; only trimming before the result enters context actually removes them.

Aggressive whole-conversation summarization treats the symptom while verbose tool results keep flooding in every turn; the source of the bloat is the untrimmed tool output, which the hook fixes at the source.
A larger context window raises cost and still leaves the irrelevant fields distracting the model — the noise problem is not a capacity problem, and switching models does not remove the clutter.

questions.stem: Downstream auditors need every extracted figure traced to where it came from: the source document name, the page, and the extraction date. Currently the merge step that combines multi-page invoice data into one record flattens everything to prose, and a general "sources reviewed" note is appended at the end. Auditors can no longer tie a specific total back to a specific page. What is the correct fix?
questions.why: Source attribution is lost when findings are compressed without preserving claim-to-source mappings. Require structured claim-to-source mappings (document name, page/location, date) per field and require downstream steps to preserve and merge them, so the final record can attribute every figure.
ww: A general bibliography at the end means individual figures are no longer traceable to specific sources — the auditor still cannot tie a particular total to a particular page. Per-claim mappings, not a document-level list, are required.
Re-deriving attributions by re-searching sources at audit time is expensive and error-prone; the mapping should be preserved through the pipeline, not reconstructed after the fact.
Flattening to uniform prose is what destroyed traceability in the first place; tabular financial data becomes imprecise and harder to verify, and per-claim source links vanish.

questions.stem: The team is redesigning extraction as a multi-agent pipeline: a coordinator delegates classification, extraction, and validation to specialized subagents. The validation subagent needs the extraction subagent's output to check it, but currently it receives nothing and reports "no data to validate." What is the root cause and fix?
questions.why: Subagents have isolated context — they do not see the coordinator's conversation history or another subagent's output unless the coordinator explicitly includes it in the subagent's prompt. The fix is for the coordinator to pass the extraction results into the validation subagent's prompt.
ww: Direct inter-agent communication breaks the hub-and-spoke pattern — subagents never talk to each other directly; all inter-agent communication flows through the coordinator, which controls what each subagent sees.
A session_id does not exist; the API is stateless and there is no server-side retrieval of another agent's turn. Context is shared only by the coordinator explicitly passing it in the prompt.

Giving the validator its own extraction tool makes it re-extract rather than validate — it breaks separation of responsibilities and defeats the point of an independent validation step, which must check the extraction agent's actual output.

questions.stem: When a document extraction subagent hits a password-protected PDF it cannot open, it currently returns a bare "failed" status to the coordinator, which then can't decide whether to retry, skip, or route to manual handling. The team wants the coordinator to make intelligent recovery decisions. How should the subagent report the failure?
questions.why: A failing subagent must return structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — not a generic status or silence. The coordinator needs this to make an intelligent recovery decision (retry, reroute, continue with partial results, or escalate).
ww: A generic status forces the coordinator to guess; a password-protected PDF is a permanent error that will always fail, so uniform retrying wastes attempts. The category must be distinguishable so the coordinator does not retry an unrecoverable failure.

Catching the error and returning a successful-but-empty result silently masks the failure — the coordinator never learns the document needs handling, and a real gap is hidden as a success. Never catch and silently return success.
Terminating the entire workflow for one subagent failure is exactly what structured error propagation avoids; one unreadable file should not fail the whole batch.

questions.stem: A single client submits a bundled packet each night: an invoice, a matching receipt, and a delivery-confirmation report, all needing extraction plus a three-way match. The coordinator currently extracts them strictly one after another, and end-to-end latency has become the client's top complaint even though each extraction succeeds. The three documents are independent to extract. What most effectively reduces latency?
questions.why: Independent subtasks should be decomposed and run in parallel: multiple Task calls emitted in a single coordinator response execute concurrently, and the coordinator synthesizes once all return. This removes the serial latency without losing the shared-context match step.
ww: Swapping in a faster model shortens each step but keeps the serial structure — the three extractions still run one after another when they could run at once. Parallelizing independent work is the structural fix.

Cramming three documents into one prompt invites attention dilution across documents and mixes their fields; the exam favors decompose-and-parallelize for independent items, not a single overloaded pass.
Direct subagent-to-subagent handoff breaks hub-and-spoke — subagents never communicate directly; all results flow through the coordinator, which owns the three-way synthesis.

questions.stem: During Aria's rollout, an engineer builds the agentic loop by hand. After each Claude API call the code must decide whether to run the requested tools and call Claude again, or stop and send the reply to the customer. In staging, some sessions never terminate and keep re-invoking Claude after it has clearly finished answering. What should the loop use to decide whether to continue or stop?
questions.why: The orchestrator inspects the structured stop_reason after each call: tool_use means Claude wants a tool run (execute it, append the tool_result, loop again); end_turn means Claude finished (stop and return). This is the documented loop-control mechanism.
ww: Parsing natural-language text for a 'done' phrase is the explicit exam trap: control flow must key off structured stop_reason, not fragile string matching that breaks when phrasing varies.

An iteration cap is a safety backstop, not the stop decision; a hard limit of five would truncate legitimate multi-tool resolutions and still misfires on short ones. stop_reason determines termination.
Tying termination to which tool was called invents a rule the API does not use; many valid resolutions never call process_refund, and the loop would hang. The signal is stop_reason: "end_turn".

questions.stem: Aria's search_orders MCP tool returns {"results": [], "isError": true} in two very different situations: when a customer genuinely has no orders on file, and when the orders database is unreachable. Logs show that on days the database has brief outages, Aria confidently tells customers "you have no orders," and on legitimately empty accounts it retries and then escalates. How should the tool signal these two outcomes?
questions.why: An empty result is a successful query with zero matches, not a failure; conflating it with an access failure corrupts the agent's decision both ways. Signalling 'ran, no matches' as success (isError false) lets Aria confidently report 'no orders found,' while reserving isError:true for a query that could not run stops it from telling a customer they have no orders when the database was simply down.
ww: Marking a valid empty result as an error and papering over it with retry instructions treats a legitimate answer as a failure; the agent burns retries and escalates a query that worked fine, and prompt-based retry rules are probabilistic rather than fixing the signal.

Returning an empty list in both cases masks the access failure: when the database is down the agent reports 'you have no orders,' a false statement caused by hiding the failure, and latency is an unreliable, fragile proxy for whether the query actually ran.

Flagging every zero-match result as an error forces the agent to treat a valid answer as a failure and retry a query that succeeded, which is exactly the empty-result-as-error anti-pattern the corpus rejects.

questions.stem: Meridian requires that Aria verify a caller's identity with get_customer before any refund is issued. The rule lives only in Aria's system prompt ("always call get_customer before process_refund"). Audit logs show that in roughly 7% of refunds Aria skipped get_customer and called process_refund directly off a customer-supplied order number, twice refunding the wrong account. What change most reliably guarantees the verification step precedes every refund?
questions.why: When correct sequencing is mandatory—verify identity before a financial action—the enforcement must be programmatic, not prompt-based. A precondition that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified identifier makes the wrong order impossible at the code level, whereas any prompt-level rule is followed only probabilistically.
ww: Strengthening and repositioning the prompt rule is still prompt-level enforcement; instruction compliance is probabilistic, so a stronger sentence reduces but never eliminates the skips that already caused wrong-account refunds.

Few-shot examples make the correct sequence more likely but still leave it to the model's discretion on each turn; for security-critical sequencing the corpus requires code-level preconditions, not example-driven nudges.

A model self-check is the same probabilistic instance making the same judgement it already skips 7% of the time; self-reported compliance provides no deterministic guarantee that verification actually ran before the refund.

questions.stem: Meridian's four support tools run as an MCP server that six engineers use locally while iterating on Aria. Each engineer authenticates to the backend with their own personal API token. The team wants one shared, version-controlled tool configuration without committing any credentials to the repository. Which configuration approach is most effective?
questions.why: Project-scoped .mcp.json is version-controlled and shared with the team; ${VAR} substitution injects each developer's own token from the environment at runtime, keeping the config shared while credentials stay out of the repo.
ww: Putting the server in each user's ~/.claude.json gives inconsistent, un-shared tooling — the opposite of the version-controlled shared config the team wants; user scope is for personal overrides.
Committing a placeholder token is a security risk and invites accidental real-credential commits; env-var substitution exists precisely so no token, real or placeholder, lives in the repo.

CLAUDE.md is loaded instructional context, not a credential store; putting a token there both leaks it into version control and misuses the memory file. Credentials belong in env vars referenced by .mcp.json.

questions.stem: When Aria escalates mid-conversation, Meridian's human agents complain they must re-ask customers for details Aria already gathered — the customer ID, the order, what was tried. The human console shows only that escalate_to_human fired with a short free-text note; it has no access to the conversation transcript. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: Human agents lack transcript access by design, so the escalation payload must be a complete, self-contained structured handoff summary — customer ID, root-cause analysis, amount, actions taken, and recommended action — everything the human sees.
ww: Handing over the raw transcript contradicts the design (humans don't get transcript access) and forces re-reading the whole conversation; a structured summary is the documented fix.
Making the human re-run Aria's tools duplicates completed work and slows resolution — exactly the information loss the structured handoff exists to prevent.
Escalating earlier does not fix the information-transfer gap and degrades autonomous resolution; the problem is what gets passed at handoff, not when.

questions.stem: Aria's process_refund tool starts rejecting some refunds because they fall outside Meridian's 30-day return window. The tool currently returns a generic {"error": "Operation failed"}, and logs show Aria retries process_refund up to three times on these rejections before finally escalating. How should the tool's error handling be changed?
questions.why: A policy-limit rejection is a business-rule error: a valid answer that the action is disallowed. Return retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation so the agent stops retrying and communicates the policy outcome.
ww: Labeling a policy denial as transient/retryable wastes retries on an outcome that can never change — the exact misclassification the business-error category exists to prevent.

A generic "Operation failed" leaves the agent unable to distinguish policy denial from an outage, so it retries or escalates incorrectly; structured error categories fix this, not blanket first-failure escalation.
A prompt rule capping retries is probabilistic and still leaves Aria guessing the error's nature from opaque text; the deterministic fix is a structured business-error response the tool returns.

questions.stem: To bound cost, Aria keeps only the last 25 message pairs of each conversation verbatim and drops everything older. On long returns cases this backfires: a customer states an accessibility requirement and an agreed store-credit arrangement early on, and 30 turns later Aria contradicts both because those turns have fallen out of the retained window. What is the most effective way to restructure the conversation state?
questions.why: A pure sliding window drops early preferences and commitments that turn out to be critical later. The hybrid approach keeps recent exchanges verbatim for coherence, compresses older discussion into a running summary, and preserves agreed structured facts in a block that is never dropped—so early commitments survive regardless of how long the conversation runs.
ww: Widening the window from 25 to 60 pairs only delays the same failure; any fixed window still eventually discards the early turns, so a sufficiently long case reproduces the contradiction.

A bigger context window is the classic misconception here: it raises cost and merely postpones dropping, and larger inputs also invite lost-in-the-middle attention gaps rather than reliably preserving the early commitment.

Replaying the entire untrimmed history on every request is precisely what makes cost and latency scale with conversation length; the stateless API resends everything each call, so unbounded history is the problem the window was meant to solve, not a fix.

questions.stem: Aria's lookup_order tool returns 40+ fields per order (warehouse routing, carrier metadata, internal SKUs), but only order_id, status, total, items, and return_eligible matter for support. In long multi-issue sessions the accumulated tool output floods the window and Aria's later answers drift. What is the most effective way to conserve context?
questions.why: Verbose tool results consume tokens disproportionately and persist every turn; a PostToolUse hook filters each result to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context, conserving the window and reducing distraction.
ww: Telling the model to ignore fields still leaves every token in context — the attention and cost burden remains; the tokens must be removed before they enter, not mentally skipped.
More aggressive summarization treats the symptom while verbose tool results keep flooding in each turn; trimming the source is the root-cause fix.
A larger window raises cost and merely delays the same flooding; the noise from 40-field results persists. This is the bigger-context misconception.

questions.stem: In extended billing conversations, a customer says early on "apply the 15% loyalty discount I was promised," but 20+ turns later Aria quotes the wrong amount. Investigation shows the discount detail was compressed by summarization into a vague note like "promotional pricing was discussed." What fix is most effective?
questions.why: Precise transactional facts must be extracted into a persistent case-facts block carried in every prompt outside the summarized history, so they survive context compression verbatim instead of being abstracted away.
ww: Raising the threshold only delays compression; the facts still eventually get summarized into vagueness. It buys time without fixing the precision loss.
Revising the summarization prompt still relies on the summarizer executing perfectly every time; the case-facts block removes that dependency by keeping facts out of summarization entirely.
External storage plus retrieval is overkill for session-level facts; a compact in-prompt case-facts block is the documented, lighter fix.

questions.stem: Meridian wants to raise Aria's first-contact resolution by having it escalate the genuinely hard cases and resolve the rest. A vendor proposes running sentiment analysis on each message and escalating whenever the customer sounds angry. Aria's logs show calm messages describing tangled multi-account billing errors and irate messages about trivially fixable typos. How should escalation be triggered instead?
questions.why: Escalation should key off structural signals — explicit human requests, policy silence, missing data, repeated failures — because sentiment does not correlate with case complexity; a calm message can be genuinely complex and an angry one trivially resolvable.
ww: Sentiment is an unreliable complexity proxy: customer mood does not track difficulty, so an anger threshold floods the human queue with resolvable cases and misses calm-but-hard ones.
Model self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and poorly correlated with actual difficulty — the model can be confidently wrong — so a 1-10 self-score is not a reliable escalation trigger.
An automatic complexity classifier is over-engineering that needs training data the team likely lacks; the sanctioned approach is escalating on structural signals, not a bespoke model.

questions.stem: A customer messages: "This is unacceptable, I've been waiting a week!" Meridian's policy covers this delay with a standard shipping credit that Aria is authorized to issue. Aria's escalation design must decide what to do with this first expression of frustration. What is the most appropriate behavior?
questions.why: A first expression of dissatisfaction is not a request for a manager: acknowledge the emotion, propose a concrete resolution, and escalate only if the customer reiterates the desire for a human.
ww: Immediate escalation on frustration alone conflates mood with an explicit human request and needlessly hands off a case Aria is authorized and able to resolve.
Resolving silently ignores the acknowledge-emotion step; the pattern is acknowledge, then resolve — skipping acknowledgment degrades the interaction even when the fix is correct.
Interrogating the customer about whether they want a manager before helping inverts the flow; the agent should offer a resolution first and only escalate on a reiterated request.

questions.stem: Aria calls get_customer and lookup_order in two separate sequential turns even when a request plainly needs both up front ("refund order #1234 on my account"). This adds an extra API loop to most resolutions and inflates latency at holiday volume. What is the most effective way to reduce the number of loops?
questions.why: The preferred fix is to prompt the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn — Claude can naturally emit multiple tool calls simultaneously, removing the extra loop without hiding the composition.
ww: A composite tool works but is not preferred: it hides the composition and adds a bespoke tool where prompting the agent to request both in one turn is the lighter, documented answer.

Forcing tool_choice "any" on every turn guarantees a tool call but does not make Aria batch the two lookups together, and it prevents ever ending the turn with a text reply; it targets the wrong problem.
Raising the loop limit accommodates the extra loops instead of eliminating them; the latency from an unnecessary round-trip remains. Bundling removes the loop.

questions.stem: A customer asks Aria to price-match a competitor's lower price. Meridian's written policy covers refunds when Meridian's own price drops after purchase, but says nothing at all about matching other retailers' prices. Aria has already run get_customer and lookup_order and has all available system data. What should Aria do?
questions.why: A policy gap — where the agent cannot determine the correct action within defined policy — is a valid escalation trigger; the agent must escalate rather than invent policy for a case the rules do not cover.
ww: Stretching the own-site price-drop rule onto a competitor scenario is a wrong policy interpretation the agent is not authorized to make; the correct move is escalation.
Refusing with a flat 'we don't match competitor prices' asserts a rule the policy never states; silence is not a documented denial, so the agent must escalate for interpretation.
Approving at the agent's own discretion invents policy to chase a metric and risks unauthorized concessions; policy-gap ambiguity must go to a human.

questions.stem: Aria still misroutes borderline messages like "I need help with my recent purchase" between get_customer and lookup_order. An engineer plans to add few-shot examples to the system prompt to fix it and asks how to choose them. Which approach most effectively improves selection?
questions.why: Few-shot examples should target the specific ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — 4-6 examples aimed at the edge cases, each with rationale — not a pile of easy, unambiguous examples.
ww: Ten to fifteen unambiguous examples do not address the ambiguous edge cases that actually cause misrouting; the exam explicitly rejects flooding the prompt with clear-cut examples.
One common-case example per tool covers exactly the requests Aria already handles correctly and ignores the borderline cases; the examples must target the failure region.
More emphatic instructions are the failing approach already — when prose instructions produce inconsistent selection, concrete targeted examples work where more instruction text does not.

questions.stem: Meridian standardized Aria's operator runbook so every engineer's local Claude Code sessions follow the same review and safety conventions. Three engineers who set this up months ago see the conventions applied; a newly onboarded engineer reports Claude ignores them entirely, though everyone shares the same repository and up-to-date code. What is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.why: When existing members follow a convention a new member doesn't, the guidance is in the original developers' user-scope ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not version-controlled; moving it to project-level config shares it with everyone.
ww: The stem states everyone shares the same repo with up-to-date code, so a stale clone is ruled out; the missing guidance was never in the project file to begin with — it lives in user scope.
A per-user CLAUDE.md cache that must be rebuilt is a fabricated mechanism; the discrepancy comes from user-scope vs project-scope placement, not a cache. Use /memory to see which files loaded.
Re-stating the rule louder each session treats the symptom, not the root cause; the guidance simply isn't in a shared file, so the fix is relocating it to project scope.

questions.stem: A newly onboarded engineer asks Pathfinder to find everywhere the legacy `computeSurcharge` routine is actually called, so she can understand the billing flow. Pathfinder must decide which built-in tool to reach for first. Telemetry from earlier sessions shows engineers most often want the call sites, not the files whose names resemble the function. Which tool should Pathfinder use to locate the call sites?
questions.why: Grep is content search: it looks inside files for patterns like function names, call sites, and imports. 'Find all callers of computeSurcharge' is a content target, so Grep is the correct built-in.
ww: Glob matches file *paths*, not file *contents* — `**/computeSurcharge*` only finds files whose names contain the string and misses every call site inside otherwise-named files. This is the documented Grep-vs-Glob confusion.
Using Bash `find` for a filename match is the same wrong problem as Glob (it matches paths, not contents) and bypasses the tool designed for the job; content discovery is Grep's role.

Reading a directory in full upfront to 'build complete context' is the exam's discovery anti-pattern — it burns the context window on irrelevant files instead of driving discovery from a content search.

questions.stem: The same engineer now wants Pathfinder to map how a shipment record flows from ingestion to invoicing across the unfamiliar integration layer. Session logs show that when Pathfinder tries to Read every file in the integration package first, it fills the context window before it reaches the invoicing code. What investigation strategy should Pathfinder follow?
questions.why: Codebase understanding is built incrementally: Grep to find an entry point, Read it, Grep for usages, Read consumers, and repeat until the picture is complete — discovery is driven by content search plus targeted reads.
ww: Globbing the whole tree and reading every match before searching is explicitly called out as the same anti-pattern as bulk reading — it burns context on files the flow never touches.
Reading every file upfront to 'get full context' is the documented anti-pattern; it exhausts the context window on irrelevant files rather than following the actual flow.
Concatenating every file into one buffer is bulk upfront reading in disguise — it loads the same irrelevant content and defeats incremental, content-driven investigation.

questions.stem: An engineer must rename the legacy `calculateTax` function everywhere it is used. Investigation reveals that `utils/tax.ts` wraps and re-exports it as `getTax`, and `index.ts` re-exports that wrapper again. Pathfinder greps only for `calculateTax`, reports the call sites it finds, and the engineer proceeds — but a downstream module that imports `getTax` breaks in production. What should Pathfinder have done to find every caller?
questions.why: When a function is re-exported or wrapped, searching only the original name misses callers that use the wrapper's alias. The strategy is to first collect all exported names (original plus every wrapper/re-export), then search for each name across the codebase.
ww: A case-insensitive grep still searches only for `calculateTax` — it never discovers the distinct alias `getTax`, so it misses every consumer that imports the wrapper.
Globbing filenames matches paths, not the names of functions imported inside files; consumers of `getTax` need not live in tax-named files, so this misses call sites.
Bulk-reading the whole repository is the upfront-reading anti-pattern and, worse, still relies on catching the alias by eye rather than systematically enumerating exported names then searching each.

questions.stem: Pathfinder is applying a boilerplate change to a large config module and calls Edit with the anchor snippet `return config;`. The Edit fails because that exact text appears in eleven places in the file, so Edit cannot decide which occurrence to modify. What is the correct fallback for a reliable modification?
questions.why: Edit works by unique text matching and fails on non-unique anchors. The sanctioned fallback is Read the full file, modify the content, then Write the updated version — a reliable full-file modification.
ww: A shorter anchor is *more* likely to be non-unique, not less — `config` appears even more often than `return config;`, so this makes the ambiguity worse.
Forcing the change with Bash `sed` bypasses the tool designed for the job; the exam's sanctioned fallback for a non-unique Edit is Read + Write, not shelling out to sed.
Handing the edit back to a human is burden-shifting — a documented distractor mold that pushes the problem onto the user when a reliable Read + Write fallback exists.

questions.stem: Meridian wires a semantic, index-backed code-search MCP server into Pathfinder so engineers can find behavior by meaning, not just literal strings. In production, Pathfinder keeps falling back to built-in Grep even for conceptual queries the semantic server handles far better. The MCP tool's description currently reads only "Searches the codebase." What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions; agents fall back to a familiar built-in when an MCP tool's description doesn't make its superior capability explicit. Enhancing the description to highlight the semantic advantage fixes the root cause. This is the fix-the-signal-before-adding-a-layer distinction.
ww: Disabling Grep breaks legitimate literal-content search; the root cause is an under-specified description, not the built-in tool's existence.

A blanket 'always prefer MCP tools' rule is blunt and keyword-sensitive, misrouting cases where the built-in genuinely is the right tool — it patches a symptom rather than fixing the description signal.
A pre-routing classifier adds an infrastructure layer to compensate for a bad signal; the exam's rule is to fix the tool description first before adding a routing layer (Key Distinction #10).

questions.stem: An engineer asks Pathfinder to split the shipping-integration layer out of the Java monolith into its own service — a change that touches dozens of files and forces decisions about service boundaries and shared data models. The engineer is tempted to let Pathfinder start editing immediately. Which execution approach should Pathfinder use?
questions.why: Large scope, architectural decisions, and changes across many files call for planning mode: Claude explores and designs with Read/Grep/Glob only, presents a plan before executing, and avoids expensive rework from premature execution.
ww: 'Start direct, switch to planning when it gets hard' is the exact reactive-switching trap the exam rejects — reactive switching is expensive; plan upfront when the task demands it.
Generating a whole architectural extraction in one pass is premature execution on an ill-defined design; it produces exactly the expensive rework planning mode exists to prevent.
Forcing the human to pre-decompose the architectural work is burden-shifting; the boundary decisions are precisely what planning mode is meant to explore and propose.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Pathfinder to generate a boilerplate carrier-integration adapter, described only in prose. After two iterations the generated adapter still shapes its output differently each time — one run nests the tracking fields, another flattens them, and timestamp formats vary. The engineer keeps re-describing the requirements in more detail. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: When natural-language descriptions of a transformation are interpreted inconsistently, 2-3 concrete input/output example pairs unambiguously show the expected format and decision logic, and the model generalizes the pattern — the fastest route to consistent shape.
ww: More prose adjectives leave the transformation ambiguous — the description is already failing, and adding text to a failing instruction doesn't fix inconsistent format.
Temperature controls randomness, not which specific output structure the model chooses; the inconsistency is an underspecified-format problem, not a sampling one.
A post-processing reshaper patches the symptom downstream instead of fixing the root cause (the ambiguous spec); examples fix generation itself.

questions.stem: Pathfinder's project CLAUDE.md has grown into a wall of rules. Engineers want the Java files to follow the billing team's exception conventions, the Python routing files to follow async patterns, and the co-located test files to follow one shared testing convention — but only when Pathfinder is actually working on files of that kind. The test files are scattered next to the code they cover. What configuration best applies the right conventions automatically?
questions.why: Conventions scoped to a file type or directory belong in `.claude/rules/` with glob patterns; the rules load automatically only when Claude works on matching paths, which handles co-located test files correctly regardless of directory.
ww: Root CLAUDE.md headings rely on model inference to decide which conventions apply, rather than deterministic file-path matching — the exam prefers glob-based rules for path-scoped conventions.
A CLAUDE.md per subdirectory doesn't work well when the relevant files (co-located tests) are spread across many directories; you'd have to duplicate the rule everywhere.
Universal, path-triggered conventions shouldn't require manual invocation each time; skills are for on-demand workflow guidance, not automatic path-scoped rules.

questions.stem: The team builds a `/audit-deps` skill that makes Pathfinder do a deep, verbose dependency and coverage scan. Engineers report that after running it mid-task, Pathfinder becomes less responsive and loses track of the original task they were working on, because the scan's large output floods the conversation. How should the skill be configured to fix this while keeping full analysis capability?
questions.why: When a skill generates large output or exploration context, `context: fork` runs it in an isolated subagent context so the output does not pollute the main conversation window, while full analysis capability is retained.
ww: A faster model doesn't fix context pollution — the verbose output still floods the main window and displaces the original task.
Compressing the scan to a short summary sacrifices the analysis capability the skill exists to provide; forking isolates the verbose work instead of discarding it.
Splitting into two skills doesn't prevent context leakage — each still dumps its output into the main session; isolation, not smaller chunks, is the fix.

questions.stem: An engineer resumes yesterday's named Pathfinder session that had mapped the entire routing service. Overnight, three files in that service were refactored by another team. The engineer wants to continue the investigation efficiently without trusting stale analysis. What is the best way to continue?
questions.why: If you resume after code modifications, tell the agent exactly which files changed so it performs targeted re-analysis of just those files, rather than trusting stale results or re-exploring the whole codebase.
ww: Resuming as-is makes the agent reason over stale tool results for the changed files — the exam's explicit wrong choice when files have changed.
Always starting from scratch is wasteful when most of the mapping is still valid; only three files changed, so a full re-analysis discards good context.
`/compact` compresses context and risks losing precise details, but does nothing to refresh the stale analysis of the three changed files — it addresses the wrong problem.

questions.stem: After Pathfinder completes an expensive analysis of the billing monolith, the team wants to evaluate two competing refactoring strategies — one that introduces a repository layer and one that keeps direct data access — both starting from that same completed analysis, without the two explorations contaminating each other. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: `fork_session` creates divergent branches that inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently — exactly the pattern for comparing two approaches from one shared, expensive analysis baseline without re-analyzing or cross-contaminating.
ww: Running both strategies sequentially in one session biases the second evaluation by the first's reasoning and conclusions — the two must stay independent.
Two brand-new sessions each must redo the shared baseline analysis, wasting the expensive work that forking would reuse.
Compacting between strategies still runs them in one lineage (so the second is contaminated by the first) and risks losing analysis precision — it solves neither independence nor reuse.

questions.stem: The team asks Pathfinder to add comprehensive test coverage to the legacy shipping-integration layer, whose full scope no one knows in advance — some modules have no tests, some have partial coverage, and hidden external-API dependencies keep surfacing as work proceeds. Which decomposition strategy should Pathfinder use?
questions.why: An open-ended task whose scope is unknown up front, where each step depends on prior discoveries and dependencies emerge during work, calls for dynamic adaptive decomposition: map structure first, prioritize high-impact areas, and adapt the plan as dependencies surface.
ww: A fixed pipeline with predetermined steps can't react to discoveries; the scope and hidden dependencies are unknown up front, so a fixed script breaks when reality deviates.
One giant single-pass prompt over everything causes attention dilution — deep on some modules, shallow on others — and is the documented anti-pattern for large multi-part work.
Reusing a fixed prompt-chaining template is right only for predictable, reproducible workflows; here the structure is unknown, so a fixed chain is the wrong pattern.

questions.stem: Pathfinder generates a batch of migration wrappers and, in its own reasoning trace, notes and then dismisses a possible edge case around null carrier IDs; the bug is only caught later when a human reviews the PR. The team wants to catch these self-dismissed issues automatically before human review. Which approach directly addresses the root cause?
questions.why: The self-check limitation is confirmation bias — the generating instance retains its reasoning and rationalizes its own choices. A second independent instance reviewing without the generator's reasoning context mirrors peer review and catches what the author dismissed.
ww: Extended thinking on the generation stage still runs in the same biased instance and does not fix the self-check limitation.
Self-review instructions keep the same instance and the same confirmation bias — it already 'considered' the case and dismissed it, so asking it to re-check itself repeats the failure.
More max_tokens gives room to write more code but does nothing about the biased self-assessment; the problem is who reviews, not output length.

questions.stem: As Pathfinder rolls out to the whole engineering org, long automation sessions start exhausting the context window. The culprit is a `get_build_status` MCP tool that returns 40+ fields per call — build logs, timestamps, runner metadata — when only the status, failing step, and commit hash matter, and every bloated result lingers in context for every later turn. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Verbose tool outputs consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance and persist across turns; a PostToolUse hook that filters results to the relevant fields before they accumulate conserves context and reduces noise at the source.
ww: Telling the model to 'ignore irrelevant fields' still consumes the tokens — the attention and context cost remains because the fields are already in context.
More aggressive conversation summarization treats the symptom; verbose tool results keep flooding in every turn, so the root cause is untouched.
A larger context window raises cost and merely delays the same problem — the noise and per-turn accumulation remain.

questions.stem: Across the org, Pathfinder reliably picks the right built-in tool for clear requests, but on genuinely ambiguous asks like "help me understand the recent purchase-order changes" it inconsistently chooses between the semantic MCP search and Grep. The team wants to raise selection accuracy on exactly these ambiguous cases. What few-shot strategy is most effective?
questions.why: Few-shot examples should target the specific ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — 4-6 examples aimed at those cases, each with rationale, rather than many examples of clear cases.
ww: 10-15 examples of clear, unambiguous requests don't address the ambiguous edge cases where misrouting actually occurs — the documented wrong move.
A single ambiguous example is too thin to cover the range of ambiguous phrasings; the exam calls for 4-6 targeted examples, not one.
Reverting to longer prose instructions is exactly what fails on ambiguous selection; examples, not more instruction text, give the model the concrete pattern.

questions.stem: Northwind's first CI job invokes `claude "Review the changed files in this PR for correctness issues"` inside a GitHub Actions step. The job never finishes; the Actions runner eventually times out at the 60-minute limit, and the step logs show Claude Code printed a prompt and then produced no further output. What is the correct way to run Claude Code in this pipeline?
questions.why: Without a non-interactive flag, Claude Code waits for interactive input and the pipeline hangs. `-p`/`--print` is the documented way to process a single prompt, print to stdout, and exit — exactly what a CI step needs.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is a fabricated environment variable; it does not exist and has no effect on Claude Code's interactivity. This is the canonical non-existent-feature trap for CI invocation.
`--batch` is not a real Claude Code CLI flag; batch processing is a Message Batches API concept, not a CLI switch, and would not fix an interactive-input hang. Fabricated flag.
Redirecting from `/dev/null` is an undocumented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned approach; the exam names `-p` as the correct mechanism and treats stdin tricks as a fragile substitute.

questions.stem: With `-p` working, Northwind's job pipes Claude's review into a script that must open one inline GitHub comment per finding, each carrying a file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix. Claude currently returns prose paragraphs, so the script parses them with brittle regex that breaks whenever wording shifts. What is the most reliable way to get machine-parseable findings?
questions.why: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` guarantees well-formed, schema-conformant output that downstream tooling can parse reliably — the sanctioned mechanism for structured CLI output feeding the GitHub API.
ww: A CLAUDE.md 'Output Format' section is guidance loaded into context, not an enforcement mechanism; compliance is inconsistent, so the parser still breaks. The corpus explicitly rejects this for structured CI output.
A prompt instruction to emit JSON has variable compliance — the model can still return prose preambles or markdown fences. Prompt-based JSON is the exact anti-pattern the schema flag removes.
A JSON-repair library treats the symptom (reconstructing structure after the fact) instead of removing the problem at the source; the schema flag makes repair unnecessary.

questions.stem: Northwind's findings are now structured, but developers say the suggested-fix field is uneven: some findings give a concrete diff-level change, others say only 'refactor the retry logic' or 'possible null issue.' The team already added the instruction 'always include a specific, concrete fix suggestion,' yet the output stays inconsistent. Which change most reliably produces consistently actionable fixes?
questions.why: When prose instructions produce inconsistent format, few-shot examples showing the exact required shape are the most effective fix — they give the model a concrete pattern to reproduce rather than more text to interpret.
ww: Adding more explicit instructions is the debunked move: the instruction is already failing, and more text does not resolve format inconsistency. Few-shot beats instruction-refinement here.
Temperature controls randomness, not adherence to a specific output structure; lowering it does not make the fix field consistently concrete. Wrong mechanism.
A post-processing rewrite patches the symptom downstream instead of fixing the generation; it cannot invent a concrete fix the model never reasoned about. Symptom-level fix.

questions.stem: Northwind's reviewer assigns a severity to each finding, but the prompt only says "rate severity appropriately." Analytics show the same class of issue—an unchecked null dereference—is labelled critical on one PR and medium on another, and developers say the levels feel arbitrary. What change most reliably makes severity ratings consistent across PRs?
questions.why: The root cause is an abstract instruction ("rate severity appropriately") that leaves the boundary between levels undefined, so identical issues land in different buckets. Replacing it with explicit, testable criteria for each level, each anchored by a concrete example, gives the model a consistent rubric to apply—moving from vague intent to concrete, example-backed definitions.
ww: Shifting every rating down one level applies a blanket strictness change that damages the accurate levels without fixing the underlying inconsistency; the same issue would still be rated differently across PRs, just uniformly lower.

Bolting self-reported confidence onto severity adds infrastructure without addressing the root cause; uncalibrated model self-confidence is unreliable and does not encode the missing criteria for what makes an issue critical versus medium.

A larger context window does not fix a definitional gap; severity is inconsistent because the levels are undefined, not because the model lacked room to see the PR, so a bigger model changes cost, not consistency.

questions.stem: Adoption analytics show Northwind's finding categories have very different reliability: correctness findings are dismissed 9% of the time, performance 19%, naming 51%, and documentation 47%. Developer comments say 'half of what it posts is noise, so I skim past all of it.' Trust in the accurate categories is now eroding too. Which approach best restores developer trust while the team improves the noisy categories?
questions.why: High-false-positive categories cause developers to dismiss everything, including accurate findings. Surgically disabling the noisy categories stops the trust bleed immediately while their prompts are fixed, preserving the value of the precise categories.
ww: Displaying confidence scores still surfaces all the noisy findings; developers keep seeing the noise and trust keeps eroding. It does not stop the bleed.
A uniform strictness reduction damages the already-precise correctness category unnecessarily while only partly reducing the noisy ones; the problem is category-specific, not global.
Adding few-shot examples across all categories is slow; trust continues to erode during the weeks it takes, and it wastes effort on categories that are already accurate.

questions.stem: As Northwind fixes the noisy categories, the team wants to learn which specific code constructs drive the naming false positives rather than guessing. Developers dismiss findings frequently but the team cannot aggregate why. What change most effectively lets them analyze which finding types are noise?
questions.why: A `detected_pattern` field labels which construct triggered each finding, so dismissals can be grouped by pattern to reveal which types drive false positives systematically instead of case by case.
ww: Capturing full reasoning logs bloats storage and still leaves the team reading prose per finding; it does not give the aggregate per-pattern dismissal signal.
Free-text dismissal reasons are unstructured and do not aggregate; the team cannot cleanly group them by pattern, which is exactly the analysis they need.
Classifying each dismissal with a second model adds cost and latency and still produces unstructured, non-aggregated labels; the structured field is the direct mechanism.

questions.stem: Northwind's CI also generates test cases for changed modules. On a PR adding shipment-status tracking, Claude proposes 11 tests, but reviewers note that 7 of them re-test scenarios the existing suite already covers. The generation prompt and CLAUDE.md are thorough. What change most effectively reduces duplicate test suggestions?
questions.why: Claude can only avoid duplicating tests it can see. Putting the existing test files in context gives it the coverage map, so it generates genuinely new scenarios.
questions.cite: Domain-3_v2 §3.8 (existing test files in context); Domain-4_v2 §4.18
ww: Instructing Claude to avoid existing coverage is useless when it has no visibility into what the suite already contains; the instruction cannot compensate for missing context.
Capping the count assumes the model orders tests by priority and that duplicates fall off the end; it may drop novel tests and keep duplicates. Wrong assumption.
Keyword matching is fragile and misses semantic duplicates worded differently while dropping distinct tests that happen to share names. Symptom-level and unreliable.

questions.stem: When an author pushes follow-up commits to a Northwind PR, the CI re-runs the review from scratch. Developers complain that each re-run re-posts near-duplicate comments on code that was already addressed, with slightly reworded findings piling up on the same lines. What is the most effective way to keep re-runs consistent and stop the duplicate flood?
questions.why: Including the prior findings in the re-run prompt and asking Claude to report only new or unresolved issues keeps the reviewer consistent across runs and prevents duplicate comments on unchanged code.
ww: After-the-fact text de-duplication is a fragile symptom patch that misses reworded duplicates and cannot tell a genuinely new issue from a reworded old one; feeding prior findings fixes the cause.
A blank-slate re-run re-litigates old findings and floods the PR with duplicates; the corpus explicitly rejects the 'objectivity' rationale for starting fresh each time.
Re-running only the latest-commit files can miss issues introduced by cross-file interactions and still re-posts duplicates within those files; it does not address run-to-run consistency.

questions.stem: Northwind wants to cut CI cost by moving analyses to the Message Batches API's 50% discount. Three workloads exist: a style check that blocks PR merge until it completes, a nightly test-generation job for changed modules, and a weekly full-codebase security audit. Which assignment correctly matches each workload to an API approach?
questions.why: Batch fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads: the nightly test generation and weekly audit both tolerate the up-to-24h window and gain 50% savings, while the merge-blocking style check must stay synchronous.
ww: Putting the blocking style check on Batch is wrong: developers wait on it to merge and Batch has no latency SLA (up to 24h), which is unacceptable for a blocking check.
Leaving nightly test generation synchronous forgoes an easy 50% saving on a scheduled, non-blocking job whose 24h window is perfectly acceptable.
Keeping all three synchronous captures none of the batch savings on the two workloads that clearly tolerate the window; off-peak scheduling does not reduce per-call cost.

questions.stem: Northwind batches the weekly security audit across 400 changed files. The batch returns with 388 files analyzed and 12 failed on context-limit errors because those files were unusually large. The team needs the results reconciled and the failures reprocessed with minimal cost. How should they handle the partial failure?
questions.why: `custom_id` identifies exactly which items failed; the fix is to modify the strategy for those items (chunk the oversized files) and re-submit only the failures, avoiding re-paying for the 388 successes.
ww: Batch results can arrive in any order, so matching by submission order silently mis-joins data; `custom_id` is the required join key.
Re-submitting all 400 pays again for 388 successes and can produce duplicate downstream results; selective re-submission by custom_id is the sanctioned approach.
Context-limit errors are not transient — the files are too large; re-submitting unchanged fails again. The cause (size) must be fixed via chunking before retry.

questions.stem: Northwind wants CI-invoked Claude to generate tests that match the team's fixture conventions, mock the shared HTTP client the same way every time, and use the project's assertion helpers — yet generated tests keep inventing their own fixtures and ad-hoc mocks. The pipeline invokes Claude with only the changed diff and a short prompt. What most reliably makes generated tests follow the team's conventions?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude durable project context — testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria — which improves generation quality and reduces low-value output across every run.
ww: A one-line prompt reminder cannot convey the team's actual fixture and mocking conventions; the model has no way to know the specifics, so it keeps improvising. Guidance without the concrete conventions in context.
max_tokens governs output length, not adherence to conventions; more room does not teach the model the project's patterns. Wrong mechanism.
Plan mode defers execution for architectural decisions; test generation for a scoped diff is routine, and planning does not inject the missing convention knowledge that CLAUDE.md provides.

questions.stem: Northwind wants a new CI job that adds comprehensive tests to a large legacy module with no existing coverage; the full scope is unknown up front, and each area's needs depend on what earlier exploration reveals (some sub-modules have hidden external-API dependencies). An engineer proposes a fixed pipeline: enumerate every file, then generate tests for each in a predetermined order. Which decomposition strategy fits this task?
questions.why: The scope is open-ended and each step depends on prior discoveries (e.g., hidden external-API dependencies), which is exactly when dynamic adaptive decomposition applies: map structure first, prioritize by risk, and adapt as dependencies emerge.
ww: A fixed pipeline suits predictable, fully-known structures; here the scope is unknown up front and a rigid script cannot react to discoveries like a newly-found API dependency. Wrong pattern for open-ended work.
A single giant pass over the whole module causes attention dilution — deep on some files, shallow on others — the anti-pattern for large multi-file work.
Running a fixed pipeline twice inherits the same rigidity and cannot adapt to discovered dependencies; it doubles work without adding adaptability.

questions.stem: A Northwind PR touches 16 files in the routing engine. A single review pass over all files at once gives deep feedback on a few files and shallow feedback on the rest, misses an obvious off-by-one bug, and flags a pattern in one file while approving the identical pattern in another. How should the team restructure the review?
questions.why: The inconsistency is attention dilution across many files at once. Per-file passes give each file full attention for local issues, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file problems — the sanctioned multi-pass structure for large PRs.
ww: Forcing developers to split the PR shifts the burden onto humans instead of fixing the review architecture, and does not address cross-file issues within a legitimately large change.
A bigger context window does not fix attention quality; more available tokens is not the same as consistent attention per token. This is the explicitly debunked 'bigger context' trap.
Consensus voting across two noisy full-PR runs suppresses real single-run findings and still inherits the diluted attention of each pass; it hides signal rather than improving depth.

questions.stem: In Northwind's review flow, the same Claude session that generates a suggested refactor is then asked, in that same conversation, to 'review your change carefully for bugs before finishing.' Subtle bugs the model reasoned about during generation still reach production — its self-review consistently reaffirms its original approach. What most directly addresses this self-check limitation?
questions.why: A model retains its generation reasoning and is anchored to its own decisions, so same-session self-review inherits the same blind spots. An independent instance with only the artifact and criteria evaluates the code on its merits and catches what the generator rationalized away.
ww: A stronger self-review instruction runs in the same instance with the same confirmation bias; it does not create independence.
More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny; extended thinking does not remove the generator's anchoring to its own choices.

A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context; the model re-reads its own justifications and confirms them. Same-conversation second pass is not independent review.

questions.stem: Northwind's CI reviewer reads Unix epoch timestamps from a `git_blame` tool, ISO 8601 dates from a `pr_metadata` tool, and numeric CI status codes (1=queued, 2=running, 3=passed) from a third-party build tool it cannot modify. The reviewer keeps misreading these mixed formats when it composes feedback. What is the most maintainable way to normalize the tool outputs?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook is deterministic code that fires after each tool returns, normalizing all outputs centrally regardless of which tool produced them — the maintainable single point of control, including for third-party tools you cannot modify.
ww: Documenting formats in the system prompt relies on the model interpreting mixed formats correctly every time — probabilistic, and it is already failing. Hooks are deterministic.
Modifying owned tools plus separate wrappers fragments the normalization logic across multiple places, which is exactly the maintenance problem the central hook avoids.
A `normalize_data` tool the model must remember to call adds an LLM call each time and relies on probabilistic compliance; the deterministic hook needs no model cooperation.

questions.stem: Ledgerline's extraction schema marks every field — including purchase_order_number and tax_id — as required and non-nullable, reasoning that downstream ERP posting needs a complete record. In a 5,000-invoice audit, 11% of outputs carry a plausible-looking PO number that appears nowhere in the source document; those invoices simply had no PO. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: A required, non-nullable field pressures the model to fabricate a value to satisfy the schema when the data is absent. Making the field nullable and non-required lets the model emit null instead of hallucinating — completeness by honest extraction, not by fabrication.
ww: Relying on a prompt instruction against fabrication is probabilistic; the schema constraint (required + non-nullable) still structurally demands a value, and the prompt cannot reliably override that pressure. The fix is the schema, not another instruction.
A downstream reconciliation job is a symptom-level patch that detects fabrications after they are produced rather than preventing them; the model is still forced to invent values at extraction time.

Temperature controls randomness, not the schema-driven pressure to fill a required field; the model fabricates because the contract demands a non-null value, and lowering temperature does not change that requirement.

questions.stem: Incoming documents are a mix of invoices, receipts, and PO confirmations, and the pipeline must ALWAYS hand the ERP schema-valid JSON — never a prose reply. The team defined three extraction tools (one per document type) but sometimes Claude answers a hard-to-classify scan with an explanatory paragraph instead of calling any tool. Which configuration guarantees a structured tool call every time?
questions.why: tool_choice {"type": "any"} guarantees the model will call some tool rather than return conversational text; with multiple extraction schemas it still picks the best-fitting one, so the output is always structured. That is the output guarantee the pipeline needs.
ww: tool_choice "auto" permits a plain-text response instead of a tool call, and a system-prompt instruction to "always return JSON" is probabilistic — exactly the prose-preamble failure being observed. "auto" gives no structure guarantee.

A JSON-repair library treats the symptom (fixing malformed prose after the fact) instead of removing the problem at the source; forcing a tool call eliminates the free-text response entirely rather than patching it.

Forcing extract_invoice specifically guarantees a tool call but the WRONG tool for receipts and PO confirmations — it would run invoice extraction on every document type. "any" lets the model choose the correct schema.

questions.stem: After moving extraction to tool_use with strict JSON schemas, Ledgerline's JSON parse failures dropped to zero.
