But the downstream ERP reconciliation still rejects about 3% of invoices because the extracted total does not equal the sum of the extracted line items. An engineer proposes tightening the schema further to "catch" the mismatches. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate the entire syntax-error class but do nothing for the semantic class — a response can be perfectly schema-valid and still state a total that doesn't match the line items. The remaining failures are semantic and require validation plus retry/self-correction, not a tighter schema.
ww: No JSON Schema constraint can express or verify that numbers sum correctly — arithmetic relationships are business-rule (semantic) checks that live in code (e.g., Pydantic validators), not in the schema shape.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the entire syntax-error class on top of the unchanged semantic class — strictly worse. tool_use is not the cause of the arithmetic mismatch.

A passing schema validator proves only structural validity, not content correctness; assuming the mismatches are all genuinely bad invoices ignores that extraction itself can pick up the wrong number — semantic errors sail through schema validation by definition.

questions.stem: The validate-then-retry loop resubmits a failed extraction with the document, the previous output, and the specific validation error. It works well for format and arithmetic errors. But on 40 documents, purchase_order_number keeps failing validation across all 3 retries; investigation shows those documents never contained a PO number at all. An engineer wants to raise max retries from 3 to 10. What should the team do instead?
questions.why: Retry-with-feedback only fixes errors the model can correct from the provided context (format, structure, arithmetic). When the information is genuinely absent from the source, no number of retries can extract what isn't there — the fix is schema design (nullable, accept null) not loop tuning.
ww: Absent information stays absent regardless of retry count; increasing retries from 3 to 10 burns tokens for nothing and, worse, the repeated pressure to fill a required field invites fabrication.
No feedback message can conjure data that is not in the document; a more forceful demand only increases fabrication pressure on a field that cannot be legitimately filled.

Keeping the field required "for data quality" guarantees fabricated values on documents that lack a PO; routing all 40 to humans mistreats a legitimate "not present" answer as a failure — null is the correct extraction, not a defect.

questions.stem: Weeks after posting, monthly reconciliation keeps surfacing invoices where the extracted total silently disagrees with the line items — sometimes the model grabbed a subtotal, sometimes the source invoice itself was internally inconsistent. The team wants to catch these at extraction time, not weeks later. What extraction design catches this?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern is structural: extract both the value as written (stated_total) and an independently re-derived value (calculated_total), plus a conflict_detected flag. This surfaces arithmetic drift as machine-readable data on every extraction and lets the pipeline route conflicts to review instead of silently trusting either number.
ww: "Be careful with totals" is a vague instruction with no detection mechanism — it cannot surface a mismatch as a signal the pipeline can act on, so silent disagreements still slip through.
Running reconciliation weekly still detects errors after posting rather than at extraction time; the self-correction pattern moves detection to the moment of extraction, which is the stated goal.

Self-correction here is not an optional conversational "are you sure?" follow-up — the exam pattern builds the re-derivation into the output schema so checking happens on every extraction and produces a machine-readable conflict signal.

questions.stem: Ledgerline's process_payment_hold tool rejects a hold because the invoice amount exceeds the client's per-invoice auto-hold policy limit. The extraction agent keeps re-calling the tool, treating the rejection like a transient outage, and burns retries. How should the tool's error handling be structured?
questions.why: A business-rule violation (policy limit exceeded) is not a tool failure — it is a valid answer that the action is disallowed. Structure it as retriable: false with a customer-friendly explanation so the agent stops retrying and communicates the policy outcome appropriately.
ww: A generic "Operation failed" leaves the agent unable to distinguish policy denial from a transient outage, so it retries or escalates incorrectly — the error category and its non-retryability must be explicit.
Marking a policy denial as a transient, retryable error wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change — re-invoking the tool cannot make a policy limit disappear.
Returning success with embedded error metadata masks the failure — the agent believes the hold succeeded when it did not, which is exactly the silent-failure anti-pattern.

questions.stem: Ledgerline needs to reprocess a 240,000-document monthly archive for a new client, with results due by 9 a.m. the next day — no human is waiting per-document. The team plans to use the Message Batches API for the 50% savings. Before committing all 240,000 documents, what is the most effective way to de-risk the run?
questions.why: Sample-first iteration validates the prompt/schema on a small synchronous sample for fast feedback, then submits the full batch only once the sample passes. This maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying (and waiting up to 24h) to discover a prompt defect replicated across all 240,000 requests.
ww: Submitting the full batch and iterating on the whole thing costs a full batch and up to 24h per iteration — a prompt defect is replicated across every request before it is caught. The point of the sample is to catch defects cheaply first.

Spreading submissions across the day does nothing to validate the prompt; it addresses scheduling, not the risk that a prompt defect ruins all 240,000 extractions. Sample-first is what de-risks the run.

custom_id joins results to inputs and identifies failures, but it cannot fix a systematic prompt defect — skipping sample validation means every document may fail the same way, and custom_id only tells you which (all of them).

questions.stem: One client's onboarding step runs extraction from a nightly CI job that shells out to the Claude Code CLI in --print mode, then posts the parsed fields to the client's ERP via an API call. The job intermittently breaks because the CLI sometimes returns a prose preamble around the JSON, so the parser chokes. What is the most reliable way to get downstream-parseable output?
questions.why: For the Claude Code CLI in print mode, --output-format json combined with --json-schema enforces the schema and guarantees well-formed output that downstream tools can parse reliably — the correct mechanism for structured CLI output feeding an API.
ww: A CLAUDE.md "Output Format" section is not guaranteed to produce consistent output — it is guidance the model may or may not follow, which is exactly the intermittent-preamble failure being seen.

A prompt instruction to return only JSON yields variable compliance; the CLI can still emit a preamble on some runs, so the parser keeps breaking. The flag-level enforcement is deterministic where the instruction is not.

A regex strip is a fragile post-hoc workaround that fails whenever the JSON itself is malformed or the preamble contains a brace; --json-schema removes the problem at the source instead of patching the symptom.

questions.stem: Ledgerline's extraction reports 97% overall accuracy on a labeled audit, and the team proposes auto-processing every high-confidence extraction with no human review. A skeptical lead notes that handwritten-receipt scans are a small fraction of volume. Before turning off review, what should the team do first?
questions.why: An aggregate 97% can hide a 40% failure rate on one rare document type — overall metrics average away segment-level failures. Before reducing human review, validate accuracy by document type and field, and add stratified random sampling so every segment independently meets the bar and novel error patterns are caught.
ww: Auto-processing on the aggregate threshold is exactly the masking trap: the 97% average conceals that the rare handwritten-receipt segment may fail 40% of the time, and those failures post as wrong payments.
Raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until calibrated against a labeled validation set; trusting it directly means the threshold itself may be miscalibrated per segment.

Auditing only low-confidence extractions leaves novel error patterns in the high-confidence automated path undetected — stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream is what measures the true error rate of automation.

questions.stem: To route extractions to human review, Ledgerline has the model emit a single 1–10 confidence score per document and reviews anything under 8. Reviewers report that many "high-confidence" extractions are still wrong on specific fields, while some flagged documents are perfectly fine. What is the most effective redesign of the confidence signal?
questions.why: The design should output confidence per extracted field (not one score per document) and calibrate the thresholds against a labeled validation set, because raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until calibrated against ground truth. This targets reviewer capacity at the specific fields that are actually uncertain.
ww: Raising the cutoff on an uncalibrated single document score does not fix miscalibration — it floods review with correct documents while still missing per-field errors hidden under a high document-level score.

Averaging two self-ratings from the same model does not calibrate confidence against ground truth; the model can be confidently wrong twice. Calibration requires a labeled validation set, not repeated self-assessment.
A flat unstratified 10% wastes reviewer capacity on easy segments and undersamples the problem fields; calibrated field-level routing directs oversight where accuracy is actually at risk.

questions.stem: Each lookup_vendor call in Ledgerline's enrichment step returns 40+ fields (full address history, tax registrations, contact log), but only vendor_id, name, and remit_to matter for extraction. On long multi-invoice sessions, the context fills with these fields turn after turn, and the model starts confusing remit-to addresses. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Verbose tool results consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance and stay in context every subsequent turn. A PostToolUse hook trims the result to only the relevant fields before it enters context, conserving the window and removing the noise that distracts the model.
ww: Instructing the model to ignore fields still leaves the tokens in context — the attention cost and clutter remain; only trimming before the result enters context actually removes them.

Aggressive whole-conversation summarization treats the symptom while verbose tool results keep flooding in every turn; the source of the bloat is the untrimmed tool output, which the hook fixes at the source.
A larger context window raises cost and still leaves the irrelevant fields distracting the model — the noise problem is not a capacity problem, and switching models does not remove the clutter.

questions.stem: Downstream auditors need every extracted figure traced to where it came from: the source document name, the page, and the extraction date. Currently the merge step that combines multi-page invoice data into one record flattens everything to prose, and a general "sources reviewed" note is appended at the end. Auditors can no longer tie a specific total back to a specific page. What is the correct fix?
questions.why: Source attribution is lost when findings are compressed without preserving claim-to-source mappings. Require structured claim-to-source mappings (document name, page/location, date) per field and require downstream steps to preserve and merge them, so the final record can attribute every figure.
ww: A general bibliography at the end means individual figures are no longer traceable to specific sources — the auditor still cannot tie a particular total to a particular page. Per-claim mappings, not a document-level list, are required.
Re-deriving attributions by re-searching sources at audit time is expensive and error-prone; the mapping should be preserved through the pipeline, not reconstructed after the fact.
Flattening to uniform prose is what destroyed traceability in the first place; tabular financial data becomes imprecise and harder to verify, and per-claim source links vanish.

questions.stem: Ledgerline is redesigning extraction as a multi-agent pipeline: a coordinator delegates classification, extraction, and validation to specialized subagents. The validation subagent needs the extraction subagent's output to check it, but currently it receives nothing and reports "no data to validate." What is the root cause and fix?
questions.why: Subagents have isolated context — they do not see the coordinator's conversation history or another subagent's output unless the coordinator explicitly includes it in the subagent's prompt. The fix is for the coordinator to pass the extraction results into the validation subagent's prompt.
ww: Direct inter-agent communication breaks the hub-and-spoke pattern — subagents never talk to each other directly; all inter-agent communication flows through the coordinator, which controls what each subagent sees.
A session_id does not exist; the API is stateless and there is no server-side retrieval of another agent's turn. Context is shared only by the coordinator explicitly passing it in the prompt.

Giving the validator its own extraction tool makes it re-extract rather than validate — it breaks separation of responsibilities and defeats the point of an independent validation step, which must check the extraction agent's actual output.

questions.stem: When a document extraction subagent hits a password-protected PDF it cannot open, it currently returns a bare "failed" status to the coordinator, which then can't decide whether to retry, skip, or route to manual handling. The team wants the coordinator to make intelligent recovery decisions. How should the subagent report the failure?
questions.why: A failing subagent must return structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — not a generic status or silence. The coordinator needs this to make an intelligent recovery decision (retry, reroute, continue with partial results, or escalate).
ww: A generic status forces the coordinator to guess; a password-protected PDF is a permanent error that will always fail, so uniform retrying wastes attempts. The category must be distinguishable so the coordinator does not retry an unrecoverable failure.

Catching the error and returning a successful-but-empty result silently masks the failure — the coordinator never learns the document needs handling, and a real gap is hidden as a success. Never catch and silently return success.
Terminating the entire workflow for one subagent failure is exactly what structured error propagation avoids; one unreadable file should not fail the whole batch.

questions.stem: A single client submits a bundled packet each night: an invoice, a matching receipt, and a delivery-confirmation report, all needing extraction plus a three-way match. The coordinator currently extracts them strictly one after another, and end-to-end latency has become the client's top complaint even though each extraction succeeds. The three documents are independent to extract. What most effectively reduces latency?
questions.why: Independent subtasks should be decomposed and run in parallel: multiple Task calls emitted in a single coordinator response execute concurrently, and the coordinator synthesizes once all return. This removes the serial latency without losing the shared-context match step.
ww: Swapping in a faster model shortens each step but keeps the serial structure — the three extractions still run one after another when they could run at once. Parallelizing independent work is the structural fix.

Cramming three documents into one prompt invites attention dilution across documents and mixes their fields; the exam favors decompose-and-parallelize for independent items, not a single overloaded pass.
Direct subagent-to-subagent handoff breaks hub-and-spoke — subagents never communicate directly; all results flow through the coordinator, which owns the three-way synthesis.

questions.stem: Compendium's coordinator, Halcyon, is being configured for a new client request: a cross-jurisdiction report on renewable-energy grid-storage policy. The current coordinator prompt reads like a script: "Step 1: query the EU, US, and Japan regulatory trackers. Step 2: open the first 10 filings from each. Step 3: summarize each filing in 150 words." QA shows the report is thin and misses a major policy shift that only became visible after the subagents' first pass. Which change to Halcyon's prompt is most effective?
questions.why: A rigid, numbered script locks the system into a fixed decision tree that cannot react when reality (a mid-research policy shift) deviates from the plan. Goal-oriented prompts that state research goals and quality criteria let subagents adapt their search strategy as findings emerge, which is exactly what a fixed script cannot do. This mirrors the agentic loop's model-driven decision-making applied at the orchestration level.
ww: Adding more procedural detail deepens the exact rigidity that caused the shallow, checklist-like output in the first place — it does not let the system adapt to what the subagents actually discover.
More subagents executing the same brittle script does not fix the script; it just runs the flawed procedure in parallel across more jurisdictions.
A self-check instruction added to the same coordinator instance does not address the underlying issue, since the prompt style itself — not oversight of the steps — is what constrains adaptability.

questions.stem: Halcyon delegates the grid-storage research and every subagent completes successfully: Scanline (web-search) finds relevant articles, Foliant (document-analysis) summarizes filings correctly, and Weftloom (synthesis) produces a coherent draft. The final report, however, covers only lithium-ion battery chemistry advances and says nothing about interconnection permitting, financing incentives, or utility procurement rules. Halcyon's logs show it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: "battery cost trends," "battery cycle-life research," and "battery recycling policy." What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: Every subagent performed correctly within the scope it was given — the problem is that the scope itself, set by the coordinator's decomposition, never included interconnection, financing, or procurement. When subagents execute correctly but the output covers the wrong ground entirely, the root cause traces to how the coordinator partitioned the research space before delegating, not to any individual subagent's execution quality.
ww: Weftloom cannot flag gaps for subtopics it was never given findings about — the subagents completed successfully because they were never asked about the missing areas, so there was no synthesis-level signal to surface.
Query wording is a subagent-execution concern; the corpus's exam pattern for this exact failure shape (all subagents correct, output wrong-domain) explicitly rules out query-quality as the cause.
Document filters would explain missing filings within an assigned subtopic, not the complete absence of three entire subtopics that were never assigned in the first place.

questions.stem: Compendium's final grid-storage report states "Battery storage deployment increased 28% year-over-year" with no source attached. Tracing the pipeline shows that Scanline and Foliant both returned their findings as long free-text paragraphs, which Halcyon concatenated and forwarded to Weftloom as one merged block. What is the most effective fix for the missing citations?
questions.why: The root cause is that content and metadata were merged into free text before ever reaching Weftloom — attribution was lost during aggregation because it was never captured in a form that survives concatenation. Structured formats that separate a claim from its source metadata preserve the claim-to-source mapping through the whole pipeline, so Weftloom can cite what it was actually given.
ww: Weftloom cannot cite metadata it never received in structured form — no prompt instruction can recover information that was never passed through in the first place.
Re-searching after the fact duplicates work and risks attaching a claim to the wrong source entirely, since Cartouche has no way to verify which source Scanline or Foliant actually used.
A blanket disclaimer does not restore claim-level attribution and undermines the credibility of every claim in the report, including ones that were properly sourced.

questions.stem: Scanline is now working against RegTrack, a third-party regulatory-filing index covering all three jurisdictions in the grid-storage project. Telemetry shows Scanline burns 6-8 tool calls per session issuing guessed `search_filings` queries just to figure out what filing categories even exist in RegTrack before it can search productively. RegTrack exposes a filing-category index as part of its MCP server. What is the most effective way to reduce this exploratory overhead?
questions.why: MCP resources are built for exactly this: exposing a content catalog that gives the agent an immediate map of available data without exploratory tool calls. Reading a resource costs no LLM round-trip the way a tool call does, and it stays current since it's requested on demand rather than baked into a prompt.
ww: A tool still requires an LLM call and relies on Scanline remembering to invoke it first — a resource provides the same map as readable context without either cost.
A static dump in the system prompt bloats every request with data most sessions won't need and goes stale as RegTrack's categories change, whereas a resource is requested on demand.
A prompt instruction is probabilistic — it depends on Scanline reliably remembering to check first, which is exactly the unreliable behavior the current telemetry shows.

questions.stem: Weftloom's first synthesis draft on the grid-storage report reads as coherent but Halcyon's own review catches that it never addresses financing-incentive mechanisms at all, even though Foliant separately logged several relevant filings on the topic earlier. What should Halcyon do next?
questions.why: Synthesis is not necessarily one-shot: the coordinator owns gap evaluation and loop termination as part of its aggregation-and-validation responsibility. The correct pattern is to evaluate the synthesis output for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries aimed specifically at what's missing, and re-invoke synthesis with the enriched findings — repeating until coverage is sufficient.
ww: A coverage-gap annotation is reserved for gaps that are unrecoverable after the refinement loop has run — here re-delegation is clearly available, since Foliant already logged the missing filings, so shipping with a caveat skips a step that would actually close the gap.
Re-running the identical prompt without a targeted query wastes a cycle; the refinement loop's value comes from aiming the re-delegation at the specific gap identified.
Giving Weftloom web-search access to self-serve the gap breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling — gap-filling research belongs to the research subagents, not synthesis.

questions.stem: Foliant is comparing two credible sources on grid-storage capacity growth: a national energy-ministry report states 34% year-over-year growth, while an independent grid-operator association study states 19% for the same period. Both documents pass Foliant's credibility checks and the discrepancy could change which policy recommendation the report ultimately makes. What should Foliant do?
questions.why: When processing genuinely conflicting credible sources, the agent should not resolve the conflict autonomously. It should complete the analysis while preserving both values with source attribution, explicitly annotate the discrepancy, and let the coordinator or a human reconcile it — a decision above the subagent's scope.
ww: Picking a value by heuristic (source type, recency, or otherwise) abandons a reconciliation decision that is above the subagent's scope and silently discards a credible data point.
Stopping the pipeline to ask before completing analysis blocks progress unnecessarily — the correct pattern is to finish the analysis with the conflict annotated, not halt on it.
Averaging fabricates a number neither source reported and discards the attribution both figures need — it manufactures false precision rather than preserving the actual conflicting evidence.

questions.stem: Compendium's finance team is worried that a poorly scoped research request could trigger a paid RegTrack API tier upgrade if Scanline's cumulative document-retrieval calls exceed 5,000 in a single project — an outcome the team wants blocked outright, not merely discouraged. Halcyon's system prompt currently says "avoid excessive retrieval calls; stay mindful of cost." Which change most reliably prevents the threshold from being crossed?
questions.why: Blocking an operation above a defined threshold is a textbook `PreToolUse` use case: it fires before the tool executes and enforces the block deterministically, regardless of what the LLM decides to do. This is the correct mechanism for safety- or cost-critical enforcement where a prompt instruction is not an acceptable guarantee.
ww: A prompt instruction, however explicit, is still probabilistic — the LLM may not reliably honor it, which is exactly the gap a hard block is meant to close.
A `PostToolUse` hook fires after the tool has already executed, so logging at call 5,000 only reports the threshold breach after it has already happened rather than preventing it.

Relying on the model's own reasoning to track and self-enforce a running count is probabilistic and unverifiable — the same category of unreliable self-governance the corpus repeatedly rejects in favor of deterministic gates.

questions.stem: Foliant's query against RegTrack for the Japan jurisdiction fails outright: the jurisdiction code the coordinator passed down, "JPN," doesn't match RegTrack's expected two-letter code "JP," so the query is rejected as malformed before it ever runs. Foliant currently returns only `{"status": "failed"}` to Halcyon, which then cannot tell whether retrying is worth attempting. What should Foliant's failure report include instead?
questions.why: A subagent failure must return structured error context — the failure type, what was attempted (the exact malformed code), and whether retrying makes sense — not a generic failure status. This is a permanent, non-transient error (a validation failure): retrying the identical query cannot succeed, so the payload should tell Halcyon that plainly so it can correct the code and re-issue, rather than wasting a retry cycle.
ww: A bare status flag gives Halcyon nothing to act on — it cannot distinguish a malformed-code problem from a timeout or an access failure without the structured detail of what was actually attempted.

A rejected malformed query never ran, so it is not a valid empty result — conflating a query that could not execute with one that executed and found nothing would tell Halcyon the wrong thing about Japan's actual filing activity.

This is a permanent error (a validation failure), not a transient one — retrying the identical malformed code will fail every time, so automatic retries only waste cycles instead of surfacing the fixable root cause.

questions.stem: Foliant's document-intake step must always begin by calling `extract_filing_metadata` before any deeper analysis tool runs, because downstream steps depend on knowing the filing's jurisdiction and date first. With `tool_choice` left at its default, Foliant sometimes skips straight to an analysis tool without extracting metadata first, about 12% of the time. What configuration most reliably guarantees the correct first step?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool on the first turn guarantees the required first step deterministically, then relaxing `tool_choice` afterward lets Foliant continue with the remaining analysis tools as needed. This forced-first-step pattern guarantees execution order exactly where a prompt instruction alone is only followed probabilistically.
ww: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees *some* tool call but not which one — Foliant could still call an analysis tool first and satisfy the constraint.
A stronger prompt instruction is still probabilistic; the 12% skip rate is exactly the kind of instruction-compliance gap that a forced tool_choice closes deterministically.
Forcing the same specific tool on every turn would prevent Foliant from ever calling the subsequent analysis tools it needs after metadata extraction is done.

questions.stem: Weftloom increasingly needs to verify individual facts (a filing date, a named agency, a cited percentage) while drafting synthesis text. Analysis shows 90% of these are simple, single-fact lookups and 10% require deeper cross-referencing across multiple filings. Currently every verification, simple or complex, routes back through Halcyon to Foliant and Scanline, adding a full extra loop each time. What is the most effective tool configuration for Weftloom?
questions.why: Strict role scoping has one sanctioned exception: a high-frequency need that would otherwise force constant round-trips through the coordinator. Giving Weftloom a narrowly scoped tool for the simple, high-frequency case while still routing the rare complex case through the coordinator applies least privilege without accepting the round-trip cost on 90% of Weftloom's needs.
ww: Full search access is cross-specialization misuse — Weftloom would start doing open-ended research instead of synthesizing, exactly the scope creep least-privilege tooling exists to prevent.
This preserves correct scoping in principle but ignores the round-trip overhead on a high-frequency need — which is exactly the situation the scoped cross-role tool exception exists to avoid.
Batching to the end is blocking: later drafting steps may depend on facts verified earlier, so deferring all verification until drafting is complete stalls the synthesis process itself.

questions.stem: Compendium's engineering team is scoping Scanline's tooling and discovers that a well-maintained community MCP server already exists for querying the U.S. Federal Register — the exact source Scanline needs for one jurisdiction. A team member proposes building a custom Federal Register MCP server from scratch instead, arguing it would give the team full control over the integration. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: For standard integrations that already have an existing, well-maintained community server, the effective choice is to adopt it rather than reinvent it. Custom server development is reserved for unique, team-specific workflows that no existing server covers — which the Federal Register clearly is not, since a community server already handles it.
ww: Building a custom server for a standard, already-served integration reinvents a maintained standard integration rather than investing engineering effort where it is actually needed.
Pre-committing to a rebuild regardless of whether the community server actually shows gaps repeats the same reinvention mistake on a delay, without evidence that a custom server is warranted.
Bypassing MCP entirely discards the standardized tool/resource interface the rest of Compendium's architecture relies on, and forces Scanline to handle raw API integration itself.

questions.stem: Weftloom's draft states: "A 2022 industry survey found grid-storage capacity growth of 11%, while a 2024 regulatory filing puts growth at 17% — a contradiction that undermines confidence in the trend." Both figures came from credible sources that Foliant tagged with different collection years, but Weftloom's output flags them as conflicting rather than as sequential data points. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Without dates, temporal differences get misinterpreted as contradictions. Requiring publication or collection dates in every structured output — and having synthesis reason about differing years as likely reflecting real change over time — prevents normal year-over-year growth from being falsely reported as a source conflict.
ww: This is the exact failure the corpus identifies: without publication dates, flagging every numeric disagreement as a conflict misreports normal temporal change as contradiction.
Blending figures from different time periods into one statistic manufactures a number that describes neither year accurately and destroys the very temporal signal that resolves the apparent conflict.
Discarding the earlier data point loses legitimate historical context and sidesteps the actual fix — the two figures were never really in conflict once dated correctly.

questions.stem: Halcyon hits a policy question it cannot resolve on its own: the client's research brief is silent on whether Compendium should include proprietary industry-consortium data behind a paywall, and getting it wrong could mean a licensing violation. Halcyon escalates to a human research director who has no access to the underlying agent conversation. What must the escalation payload include to avoid the director having to reconstruct context from scratch?
questions.why: The human agent does not have access to the conversation transcript, so a complete, self-contained structured handoff is everything they see. It must include the issue summary, the root cause of the escalation (here, the licensing policy gap), what has already been done, and a recommended action — otherwise the director has to re-ask for information Halcyon already has.
ww: A bare flag with no context forces the director to re-derive everything through follow-up questions, defeating the purpose of a self-contained handoff.
The human agent lacks transcript access by design, and dumping a raw transcript forces the director to re-read an entire multi-agent conversation instead of reviewing a concise, actionable summary.
Asking the director to re-run the subagents' queries duplicates work that has already been completed and slows resolution rather than transferring the existing findings.

questions.stem: Compendium wires a semantic, citation-aware filing-search MCP server into Foliant so it can find relevant passages by legal and regulatory meaning rather than exact keyword match. In production, Foliant keeps falling back to a generic `fetch_url` call to grab whole filing pages instead of using the semantic server, even on queries the semantic tool is built to handle far better. The MCP tool's description currently reads only "Searches filings and returns matches." What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions, and agents default to a familiar tool when a more capable one's description doesn't make its superior capability explicit. Enhancing the semantic tool's description to spell out its concrete advantages and unique outputs is the fix that addresses the actual root cause — an under-specified description.
ww: Removing `fetch_url` breaks legitimate cases where a generic fetch genuinely is the right tool, and does not address the actual root cause, which is the semantic tool's under-specified description.

A blunt "always prefer X" system-prompt rule is keyword-sensitive and can misroute the legitimate cases where `fetch_url` is actually the right choice, rather than fixing the signal the model uses to choose.

Tool selection is in fact driven primarily by tool descriptions, which is exactly why the current thin description causes the fallback — this option misstates the mechanism the corpus identifies as the primary lever.

questions.stem: Weftloom's input for the grid-storage synthesis totals 118K tokens: Scanline's raw web pages and full search reasoning make up 64K, Foliant's complete filing excerpts and analysis notes make up 54K. QA finds Weftloom's draft cites Scanline's opening search summary and Foliant's closing recommendations accurately, but omits a load-bearing interconnection-permitting finding that sat in the middle of Foliant's output. Recommended synthesis inputs top out near 45K tokens. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The root cause of missed middle-content is volume: full page content and reasoning traces from the subagents inflate the input far past what synthesis reliably attends to. Having Scanline and Foliant emit structured facts, quotes, and relevance scores instead of verbose raw content fixes the problem at its source, shrinking the input toward the ~45K range where lost-in-the-middle effects are minimized.
ww: An intermediate summarization agent adds latency and introduces a new point of failure — it treats the volume symptom downstream rather than fixing the verbose upstream outputs causing it.

Reordering which agent's output comes first does not fix the fundamental attention pattern — a finding still sitting in the middle of Foliant's own 54K-token block is just as likely to be missed regardless of which subagent's content leads.

Truncating to the first 20K tokens of each subagent's output risks discarding exactly the kind of load-bearing finding that happens to fall later in that subagent's own content, rather than addressing why the content is so verbose in the first place.

questions.stem: Fernbank's expense-reconciliation platform, Ostrakon, has an engineer, Priya, who personally built a `/recon-trace` slash command at `~/.claude/commands/recon-trace.md` to trace a transaction through the matching pipeline. The rest of the eight-person team likes it after watching her demo it and wants `/recon-trace` available automatically to everyone the moment they clone or pull the repo, with no per-developer setup. Where should the command file live to achieve this?
questions.why: Commands (and skills) placed under the project's `.claude/commands/` directory are checked into version control, so every teammate who clones or pulls the repo gets `/recon-trace` automatically with zero manual setup. This is the documented mechanism for project-wide, auto-available custom commands.
ww: This keeps the command in Priya's personal, non-version-controlled scope and pushes the distribution problem onto a manual wiki instruction — every new clone or pull still requires a manual copy step, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid.

`context: fork` controls whether a skill's execution runs in an isolated subagent context to protect the main session from pollution — it has nothing to do with where the file lives or whether teammates receive it automatically.

Converting the command to a skill under the personal `~/.claude/skills/` path doesn't fix the distribution problem — it is still a user-scoped location invisible to the rest of the team; the fix is the project-scoped directory, not the command-vs-skill format.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's team maintains a shared `/close-books` skill at `.claude/skills/close-books/SKILL.md` for the month-end reconciliation checklist. A new hire, Devon, clones the repo, then also copies a `close-books` skill folder from an old personal project into his own `~/.claude/skills/`, not realizing the name collides. When Devon runs `/close-books`, he gets different behavior than the rest of the team and can't figure out why, since his repo checkout is identical to everyone else's. What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: When a personal skill and a project skill share the same name, the personal skill takes precedence — this lets individuals customize without forking the team command, but it also means an accidental same-name personal skill silently shadows the shared one. Devon's leftover personal `close-books` skill is overriding the project's version for him specifically.
ww: Nothing in the scenario suggests the repo file is missing — Devon's checkout is stated to be identical to the team's, and the actual mechanism (personal-overrides-project on name collision) fully explains the symptom without needing to assume file corruption.

This states the precedence backwards — it is the personal skill that overrides the project skill on a name collision, not the other way around, and there is no caching or reinstall mechanism documented for this behavior.
This invents a version-dependent behavior that isn't documented anywhere in the corpus; the actual root cause is the same-name precedence rule, which applies regardless of Claude Code version.

questions.stem: A merchant-data vendor Ostrakon depends on just changed its category-code rules for the third time this quarter, and Priya is asked to have Claude Code build a re-categorization layer for multi-currency transactions before the next feed lands. She has never worked in this vendor's taxonomy before and worries she doesn't know what edge cases matter. Her first attempt at a prompt just describes the goal in one paragraph and asks Claude Code to implement it directly. Which approach is most effective for her next attempt?
questions.why: The interview pattern is designed for exactly this situation: an unfamiliar domain with non-obvious implications (conversion timing, unmapped codes, retroactive tagging) where the best choices depend on context Priya hasn't articulated yet. Having Claude Code ask clarifying questions up front surfaces these considerations before implementation, replacing several likely correction cycles with one interview turn.
ww: This is the reactive-iteration approach the interview pattern is meant to replace — generating first and fixing one missed requirement at a time is slower here precisely because Priya doesn't know the domain well enough to spot what's missing until it breaks.

This is the same underlying misconception the corpus calls out directly: adding more descriptive language to an already-ambiguous prose brief doesn't surface the domain-specific unknowns Priya doesn't know she's missing — only a clarifying dialogue does that.

Generating parallel alternatives doesn't help when the underlying requirements themselves are unclear — Priya would still be comparing three implementations against a spec she hasn't fully worked out, rather than gathering the missing requirements first.

questions.stem: Ostrakon has accumulated fourteen vendor-feed adapter modules over two years, several written by contractors long gone, and the team suspects heavy duplicated logic across them before committing to a consolidation plan. Priya asks Claude Code to survey all fourteen directly in her main working session; the resulting comparison — module-by-module notes and overlap candidates — grows so large the context window is nearly full before she can even discuss which adapters to merge first. What is the most effective way to complete the survey while preserving context for the consolidation design conversation?
questions.why: An Explore subagent isolates the verbose adapter-by-adapter comparison — the structure notes and overlap candidates across all fourteen modules — in its own subagent context, and returns only a concise summary to the main session. This preserves the main session's context window for the consolidation design conversation that follows, which is exactly the pattern needed when a broad survey threatens to fill the window before the real decision-making starts.
ww: `/compact` compresses context but risks losing exact details — which specific adapters overlap on which logic, exact module paths — that the consolidation design conversation needs precisely intact; it treats the symptom of a full window rather than isolating the verbose survey at the source.

Asking the same session to self-summarize periodically still runs the full verbose comparison in the main conversation before any summarization happens — the tokens are already spent by the time a summary is requested, and repeated summarization requests add overhead without isolating the underlying verbosity.

`--resume` continues a specific saved session — it doesn't parallelize the survey across adapters or isolate verbose output; manually merging per-adapter sessions also introduces coordination overhead and consistency risk that the Explore-subagent pattern avoids entirely.

questions.stem: After Claude Code finishes a full architectural analysis of Ostrakon's settlement-retry logic, Priya's team wants to evaluate two competing designs for making retries idempotent: one based on a client-generated idempotency key stored per request, the other based on a server-side dedup window keyed on transaction hash. Both designs should start from the same completed settlement-retry analysis, and the team wants to avoid paying for that expensive analysis twice or having the two evaluations bias each other. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: `fork_session` creates independent branches that both inherit context up to the branch point — here, the completed settlement-retry analysis — and then diverge. This lets the idempotency-key and dedup-window designs each be evaluated from the same expensive shared baseline without re-running the analysis twice and without either evaluation's reasoning contaminating the other.
ww: Evaluating both designs sequentially in one session means the second evaluation happens with the first design's reasoning and conclusions already in context — it is biased by whatever was just concluded about the first approach, which is the opposite of the independent comparison the team wants.

Two brand-new sessions would each have to redo the full settlement-retry analysis from scratch before getting to the design evaluation — exactly the duplicated, expensive work the team wants to avoid.

Resuming the same named session twice does not create two divergent, isolated branches — each resume continues the identical accumulating history, so the second design's evaluation would still see everything reasoned about the first design, not a clean independent perspective.

questions.stem: Fernbank's compliance team wants a nightly job where Claude Code reviews the day's reconciliation-engine commits and automatically opens a ticket in Ostrakon's internal tracker for every finding, with each ticket requiring a module path, line number, severity level, and a one-line remediation note as distinct fields the ticketing API expects. The team's first attempt just prompts Claude Code to "list findings in a clear, structured way," and the ticket-creation script frequently fails to parse the output into those four fields. Which approach is most effective?
questions.why: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` enforces schema-conformant output on every invocation, guaranteeing the module path, line number, severity, and remediation note arrive as distinct, reliably parseable fields — exactly what a downstream ticket-creation script needs to run unattended every night.
ww: A CLAUDE.md section describing the desired output shape is not enforced — it's guidance the model may or may not follow consistently, which is exactly the unreliable behavior the compliance team is already experiencing with prose-based instructions.

A more forgiving regex still depends on Claude's free-text output staying in a parseable shape run after run — this patches the symptom of unreliable parsing without fixing the underlying lack of a structural guarantee.

A prompt instruction naming the exact field order is still a probabilistic request, not a structural guarantee — variable compliance is the documented failure mode this exact scenario is built to catch.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's dev tools expose two MCP tools to Claude Code: `flag_ledger_entry`, for marking one transaction row as needing manual review, and `flag_reconciliation_run`, for marking an entire nightly batch as needing review. Both descriptions currently read only "Flags an item for review." Telemetry shows Claude Code calls `flag_ledger_entry` when a developer actually wants to flag the whole run about a third of the time, since both accept a numeric ID and the descriptions give no way to distinguish scope. How should this misrouting problem be fixed?
questions.why: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses for tool selection, and here both tools are effectively indistinguishable to the model. Expanding each description to state what its ID refers to, with example inputs and explicit scope boundaries, fixes misrouting at its root rather than adding infrastructure around an unclear signal.
ww: Merging into a single tool with a `scope` parameter loses the semantic precision that made two distinct, well-described tools useful in the first place — the corpus explicitly rejects consolidation as the fix for a description-ambiguity problem.

A pre-routing classifier adds new infrastructure to compensate for an ambiguous signal instead of fixing the signal itself — the root cause is the underspecified descriptions, and a classifier layered on top doesn't address that.

A system-prompt instruction to "double-check scope" is a probabilistic nudge riding on top of the same ambiguous descriptions — it doesn't give the model any new information to actually distinguish the two tools, so the misrouting is likely to persist.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's reconciliation matcher occasionally leaves a one-cent residual unmatched when a refund is split across two partial settlements in different currencies, because the rounding happens in a different order than the original charge used. Priya has described the bug to Claude Code twice in prose ("make sure split-currency refunds round the same way the original charge did"), and each attempt fixes the specific split ratio she mentioned but leaves other split ratios still off by a cent. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: A concrete failing test with a specific split-refund example and exact expected per-leg amounts gives Claude Code an objective, machine-checkable definition of correct rounding behavior, and iterating against that test's pass/fail signal is targeted rather than guesswork — this is the fastest documented way to converge on a fix for an arithmetic edge case like this one.
ww: This is exactly the failure mode already occurring — restating the requirement more emphatically in prose has already produced two rounds of partial fixes tied to one split ratio, because prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently run to run.

Asking the same instance to confirm its own fix is complete relies on the same reasoning that already produced two incomplete fixes reviewing itself — it isn't grounded in an objective, external check like a concrete test case.

Rolling back and deferring the fix doesn't resolve the rounding bug at all — it avoids the problem rather than converging on a correct fix, and abandons a currently-shipped matcher with a known off-by-a-cent defect.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's architecture channel has hosted a running design discussion for eleven weeks about how the ledger should represent multi-currency balances, with the conversation history now well past 90,000 tokens across many sessions. A new engineer asks Claude, "Why did we settle on storing balances in minor units instead of decimal, again?" — a decision made and justified in detail back in week 3, buried among many later, unrelated tangents. What is the most effective way to answer this kind of question reliably?
questions.why: For recalling one specific past exchange out of many months of accumulated discussion, semantic retrieval over the full history is the pattern that finds and surfaces the exact relevant exchange on demand — here, the week-3 minor-units justification — rather than depending on where it happens to sit in a compressed or windowed representation.
ww: A rolling window keeping only recent sessions verbatim discards the week-3 exchange entirely — it is exactly the kind of buried early-history detail a rolling window is documented to lose.
Progressive summarization compresses specific justifications like "why minor units over decimal" into vague abstractions, losing exactly the precise reasoning the new engineer is asking to recall.

Manually tagging every concluded decision doesn't solve retrieval at this scale — it depends on remembering to tag consistently across eleven weeks and many sessions, and doesn't address the fundamental problem of finding one exchange among tens of thousands of tokens.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's project CLAUDE.md already states universal rules the whole team follows on every task — for example, "all monetary values are integers in minor units, never floats." The team also runs a quarterly-close procedure: a specific multi-step checklist (freeze the ledger, reconcile outstanding batches, generate the compliance export, notify finance) that only applies during the close window, a few days per quarter, and nobody wants that checklist loaded into every session's context the rest of the year. Which restructuring approach is most effective?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md content loads into every session, so it's the right home for a rule that must always apply, like the minor-units convention. The quarterly-close checklist is workflow-specific and rarely needed, so it belongs in a Skill that's invoked on demand — keeping it out of the context budget for the other 360-odd days of the year while still being one command away when the close window opens.
ww: `.claude/rules/` is path-scoped, triggered by which files Claude is currently working on — it isn't designed for a workflow-scoped, occasion-based procedure like a quarterly close, which isn't tied to any particular file glob but to a calendar event.

Leaving the rarely-needed, multi-step close checklist permanently in CLAUDE.md means it loads into every single session all year, wasting context on guidance that's relevant only a few days per quarter — the whole point of separating universal standards from workflow-specific guidance is to avoid this.

Moving the universal minor-units rule into a Skill means it now requires an explicit `/command` invocation to take effect — but it's meant to apply on every task, so demoting it from always-loaded CLAUDE.md content to on-demand Skill content would let engineers forget to invoke it and violate the convention.

questions.stem: Ostrakon is splitting into three packages (`ledger-core`, `recon-engine`, `finance-export`), each with its own maintainers and coding standards file. The root CLAUDE.md currently pastes the full text of all three standards documents inline, so every engineer's session loads all three regardless of which package they're touching. The `finance-export` maintainers want their package's CLAUDE.md to pull in only their own standards file, not the other two, while still keeping that content in the context Claude sees. Which approach best achieves this?
questions.why: The `@path` import syntax lets a CLAUDE.md reference an external file so its content is pulled into context without needing to paste it inline — `finance-export`'s CLAUDE.md can import just its own standards file (relative paths resolve relative to the importing file), leaving `ledger-core` and `recon-engine` engineers' sessions free of content irrelevant to them, while the imported content still becomes part of the concatenated context Claude sees.
ww: `.claude/rules/` triggers on which file paths Claude is actively editing, not on which package's CLAUDE.md is loaded — it solves a different problem (path-scoped conditional loading) than selectively importing one package's own standards file into its own configuration.

This is true that discovered CLAUDE.md files concatenate rather than override each other, but it wrongly concludes there's no way to control what content goes into a given package's own CLAUDE.md file in the first place — `@import` exists precisely to let each file selectively pull in only the external content relevant to it.

Converting always-applicable coding standards into a Skill requiring explicit invocation risks maintainers forgetting to invoke it, and it doesn't solve the stated goal — the team wants the standards to remain part of what Claude always sees for that package, just without every package loading every other package's standards.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's automated code-review pass for reconciliation-matcher changes is instructed to "flag risky changes to the matching logic." Reviewing three recent PRs, the same class of change — widening a currency-comparison tolerance from 0.001 to 0.01 — is flagged as high severity in one PR and left uncommented in another, with no clear pattern to which PR gets flagged. Which change most reliably makes the flagging consistent?
questions.why: "Risky" is an abstract judgment call that the model can reasonably interpret differently across otherwise-similar changes. Replacing it with explicit, testable criteria — naming the exact construct (tolerance/threshold/rounding constants) and what to report about it — removes the ambiguity that's producing inconsistent flagging, moving the instruction from abstract to concrete.
ww: A same-conversation double-check doesn't introduce any new information about what "risky" means — it just asks the same reasoning that already produced the inconsistency to evaluate itself again, which doesn't fix an underspecified criterion.

Temperature controls output randomness broadly; it doesn't resolve a genuine ambiguity in what counts as "risky" — the inconsistency here comes from an underspecified concept, not from stochastic sampling variance.

Restating the same vague word ("consistently apply the risk criteria") without ever defining what the criteria actually are doesn't give the model any new concrete signal — it's the abstract-instruction problem repeated, not resolved.

questions.stem: A review of Ostrakon's settlement module turns up three issues in one function at once: a race condition in how the retry lock is acquired, a backoff calculation that assumes the old locking behavior and will misbehave once the lock logic changes, and an unrelated log message with a typo. Priya is deciding how to hand these findings to Claude Code for fixing. Which approach is most effective?
questions.why: The lock fix and the backoff fix interact — the backoff logic's correctness depends on the new locking design, so fixing them separately risks the backoff patch conflicting with or assuming stale details about the lock. Presenting the two interacting issues together lets Claude Code design one coherent change; the independent typo can be handled either way without affecting the others.
ww: Splitting the interacting lock and backoff fixes into strictly sequential, separate messages is the documented failure case: the backoff fix produced without full knowledge of the new locking design can contradict or misalign with it, forcing another round of correction.

Deferring the interacting backoff fix to a separate future sprint, after the lock change has already shipped independently, doesn't prevent the interaction problem — it just delays discovering that the backoff logic needs to account for the new lock behavior, and ships an interim state where the two are already out of sync.

Sequencing the typo before the two genuinely interacting fixes doesn't address the core problem — the lock and backoff issues still need to be reasoned about together as one coherent change; an arbitrary fix order doesn't substitute for presenting the interdependent pair jointly.

questions.stem: Claude Code fixes a flaky integration test in Ostrakon's settlement-retry suite by loosening an assertion that compared exact retry counts to a range check instead. In its own reasoning it considers whether this masks a real timing bug, and concludes the range check is safe because retries are inherently variable. The change ships; weeks later, an incident review finds the range check was hiding a real race condition that occasionally double-submits a settlement. Which approach most directly addresses this self-check limitation?
questions.why: The same instance that generated the fix retains its own reasoning context and is anchored to the conclusion it already reached — that the range check is safe. A second, independent instance that never sees that justification evaluates the change fresh, without inheriting the same rationalization, which is what's needed to catch a masked bug the generator talked itself into accepting.
ww: Asking the same conversation to re-examine its own reasoning still carries the full generation context, including the justification it already accepted — it tends to re-confirm its prior conclusion rather than challenge it, which is exactly the same-session self-check limitation, not independent review.

Extended thinking makes the same anchored instance reason more, but it's still the same instance reaching for the same justification it already found convincing — more reasoning by an anchored instance isn't equivalent to independent scrutiny.

A self-review instruction added to the generation prompt still runs inside the same session and reasoning trail that already concluded the range check was fine — it's the same confirmation-bias risk, not a genuinely independent second look.

questions.stem: Ostrakon's team is migrating the settlement module off a deprecated retry library across roughly 70 call sites, a multi-day effort involving many Claude Code tool calls to locate, evaluate, and update each site. Midway through day two, Priya's laptop restarts unexpectedly and the session is lost. She doesn't want to re-discover which call sites were already migrated and which weren't, and wants to resume efficiently from wherever the work actually stood. What is the most effective way to design the migration so it survives an interruption like this?
questions.why: Writing intermediate state and key findings to a scratchpad file — which call sites are migrated, which remain, and what's been learned along the way — lets the task survive an interruption like a crash. Reading from the scratchpad at the start of each continuation picks up exactly where the work stood, without holding all of it in a single context window that could be lost.
ww: `/compact` operates on the conversation's context within a still-running session — it doesn't help once the session itself has crashed and its context is gone; it's also documented as risking loss of exact details like which specific call sites were completed.

The API is stateless and a crashed session's context is gone — keeping migration progress only in the conversation history means the laptop restart wipes out the record of what was already done, which is exactly the failure mode a scratchpad file is meant to prevent.

Restarting from call site one after every interruption wastes the substantial work already completed and risks re-applying changes to sites already migrated — the scratchpad exists precisely so completed work doesn't need to be re-verified from scratch.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight's engineering team runs its CI review pipeline, internally named Vanguard, as a scheduled stage in their freight-routing monorepo's build system: `claude "Review the changed files in this build for correctness issues"` is invoked as a build step rather than a one-off script. Over two weeks, the runner pool backing this stage slowly saturates — queue depth climbs from 2 to 40 pending jobs — because each Vanguard invocation never exits on its own; operators have to manually kill the process after it sits idle. What is the correct way to run Claude Code so this pipeline stage completes and releases its runner?
questions.why: Without `-p`/`--print`, Claude Code runs in its interactive mode and waits for further input that a CI runner will never provide, which is exactly why the process sits idle until an operator kills it and the runner pool backs up. The `-p` flag processes the given prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits cleanly — the documented mechanism for running Claude Code non-interactively in any automated pipeline, scheduled or triggered.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is not a real Claude Code environment variable or flag; it sounds plausible but does not exist, so setting it changes nothing about the hang.
`--batch` is not a Claude Code CLI flag — that name describes the separate Message Batches API, not a CLI execution mode, and passing it would simply be an unrecognized argument.

Redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` is a Unix workaround some teams stumble onto, not the documented approach, and it does not reliably replace `-p` across environments or guarantee clean stdout capture.

questions.stem: With `-p` now fixed, Vanguard runs three independent analyses on every PR to the freight-routing monorepo: a style check, a security scan, and a performance review. The pipeline currently invokes Claude Code three times in sequence within one orchestrating session — style, then security, then performance — and the stage now takes 9 minutes end to end even though none of the three analyses depends on another's output. Engineers want to cut wall-clock time without losing any of the three analyses. What is the most effective architectural change?
questions.why: Style, security, and performance review are independent subtasks with no data dependency between them, which is exactly the profile for parallel execution: multiple `Task` calls issued in a single coordinator response run concurrently, and the coordinator aggregates once all three finish. This cuts the 9-minute sequential wall-clock to roughly the duration of the slowest single analysis instead of the sum of all three.
ww: Combining three distinct analytical lenses into one pass reintroduces the attention-dilution problem the corpus warns about — a single pass covering multiple concerns at once tends to go shallow on some dimensions, not faster and equally thorough on all three.

This PR-blocking check is exactly the latency-sensitive, developer-waiting workload the corpus says must stay synchronous — moving it to Batch trades a 9-minute wait for a process with no latency SLA (up to 24 hours), which is worse, not better, for a blocking pre-merge stage.

Trimming the diff addresses token volume, not the root cause of the 9-minute total, which is that three independent calls are being forced to run one after another instead of concurrently — smaller inputs per call would not eliminate the sequential wait.

questions.stem: Vanguard's security-scan analysis includes a cross-service consistency check: it compares the retry-and-backoff logic across Solstice Freight's five microservices (dispatch, tracking, billing, notifications, and routing) to flag services whose retry budgets have silently diverged from the others. On PRs touching two or more of these services, the check frequently misidentifies which service is the outlier, sometimes flagging the one service that actually matches the majority pattern. The comparison genuinely requires reasoning through five services' worth of retry-budget values before concluding which ones diverge. What change would most reliably improve accuracy on this specific check?
questions.why: Comparing retry-budget logic across five services is a multi-stage comparison task — exactly the class of problem where an explicit step-by-step reasoning cue measurably improves accuracy, because it forces the model to enumerate and hold each service's value before judging divergence rather than pattern-matching to an answer. This is a targeted, low-cost fix for a task that inherently requires multi-step comparison across N items.
ww: Splitting into five isolated single-service prompts removes the very information the check needs — comparison across services requires seeing all five values together; a later manual merge step also reintroduces the human bottleneck the automated check was meant to remove.

Temperature controls response randomness/creativity, not reasoning depth on a structured multi-step comparison — this is the same category of non-fix as adjusting temperature to suppress a specific unwanted phrase.

More emphatic wording about the stakes of the comparison does not give the model a mechanism for holding five values in mind and comparing them systematically — instruction intensity is not a substitute for a reasoning-cue technique matched to the task's structure.

questions.stem: Vanguard's root CLAUDE.md has grown to cover universal style conventions that apply to every PR, plus a rarely-invoked deploy-hotfix procedure (used a few times a year during incident response) and a database-migration rollback checklist (used only when a migration needs reverting). Every Vanguard invocation loads the full file, and engineers report the hotfix and rollback sections add noticeable irrelevant context to routine style-and-security PR reviews. Which restructuring most effectively keeps universal conventions always available while loading the rare procedures only when actually needed?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md content loads in every session, so it is the right home for content that truly applies always — the universal style conventions. Workflow-specific guidance that's only relevant when performing a specific task (deploy hotfixes, migration rollbacks) belongs in Skills, which load on demand via slash-command invocation rather than bloating every routine review with rarely-needed procedure text.
ww: `.claude/rules/` is path-scoped (loaded when working on files matching a glob), not workflow-scoped — deploy-hotfix and rollback procedures aren't tied to a particular file path, they're tied to which task an engineer is doing, which is what Skills are for, not rules.

Better visual formatting doesn't stop the full file — hotfix and rollback text included — from loading into every single Vanguard invocation's context; the token cost and irrelevant-content problem persists regardless of how readable the file looks to a human.

Moving the universal conventions into a Skill means they would only load when explicitly invoked, but universal standards need to apply to every session automatically — exactly the opposite of what CLAUDE.md's always-loaded behavior is for.

questions.stem: Vanguard's finding-reporting tool defines its own hand-written JSON schema for structured findings (file, line, severity, description, suggested_fix), and a separate internal validation script checks incoming findings against a second, independently maintained set of field definitions. Twice in the last quarter, someone updated one definition (adding a `detected_pattern` field) without updating the other, and findings silently failed validation in production until the mismatch was traced. What change most directly prevents this class of drift going forward?
questions.why: The root cause is that two independently hand-maintained definitions of the same structure will drift apart over time, no matter how careful anyone is. Generating both the tool's input schema and the code-side validator from one Pydantic model makes drift structurally impossible — there is only one source of truth, and both consumers derive from it rather than being kept in sync by hand.
ww: A checklist reminder is a process patch for what is fundamentally an architecture problem — it depends on every future editor remembering and correctly executing a manual step, which is exactly the failure mode that already happened twice.

Retrying doesn't address a definitional mismatch between two schemas — if the validator's field list genuinely differs from the tool's output shape, retrying the same request produces the same failure every time; this isn't a transient error.

Removing code-level validation eliminates defense-in-depth entirely — the corpus is explicit that programmatic validation should still check semantic/business rules and guard downstream consumers even when tool_use enforces shape at generation time; the fix is unifying the source of truth, not dropping one of the two checks.

questions.stem: Vanguard calls a `get_pr_diff` tool at the start of every review to fetch the changed files. The tool returns 50+ fields per invocation — full commit metadata, author history, CI runner IDs, branch protection settings — when only the file path, diff hunk, and change type matter for the actual review. On PRs that touch many files, engineers notice review quality degrading partway through as the accumulated tool output crowds the context, and Vanguard's later comments start referencing the wrong file. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The problem is that irrelevant fields consume context tokens and attention regardless of whether the model is told to ignore them — a `PostToolUse` hook trims the tool's raw output down to only the fields the review actually needs before it ever enters the conversation, conserving context and removing the noise at its source rather than asking the model to mentally filter it out turn after turn.
ww: Telling the model to ignore fields in the system prompt doesn't reduce token consumption — the 50+ fields are still present in context on every subsequent turn, and the attention cost of the clutter remains even if the model tries to comply.
More aggressive summarization treats the symptom, not the source — the verbose tool results keep flooding in on every new `get_pr_diff` call regardless of how hard earlier output gets compressed.

A bigger context window increases cost and still leaves the underlying noise problem intact — the fix the corpus prescribes is trimming irrelevant fields at the tool-output layer, not paying for more room to hold clutter.

questions.stem: Vanguard's review currently uses one prompt that asks Claude to both identify issues in the diff and immediately propose a fix for each one in the same response. Reviewers notice that on PRs with several interacting issues, the proposed fixes are sometimes shallow or miss an issue's downstream implications, as if fix-generation is being rushed alongside issue-identification. An engineer wants Claude to reason more thoroughly about each fix without changing what issues get flagged. What is the most effective restructuring?
questions.why: Splitting identify-issues and generate-fixes into two sequential, focused prompts — where the first stage's output feeds the second — is prompt chaining: each stage gets Claude's full attention on one well-defined job instead of splitting effort across identification and fix-generation simultaneously. This produces more focused, consistent output at each stage than asking for both at once.
ww: A vague instruction to "think more carefully" doesn't restructure how the work is decomposed — it asks the same single-pass prompt to somehow do a better job at two competing objectives at once, without giving it a mechanism to actually separate them.

Capping the number of flagged issues to buy more effort per fix trades completeness for depth rather than fixing the actual problem, which is that identification and fix-generation are competing for attention within one response — chaining removes that competition without discarding any valid finding.

Generating three candidates per issue multiplies token cost and reintroduces a human bottleneck of picking among options for every single finding — it doesn't address why the single combined pass produces shallow fixes in the first place.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight assigns Vanguard a new initiative: backfill test coverage for the legacy webhook-retry module, which has no owner and no documentation. Nobody knows up front how many retry paths exist, which ones are already covered, or whether the module depends on anything external. An engineer proposes a fixed pipeline: enumerate every function in the module first, then generate a test for each one in file order. Partway through, Vanguard discovers the module silently depends on an internal rate-limiter service that must be mocked before several of the retry paths can be tested at all. Which decomposition strategy best fits this task from the outset?
questions.why: This task's full scope is unknown up front, and dependencies (the rate-limiter) surface only as work proceeds — exactly the profile for dynamic adaptive decomposition rather than a fixed script. Mapping structure first, prioritizing by risk, and adapting the plan as new dependencies are discovered lets Vanguard react to what it actually finds instead of executing a predetermined order that cannot account for a dependency nobody knew about at the start.
ww: A fixed pipeline assumes the steps are known and stable in advance — this module's scope and dependencies were explicitly unknown until work was underway, which is exactly the situation the corpus says breaks a predetermined script; enumeration order also doesn't guarantee coverage if the rate-limiter dependency blocks entire retry paths that weren't anticipated.

A single giant pass covering the whole module reintroduces attention dilution across many functions at once rather than adapting the plan as discoveries emerge — it also doesn't help identify the rate-limiter dependency any faster than a structured mapping step would.

You cannot know a specific dependency needs mocking before discovering it exists — the rate-limiter dependency was found only partway through the work, so requiring its mock as a fixed first step is not something the team could have specified up front; this still tries to force an unknown-scope task into a predetermined sequence.

questions.stem: Weeks after the webhook-retry test backfill merges, a race condition surfaces in production: two retry attempts fire concurrently under load and double-post the same webhook. The original Claude Code session that wrote the retry-and-lock fix, still open, is asked in that same conversation to "double-check your fix for any thread-safety issues before we close this out" — it re-examines its own change and reports the locking approach is sound. A human reviewer, looking at the diff cold days later, spots the race immediately. What most directly addresses why the same-session check missed it?
questions.why: A session that generated the locking logic retains the reasoning that convinced it the approach was safe, and re-checking within that same context tends to reaffirm the original decision rather than genuinely question it. Sending the diff to a second, independent instance that never saw the first session's justification removes that anchoring — it evaluates the code on its own merits, the same way a human reviewer coming in cold caught the race immediately.
ww: Extended thinking gives the same anchored instance more reasoning steps, but it is still the same instance carrying the same justification for why the lock is correct — more reasoning by an anchored reviewer is not equivalent to independent scrutiny.
