A more specific instruction to look for race conditions still runs inside the same context that already convinced itself the locking was safe — strengthening the ask doesn't remove the anchoring effect that caused the original miss.

A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context — the model re-reads its own justification for the lock and confirms it again; genuine independence requires a separate request without that reasoning history, not a relabeled follow-up message in the same session.

questions.stem: Vanguard has recently added two new finding categories beyond its original correctness and style checks: `dependency-upgrade-risk` (flagging PRs that bump a dependency with known breaking changes) and `test-coverage-gap` (flagging changed code with no corresponding new test). Three months of dismissal data show `dependency-upgrade-risk` findings are dismissed 61% of the time and `test-coverage-gap` findings 55% of the time, while the original correctness findings are dismissed only 6% and style findings 22%. Developers report they've started skimming past dependency and coverage findings entirely, and now catch themselves skimming past correctness findings too out of habit. Which approach best restores trust while the two new categories are improved?
questions.why: The two new high-dismissal categories are actively bleeding trust into the well-performing correctness and style categories — developers have started skimming past everything, including findings that are usually right. Temporarily disabling just the noisy categories stops that bleed immediately while leaving the two reliable categories active and useful, buying time to fix the new categories' prompts without their noise contaminating trust in the whole system.
ww: Showing a confidence score still surfaces every noisy finding to developers — the two problem categories keep flooding the review with high-dismissal noise, and trust continues eroding while developers wait for a number they may not trust either.

A uniform strictness cut damages the two already-reliable categories (6% and 22% dismissal) to compensate for problems that are isolated to the two new categories — it punishes the accurate findings instead of surgically addressing the noisy ones.

Few-shot refinement is a reasonable long-term fix for the two new categories' prompts, but it takes weeks to show results while the noise keeps flowing to developers in the meantime — trust keeps eroding during that window instead of being stopped immediately.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight's five microservices share a near-identical pattern for validating incoming webhook payloads, copy-pasted years ago with minor variations. When a PR fixes a payload-validation bug in the dispatch service, Vanguard's review — running per-service as each one gets touched over the following days — independently proposes the exact same fix again on tracking, then again on billing, even though the team already applied and merged the dispatch fix using the identical approach across services deliberately. Developers say re-reviewing the same already-known fix three more times wastes time. What is the most effective way to stop Vanguard from re-suggesting a fix that has already been applied elsewhere?
questions.why: Vanguard can only avoid re-proposing an already-applied fix if it actually knows the fix exists — including the merged dispatch diff directly in context when reviewing the sibling services gives it the concrete information needed to recognize the pattern is already addressed, the same way including existing tests in context prevents duplicate test suggestions.
ww: Capping the finding count assumes some priority ordering that has nothing to do with whether a specific fix was already applied elsewhere — it might just as easily suppress a genuinely new issue while still leaving the duplicate-fix problem unaddressed.

Keyword matching against commit messages is fragile — it depends on wording overlap and misses semantically identical fixes phrased differently, the same failure mode as trying to catch duplicate suggestions with surface-level text matching.

An instruction to "check whether a similar fix exists" without actually providing that fix in context asks the model to recall information it was never given — Vanguard has no way to know about the dispatch merge unless it's explicitly included in the prompt.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight wants Vanguard's findings to auto-populate an internal engineering-metrics dashboard (tracking finding counts, categories, and resolution time per team) via a nightly ingestion job that calls a REST endpoint. Vanguard currently prints narrative prose to stdout, and the ingestion job's parser — built to expect a specific field set for the dashboard's schema — regularly throws validation errors and drops entire nights of data whenever Claude's phrasing varies. What change most reliably produces output the ingestion job can consume?
questions.why: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` enforces well-formed, schema-conformant JSON output from the Claude Code CLI, which is exactly what a downstream ingestion job needs to parse reliably regardless of which specific consumer (GitHub comments, a dashboard, any other system) is reading it — the mechanism guarantees the shape rather than hoping for consistent prose.
ww: A CLAUDE.md section describing the desired format is not guaranteed to be consistently followed — it's a prompt-level request, and the ingestion job would still be vulnerable to the same phrasing variance that's already breaking it.

A prompt instruction to format as JSON is exactly the "asking nicely" approach that can still produce prose preambles, markdown fences, or malformed JSON — it doesn't carry the same schema guarantee as the CLI's dedicated output-format and schema-validation flags.

Widening the parser's tolerance treats the symptom of inconsistent output rather than the cause — the source (Claude's freeform prose) keeps varying, so the parser will keep needing further expansion indefinitely instead of the format simply being guaranteed at the source.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight schedules a full-repository dependency and security audit across the entire freight-routing monorepo to run weekly via the Message Batches API, taking advantage of the 50% cost savings since the audit isn't blocking anyone. Leadership wants the completed audit results available by 8 a.m. every Monday for the weekly engineering review. Given that batch processing has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours in the worst case, when is the latest the team can submit the batch and still safely expect results by the Monday deadline?
questions.why: Batch processing has no latency SLA — the documented window is up to 24 hours, and a submission plan must budget against that worst case, not the typical case. To guarantee results are ready by 8 a.m. Monday, the batch must be submitted no later than 24 hours earlier, i.e., by 8 a.m. Sunday, so that even a batch that takes the full 24 hours still finishes in time.
ww: Planning around "usually finishes in about an hour" ignores that there is no SLA — the one week a batch takes closer to the full 24 hours, the Monday deadline is blown; historical typical-case timing does not bound the worst case.

Batch requests do complete and post results by some point, and a fixed weekly deadline (8 a.m. Monday) does exist for this audit — treating the submission timing as irrelevant ignores the real downstream deadline leadership set.

Submitting the morning of the deadline itself leaves zero buffer — if the batch takes anywhere close to its documented worst case of 24 hours, results would arrive a full day late, well past the 8 a.m. review.

questions.stem: A developer opens a PR with the one-line description "add tests for the new pricing logic" and triggers Vanguard's test-generation step. The new pricing logic actually touches three distinct calculations (surcharge, discount stacking, and currency rounding), and the description doesn't specify which of the three — or whether all three — should be covered. Rather than blocking the pipeline to ask the developer for clarification, Vanguard proceeds by generating tests for all three calculations and includes a short note listing the assumption it made. Is this the right way to handle the ambiguous instruction, and why?
questions.why: For a vague request, proceeding with clearly stated assumptions and inviting correction is the pattern that avoids the abandonment and friction that comes with blocking on clarifying questions — it keeps the pipeline moving and gives the developer an easy, low-effort way to redirect scope if the assumption about test coverage is wrong, rather than forcing a synchronous back-and-forth in an automated CI step.
ww: Pausing a CI pipeline to demand a precise specification before doing any work is exactly the pattern the corpus warns against for vague requests — it introduces a blocking round-trip and demands upfront effort from the developer instead of proceeding with a reasonable, correctable assumption.

A hidden default is worse than a stated one — the developer has no way to know surcharge-only coverage was assumed, and would only discover the gap later when discount stacking or currency rounding bugs slip through untested.

Bundling every possible ambiguity into one compound clarifying message still demands the developer stop and respond before any work happens — it still incurs the friction cost of blocking, just packaged as a single message instead of several.

questions.stem: Solstice Freight is designing Vanguard's auto-approve behavior: findings above a certain bar should be auto-resolved with a suggested fix applied automatically, while others should route to a human reviewer. A vendor proposes having Vanguard self-rate its own confidence in each finding on a 1-to-10 scale and auto-apply any fix scoring 8 or above. Early testing shows several confidently-scored auto-applied fixes were actually wrong, while some fixes scored below the threshold turned out to be fine. What is the most effective way to design this routing decision instead?
questions.why: The failure here is that self-rated numeric confidence is not a reliable signal of actual safety — the model can be confidently wrong, and the vendor's early test data already shows scores don't track real outcomes. Explicit, concrete escalation criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing the two cases gives Vanguard a clear, testable boundary to apply consistently, rather than relying on an uncalibrated confidence number to make the call.
ww: Raising the threshold from 8 to 9 still relies on the same fundamentally unreliable signal — self-rated confidence — and the test data already shows confident scores don't reliably track correctness; a stricter cutoff on a broken measure doesn't fix the measure.

Building a separate trained classifier is significant infrastructure overkill for what the corpus treats as a prompt-design problem — the root cause is unclear decision boundaries in the routing logic, not the absence of a dedicated model.

A second instance re-confirming the same self-rated confidence score is still built on the same unreliable signal — two uncalibrated confidence ratings agreeing with each other doesn't make the underlying number any more trustworthy.

questions.stem: Claimwise runs an auto-insurance claim-intake pipeline. Incoming packets are a mix of accident report forms, repair-shop estimates, and medical-visit summaries, and three separate extraction tools exist (one per document type). The pipeline must always hand the adjuster queue a schema-valid record for classification metadata before any downstream enrichment tool touches the document, but a prompt instruction telling Claude to 'always classify the document type first' is only followed on about 88% of runs. Which configuration most reliably guarantees the classification step runs before enrichment?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool by name on the first turn guarantees that exact tool runs before anything else — this is the forced-first-step pattern for a mandatory execution order. Relaxing `tool_choice` back to `auto` afterward lets Claude proceed normally with enrichment tools once classification is done.
ww: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees Claude calls *some* tool, but not that it calls classification specifically — Claude could call an enrichment tool first and still satisfy `"any"`.
Strengthening a prompt instruction is still probabilistic; the pipeline already has 88% compliance from a similar instruction and needs a guarantee, not a stronger suggestion.

Leaving the tool forced for the entire workflow means Claude can never call the enrichment tools afterward — the forced-first-step pattern requires relaxing `tool_choice` once the mandatory step completes.

questions.stem: Claimwise's intake pipeline always follows the same five steps for every claim packet: document classification, field extraction, cross-field validation, coverage-limit enrichment, then adjuster-queue formatting — the template never changes regardless of claim type. An architect proposes replacing this with a dynamic decomposition step where the coordinator generates a custom subtask plan for each incoming packet based on what it discovers during initial parsing. Which structure is actually most appropriate here?
questions.why: When every task instance follows the same known steps in the same order, a fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) is the correct choice — it gives stability and reproducibility, which matters for a repeatable extraction template. Dynamic decomposition is reserved for open-ended tasks where the scope isn't known up front.
questions.cite: Domain-1_v2 §1.7 (fixed sequential pipeline vs dynamic adaptive)
ww: Dynamic adaptive decomposition is for tasks where full scope is unknown up front and each step depends on discoveries — the opposite of Claimwise's situation, where every claim follows the identical five-step template. Introducing this here adds unneeded complexity.

The five stages are sequentially dependent (validation needs extraction's output, enrichment needs validation's output) — this isn't the independent-subtask situation that parallel `Task` calls are for.

Collapsing a five-stage template into one open-ended prompt abandons the reproducibility that a fixed pipeline is chosen specifically to preserve, and reintroduces the attention-dilution risk of doing too much in one pass.

questions.stem: Claimwise's extraction agent frequently needs to check which coverage categories and per-incident limits apply to a policy while extracting a claim — information that rarely changes and would otherwise require the agent to guess at query terms for a `search_policy_rules` tool. An engineer wants the agent to see, up front, what coverage categories and limit structures exist without burning tool calls on exploratory guesses. Which MCP design best fits this need?
questions.why: MCP resources expose read-only content catalogs the agent can access without an exploratory tool call — exactly the 'map of what data exists' need described here. A resource gives this visibility for free, whereas the agent would otherwise burn turns guessing at query terms.
ww: A tool the agent 'must remember to call' still costs an LLM call and relies on the agent thinking to invoke it first — a resource provides the same map as readable context without that dependency.
A static system-prompt dump bloats context on every single turn and goes stale as coverage rules change, whereas a resource is requested on demand.

Standard integrations should use existing solutions where possible; building a custom server to re-implement a policy-rules API 'for control' reinvents infrastructure that a resource-based approach against the existing API would already solve.

questions.stem: Claimwise's accident-report extraction schema marks `police_report_number` as required and non-nullable, on the reasoning that every accident should have an official filing. An audit of 3,000 extracted accident reports finds that 9% carry a police report number that traces to no real filing in the department's system — the model appears to be inventing plausible-looking numbers. Investigation confirms these claims were minor fender-benders where no police report was ever filed. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: A required, non-nullable field pushes the model to fabricate a value when the underlying information is genuinely absent from the source. Making the field nullable and non-required lets the model honestly return `null` for the many minor claims where no police report was ever filed, which is a legitimate real-world outcome rather than an extraction failure.
ww: Adding a confidence score alongside a still-required, still-non-nullable field does nothing to stop the fabrication itself — the model is still pressured to produce a number when none exists; a confidence score only measures the symptom after the fabricated value is already produced.

A format validator only catches syntactically malformed numbers; a fabricated number that happens to match the correct format (which is exactly what a plausible-looking invented number would do) passes the check cleanly. This is a semantic error, not a syntax error, and no schema format constraint can catch it.

Discarding structured extraction for a free-text field abandons the schema guarantee entirely for a field that is genuinely present and extractable in the majority of cases — the fix for occasional absence is nullability, not giving up structure altogether.

questions.stem: Claimwise's intake coordinator delegates classification, extraction, and validation work across dozens of claim packets in a long-running overnight batch, tracked in-memory across many tool calls. Midway through processing claim #4,412, the orchestration host crashes and restarts. Currently, the coordinator has no way to know which claims were already fully processed, so the restart script simply reprocesses the entire overnight queue from claim #1. What is the most effective way to prevent this waste on the next crash?
questions.why: Structured state persistence lets each processing stage export status and findings to a known location, with the coordinator reading a manifest on resume to pick up exactly where it left off — this survives a crash because the state lives outside any single in-memory session. This is the correct pattern for crash recovery in long-running, multi-step pipelines.
questions.cite: Domain-5_v2 §5.12 (structured state persistence for crash recovery)
ww: The API is stateless and a crashed process's in-memory conversation history does not survive a restart — there is no server-side session to recover from, which is exactly why external, persisted state is required.

Shrinking the batch size limits the blast radius of a crash but does not solve the underlying problem — the restart script still has no way to know what was already completed, so it still reprocesses from the start of whatever chunk it's in.
Keeping findings only in each stage's own context window means nothing survives a crash at all — context fills and, more importantly, in-memory context is lost the moment the process dies.

questions.stem: Claimwise's adjuster-support agent, when reviewing a flagged claim, almost always needs both the policy's coverage terms and the claimant's prior claim history together — the two calls are made in sequence on nearly every review, adding a full extra API loop each time. An engineer considers building a single `get_policy_and_history` tool that fetches both in one call. What does the corpus favor instead?
questions.why: When an agent frequently calls multiple tools in sequence for the same operation, the preferred fix is prompting the agent to request them together in one turn rather than building a composite tool — the agent can naturally bundle multiple tool calls into a single response when it already knows both are needed.
ww: A composite tool is explicitly called the not-preferred approach in the corpus for this situation — it hides the composition rather than letting the agent bundle related, already-known calls into one turn.

Giving unrestricted tool access breaks the least-privilege principle and increases the tool count the agent must discriminate between on every turn, which degrades selection reliability rather than fixing the sequencing inefficiency.

Pre-fetching in the coordinator before the subagent even runs removes the subagent's own judgment about what it needs for a specific case and adds unnecessary coordinator-side logic for a need the subagent itself already reliably identifies.

questions.stem: When Claimwise's extraction pipeline cannot resolve a claim automatically — conflicting figures between the repair estimate and the medical summary, for instance — it calls `escalate_to_adjuster`. The human adjusters who receive these escalations report they must re-derive the claim's basic facts from scratch: the claimant, the policy number, which fields conflicted, and what the extraction agent already tried. The escalation console shows only that the tool fired with a one-line note, and adjusters have no access to the extraction agent's internal reasoning. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: Since the human reviewer has no access to the agent's transcript or reasoning, the escalation summary is the entirety of what they see — it must be a complete, self-contained structured payload with the identifying details, root cause, conflicting values, actions taken, and a recommendation, exactly mirroring the required handoff fields the corpus specifies.
ww: Adjusters lack transcript/reasoning access by design in this workflow, and dumping a raw reasoning trace on them forces them to read through an entire internal deliberation rather than receiving a concise, actionable summary.

Having the human re-run the same tools the agent already called duplicates work and slows resolution — the whole point of a structured handoff is to avoid making the receiving party rebuild context that was already gathered.

Escalating earlier doesn't fix the information-loss problem — it just means less context was gathered before handoff, and the same generic-note limitation still leaves the adjuster without the specifics they need; it also degrades the agent's autonomous resolution rate.

questions.stem: Claimwise defines one extraction tool per document type (accident report, repair estimate, medical summary) so that every processed page always yields a schema-valid record for the adjuster queue. On a batch of scanned, low-quality faxes, Claude occasionally responds with an apologetic paragraph explaining the scan is hard to read instead of calling any of the three extraction tools — leaving that page with no structured output at all. Which configuration change most reliably eliminates this gap?
questions.why: `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` forces Claude to call some tool rather than answer in free text — even on a poor-quality scan, the model must pick the best-fitting extraction tool (nullable fields can then absorb whatever it genuinely cannot read), guaranteeing structured output on every page.
ww: `"auto"` permits Claude to answer in plain text regardless of any prompt instruction telling it not to — this is exactly the failure mode observed, since prompt-based JSON requests can still return prose instead of a tool call.

Repairing free text after the fact treats the symptom rather than removing the root cause; `tool_use` prevents the prose response from happening in the first place rather than patching it after generation.

Adding a fourth tool option doesn't help if `tool_choice` remains `"auto"` — Claude can still choose to respond in prose regardless of how many tools exist, since `auto` never removes the free-text option.

questions.stem: Claimwise's field-extraction subagent was originally scoped to five tools (extract per document type, plus a lookup helper) and selected correctly. Over several sprints, engineers kept adding convenience tools directly to this subagent — currency conversion, address standardization, a legacy OCR fallback, a duplicate-claim checker, and more — until it now has 16 tools. Selection accuracy has dropped noticeably, and the subagent now occasionally calls the wrong helper for a field it could have extracted directly. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Too many tools on one agent degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity — each additional near-miss tool is another candidate to discriminate between on every turn. Restricting the subagent back to the small set core to its role directly reduces that decision space, which is the root-cause fix.
questions.cite: Domain-2_v2 §2.5 (too many tools degrades selection reliability)
ww: Better descriptions help at the margin, but the tool count itself is named as the root cause here — description tuning alone doesn't reduce the number of near-miss candidates the model must discriminate between on every turn.

Giving every agent the full catalog 'for flexibility' is explicitly the wrong direction — agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them, which is exactly the drift already observed here.

Adding a pre-routing classifier is infrastructure layered on top of an inflated tool set rather than fixing the underlying cause; it doesn't reduce the subagent's actual tool count or its selection burden once invoked.

questions.stem: A regional carrier hands Claimwise a one-time backlog of 180,000 legacy claim packets to extract, with results due to feed a year-end reconciliation report at 8 a.m. two days from now — no adjuster is waiting on any individual document. The team plans to submit the whole backlog as a single Message Batches API run to capture the 50% discount. Given the batch has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, how should the team plan the submission window to be safe?
questions.why: Because the Batches API carries no latency SLA, deadline planning must budget the full 24-hour worst case, not the typical faster completion time — submission deadline should be the downstream deadline minus 24 hours. With a two-day window before an 8 a.m. deadline, submitting with at least a full 24-hour buffer protects against the one run that takes close to the maximum.
questions.cite: Domain-4_v2 §4.11 (SLA planning: budget the 24-hour worst case)
ww: Planning around 'batches usually finish fast' ignores that there is no SLA — the one run that takes close to 24 hours would blow the deadline if submission happened late in the window based on typical-case assumptions.

Splitting into many small sub-batches doesn't address the core planning requirement — each sub-batch still needs its own 24-hour buffer before the deadline, and arbitrary hourly slicing doesn't guarantee that buffer for the last slices submitted late in the window.

Submitting 'the evening before' with only slightly more than 24 hours of margin leaves very little safety buffer against the documented worst case, especially since real-world submission and processing overhead can eat into that thin margin.

questions.stem: Claimwise's extraction system reports 96% field-level accuracy in aggregate across all claim types, and leadership proposes ending human review for every extraction above the confidence threshold. A data scientist points out that windshield-only glass claims are a small slice of total volume and asks the team to check accuracy specifically within that segment before proceeding. The check reveals glass claims fail extraction 33% of the time, hidden inside the reassuring 96% aggregate. What should the team do before reducing human review?
questions.why: An aggregate accuracy figure can hide a much worse failure rate on a rare segment — exactly what happened here, where a 96% overall number concealed a 33% failure rate on glass claims. The fix is to validate accuracy by document type and field before reducing review, and to implement ongoing stratified random sampling across claim types so novel segment-level problems are caught on a continuing basis, not just when someone happens to ask.
ww: Proceeding on the aggregate number alone is exactly the masking trap — a 96% overall figure does not guarantee every segment independently clears the bar, and this glass-claims example proves a rare segment can fail dramatically underneath it.

A small threshold adjustment is a blunt, aggregate-level tweak that doesn't address the actual problem — a systematically underperforming segment needs its own investigation and likely its own handling, not a marginally stricter global cutoff.

A single self-reported confidence score per document is uncalibrated and unreliable until validated against ground truth, and collapsing to one document-level number is a step backward from the field-level granularity the corpus calls for.

questions.stem: Claimwise's extraction subagent occasionally receives a scanned repair estimate where the image is so severely truncated mid-page that the OCR layer throws a hard parsing exception. Today, the subagent simply returns the bare status `"failed"` to the coordinator, which then has no way to decide whether to request a rescan, skip the document and flag it, or route it to manual entry. What change would most effectively let the coordinator make an intelligent recovery decision?
questions.why: The coordinator needs structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — to make an intelligent recovery decision rather than being stuck choosing blindly between retry, skip, or escalate. A bare failure status gives it nothing to reason with.
ww: Blind internal retries on an image-truncation failure waste effort on a failure type that retrying the same OCR pass is unlikely to fix — the corpus draws a clear line between failures a component can resolve locally and ones that need to be escalated with context.

A generic, undifferentiated error payload is explicitly the pattern to avoid — it prevents the coordinator from distinguishing this failure from any other and only allows a crude retry-or-abort response instead of an informed one.

Halting the entire batch for one truncated document is a wildly disproportionate response — the corpus's design principle is to never terminate the whole workflow for a single subagent failure; a targeted structured error report lets the coordinator handle just that one item.

questions.stem: Claimwise's `submit_settlement_offer` tool starts rejecting some settlement calculations because the proposed payout exceeds the claimant's policy per-incident coverage cap. The extraction agent currently treats every rejection the same way it treats a database timeout — it retries the exact same settlement calculation up to three times before finally escalating. How should the tool's error handling be restructured?
questions.why: A coverage-cap rejection is a business-rule error, not a tool malfunction — it's a valid answer that the requested payout is disallowed, and no amount of retrying changes that outcome. Marking it `retriable: false` with a customer-appropriate explanation lets the agent stop wasting attempts and correctly communicate the policy outcome instead of treating it like a transient failure.
ww: Marking a business-rule denial as retryable is exactly the failure mode already observed — a per-incident cap doesn't change no matter how many times the same or adjusted figure is resubmitted, so this wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change.

A generic failure message makes a business-rule denial indistinguishable from a genuine transient outage, so the agent can't tell it should stop retrying and instead applies the same blind retry-or-escalate behavior already causing the problem.

Silently overriding the settlement figure without informing the agent hides a real business-rule outcome behind an apparent success, masking the coverage-limit decision from both the agent and, ultimately, whoever needs to explain the payout to the claimant.

questions.stem: Claimwise's weekly reprocessing job for disputed claims uses the Message Batches API, and each request includes the claim-review tool definitions plus the full multi-turn conversation for that claim so far, because some disputes require the model to call a supplementary-document tool mid-review. A new engineer claims 'the Batches API doesn't support tool use at all, so this design is invalid and we need to move disputed-claim reprocessing to synchronous calls.' Is this assessment correct?
questions.why: The Batches API does support tool use and multi-turn conversation histories — a batch request's params mirror a normal Messages API call, including `tools`. The real constraint is narrower: each batch request is self-contained, so if the model's response ends in `tool_use`, that request completes there, and continuing the loop requires a separate follow-up request with the tool result appended.
questions.cite: Domain-4_v2 §4.11 (accuracy note: tool use in batches)
ww: This claims tool definitions are silently dropped, which is false — the Batches API accepts `tools` in a request's params exactly as the synchronous Messages API does; the limitation is about mid-request execution, not about the field being ignored.

Batch requests can include full multi-turn message histories, not just a single fresh message — this option misstates the actual, narrower limitation (no mid-request tool execution) as a much broader one that doesn't exist.

A batch request cannot pause mid-processing to receive a tool result and continue as one unit — each request is a single submit-then-respond cycle; expecting it to behave like an uninterrupted synchronous loop misunderstands the one-shot nature of batch processing.

questions.stem: A single Claimwise policyholder submits one packet each night containing an accident report, a repair estimate, and a medical-visit summary — three genuinely independent documents that each need their own extraction before a coordinator cross-checks them against each other. The coordinator currently extracts them strictly one after another, and end-to-end turnaround for this nightly packet has become the client's top complaint even though every individual extraction succeeds. What is the most effective way to reduce turnaround here?
questions.why: Because the three documents are independent to extract, issuing their `Task` calls together in one coordinator response runs them in parallel instead of one after another — this is the standard fix for independent work items being processed sequentially, and it directly reduces end-to-end latency without sacrificing correctness.
ww: Trimming fields might shave some time per call but doesn't address the actual bottleneck — the documents are still processed sequentially, so the latency savings are marginal compared to running the three independent extractions concurrently.

Combining three independent documents into a single extraction call reintroduces the attention-dilution risk of processing too much in one pass, and loses the clean per-document separation that made each individual extraction reliable in the first place.

Batch processing addresses cost, not latency — it has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, which is the opposite of what a client complaining about turnaround needs; it also doesn't address the sequential-submission pattern itself.

questions.stem: Your support agent's loop keeps calling Claude until its reply text contains the phrase 'issue resolved.' Logs show cases where Claude calls `process_refund` and returns a clear final answer, but the loop invokes Claude again anyway because the reply lacks that exact phrase, wasting a round-trip on 9% of resolved cases. What should the loop check instead?
questions.why: The agentic loop must check stop_reason, not parse response text — tool_use means continue and execute the next tool call, end_turn means Claude has finished. Text-matching for phrases like 'issue resolved' is exactly what causes premature or delayed loop exits.
ww: This encodes the documented exam trap of parsing Claude's text for completion language instead of using the structured stop_reason signal — unreliable and unrelated to what actually signals the loop should stop.

A fixed call-count cap doesn't reflect whether Claude has actually finished — it would cut off legitimate multi-tool cases early or let an already-finished case loop needlessly before hitting the cap.
A wall-clock timeout is an operational safety net at best, not a completion signal — a finished case could linger until the timeout while a legitimately in-progress case gets cut off early.

questions.stem: Your `process_refund` tool accepts a `dry_run: boolean` parameter so the agent can preview a refund's impact before committing it. Production monitoring shows the agent sometimes calls `process_refund` with `dry_run=false` on the first attempt, skipping the preview step policy requires. Which redesign makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible?
questions.why: The two-tool token-binding pattern makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible — execute_refund cannot succeed without a token that only preview_refund ever produces, a code-level guarantee rather than a hope.
ww: Adding a second boolean to the same tool is still a single-tool design the agent can set directly — the same structural flaw as dry_run itself, just renamed.
Relying on a prompt instruction to enforce a mandatory sequencing rule is probabilistic, not guaranteed — the exact class of fix the corpus documents as inferior to token-binding.
A hook that only logs and flags after the call happened is detection, not prevention — it doesn't stop the skipped-preview refund from executing.

questions.stem: Policy authorizes your agent to waive return-shipping fees for domestic returns when an item arrives damaged. A customer requests the same waiver for an international return; written policy is silent on international shipping fees entirely. `get_customer` and `lookup_order` both confirm the order and damage claim. What should the agent do?
questions.why: A policy gap — where the agent cannot determine the correct action within defined policy — is an explicit escalation trigger; the agent must not invent an interpretation for an uncovered case.
ww: Extending the domestic rule to an unaddressed case is exactly the invented-interpretation failure the corpus warns against for policy gaps.
Treating policy silence as an implicit denial is the mirror-image invented interpretation — silence means undefined, not 'no.'
Inventing a new remedy that policy never authorizes is scope creep beyond the agent's defined authority — the same class of error as guessing at an uncovered rule.

questions.stem: A new compliance rule requires that the moment a customer explicitly asks for a manager, the agent's very next turn must call `escalate_to_human` — not offer reassurance first. Engineers want this guaranteed for that one turn only, then normal behavior resumes. Which `tool_choice` configuration guarantees it?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool guarantees exactly that call on the triggering turn; relaxing back to auto afterward preserves normal operation on every later turn — the documented forced-first-step pattern.
ww: `auto` permits Claude to answer in plain text instead of calling any tool — an instruction layered on top is still probabilistic, not a guarantee.
`any` guarantees a tool call but not which one — with get_customer, lookup_order, and process_refund also available, the model could satisfy 'any' with a different tool entirely.

Forcing that one tool for the rest of the conversation blocks the agent from ever calling get_customer, lookup_order, or process_refund again — it fixes the triggering turn but breaks every turn after it.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes fixing a bug where the agent forgets a customer's stated preference from two turns earlier by adding a session ID parameter so 'the API remembers the conversation.' A colleague pushes back. Investigation confirms the application's own request builder omits prior turns. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.why: Claude's API is fully stateless; the only mechanism for memory is including prior turns in the messages array on every request — there is no session_id parameter that substitutes for this.
ww: This is the documented exam trap verbatim — 'Claude needs a session_id parameter' is false; the API has no session state to attach to.
A two-turn conversation is nowhere near exhausting a context window — this misdiagnoses a request-construction bug as a capacity problem.
A vector database addresses retrieval over long, multi-session histories, not standard short multi-turn memory, and does nothing to fix a request builder that omits prior turns.

questions.stem: Your team builds a `/audit-refund-errors` skill that runs a deep scan of weeks of refund logs, correlating `process_refund` calls with disputed charges. Engineers report that after invoking it mid-debugging-session, Claude becomes sluggish and loses track of the original bug they were investigating. How should the skill be configured to fix this?
questions.why: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent context so its large output does not pollute the main session — the documented fix for exactly this exam pattern.
ww: argument-hint only displays a prompt for an argument value at invocation — it doesn't isolate context and wouldn't stop a large scan's output from filling the main session.
A faster model doesn't address context pollution — the same verbose output still lands in the main conversation regardless of model speed.
Compressing the output loses the analysis detail the skill exists to produce; the documented fix is isolation via context: fork, not shrinking the result.

questions.stem: A customer disputes charges on two orders in one message. `get_customer` succeeds and `lookup_order` returns full details for the first order, but times out on the second. The agent has enough to resolve one order now. What should it do with the incomplete second order?
questions.why: Complete the response using what the data supports, explicitly annotate what could not be confirmed, and propagate that gap forward rather than hiding it or blocking on it.
ww: A single transient timeout on one of two lookups isn't a policy gap or a pattern of repeated failure — escalating the whole case, including the already-resolvable order, is unwarranted.
Reporting both orders as resolved regardless of what the lookup actually returned is the return-success-with-embedded-failure anti-pattern — it tells the customer something false.
Refusing to act on the order the agent already has confirmed data for needlessly withholds a resolution it's able to provide.

questions.stem: Your `process_refund` tool's description reads only: 'Processes a refund for a given order.' Logs show the agent sometimes calls it for exchange requests — where the customer wants a replacement item, not money back — issuing refunds nobody asked for. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Descriptions must state boundary cases — when NOT to use a tool. This is the root-cause fix for a description that never told the model the refund/exchange boundary.
ww: Merging into a single composite tool loses the semantic precision that distinguishes a refund from an exchange, the corpus's documented anti-fix for similar-tool confusion.
A pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure to compensate for a description that simply never stated the boundary — fix the description first.
One example addressing a single case doesn't fix the description itself, which still lacks the boundary statement for every other exchange-shaped request.

questions.stem: When customers send vague openers like 'there's an issue with my order,' your agent currently asks up to four clarifying questions — which order, what kind of issue, email on file, preferred resolution — before doing anything. Abandonment on these openers is 37%. What should the agent do instead?
questions.why: Proceed with a stated, reasonable assumption and invite correction — the documented fix for vague-request abandonment.
ww: Bundling all four questions into one message still demands the same upfront effort from the customer before anything happens — it doesn't fix the over-clarification pattern itself.
A hidden default that isn't stated leaves the customer confused when the response doesn't match what they actually meant; the documented fix requires stating the assumption.
Sequential one-at-a-time clarification is the exact pattern the corpus ties to 35-40% abandonment — it changes pacing, not the number of questions asked.

questions.stem: Your agent's resolution rate looks strong at 91% overall — cases closed without human handoff. A team member wants to broaden auto-resolution to more case types on the strength of that number. A skeptical colleague points out that billing-dispute cases are a small slice of total volume. What should the team check before broadening?
questions.why: An aggregate rate can mask a much worse failure rate on a smaller segment — the exact reason to validate accuracy by case type and by segment before broadening auto-resolution, not just trust the overall number.
ww: Trusting the aggregate directly without checking segments is the documented masking trap — a rare segment like billing disputes could be failing far more often than 91% suggests.
Measurement window length doesn't address whether the aggregate is masking a per-segment failure rate — a longer window can average away the same problem just as easily.
External benchmarking doesn't reveal whether this system's own aggregate is hiding a segment-level failure — the fix is internal segment analysis, not competitive comparison.

questions.stem: Policy requires that any case flagged for suspected fraud be escalated to a human before the agent marks it resolved. Today this rule lives only in the system prompt: 'always escalate fraud-flagged cases before closing.' An audit finds 6% of fraud-flagged cases closed without escalation. What change most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: For safety-critical sequencing, enforce with a programmatic precondition rather than relying on the model to follow an instruction — deterministic where the prompt-only version was only probabilistic.
ww: A more emphatic prompt instruction is still prompt-only enforcement — the corpus documents this as unreliable for critical sequencing regardless of wording strength.
Few-shot examples improve the model's tendency to follow the sequence but remain probabilistic, not a guarantee — the same class of fix the corpus rejects for critical sequencing.
More frequent reminders address instruction drift over a long conversation, not the underlying lack of enforcement — the case could still close without escalation on any given turn.

questions.stem: Refunds above $1,000 require manager sign-off before they execute, but today that rule lives only in a system-prompt instruction: 'route refunds over $1,000 to escalation before calling `process_refund`.' A monthly audit finds 4% of large refunds are still processed without sign-off, mostly during high-volume shifts. Which change enforces this rule deterministically?
questions.why: PreToolUse fires before the tool executes and can block operations above a defined threshold, routing to escalation deterministically regardless of what the prompt says.
ww: Rewording the instruction is still prompt-only enforcement, which the corpus already shows failing 4% of the time — stronger wording adds no enforcement.
PostToolUse fires after the tool already executed — logging the violation after the fact doesn't prevent the unauthorized refund from being processed.
Few-shot examples improve compliance probabilistically but provide no guarantee — the same class of fix already shown insufficient for this threshold rule.

questions.stem: The team wants the agent to stay calm under pressure, always cite the specific policy section behind a decision, and never guess at a policy point that isn't explicitly stated anywhere in the documented rules. Where should these behavioral constraints be defined so they hold for the entire conversation?
questions.why: Persistent behavioral constraints — tone, standards of citation, honesty about unstated policy — that apply for the whole conversation belong in the system prompt.
ww: Putting the rule in the first user message loses authority as the conversation progresses — it isn't re-asserted with the same standing weight as a system prompt on every request.
An environment variable has no effect on model behavior at all — it isn't part of the request the model reasons over.
A first assistant message is just prior conversation content the model can drift away from over time — it doesn't carry the standing authority a system prompt does.

questions.stem: A customer asks the agent to refund all 42 orders on their account in one request, citing a billing error from several months ago they can't fully describe. Nothing in policy explicitly forbids a bulk refund of this kind, and `get_customer` confirms the account is legitimate. What should the agent do?
questions.why: High-stakes ambiguity — where a wrong autonomous decision could cause significant harm — is an explicit escalation trigger even absent a policy prohibition.
ww: 'Not explicitly forbidden' is not the same as 'safe to do autonomously' — the scale and ambiguity here are exactly the high-stakes-ambiguity trigger, not a green light.
Partially executing an ambiguous bulk action the agent isn't authorized to judge doesn't resolve the ambiguity — it spreads the same unauthorized decision across fewer orders first.

Demanding a per-order explanation for all 42 orders before doing anything is the over-clarification pattern the corpus separately flags as causing abandonment, not the correct response to a high-stakes case.

questions.stem: As holiday volume rises, multi-issue support conversations now often exceed 60 turns, mixing precise transactional details — order IDs, agreed refund amounts, promised delivery dates — with long stretches of routine back-and-forth. The team needs to manage growing token cost without losing that precision. Which context management strategy is most effective?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — extract structured facts verbatim, summarize general discussion, keep recent exchanges verbatim — is the documented most-tested pattern for exactly this mix of precision-critical and routine content.
ww: Uniform summarization compresses precise values like order IDs and agreed amounts into vague language, losing exactly the precision the team needs to preserve.
A fixed recent-message window drops early-conversation facts entirely if they were mentioned before the cutoff, even though they may still be operative.
A bigger window raises cost and only delays the same problem — nothing about a larger raw window prevents the same details from still needing extraction.

questions.stem: The order-fulfillment service is a 60-file legacy module the engineer has never touched. To speed up discovery, they configure a coordinator agent definition with detailed descriptions of three investigation subagents (routes, validators, retry logic) in its system prompt. In practice, Claude Code never spawns a single subagent — it investigates everything directly in the main session. What is the most likely fix?
questions.why: A coordinator's allowedTools must include `Task`, or it cannot spawn subagents at all, regardless of how detailed the subagent descriptions are.
ww: Rewriting the system prompt to instruct delegation doesn't help — the prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds; without `Task` in allowedTools, delegation is impossible regardless of wording.
More detailed subagent descriptions don't enable spawning — descriptions inform what an agent is for once delegation is possible; the `Task` tool is what makes delegation possible at all.
This doesn't address the missing `Task` tool at all, and granting unrestricted access on top of an unrelated problem violates least-privilege scoping for subagents.

questions.stem: With Task-spawned subagents investigating routes, validators, and retry logic in parallel, the retry-logic subagent hits a parsing exception on 2 of its 8 target files (malformed legacy syntax) and cannot read them; the other two subagents complete fully. What should the coordinator do when synthesizing the discovery report?
questions.why: Synthesis should complete using available data and explicitly annotate which conclusions are well-supported versus where coverage gaps exist, propagating uncertainty upward rather than blocking or hiding it.
ww: Returning an error because input is incomplete is the documented wrong response — coverage annotation, not failure, is how partial upstream input should be handled.
Proceeding without noting the gaps is the other documented wrong response — it hides a real limitation from readers of the report.
A parsing exception on malformed syntax is a permanent error, not a transient one — it will not resolve by retrying and repeated retries waste effort.

questions.stem: The routes-investigation subagent was scoped to Read, Grep, and Glob for its discovery task. After a teammate adds Bash to its allowed tools 'for convenience,' logs show it now runs ad hoc shell commands — including starting a local dev server — mid-investigation instead of just reading and searching files. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Each subagent should have only the tools its defined scope needs; a pure discovery subagent has no legitimate use for Bash, and removing it closes the scope creep at the interface level.
ww: A prompt instruction not to misuse a tool the subagent still has is probabilistic, not deterministic — this mirrors the corpus's own rejected fix for an over-scoped fetch_url tool.
A larger model doesn't fix a tool-scoping problem — the misuse happens because the tool is available, not because the model is too small to reason about it.
Logging every Bash call after the fact detects misuse but doesn't prevent it; a PreToolUse-style gate could block, but passive logging leaves the scope creep in place.

questions.stem: The team's quick-fix suggestion feature, built with Claude Code, calls the Claude API directly with an `apply_fix` tool defined, expecting a tool call every time. On roughly 1 in 6 requests, the response is a prose paragraph explaining why no fix was proposed, and the automation has nothing to apply. What configuration change most reliably closes this gap?
questions.why: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees the model calls some tool rather than returning conversational text — the documented fix for an agent that occasionally replies in prose instead of calling any extraction/action tool.
ww: `{"type": "auto"}` (the default) still permits a plain-text answer; a prompt instruction to always call the tool is probabilistic and is exactly the failure already being observed.
Temperature controls response wording and randomness, not whether the model decides to call a tool at all — it's the wrong lever for this failure.
A hook that fires after the model has already answered in prose can't turn that response into a valid tool_use block for the automation to act on — it patches the symptom after the fact.

questions.stem: The team decides to migrate the order-fulfillment service off its templating engine to a new one. The change touches views across roughly 50 files, and it's not yet settled whether migration should happen module-by-module or via a compatibility shim first. Which Claude Code approach should the engineer use to start this work?
questions.why: Large scope, an unsettled architectural decision (shim vs. module-by-module), and changes crossing many files are exactly when planning mode avoids expensive rework from premature execution.
ww: Starting in direct execution and reactively switching once it gets hard is the documented exam trap — reactive switching is expensive; the task should be planned upfront.
`--resume` continues a saved session with its context — it isn't an undo mechanism, and it doesn't resolve the open shim-vs-module-by-module decision before work starts.
Fragmenting into 50 independent sessions never resolves the open architectural question and loses the cross-file consistency that a single upfront plan would establish.

questions.stem: Across the order-fulfillment codebase, the payments module enforces a custom validation-decorator pattern, the notifications module uses an event-emitter pattern, and a no-default-exports rule applies to utility files scattered across dozens of directories. The engineer wants each convention applied automatically based on which files Claude Code is touching. What should they configure?
questions.why: Glob-pattern rules in `.claude/rules/` load automatically only when Claude works on matching files — deterministic file-path matching that works regardless of which directory a file lives in.
ww: A root CLAUDE.md organized under headings relies on model inference to apply the right section, not deterministic file-path matching.
A CLAUDE.md per subdirectory breaks down exactly when files needing a shared convention (like the scattered utility files) are spread across many directories.
Skills are invoked on demand via a slash command, not applied automatically based on which files are being touched.

questions.stem: Root CLAUDE.md imports `@./standards/coding-style.md` via `@import`, which imports another file, which imports another, continuing the chain six levels deep. Content from the sixth-level file silently doesn't appear in context. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.why: The maximum import nesting depth is documented as 5 — a sixth level in a chain exceeds that limit and does not load.
ww: Fabricated restriction — the corpus states relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import, supporting cross-directory references, not a same-directory-only rule.

Fabricated — there is no documented rule limiting loading to only the root file's direct imports; the actual limit is a numeric nesting depth, which presupposes nested imports do load up to that depth.
Fabricated — the corpus explicitly states both relative and absolute paths are supported for `@import`, not absolute-only.

questions.stem: A Claude Code session spent an afternoon mapping the order-fulfillment service's dependency graph. The next morning, five files in the inventory-sync module are rewritten before the engineer returns to the investigation. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: When resuming after code changes, tell the agent exactly which files changed so it performs targeted re-analysis of just those files, rather than trusting stale results or re-exploring everything.
ww: Resuming and continuing as-is means the agent reasons over stale tool results for the five files that actually changed.
Restarting from scratch discards a mostly-still-valid investigation — wasteful when only five of many files actually changed.
`/compact` risks losing exact details like specific file names and dependency edges during summarization, and doesn't target the specific files that changed.

questions.stem: Migrating the order-fulfillment service off its old logging library, a single prompt asking Claude Code to both enumerate every call site and rewrite each one in the same pass produces inconsistent results — several call sites are missed, and two are converted twice. What restructuring is most effective?
questions.why: Breaking a complex combined task into sequential focused prompts, where each step's output feeds the next, produces more focused and consistent output at each stage.
ww: 'Work faster' isn't a documented technique — it doesn't address why a combined enumerate-and-rewrite pass produces inconsistent results.
Forcing a tool call guarantees a tool gets called, not that a single combined pass becomes internally consistent — it misapplies a structured-output mechanism to a decomposition problem.
Adding more detail to an already-failing combined instruction doesn't fix it — this mirrors the rejected 'lengthen the prose description' fix for inconsistent transformations.

questions.stem: The engineer's CLAUDE.md instructs Claude Code to 'make sure new endpoints have good test coverage.' Generated tests for a newly scaffolded endpoint cover only the happy path — no validation errors, no empty-input case. What change most reliably improves test quality?
questions.why: Moving from an abstract instruction to explicit, testable criteria is the documented fix for vague guidance producing inconsistent, shallow output.
ww: Repeating an already-vague instruction more emphatically doesn't add the missing concrete criteria — it mirrors the rejected 'describe the bug more emphatically' fix.
`--json-schema` guarantees output structure and format, not the substantive coverage of the tests themselves — a mismatched mechanism for this problem.
A larger model doesn't fix an under-specified instruction — the instruction stays ambiguous regardless of model size.

questions.stem: A request comes in simply as 'add export functionality to the reports module' — no format specified (CSV, PDF, or Excel are all plausible). Relayed as-is, Claude Code asks five clarifying questions before writing any code, stalling the task. What is the most effective way to handle this kind of vague request?
questions.why: Stating explicit, reasonable assumptions and proceeding, while inviting corrections, avoids the abandonment risk of front-loading multiple clarifying questions before any progress is visible.
ww: Bundling all five questions into one message still demands effort from the requester before any code exists — it doesn't solve the underlying stall.
Speculatively building every plausible format is infrastructure overkill for a request that may only need one — the documented fix is stating an assumption, not building for every possibility.
Hidden defaults leave the requester unaware of what was assumed, causing confusion when the delivered format doesn't match unstated intent.

questions.stem: A hard-to-reproduce order-fulfillment bug investigation runs 40+ turns in one Claude Code session. Early on, the exact error code (`ERR_STALE_LOCK_409`) and the specific line where it originates were pinned down precisely. By turn 35, after summarization, Claude refers only to 'a locking-related error somewhere in the reservation path.' What fix most directly addresses this?
questions.why: Extracting precise transactional facts into a persistent block kept outside the summarized history preserves them verbatim, surviving whatever compression the rest of the conversation undergoes.
ww: Revising the summarization prompt still relies on the summarizer executing perfectly every time — it doesn't structurally guarantee precision survives.
Raising the summarization threshold only buys more turns before the same precision loss eventually happens — it doesn't fix the underlying problem.
`session_id` isn't a real API mechanism, and an external database is overkill for facts that only need to persist within one session.

questions.stem: During a long refactor session, Claude Code follows the order-fulfillment service's CLAUDE.md formatting and error-handling conventions precisely for the first 15 turns, then begins drifting toward inconsistent formatting. The session is only 3,000 tokens — nowhere near any context limit. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: As assistant responses accumulate, CLAUDE.md's instructional influence dilutes relative to the growing body of the model's own prior output — not a token-limit or one-time-loading problem.
ww: Context window overflow is explicitly ruled out — 3,000 tokens is far below any practical context limit.
CLAUDE.md is included in every request, not just the first turn — the 'applies once' framing is a documented false explanation.
The scenario already shows the conventions were correctly followed for 15 turns, ruling out a never-loaded file — a `/memory` check would show it present, not missing.

questions.stem: Reviewing a 3,000-line consolidated diff spanning the templating and logging migrations, Claude Code's summary accurately covers the diff's opening import changes and its closing test updates, but never mentions a breaking API-signature change that sits in the diff's middle third. What is the most effective way to fix this pattern?
questions.why: Claude reliably attends to the beginning and end of long input but has degraded attention in the middle; placing a key-findings summary up front and adding explicit section headings surfaces mid-diff changes in the positions Claude actually attends to.
ww: Rotating which files appear first doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern — the breaking change would still land in whatever position is now the 'middle,' regardless of file order.
Compressing the diff to fit under a token target risks summarizing away the very breaking-change detail this problem is about preserving, rather than surfacing it.
A larger context window changes how much fits, not where Claude's attention is strongest — lost-in-the-middle degradation is a positional attention pattern, not a capacity limit.

questions.stem: A single marathon Claude Code pair-programming session covering the templating migration, the logging migration, and plenty of general discussion reaches 82,000 tokens. It contains exact API-contract decisions, edge cases agreed on, and casual back-and-forth. The engineer wants to cut tokens while preserving what matters. What approach best balances this?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — extracting critical structured facts, summarizing lower-density discussion, and keeping recent exchanges verbatim — preserves precision that pure summarization or truncation would lose.
ww: Uniform summarization of the entire history loses exact detail, the same precision-loss risk the corpus flags for critical values.
Keeping only the most recent tokens drops the early API-contract decisions entirely if they were established earlier in the session.
A larger context window doesn't fix the underlying precision and attention problem, and avoids reduction rather than solving it.

questions.stem: An engineer asks the agent to locate every file that still imports the deprecated helper `resolveShippingRate` before deleting it. The agent runs `Glob("**/resolveShippingRate*")` and reports two matches inside the helper's own module. A manual audit finds eleven more call sites elsewhere that the search missed. What is the most likely reason the search under-counted the callers?
questions.why: Glob is a file-path/name pattern matcher; it never inspects file contents. Grep is the tool for content search — finding what a file contains, not what it's named.
ww: Invents a recursion-depth limit on Glob that isn't documented anywhere in the corpus; the real cause is that Glob never inspects file contents at all, regardless of nesting.
Mirrors the corpus's own rejected pattern of widening a file-name Glob when the real requirement is a content search — a broader path pattern still never looks inside a file.
Invents a size ceiling for built-in Grep the corpus never documents; reaching for Bash grep bypasses the purpose-built tool without fixing why Glob was the wrong choice.

questions.stem: While standardizing a logging call across the reservation module, the agent's first `Edit` attempt targets the anchor `return response`, but it matches nineteen locations and fails. The engineer suggests shortening the anchor to just `return` to make the match 'more specific.' Before trying that, what should the agent do instead?
questions.why: When Edit's anchor is non-unique it cannot decide which occurrence to change; the sanctioned fallback is Read the full file, modify programmatically, then Write it back.
ww: Matches the corpus's documented misconception directly: a shorter, more generic anchor is MORE likely to be non-unique, not less — the opposite of what's needed.
Bypasses the tool built for the job; the corpus's sanctioned fallback for a non-unique Edit anchor is Read + Write, not a shell-level sed replacement.
Describes a disambiguation capability Edit doesn't have — the tool matches on a single anchor string, not a chained sequence of surrounding-line calls.

questions.stem: A newly onboarded engineer asks the agent to trace how order-cancellation requests move through the monolith. On the first attempt, the agent reads all 60+ files under `order/` before producing any output, and its summary ends up conflating the cancellation flow with an unrelated returns-processing flow living in the same directory. What investigation strategy would have avoided this?
questions.why: Codebase understanding should be built incrementally: Grep to find entry points and call sites, Read only what surfaces, then repeat — never bulk-read a whole directory upfront.
ww: Matches the corpus's own rejected pattern: Globbing an entire directory and reading every match before searching is the same upfront-bulk-reading anti-pattern, just routed through a different built-in tool.

A larger context window doesn't fix the anti-pattern — the agent still reads irrelevant files and still risks conflating unrelated flows that share a directory; the fix is targeted discovery, not more room.
Parallelizing the same bulk read doesn't address why it was the wrong strategy — the agent still ingests every file instead of following the flow's actual call sites.

questions.stem: The platform team defines a dedicated investigation subagent, spawned via the coordinator's `Task` tool, to map unfamiliar corners of the monolith. They want a guarantee that this subagent can explore freely but can never modify a file while doing so, even if a prompt asks it to. Which configuration most reliably enforces this?
questions.why: AgentDefinition.allowed_tools is a whitelist enforcing least privilege per subagent type; restricting it to Read/Grep/Glob makes Write/Edit/Bash structurally unavailable regardless of prompt.
ww: A prompt instruction is probabilistic, not a guarantee — the prompt cannot grant or withhold a tool that the configuration itself controls.
Contradicts least-privilege scoping; giving the full catalog and relying on the description alone is exactly the setup the corpus flags as producing scope creep, not a guaranteed restriction.
A per-call approval hook still permits the write if approved — it adds a gate, not a structural impossibility, unlike scoping allowed_tools so Write/Edit/Bash are never callable at all.

questions.stem: The team builds a `/trace-dependents` skill that catalogs every module depending on a legacy interface before a breaking change. After running it against a module's forty downstream modules, the engineer starts refactoring only that module itself — but the agent's next several suggestions keep proposing edits to downstream modules the trace merely catalogued. What fixes this?
questions.why: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent context so its large or exploratory output doesn't pollute the main conversation; only a summary returns.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected fix for this exact pattern — shrinking the output loses the analysis capability the trace exists to provide.
A faster model doesn't fix context pollution; the catalogued modules would still sit in the main session's context regardless of which model produced them.
Matches the corpus's rejected fix — splitting into two skills run in the same session doesn't prevent the catalogued findings from leaking into the next task's context.

questions.stem: The investigation subagent is asked to map every consumer of the monolith's `PricingEngine` module. Three of the eleven files it needs to read return a permission-denied error — they belong to a legacy team's locked-down directory — while the other eight read successfully. What should the subagent do with its findings?
questions.why: When upstream inputs are incomplete, the correct pattern is to complete synthesis with available data and explicitly annotate coverage gaps, not error out or hide them.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected response to partial upstream failure — aborting because input is incomplete discards the eight files that did succeed for no benefit.
Matches the corpus's rejected response — proceeding without noting the gap hides a real coverage hole from whoever consumes the map next.
Bypassing an access control to force a read isn't a sanctioned recovery pattern anywhere in the corpus and turns a permissions boundary into a security workaround instead of a reported gap.

questions.stem: The team plans to replace the monolith's decade-old job scheduler with a maintained open-source alternative — a change touching roughly 40 modules, with several viable target libraries and no agreement on which fits the monolith's retry semantics. An engineer is ready to implement against the first library that looks reasonable. Which execution approach should be used?
questions.why: Multiple valid approaches and architectural decisions across dozens of files call for planning mode: explore and design, present a plan for approval, then execute.
ww: Skips the actual architectural evaluation the task requires; picking by popularity alone is exactly the premature-execution risk planning mode exists to catch before dozens of files are touched.
Matches the corpus's documented exam trap verbatim: reactive switching from direct execution to planning mode only after trouble starts is expensive rework upfront planning avoids.
Conflates planning mode with a rigid, pre-ordered pipeline and defers the actual library decision past the point the task needs it decided.

questions.stem: The agent now drafts boilerplate PRs for new monolith modules, but engineers report it sometimes writes a module's tests directly into the module file instead of a separate test file — almost always on modules that don't yet follow the repo's usual `module/tests/test_module.py` layout. Which prompting change most effectively fixes this specific pattern?
questions.why: Few-shot examples should target the specific ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — 4-6 examples aimed at exactly those cases, not generic clear ones.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected pattern directly: examples of the clear, already-correct cases don't help the model handle the specific edge case where it's failing.
Matches the corpus's rejected pattern: the instruction is already failing, and restating it more forcefully doesn't give the model a concrete pattern to follow.

Temperature controls output randomness, not structural file-placement decisions — the corpus rejects this exact lever for fixing a specific behavioral pattern elsewhere, and the same mismatch applies here.

questions.stem: The coordinator asks three subagents to map how a fulfillment order moves from cart to shipment. Each finishes cleanly, but the combined map never covers inventory reservation or payment settlement, though all three report success. Coordinator logs show it decomposed the work into checkout UI, shipping label generation, and email notifications. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: When subagents all succeed but coverage is wrong or incomplete, the root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition, not subagent performance.
ww: Every subagent completed successfully within its assigned scope — the gap is in which subtopics were assigned, not what tools the subagents had.
Invents an interference mechanism the corpus never documents; nothing in the scenario points to cancellation code causing the omission.
Misattributes the gap to codebase structure when the coordinator's own logs show the real cause: it simply never created a subtask covering those two areas.

questions.stem: Late in a long mapping session, the agent's summaries start drifting — vague phrases like 'the relevant handler' instead of the file and line it cited accurately an hour earlier. Logs show the semantic-search MCP tool has returned full method bodies and relevance-score metadata for every hit all session. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Verbose tool results consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance; a PostToolUse hook trimming to only the fields the task needs conserves context and reduces noise.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected fix — the unwanted fields still consume tokens and attention even if the model is told to ignore them.
Matches the corpus's rejected fix — aggressive summarization treats the symptom while the same bloated tool results keep flooding in on every subsequent hit.
Matches the corpus's rejected fix — a bigger window raises cost and still leaves the noise problem, which is caused by field volume, not window size.

questions.stem: Two of the monolith's dozen modules handle payment adjustments and are subject to a compliance rule requiring an audit-log entry on every change — a rule that applies nowhere else. Pasting it into root `CLAUDE.md` means every session, even ones nowhere near payment code, loads it anyway. Which configuration applies the requirement automatically only where it's needed?
questions.why: .claude/rules/ with glob-pattern frontmatter loads automatically only when Claude works on matching file paths, keeping irrelevant sessions free of the rule and saving tokens.
ww: Skills are invoked on demand by name, not automatically by file path — an engineer has to remember to run it, exactly the reliability gap automatic path-scoping is meant to close.
Matches the corpus's rejected pattern: a labeled heading relies on the model inferring which section applies, not on deterministic file-path matching.

Doesn't use the supported modularization mechanism for this need and stops scaling as soon as a third payment-adjacent module appears; .claude/rules/ scopes by pattern instead of hand-maintained per-directory files.

questions.stem: The coordinator's prompt for the boilerplate-PR subagent is procedural: create the module file, then create `tests/test_<name>.py`, then create `docs/<name>.md`. On the twelve modules that don't yet have a `tests/` folder at all, the subagent halts with a path-not-found error instead of creating one. Which change to the prompt would most effectively prevent this class of failure?
questions.why: Procedural, step-scripted prompts are brittle when reality doesn't match the script; goal-oriented prompts stating what to achieve let the subagent adapt to structural variation it discovers.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected pattern — adding another scripted step for each newly discovered edge case deepens the same rigidity that caused the failure.
Matches the corpus's rejected pattern — running more passes through the same fixed script doesn't fix the script itself.
Still a rigid, procedural script underneath — swallowing the error avoids the crash but doesn't let the subagent reason about what structure the module actually needs.

questions.stem: Partway through debugging a slow order-cancellation endpoint, the agent's investigation into why it calls `PricingEngine` three times expands into tracing all nineteen of `PricingEngine`'s callers across the monolith, filling most of the session's context before the engineer can start on the actual fix. What should the agent have done once the investigation began expanding this far?
