questions.why: An Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output in its own context and returns only a summary, preserving the main session's context for the actual implementation work.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected fix — /compact mid-task loses the precision the engineer still needs to write the actual fix.
Matches the corpus's rejected fix — splitting across multiple sessions adds coordination overhead and consistency risk instead of isolating the verbose output.

Shifts the exploration burden onto the human instead of using the isolation mechanism the corpus prescribes for exactly this situation — verbose discovery belongs in a subagent, not offloaded to the engineer.

questions.stem: The same agent session that drafts a boilerplate refactor for `inventory/reservation.py` is then asked, in that conversation, to 'review your own change before we merge it.' It reports the refactor is safe. A human reviewer looking at the diff days later spots a locking bug within minutes. What most directly explains why the same-session check missed it?
questions.why: A model that generated code retains its own reasoning within the session and is anchored to its own decisions; true independence requires a separate instance with no access to that reasoning.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected fix — more reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny; extended thinking doesn't remove the anchoring.
Matches the corpus's rejected fix — adding self-review instructions to the generation prompt still runs inside the same context, inheriting the same confirmation bias.
Matches the corpus's documented misconception directly: a second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context and is not an independent review.

questions.stem: Once the investigation subagent maps the reservation module, its findings pass to a second subagent that drafts a refactor plan. The report is one free-text paragraph blending file names, line numbers, and reasoning together. The resulting plan cites structural issues but can't say which file or line each came from. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Structured formats that separate content from metadata (file paths, line numbers) preserve attribution through the pipeline; merged free text is where that traceability gets lost.
ww: Matches the corpus's rejected fix — re-deriving the same information duplicates work and risks attributing an issue to the wrong location the second time around.
Matches the corpus's documented misconception directly — the subagent cannot cite metadata it never received in structured form; an instruction can't manufacture data that was never passed.

Collapses the separation of responsibilities between investigation and planning without fixing the actual cause — the metadata loss happens in how findings are formatted, not in there being two subagents.

questions.stem: The review job runs `claude -p` from the monorepo's `services/billing/` directory on every PR touching that service, so review context stays scoped locally, but engineers worry the subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` there will silently replace the root `CLAUDE.md`'s org-wide review criteria for those PRs. What actually happens to the two files' instructions?
questions.why: Discovered CLAUDE.md files (root down to working directory) are concatenated into context in load order; there is no documented override mechanism between levels. Conflicting instructions must be resolved by editing the files themselves, not by relying on one level to win.
ww: Misconception: a directory-level file does not replace a higher-level one. Both sets of instructions load together — treating this as override precedence is the exact trap the corpus flags.
Fabricated restriction — nothing scopes subdirectory CLAUDE.md discovery to interactive local sessions only; `-p` mode discovers the same hierarchy.
No such mechanism exists. The documented model is concatenation by directory level, not a modification-timestamp precedence rule.

questions.stem: The review job's finding layer exposes `flag_line_finding` (single line) and `flag_file_finding` (whole file, e.g. missing coverage) — both described only as "Flags an issue for review." Across roughly 40 PRs a week, logs show file-wide issues get filed via `flag_line_finding` attached to line 1 in 30% of cases. What should the team check first?
questions.why: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses for selection. When misrouting occurs, check whether descriptions distinguish the tools' scope and boundary cases before reaching for any other fix — the exact fix the corpus applies to near-identical tool descriptions.
ww: A post-hoc rewrite hook patches the symptom after the wrong tool already fired with the wrong location semantics — it doesn't fix why the model chose wrong in the first place.
Adding a pre-routing classifier is infrastructure layered on top of an ambiguous signal instead of fixing the signal — the documented anti-pattern for tool misrouting.
Merging into one tool loses the semantic precision that lets the model distinguish scope at a glance — the corpus rejects consolidating similarly-purposed tools for this reason.

questions.stem: The team added 12 few-shot examples to the review prompt to fix inconsistent severity labels — all obviously-critical security bugs or obviously-trivial style nits. On a 200-finding audit sample, misclassification at the high/medium boundary (e.g., a null-dereference behind an already-checked guard) stays around 35%. Which change most reliably improves boundary accuracy?
questions.why: Few-shot examples work best when targeted at the specific ambiguous cases causing errors, not generic unambiguous ones. 4-6 examples at exactly the boundary, each with a rationale, is the documented fix for misrouting/misclassification driven by edge cases.
ww: More clear-cut examples repeats the failed approach at greater volume — 10-15 unambiguous examples don't help with the edge cases actually being misclassified.

Lengthening written instructions when the format/consistency problem already survived one round of prose refinement repeats a distinct, already-failing pattern; examples anchor a boundary judgment better than more prose.
Fabricated flag — no `--severity-strict` flag exists in the documented CLI reference; severity is a model judgment, not something a CLI flag can enforce.

questions.stem: The pipeline now routes large PRs through a coordinator that delegates security, performance, and style analysis to separate subagents. On a PR flagged for a possible injection risk, logs show the coordinator's own reasoning states it should hand off to the security subagent, but no subagent ever runs. What should the team check?
questions.why: A coordinator's `allowedTools` must include `"Task"` or it cannot spawn subagents regardless of how well it reasons about wanting to — the tool grant, not the prompt, is what enables delegation.
ww: The prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds — this is the exact named pattern in the corpus: instructing delegation in the system prompt does nothing if `Task` was never whitelisted.

Subagent descriptions matter for choosing AMONG available subagents once delegation is possible, but they don't enable delegation itself if `Task` was never granted — this addresses a downstream concern, not the actual blocker.
Context window size has no bearing on whether a tool is present in an agent's whitelist — this misdiagnoses a configuration gap as a capacity problem.

questions.stem: To cut startup overhead on a branch now receiving 6-8 PRs a day, an engineer proposes having the review job `--resume` the same named session across every PR opened against that fast-moving feature branch, instead of starting a new session per PR. What is the most effective way to evaluate this idea?
questions.why: When the underlying files a session's tool results describe are going to differ from run to run, a resumed session reasons over old tool results as if they were current. Starting fresh is preferred whenever prior tool results would be stale.
ww: Optimizes for the wrong variable — the risk isn't reload cost, it's that the resumed session treats a previous PR's file contents as still current when reviewing a different PR's diff.
An arbitrary file-count threshold doesn't address the actual failure mode: a small PR can still be reviewed against stale assumptions carried over from the last resumed review.
Fabricated claim — the corpus documents no such incompatibility. The reason to avoid resuming here is context staleness, not a nonexistent CLI restriction.

questions.stem: Since the review job adopted `--json-schema` output three weeks ago, zero findings have failed schema validation. A 500-finding sampling audit still finds 6% are labeled "critical" for issues that are demonstrably low-risk under the team's own rubric. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: Schema enforcement eliminates syntax errors but does nothing for semantic correctness — output can be perfectly schema-valid and still contain a wrong value. The fix is a business-rule/semantic validation layer, not a tighter schema.
ww: No JSON Schema constraint can verify that a severity judgment matches rubric intent — schema tightening only catches structural violations, never semantic ones.
Reverting to prose reintroduces the syntax-error class (malformed output, missing fields) that schema output eliminated, on top of a semantic problem that would remain either way.
A 6% mislabeling rate on severity is exactly the semantic error class the corpus flags as needing detection, not dismissal — unaddressed it erodes trust in the categories developers rely on.

questions.stem: The job's `post_finding` tool fails two different ways: on fork-originated PRs the CI token lacks comment-write permission (never succeeds no matter the retry count); on internal-branch PRs, failures are occasional network timeouts (succeed on retry). Both currently return an identical generic error, and the job retries every failure 3 times. How should the tool's error handling be restructured?
questions.why: Transient errors should be retried; permission/permanent errors never succeed regardless of retry count and should return non-retryable status with details immediately. Conflating the two wastes retries on an outcome that cannot change.
ww: Backoff only helps the transient case — no amount of retrying resolves a genuine permission denial, so uniform backoff still burns retries on the fork case for nothing.
Forcing the agent to guess the failure type from error text alone is explicitly ranked worse than structured error categorization.
Disabling review for an entire class of PRs discards legitimate coverage instead of fixing the error-handling design that already distinguishes the two failure types.

questions.stem: On a 22-file PR, the review job's analysis pass times out on 4 large generated files but completes normally on the other 18. The job currently posts its summary exactly as if the review were complete, with no mention that 4 files went unanalyzed. What should the output do differently?
questions.why: When upstream analysis is incomplete, complete with available data and annotate coverage — mark what's well-supported vs. where gaps exist — rather than erroring out entirely or proceeding as if nothing is missing.
ww: Failing the whole check over a partial timeout blocks merge over a recoverable gap and discards the 18 files' worth of legitimate findings — exactly the overreaction coverage annotation exists to avoid.
The coverage-annotation pattern is about completing with available data and marking the gap, not indefinite silent retrying that delays the whole summary and may still fail on the same files.
Posting the summary with no indication of the 4 unanalyzed files hides the gap — developers can't tell a clean 22-file pass from an 18-file pass, the exact failure mode annotation prevents.

questions.stem: On PR #4,821, a developer comments "/review focus on the risky parts," on a change touching both a payment-retry function and an unrelated formatting-only edit to a config file. "Risky" is undefined. Rather than pausing the pipeline to ask what counts as risky, how should the review job proceed?
questions.why: For vague requests, the documented approach is to proceed with stated, reasonable assumptions and invite correction — this avoids blocking on clarification while keeping the developer informed of what was assumed.
ww: Blocking the pipeline to ask a clarifying question mirrors the rejected "ask clarifying questions" pattern, which causes high abandonment — here it stalls an automated PR check for a resolvable ambiguity.
Hidden, unstated defaults leave the developer unable to tell what was assumed when the output doesn't match intent — explicitly rejected alongside asking too much.

Even one batched message of multiple questions still demands developer effort and blocks the automated check before any analysis happens — the documented fix is stated assumptions, not fewer-but-still-blocking questions.

questions.stem: On PR #2,203, the review job posts three findings on one function: a retry-lock race condition, a backoff calculation that assumes the current locking behavior, and an unrelated log-message typo. The developer will hand all three to Claude Code to fix. How should the findings be batched into prompts?
questions.why: Interacting issues — where fixing one affects the other, as with a locking change and a backoff calculation that depends on it — belong in one detailed message so Claude designs one coherent change; independent issues (the typo) don't need that coordination.
ww: Fixing the locking and backoff bugs strictly one at a time risks each patch contradicting the other, since the backoff fix's correctness depends on knowing the new locking design.
There's no documented "oldest-issue-first" sequencing rule; what matters is whether issues interact, not report order — this also still risks the same sequential-fix conflict.
Bundling every finding together regardless of relationship isn't the documented rule — the independent typo doesn't need to be coupled with the interacting pair.

questions.stem: The test-generation subagent started with Read, Write, and the repo's test runner. Over several months, engineers added a deploy-script trigger and direct database-seed access "for convenience." It then ran the deploy trigger against shared staging while generating tests for an unrelated PR, disrupting another team. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Each subagent should have only the tools its defined scope needs. Accumulated "convenience" tools outside test generation's actual role caused the incident; the fix is restoring least privilege by removing them, not managing their use after the fact.
ww: A prompt instruction limiting how a tool is used is probabilistic — the subagent already had the tool and used it outside its intended scope once; telling it not to doesn't remove the capability.
Better descriptions help a subagent choose correctly among tools it needs, but don't address the actual root cause — the subagent shouldn't have deploy/database-seed access at all for its scope.

A blanket human-approval gate on every tool call is disproportionate infrastructure that slows down routine test-generation calls, when the fix is simply not granting out-of-scope tools in the first place.

questions.stem: The review job's coordinator burns 5-8 tool calls each run issuing guessed `list_open_findings` queries just to discover which finding categories currently exist, before it can search productively. The finding-tracker MCP server could expose this information without an exploratory call. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: MCP resources expose content catalogs — giving the agent an upfront map of what data exists without exploratory tool calls — exactly the fix for a coordinator burning calls to discover categories it could just read.
ww: Building a custom server for something a resource already solves reinvents effort the corpus reserves for genuinely team-specific workflows, not category exposure a resource handles natively.
A tool the coordinator must remember to call still costs an LLM call and relies on the agent thinking to use it first — a resource provides the map as readable context instead.
A static system-prompt dump goes stale as categories change and bloats context permanently, unlike a resource requested on demand.

questions.stem: The pipeline runs three CI-triggered analyses: a pre-merge style check that blocks the PR until it completes, a nightly test-generation job for changed modules, and a weekly full-repo security audit. The team wants to cut cost by moving eligible work onto the Message Batches API's 50% discount. Which assignment is correct?
questions.why: The nightly and weekly jobs are non-blocking and latency-tolerant — ideal for the Batches API's savings. The pre-merge check blocks a developer, and batch's lack of an SLA (up to 24h) is unacceptable for something someone is actively waiting on.
ww: Frequency isn't the deciding factor — the pre-merge check is exactly the blocking, latency-intolerant task the Batches API is wrong for, regardless of how often it runs.
Refusing batch anywhere discards real savings on two workloads that are genuinely non-blocking; the batch API's latency profile is a mismatch only for the pre-merge check, not the other two.
Batching the pre-merge check would leave developers blocked for up to 24 hours with no SLA — "eventually completes" ignores that the task requires an immediate response.

questions.stem: An engineer on the eight-person platform team built `/pr-checklist` at `~/.claude/commands/pr-checklist.md`, used by both her local sessions and a CI step. The team wants it available to the CI job and to every developer automatically on clone, with no per-machine setup. Where should the command file live to achieve this?
questions.why: Project-wide commands belong in the repo's `.claude/commands/` (or the richer `.claude/skills/`) directory — version-controlled and auto-available to every developer's checkout and to CI, unlike the personal `~/.claude/commands/` location.
ww: The personal commands folder is not version-controlled — manual copying is exactly the per-machine setup the team wants eliminated, and it won't reach the CI runner either.
Restricting it to the CI runner's install defeats the stated goal of making it available to every developer locally, not just the pipeline.
`context: fork` isolates a skill's output into a subagent context to avoid polluting the main session — it has nothing to do with where the file needs to live to be shared and auto-available.

questions.stem: Weeks after a "critical" mislabeling incident on a payment-retry finding, the team wants findings to self-flag disagreements between the model's free-text severity judgment and a rubric-derived score computable from the same evidence, instead of catching mismatches only in periodic manual audits. Which schema design most directly achieves this?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern has the model re-derive and compare a claimed value against an independently computed one within the same structured output — flagging disagreement at generation time instead of relying on later manual review.
ww: A free-text explanation isn't machine-readable and doesn't structurally flag disagreement — a reviewer must still read every note to notice a mismatch, the exact after-the-fact process the team wants to move earlier.
More few-shot examples might reduce the error rate somewhat, but it's a probabilistic mitigation, not a detection mechanism — it flags nothing about the findings where disagreement still occurs.

Averaging two instances' scores produces one blended number with no signal of whether or how much they disagreed; independent review is a different pattern aimed at generation-time blind spots, not structural self-flagging.

questions.stem: A document-analysis subagent starts sending findings straight to the synthesis subagent over a shared queue, skipping the coordinator, to save a round-trip. Within a week, synthesis output silently omits findings the coordinator never sees, and a subagent failure goes unnoticed until the report is missing a whole subtopic. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Coordinator-as-hub means all inter-agent communication and error handling stays centralized: routing document-analysis output through the coordinator restores its visibility into what each subagent produced and lets it decide retries or escalation uniformly.
ww: A periodic digest still leaves synthesis and document-analysis communicating directly day-to-day; the coordinator only sees a delayed summary, not real-time visibility into failures — the direct-communication problem isn't actually undone.
Retrying a lost message treats the symptom (a dropped send) without restoring the coordinator's visibility or centralized error handling that hub-and-spoke exists to provide.
Pushing failure detection onto the synthesis subagent means each agent now handles its own errors independently — exactly the fragmented pattern the coordinator hub is designed to avoid.

questions.stem: An engineer wires a custom `verify_citation` tool into the synthesis subagent's request. When the subagent issues two tool calls in the same turn, the application's tool-execution code appends both results to the conversation, but Claude occasionally treats the second result as belonging to the first call. What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Each `tool_use` block carries a unique `id`, and the matching `tool_result` block must reference that same `id` so Claude can correctly associate results with calls. Omitting or mismatching it causes exactly this cross-attribution when multiple calls occur in one turn.
ww: Tool count affects which tool gets selected, not whether a returned result is correctly matched to its originating call — a different mechanism.
`input_schema` validates the shape of Claude's tool call arguments before execution; it plays no role in matching a `tool_result` back to its `tool_use` block.
`tool_choice` controls whether and which tool Claude must call, not how results are subsequently matched to calls already made.

questions.stem: The team wants a research system that always follows the same steps for standard competitive-landscape briefs: search, extract company profiles, validate figures, then format. Separately, they're prototyping open-ended requests like "assess this emerging technology's societal impact," where nobody knows the relevant subtopics until initial findings come in. Which decomposition strategy fits each case?
questions.why: Predictable, template-shaped work (the same four steps every time) is the textbook fit for a fixed sequential pipeline; open-ended scope that only becomes clear from initial findings needs dynamic adaptive decomposition that generates subtasks as discoveries emerge.
ww: Dynamic decomposition adds planning overhead the fixed-structure brief doesn't need — the corpus recommends the fixed pipeline specifically when steps are stable and reproducibility matters, not defaulting to adaptive everywhere.
A fixed script can't react to what the open-ended request's initial findings reveal; its scope is unknown up front by design, which is exactly when adaptive decomposition is called for instead.
This pairs each task with the wrong strategy — the predictable brief doesn't need adaptive replanning, and the open-ended request can't be scripted in advance.

questions.stem: The web-search subagent's `search_web` tool is described only as "searches the web for a query and returns results." When a researcher pastes a specific article URL into a request, the subagent calls `search_web` with the URL as the query instead of handing it to the document-analysis subagent's fetch tool. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses for selection; stating explicitly what the tool is for and naming the boundary case it should NOT handle fixes the root cause at the source.
ww: A classifier is added infrastructure that compensates for an ambiguous description instead of fixing it — checking descriptions first is the stated priority before adding routing layers.
Combining the tools loses the semantic distinction Claude needs to select between them — the corpus names this exact merge as the wrong fix for a misrouting example.
A prompt example nudges behavior probabilistically; it doesn't change what the tool's own description tells Claude about scope on every future call, which is where the fix belongs.

questions.stem: The web-search subagent's external search API returns a quota-exceeded response mid-task. Today the subagent simply reports `{"status": "failed"}` to the coordinator, which cannot tell whether to wait and retry, switch source categories, or continue with partial findings. What change would most effectively let the coordinator make an intelligent recovery decision?
questions.why: A structured error payload — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and alternatives — is what lets the coordinator choose retry, reroute, or continue with partial data instead of guessing from a bare status.
ww: Silent retrying without reporting to the coordinator hides the failure entirely and blindly burns time against a quota window of unknown length — the coordinator never gets to decide.
Reporting completion with zero results when the query never actually ran misrepresents a failure as a valid empty result, corrupting the coordinator's downstream decisions.
Bypassing the coordinator for an error it could resolve with a simple retry-or-reroute decision skips the hub's role in uniform error handling and adds unnecessary human load.

questions.stem: Before delegating research subtasks, the coordinator must survey an internal document repository of several thousand files to see what topics and date ranges exist. Doing this directly in the coordinator's own session returns hundreds of summaries and nearly fills its context before delegation starts. What is the most effective way to run this survey?
questions.why: An isolated subagent absorbs the verbose discovery output and returns only a concise summary, preserving the coordinator's context for the actual orchestration work that follows.
ww: `/compact` mid-task compresses away the specific precision the coordinator will need to decompose accurately — this is the rejected alternative to subagent isolation.
Reading every file directly in the coordinator's own session is exactly the bulk-context consumption the survey needs to avoid — the isolation subagent exists precisely to prevent this.
Without a shared map, each subagent re-discovers structure independently, duplicating effort and leaving the coordinator's own decomposition just as uninformed as before the survey was proposed.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent's `query_source_archive` tool sometimes returns `{"results": [], "isError": true}` and sometimes `{"results": [], "isError": false}` for what production logs show are actually two different situations: a genuinely empty archive section, and an archive index that is temporarily unreachable. How should the tool signal these two outcomes?
questions.why: An empty result set from a query that actually executed is a valid, successful answer; an unreachable index is a genuine access failure. Signaling them differently lets the agent trust a real 'nothing found' and correctly retry or escalate the access problem.
ww: Marking an unreachable-index case as a non-error empty result causes the subagent to confidently report 'nothing found' when the archive was never actually queried — a false statement caused by masking an access failure.
Flagging a genuine zero-match query as an error causes the subagent to retry or escalate a query that already succeeded, wasting effort on a valid finding.
The tool already has the information needed to distinguish the two cases; discarding it and returning an identical generic message forces the coordinator to guess when a clear signal was available.

questions.stem: Policy requires every source be checked for license restrictions before use in synthesis, since paywalled data can't be quoted verbatim. Today this rule lives only in the synthesis subagent's system prompt. An audit finds 8% of drafts quote paywalled sources unchecked. What change most reliably guarantees the check happens every time?
questions.why: For mandatory sequencing where getting it wrong has real consequences, a programmatic precondition enforces the rule deterministically at the code level — a prompt instruction, however strongly worded, remains probabilistic.
ww: A more emphatic prompt instruction is still guidance the model may or may not follow every time — it doesn't change the fundamentally probabilistic nature of prompt-level enforcement.
Few-shot examples improve consistency but remain a prompt-level technique; for safety- or compliance-critical sequencing the corpus calls for code-level enforcement, not better examples.
Catching violations after the report is drafted doesn't prevent them from occurring — it's detection, not the deterministic precondition the policy actually requires.

questions.stem: The research team wires a shared MCP server for a paid market-data API into everyone's Claude Code setup, but each researcher holds a separate personal subscription key. Leadership wants one configuration file everyone pulls from version control, with no working key ever committed to the repo. Which configuration approach is most effective?
questions.why: `.mcp.json` is project-scoped and version-controlled, giving the whole team the same server configuration; `${VAR_NAME}` substitution lets each researcher's own key be supplied from their environment at runtime without ever entering the repository.
ww: User-scoped `~/.claude.json` configuration isn't shared or version-controlled, so each researcher ends up with independently drifting tooling instead of one consistent team configuration.
Hardcoding any real key into a version-controlled file, even as a 'placeholder,' commits a credential to the repository — exactly what env-var substitution exists to avoid.
Keeping the whole configuration user-scoped means there is no shared, version-controlled source of truth for the team, defeating the stated goal of consistent tooling.

questions.stem: For a request needing both fresh news and analysis of an uploaded filing, the coordinator issues one `Task` call to web-search, waits for its full response, then issues a separate `Task` call to document-analysis next turn — though neither depends on the other. What most effectively reduces latency here?
questions.why: Multiple `Task` calls emitted in a single coordinator response execute in parallel; issuing them across separate turns runs them sequentially instead, which is exactly the latency this request doesn't need to pay.
ww: Merging the subagents collapses the specialized, narrowly-scoped roles hub-and-spoke design depends on, rather than fixing the actual sequencing issue.
Giving document-analysis a search tool creates cross-specialization scope creep instead of using the parallel-execution mechanism already available to the coordinator.
Caching addresses repeated identical queries, not the fact that two independent, non-cached subtasks are being run sequentially when they could run in parallel.

questions.stem: Months ago, a researcher created a personal `/cite-check` skill at `~/.claude/skills/` to tweak citation formatting to their taste. The team has since updated the shared project skill to a new house style, and every teammate's output reflects it — except this researcher's, even though their repo checkout is current. What is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.why: A personal skill at `~/.claude/skills/` overrides a project skill of the same name — a forgotten old personal copy keeps shadowing the team's updated version until it's removed or brought in line, even with an up-to-date repo checkout.
ww: The scenario states the checkout is current, ruling out a stale-pull explanation — the divergence is caused by something outside the repo itself.
There is no documented restart requirement for shared skill updates to apply; this invents a mechanism not present in the corpus.
`context: fork` isolates a skill invocation's output from the main session — it has no role in determining which of two same-named skill files takes precedence.

questions.stem: When a request needs both current news and an uploaded filing summarized, the coordinator's `Task` calls to web-search and document-analysis now run in parallel, but inside the web-search subagent, `search_web` and `fetch_snippet_details` still run in separate turns even when both are clearly needed. What most effectively reduces this?
questions.why: The corpus's preferred fix for this exact pattern is prompting the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn, since Claude can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously — creating a composite tool is explicitly the less-preferred alternative.
ww: A composite tool works but is the corpus's non-preferred approach here — it hides the composition rather than letting the model naturally request both tools together in one turn.
Caching addresses redundant identical calls, not the separate-turn pattern driving the extra round-trip — a different problem than the one described.
Adding a decision-making tool is unneeded infrastructure for a case the corpus resolves with a simple prompt instruction to bundle requests.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent's one prompt asks it to both identify which claims need a citation and write the full narrative in the same pass. Reviewers find citation coverage inconsistent — some well-supported claims go uncited while marginal ones get cited. An engineer wants more thorough citation identification without changing which claims make the report. What is the most effective restructuring?
questions.why: Breaking a task that does two things at once into a sequential chain — each step's output feeding the next — produces more focused, consistent output at each stage than asking one pass to do both jobs together.
ww: A more detailed instruction is still one prompt asking the model to do two things simultaneously; it doesn't address the attention split causing inconsistent citation coverage.

A larger context window gives the model more room but doesn't change that citation-identification and narrative-drafting are competing for attention within a single pass — this targets the wrong problem.
Generating two full independent drafts and merging them adds cost and complexity without directly separating the citation-identification step from the drafting step the way a focused chain does.

questions.stem: While configuring the three research subagents, an engineer proposes giving each one the full tool catalog — web search, document fetch, citation verification, and formatting — reasoning that any subagent could then substitute for another during a bottleneck. What is the most effective response to this proposal?
questions.why: `AgentDefinition`'s `allowed_tools` whitelist per subagent type IS the mechanism for least privilege and separation of responsibilities — the corpus explicitly rejects 'give every subagent the full tool set for flexibility' as backwards reasoning.
ww: Full tool access for every subagent breaks the least-privilege scoping that separation of responsibilities depends on — a subagent outside its specialization is prone to misuse, not a safety net.

A prompt note asking subagents to self-restrict is probabilistic; it doesn't change what `allowed_tools` actually grants, so nothing structurally prevents a subagent from calling a tool outside its role.

Building an extra subagent for overflow calls doesn't address the actual proposal to grant blanket tool access, and adds infrastructure where `allowed_tools` scoping already solves the problem directly.

questions.stem: The research team's system also maintains an archive of every completed research project going back months, totaling well over 100K tokens. A researcher asks the coordinator to recall a specific caveat one project's synthesis flagged about a data source's methodology three months ago. What is the most effective way to support this kind of recall?
questions.why: For specific recall from months of accumulated history, semantic embeddings with retrieval of the relevant past exchange find the precise caveat on demand — unlike a rolling window or summarization, retrieval doesn't discard or compress away the specific detail.
ww: A rolling window keeps only recent projects, and the caveat in question is three months old — this discards exactly the content the recall needs.
Progressive summarization compresses specific quoted conclusions like a methodology caveat into vague abstractions that can no longer be recalled precisely — the same failure mode this warns against.
Section headings address lost-in-the-middle attention within a single long input, not retrieval of a specific past exchange from months of separate archived projects — a different problem entirely.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline's review-flagging step is instructed to 'flag any document with an unclear or possibly incorrect field appropriately for manual review.' Audit of 200 documents shows a missing `tax_id` field is flagged in some documents but not others with the identical gap, and reviewers say the flagging feels arbitrary. What change most reliably makes flagging consistent?
questions.why: Vague instructions like "flag appropriately" produce inconsistent behavior; the documented fix replaces abstraction with explicit, testable criteria, not more emphasis or more instructions.
ww: More emphatic wording is still the same abstract instruction — the corpus explicitly rejects "add more detailed/explicit instructions" as a fix when the instruction itself, not its intensity, is the problem.
An independent second-instance review addresses self-review confirmation bias, not an undefined flagging rule — the criteria ambiguity persists regardless of who reviews.
One-sided examples of only the positive case don't establish where the boundary is, and don't replace the underlying vague criteria with testable ones.

questions.stem: Your extraction pipeline has three tools — one each for invoices, receipts, and PO confirmations — and an upstream classifier tags each file's type. To guarantee a structured call every time, an engineer hard-codes `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}` on every request, ignoring the classifier's tag. Receipts and PO confirmations now come back with invoice-only fields full of nulls and guesses. What should the team change?
questions.why: The `tool_choice` table shows `{"type": "any"}` guarantees Claude calls some tool — it never returns plain text — while still leaving the choice of which tool to Claude's judgment. Unlike `{"type": "tool", "name": "X"}`, which locks every single request to that one named tool no matter what the document actually is, `any` keeps the structured-output guarantee while restoring correct per-document tool selection.
ww: Falling back to `{"type": "auto"}` reintroduces the exact problem the engineer set out to prevent: auto permits Claude to skip tool calls entirely and answer in plain text, so the pipeline would lose its guarantee of a structured call on any document — not just the misrouted ones.

`PostToolUse` hooks fire only after a tool call completes; they can discard a bad result but cannot stop the wrong tool from being invoked in the first place, since `tool_choice` already forced `extract_invoice` before the hook ever runs.

Once `tool_choice` names a specific tool, Claude has no discretion to decline that call based on its description — tool_choice, not the description, is what controls selection here, so rewriting the description changes nothing while tool_choice stays hard-coded to it.

questions.stem: One legacy onboarding path still requests JSON via prompt instructions only, without `tool_use`. Responses often open with "Certainly! Here is the extracted data:" before the JSON body, and the downstream parser — which expects the response to start with `{` — throws on roughly 8% of calls. Migrating this path to `tool_use` is scheduled for next quarter. What should the team do in the meantime?
questions.why: Prefilling seeds the start of the assistant's message so Claude continues from it rather than generating a fresh response; this is the documented technique for suppressing a filler/preamble phrase, and applies directly here to force immediate JSON continuation ahead of the scheduled migration.
ww: Temperature controls randomness across generations broadly, not a specific recurring phrase — it doesn't reliably suppress a particular preamble.
A prompt instruction to avoid a specific opening is probabilistic; the corpus ranks this less reliable than prefilling for suppressing filler phrases.
Fixes the symptom in the parser after generation rather than at generation time, and stays fragile to any drift in how the preamble is worded.

questions.stem: A single prompt call extracts obligations from a 45-page merger agreement concatenated into one document. Party names and the closing signature block extract reliably every time, but financial covenants embedded in pages 20–25 are frequently missed or returned with generic placeholder values. What is the most effective way to restructure the extraction input?
questions.why: Content in the middle of long input suffers degraded attention; the documented mitigation is a key-findings/navigation summary at the start plus explicit section headings, not shrinking, reordering, or enlarging the input.
ww: Summarizing to fit a smaller budget risks discarding exactly the covenant language the extraction needs — the corpus explicitly rejects "summarize to under [X] tokens" as losing critical information.
Rotating presentation order doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern — the corpus explicitly rejects rotation as a lost-in-the-middle fix.
A bigger context window doesn't fix attention quality at a given position; the covenants already fit within the current window and are still missed.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline handles three workloads: a single-document lookup a support rep waits on live during a call, a nightly re-run of the previous day's failed extractions, and a one-time 300,000-document historical backlog with no one waiting on results. Which assignment of each workload to an API approach is correct?
questions.why: Match the API to latency tolerance: the rep waiting live needs an immediate synchronous response, while both the nightly re-run and the one-time backlog are non-blocking and latency-tolerant, so both qualify for the Batches API's 50% discount.
ww: Routes the live, latency-sensitive lookup to Batches, whose up-to-24-hour window with no SLA is unacceptable for a rep waiting on an active call.
Leaves the nightly re-run on synchronous, paying full price for a workload that is explicitly non-blocking and a textbook batch candidate.
Forcing the live lookup onto Batches ignores latency tolerance entirely — "batch everywhere for the discount" is the documented misconception.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline's classification, extraction, and validation subagents each report success on every document, yet the coordinator's logs show it routes only `invoice` and `receipt` categories to those subagents, even though roughly 20% of the incoming stream is purchase-order confirmations that silently fall through unclassified. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: When every subagent executes correctly but coverage is wrong, the root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition; here it never assigned the purchase-order category to any subagent in the first place, not a failure inside a subagent.
ww: Subagents are reported succeeding on everything they're given; the missing coverage happens upstream of extraction, in what gets routed to it at all.
Nothing in the logs shows validation rejecting purchase orders — they never reach the pipeline's subagents to be validated in the first place.
A description problem would cause misrouting between existing categories, not the wholesale absence of a category from the decomposition.

questions.stem: Since moving to `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema, extraction responses always parse and every field passes type validation. But reconciliation still flags 4% of invoices where `total_due` holds the pre-tax subtotal instead of the tax-inclusive total the schema description asked for. How should the team respond?
questions.why: Strict schemas via `tool_use` eliminate the syntax-error class entirely but do nothing for semantic errors (valid JSON, wrong content); a value in the wrong field passes schema validation by definition, and the fix is business-rule validation plus retry with the specific error, not the schema itself.
ww: Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce syntax errors on top of the semantic error already present — the corpus explicitly rejects this reasoning.
No type constraint (string vs number, required vs optional) can verify which of two numerically valid values is the semantically correct one.
Nothing in the scenario points to validation-set sizing; the described failure is a category of error type validation cannot catch, regardless of test-set size.

questions.stem: A vendor sends periodic amendments to the same service contract. The extraction pipeline pulls a price clause from the original contract and, months later, a different price from an amendment covering the same clause. Downstream reconciliation flags this as a data conflict requiring manual reconciliation. What extraction design change most directly prevents this false conflict?
questions.why: Without dates, temporal differences between documents are misread as contradictions; capturing the effective/publication date lets downstream logic recognize a later, dated amendment as an update rather than a conflict.
ww: Silently picking a value without surfacing the reasoning discards the audit trail entirely, and an amendment doesn't always supersede the original for every downstream purpose.

This is the documented failure mode itself — flagging every numeric disagreement as a conflict without dates misreports normal temporal change as contradiction, which is what's already happening here.
Merging documents before extraction destroys the provenance the pipeline needs and doesn't scale as more amendments arrive; the fix is metadata, not document flattening.

questions.stem: A classification step routes each intake document to one of three extraction tools by type. Clear invoices and clear receipts route correctly nearly every time; documents that are simultaneously a receipt and a tax-deductible donation acknowledgment are misrouted about 40% of the time. An engineer plans to add few-shot examples to fix this. Which set of examples is most effective?
questions.why: Target 4–6 examples at exactly the ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong, each with rationale, rather than broad coverage of the easy cases.
ww: Examples of the clear, unambiguous cases don't address the specific boundary the model is failing on — the documented anti-pattern.
A schema/format example addresses output shape, not the routing decision that is actually failing here.
Random sampling isn't targeted at the known failure mode and will mostly reinforce cases the model already handles correctly.

questions.stem: A due-diligence run cross-checks a bundle of 12 related loan documents for consistency in a single prompt call. QA finds thorough, accurate flags on the first two or three documents, but shallow coverage after that — and an identical missing-signature pattern is flagged in document 3 while the same pattern is missed in document 9. What is the most effective restructuring?
questions.why: Single-pass review over many items causes attention dilution: detailed on some items, shallow on others, with inconsistent flagging of the same pattern; the fix is per-item passes plus a separate integration pass, not a bigger single pass.
ww: A larger context window doesn't fix attention quality — the corpus explicitly names this exam trap, and the documents already fit in the current window.
Shrinking the batch without restructuring into per-item passes still risks the same dilution within whatever subset is processed together, and leaves the rest unplanned.
Asking for self-checking within the same pass doesn't address attention dilution across many items — the same cognitive-overload conditions still apply within one response.

questions.stem: An extraction system routes low-confidence fields to human review and auto-processes everything else. Six months after launch, no auto-processed extraction has been re-examined. A new invoice layout was introduced by a major vendor three months ago. What should the team implement to catch a hidden failure mode in that auto-processed stream?
questions.why: Even high-confidence, auto-processed extractions need regular stratified sampling across document types and layouts; this is the documented way to detect novel error patterns, like an unvalidated new vendor layout, before they compound, since the automated path is otherwise never re-examined.
ww: Lowering the threshold shifts the boundary but still leaves the auto-processed segment unaudited — it doesn't measure whether the new layout is actually handled correctly.
Reviewing everything defeats the purpose of automation and doesn't scale — the corpus explicitly rejects universal human review as the fix for targeted oversight.
Waiting for downstream complaints is reactive; stratified sampling exists precisely to catch the error before it compounds and reaches reconciliation.

questions.stem: The validate-then-retry loop resubmits failed extractions with only the message "Extraction failed, please retry" — no specifics. On documents with wrong-format dates and misplaced currency symbols, all three retries still fail, though the source clearly contains the correct data. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The retry-with-feedback loop must carry the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error; format and structural errors are exactly the class retry can fix when the model is told precisely what's wrong, and a generic "try again" gives it nothing to correct.
ww: More attempts don't help when every attempt receives the same uninformative feedback — the loop is information-limited, not retry-count-limited.
Nullable fields are the correct fix when information is genuinely absent from the source, the corpus's other documented case; here the data is present and the model just needs the specific error.
Skipping retries entirely burns human review capacity on errors the model could fix itself if simply given the specific validation error.

questions.stem: An intake document arrives as a one-page scan with ambiguous formatting — it plausibly matches either the receipt schema or the invoice schema, and nothing in the document definitively resolves which. The pipeline currently pauses and queues the document for a human to specify the type before continuing. Backlog on these ambiguous scans is now three days deep. What should the pipeline do instead?
questions.why: For ambiguous input, proceed with a stated, reasonable assumption and record it for correction rather than blocking; blocking to ask causes exactly the backlog described, and the assumption must be explicit, never a silent default.
ww: Waiting on the sender to respond keeps the document blocked exactly as before, just through a different channel — it doesn't fix the backlog.
Adding another required field at intake burdens every sender on every document to solve a problem that affects only a minority of ambiguous scans.
Continuing to queue every ambiguous document is the status quo generating the three-day backlog; the corpus explicitly rejects blocking over stating assumptions.

questions.stem: A reconciliation specialist works an extended interactive session correcting a batch of vendor credit notes, one after another, in a single long-running conversation. Early on, an agreed $12,450 credit adjustment is confirmed. Forty exchanges later, the session's summary of that adjustment reads only "a credit adjustment was discussed," and the final reconciliation entry uses the wrong amount. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Precise transactional facts get compressed into vague references during summarization; the documented fix is a persistent case-facts block held outside the summarized history and included verbatim in every prompt, not a better summarizer.
ww: A higher threshold only delays the same compression — the exact figure is still eventually summarized away.
Still relies on the summarization step executing perfectly every time — the corpus explicitly rejects this as an incomplete fix.
Restarting periodically loses conversational continuity and doesn't address why precise facts get compressed in the first place — it just resets the clock.

questions.stem: A long interactive extraction session processes a stream of scanned invoices one at a time in the same conversation. The system prompt states that a missing purchase-order number must be returned as `null`, never invented. Through the first 14 documents this holds; by document 15, with the session still only 4,000 tokens, the model starts fabricating plausible-looking PO numbers. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: As assistant responses accumulate, system prompt influence dilutes relative to the growing body of the model's own output, even at low token counts; this is the documented root cause, distinct from context overflow.
ww: 4,000 tokens is far below any context limit, so overflow cannot be the cause, and the system prompt is included in full on every request regardless of length.
The system prompt is sent with every API call, not just the first — this exact misconception is explicitly named and rejected in the corpus.
Nothing in the scenario suggests the schema configuration itself changed; the drift described is behavioral (rule-following), not a change to the schema.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Claude Code to always run an extra local formatting pass before finishing, a habit the rest of the eight-person team doesn't want imposed on their sessions. They want it active only in their own use, with no change to what teammates see after cloning the same repo. Where should this instruction go?
questions.why: User-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies only to that developer and is never version-controlled or shared with teammates, exactly matching a personal habit that shouldn't reach the rest of the team.
ww: `.claude/rules/` is a project-level, version-controlled mechanism for path-scoped conventions — still shared with the whole team regardless of which glob is chosen, so it doesn't solve the personal-vs-shared distinction.
Root `CLAUDE.md` is checked into version control and available to all team members — the opposite of what's needed here.
Skills in `.claude/skills/` are project-shared by default and require deliberate slash-command invocation — neither automatic nor personal-only, and every teammate who pulls the repo would see it.

questions.stem: Your team wants a stricter commit-message format enforced automatically whenever Claude Code touches files inside the `release/` branch-prep directory, but nowhere else — most sessions never open that directory and shouldn't load the extra convention. Which configuration achieves this without adding the rule to every session's context?
questions.why: Rules load automatically only when Claude works on files matching the glob pattern in their frontmatter, which is exactly the mechanism for a convention scoped to one directory.
ww: Root `CLAUDE.md` under a heading loads every session and relies on model inference rather than deterministic path matching — the corpus's own exam scenario rejects this approach.
Fabricates how `.claude/rules/` works — the corpus specifies YAML frontmatter with a `paths` glob array as the trigger; omitting it doesn't produce inference-based loading.
Skills are invoked on demand via a slash command — not automatically applied when Claude touches matching files.

questions.stem: A coordinator spawns subagents via Task to migrate a codebase off a deprecated logging library. Its prompt reads: 'Step 1: find files importing old-logger. Step 2: replace with new-logger. Step 3: run tests.' Migration stalls whenever a file uses old-logger in a way the fixed steps didn't anticipate. What change to the prompt fixes this?
questions.why: Goal-oriented prompts that state goals and quality criteria let subagents adapt as findings emerge; this matches the documented fix for shallow, script-locked coordinator behavior.
ww: The corpus explicitly rejects this — adding more detailed steps "deepens the rigidity that caused the problem."
The corpus explicitly rejects this — more agents executing the same bad script doesn't fix the script.

Bolts a vague escape hatch onto an otherwise still-fixed, still-procedural script; it never states goals or quality criteria, so it doesn't grant the genuine adaptive investigation the corpus describes.

questions.stem: Your team's `/scaffold-endpoint` skill writes new API endpoint files and explains its naming choices so the developer can keep refining them in the same conversation. An engineer proposes adding `context: fork` to the skill's frontmatter "to keep the main session clean." What is the effect of doing this, and is it appropriate here?
questions.why: `context: fork` runs a skill in an isolated subagent context, best for discovery/exploration whose output shouldn't pollute the main session; implementation work meant to be continued in conversation belongs in the main session, so forking here removes needed continuity.
ww: Fabricated — `context: fork` doesn't disable tool access; scoping what a skill can do is `allowed-tools`'s role, a separate mechanism.
Fabricated interaction — `context: fork` and `argument-hint` are independent frontmatter keys with no documented gating relationship.
Inverts the mechanism — fork isolates output rather than merging it, and this pattern reserves it for exploration, not as a universal default.

questions.stem: Your team's `generate-component` CI script calls the Claude API directly with a `write_component_file` tool so Claude can scaffold new React components. A new engineer's version sends the request and marks the run complete as soon as the response contains a `tool_use` block, but no file ever appears on disk. What is missing from the script?
questions.why: Claude only returns a `tool_use` content block requesting that a tool run — it never executes anything itself. The application executing the tool and appending a `tool_result` content block are the calling application's own responsibility. The script is missing exactly that step: nothing in it reads the `tool_use` block, performs the write, or reports the result back.
ww: `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` only guarantees Claude requests some tool call instead of replying in prose — Claude is already calling `write_component_file` correctly here, so forcing a tool call changes nothing about whether the file gets written.

A richer description is the corpus's fix for tool-selection ambiguity between similarly-named tools — Claude is already selecting the right tool, so the problem isn't which tool gets picked, it's that nothing ever executes it.

`PostToolUse` hooks are a Claude Code harness feature that fires around tool calls the harness itself executes; a standalone script calling the Messages API directly has no such hook mechanism, and even inside Claude Code a hook doesn't substitute for the application's own responsibility to execute the tool.

questions.stem: An engineer wrote `/scaffold-endpoint` as a plain file at `.claude/commands/scaffold-endpoint.md`, predating the team's skills. It reads the endpoint name typed after the command. A teammate insists this legacy file no longer works and must become a `.claude/skills/` folder first. Is the teammate correct, and what holds the typed text?
questions.why: Legacy `.claude/commands/` remains supported and creates the same `/name` invocation as skills; the text typed after the command name is available inside the file as `$ARGUMENTS`.
ww: Fabricated obsolescence — the corpus confirms legacy commands still work; `.claude/commands/` and `.claude/skills/` are unified, not sequential replacements.
`context: fork` is an isolation mechanism unrelated to whether a legacy command file functions — a fabricated fix for a nonexistent problem.
Confuses `argument-hint` (a displayed prompt hinting what args are expected) with `$ARGUMENTS` (the actual variable holding the typed text) — two distinct mechanisms.

questions.stem: During a multi-day session migrating a payment SDK, the team agreed to pin the library to v4.2.1 (not v4.3.0, a known regression) and keep a 750ms retry-timeout override. Forty exchanges and several summarization rounds later, Claude proposes pinning v4.3.0 and drops the override. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A persistent case-facts block outside summarized history survives compression, preventing exactly this kind of precision loss on technical values.
ww: The corpus explicitly rejects this — raising the threshold "still eventually gets compressed," just delays the same failure.
The corpus explicitly rejects this — still relies on the summarizer executing the instruction perfectly every time.
The corpus explicitly rejects this — external storage plus a new retrieval tool is overkill for session-level facts.

questions.stem: Adding multi-currency checkout support touches pricing, cart, and receipt modules, and the team hasn't settled whether amounts should be integer minor units or decimals, or how per-currency rounding should work. An engineer is ready to have Claude Code start implementing immediately and adjust once problems surface. What should they do instead?
questions.why: Large scope, cross-module architectural decisions, and multiple valid approaches (representation, rounding) call for planning mode first, then direct execution once approved — the documented combined approach.
ww: The corpus's own exam trap — "start in direct execution and switch to planning when it gets hard"; reactive switching is expensive, plan upfront when the task demands it.
Ignores that the representation/rounding decision is cross-cutting and must be made once, not independently per module — risks inconsistent designs across pricing, cart, and receipts.
Over-engineering — generating three competing implementations doesn't resolve the undecided design question, just multiplies unreviewed code three ways.

questions.stem: A developer unfamiliar with tax rules asks Claude Code to implement a discount-stacking calculator. The first attempt applies discounts in the wrong order; the second fixes that but ignores a tax-exempt category; the third fixes that but mishandles a coupon-plus-loyalty combination. Each fix only addresses the most recently discovered gap. What should the developer do on the next attempt?
questions.why: The interview pattern surfaces unfamiliar-domain requirements up front, replacing several correction cycles with one clarifying turn.
ww: The corpus explicitly names this the slow, inferior path — "each fix can disturb the last."

Concrete examples fix format/transformation-shape inconsistency when requirements are already known but described ambiguously — they don't surface domain rules the developer never stated because they didn't know them; wrong mechanism for this failure.
Over-engineering — two independent parallel implementations both face the same unknown-domain gap, so duplicating generation doesn't surface the missing requirements either.

questions.stem: Asked to bump a feature-flag timeout, Claude Code finds the flag defined in three config files — `dev.yaml`, `staging.yaml`, and `prod.yaml` — with different existing values, and the request doesn't say which environment(s) to change. Rather than guessing, what should Claude Code do?
questions.why: This is the Multiple-Match Disambiguation pattern: when several genuine candidates exist and the request doesn't disambiguate, request additional identifiers rather than picking by heuristic.
ww: The corpus explicitly rejects heuristic selection ('select the most recently active account') — the same failure class here, since recency risks the wrong target.
Silently over-scopes the change to resolve ambiguity instead of asking — risks an unintended `prod.yaml` change, the opposite of the corpus's caution.
Still a guess (production-first assumption) dressed as risk reasoning, rather than confirming the actual intended scope.

questions.stem: An engineer wraps Claude Code in a nightly script that regenerates typed client bindings: `claude "Regenerate the TypeScript client from openapi.yaml"`. Cron logs show the process starts, prints the prompt, and produces no further output until it's killed two hours later. What is the correct way to invoke Claude Code so the script completes on its own?
questions.why: `-p`/`--print` processes the prompt, prints to stdout, and exits; without it, Claude Code waits for interactive input and the pipeline hangs.
ww: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` does not exist.
A documented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned approach.
`--batch` does not exist as a Claude Code CLI flag.

questions.stem: Your team wired an automated review step into the Claude Code CI pipeline to flag issues in every merged PR. Three months of data show null-dereference findings dismissed only 5% of the time and resource-leak findings 11%, but import-ordering findings are dismissed 44% and variable-shadowing findings 49% — and developers now skim past every finding, including the reliable ones. What should the team do first?
questions.why: High-false-positive categories erode trust in the accurate categories too — once developers start skimming past everything, even the reliable null-dereference and resource-leak findings stop getting read. Surgically disabling the two noisy categories stops the trust bleed immediately while the two reliable categories keep providing real signal, buying time to rework the noisy ones before re-enabling them.
ww: Confidence scores still surface every import-ordering and variable-shadowing finding — developers already report skimming past everything regardless, so attaching a number to findings they've stopped reading doesn't restore trust.

Few-shot refinement is the corpus's legitimate eventual fix for the noisy categories, but it takes weeks to move dismissal rates — during that time the flood continues and trust keeps eroding, including in the two categories that were never the problem.

A uniform strictness cut damages the categories that were already reliable (5%/11% dismissal) to compensate for two unrelated noisy categories — the corpus flags this as unnecessary damage to accurate signal rather than a targeted fix.

questions.stem: A nightly automation invokes Claude Code to propose refactor suggestions for stale utility modules, then feeds the output into a script that opens one ticket per suggestion with `module_path`, `suggested_change`, and `estimated_effort` as separate fields. The script currently regex-parses Claude's prose output and breaks whenever the wording shifts. Which invocation most reliably gives the script parseable fields?
questions.why: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` guarantees well-formed, schema-parseable output for downstream tooling.
ww: The corpus explicitly rejects this — a `CLAUDE.md` format section "is not guaranteed consistent."
The corpus explicitly rejects this — a prompt format instruction has "variable compliance."
Symptom-level fix — patches the fragile parser instead of guaranteeing structured output at the source.

questions.stem: A long Claude Code session refactoring authentication middleware follows a stated instruction — 'never remove backward-compatible parameter names, only deprecate them' — for the first eight exchanges. By the eleventh exchange, at just under 3,400 tokens total, it silently drops a legacy parameter in a suggested diff. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.why: The root cause is accumulated assistant responses diluting system-prompt influence, not context overflow and not a first-turn-only misconception.
ww: The corpus explicitly rejects this — context overflow is impossible at a few thousand tokens.
The corpus explicitly names this false — the system prompt is included in every request, not just the first turn.
Fabricated mechanism — no documented session-cache-expiry behavior exists for system-prompt instructions.

questions.stem: Your team runs three workloads: (1) generating docstrings interactively while a developer pairs with Claude Code, (2) a nightly job drafting a changelog from the day's merged PRs, and (3) a one-time bulk pass documenting 50,000 legacy functions with no deadline pressure. Which assignment to the Message Batches API is correct?
questions.why: Synchronous for blocking/interactive work; batch for scheduled, non-blocking tasks that tolerate up to 24 hours, generalized here to nightly changelog drafting and one-time bulk documentation.
ww: Misclassifies the nightly changelog job as urgent — nightly, non-blocking jobs are exactly the batch-appropriate case.
Batch's no-SLA, up-to-24-hour window is incompatible with (1)'s live interactive requirement — the same reasoning behind never batching interactive, iterative work.
Fabricates a scope restriction; batch applies to any latency-tolerant Claude workload, not only extraction.

questions.stem: Your repository automation must always run `format_code` before `commit_changes` fires, so every commit is consistently formatted. Today this rule lives only in the system prompt: 'always format before committing.' A monthly audit finds 5% of automated commits skip formatting, mostly during high-volume batch runs. Which change most reliably closes this gap?
questions.why: Critical sequencing for a mandatory step requires a programmatic precondition (deterministic code-level enforcement), not a prompt instruction, because prompt compliance is probabilistic and fails under load exactly as observed here.
ww: Strengthening the wording is still a prompt-level fix; prompt instructions remain probabilistic regardless of phrasing intensity — the corpus explicitly rejects "strengthen the system prompt" as the fix for mandatory sequencing.

Few-shot examples improve consistency for ambiguous format or selection problems, but they don't guarantee sequencing — mandatory ordering needs deterministic enforcement, not better examples of the desired order.
Human review addresses a subset of commits after the fact rather than fixing the root cause; it also adds friction to every high-volume run instead of resolving why formatting gets skipped.

questions.stem: Your boilerplate-generation harness always invokes Claude Code exactly three times per request, then stops. On simple scaffolds, the third call is wasted after Claude already finished with a clean final answer; on complex scaffolds needing four tool calls, the harness cuts off before Claude finishes. What should the harness check instead?
questions.why: The agentic loop's continue/stop decision is driven by the structured `stop_reason` field (`tool_use` → execute and continue, `end_turn` → stop), not by a fixed call count or any heuristic on response content.
ww: Parsing text for a completion keyword is the natural-language-parsing trap the corpus explicitly rejects — Claude's final answer wording varies and may never mention "done" even when it has genuinely finished.

A wall-clock or call-count budget is disconnected from what Claude actually needs to do; it produces exactly the two failure modes described — wasted calls on simple tasks, premature cutoff on complex ones.
Whether a tool result is non-empty says nothing about whether Claude intends to call another tool or has finished responding — it isn't the API's actual continuation signal.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to scaffold 12 new module files from a boilerplate template, then review all 12 in one pass for consistency. The single pass gives detailed feedback on the first few files, misses a naming-convention violation repeated in three others, and never checks whether the generated files agree with each other. How should the review be restructured?
questions.why: A single pass over many files dilutes attention (deep on some files, shallow on others) and misses cross-file inconsistencies; the corpus-favored fix is per-file local passes plus a separate integration pass for cross-file issues.
ww: A bigger context window does not fix attention quality — the corpus explicitly rejects "larger model / bigger context" as the fix for attention dilution; more tokens available doesn't mean consistent attention per token.
Sampling only 6 of 12 files trades thoroughness for focus and guarantees some files are never reviewed at all — it doesn't address why the pass was shallow, it just shrinks the problem.

Keeping only findings that repeat across two identical single-pass runs suppresses real issues that surface only once and does nothing to fix the underlying attention-dilution cause — a consensus-filtering distractor, not a restructuring.

questions.stem: A coordinator investigating an unfamiliar payment-authorization module is given only a goal: 'produce a complete map of how authorization requests flow end to end, noting any external dependencies discovered along the way.' No steps are scripted. Which named pattern does this coordinator prompt exemplify, and why does it outperform a scripted investigation checklist here?
questions.why: This is goal-oriented delegation: stating the goal and quality criteria instead of a step-by-step script lets the coordinator adapt as it uncovers dependencies, which is exactly why it fits open-ended investigation better than a fixed checklist.
ww: Prompt chaining names the opposite pattern — a fixed sequential pipeline of predetermined steps — which is the corpus's own example of what fails for open-ended, discovery-driven investigation.
Least-privilege tooling is a real named pattern but describes tool-access scoping, not how the goal itself is framed; it answers a different question than what this prompt exemplifies.
Coverage annotation describes how a synthesis output marks confidence and gaps after research completes — it isn't a description of how the initial goal-stating prompt itself is structured.

questions.stem: An investigation subagent scanning legacy modules for a deprecated API pattern hits two kinds of failure: some files are on a network-mounted share that occasionally times out, others are binary artifacts that can never be parsed as text. Today both failures return a bare 'failed' status, and the coordinator retries the binary-artifact failures three times before giving up. What should the subagent report instead?
questions.why: Transient failures (timeout, network) merit retry with backoff, while permanent failures (a file that can never parse as text) will always fail and should be logged and skipped, not retried; the subagent must return structured error context distinguishing the two.
ww: A blanket "always retryable" signal wastes retries on the binary-artifact failures, exactly the wasteful pattern described in the stem — it doesn't distinguish the two failure types at all.
Pushing cause-diagnosis back onto the coordinator for every failure defeats the purpose of structured error reporting and adds manual work the subagent is better positioned to do automatically.
A shared generic code collapses two failure types that need opposite responses (retry vs never-retry) back into one undifferentiated signal — the same problem the stem describes today.

questions.stem: A coordinator investigating three independent legacy modules — authentication, billing, and notifications — for a deprecation audit spawns one investigation subagent via `Task` per module, but issues each `Task` call in its own separate coordinator turn, one after another. Investigation latency triples versus running them together. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Multiple `Task` calls only run in parallel when emitted together in a single coordinator response; issuing them across separate turns runs them sequentially regardless of how independent the modules are, so the fix is batching the calls into one response.
ww: Collapsing three independent, differently-scoped investigations into one subagent trades away specialization and least-privilege benefits without addressing the actual latency cause, which is sequential turns, not subagent count.
Adding more subagents doesn't fix latency if the coordinator still emits their `Task` calls one turn at a time — the root cause is turn structure, not subagent count.
A larger token budget per turn has no bearing on whether `Task` calls execute in parallel; parallelism is determined by whether the calls appear together in one response, not by available tokens.

questions.stem: An automation renaming a deprecated config key across the codebase discovers the key is also referenced inside a third-party vendor plugin directory that sits outside version control, with no record of whether anything in production still depends on it. Nothing in the runbook addresses vendor-owned code. What should the automation do?
questions.why: This combines a policy gap with high-stakes ambiguity: the runbook doesn't cover vendor-owned code, and guessing wrong could break production dependencies, so escalation criteria call for escalating rather than inventing policy.
ww: Applying the rename anyway invents a policy stance the runbook never stated — the same "apply own-site rules" mistake the corpus rejects when policy is genuinely silent on a case.
Silently skipping and reporting completion hides the gap from whoever relies on the automation's output — the corpus explicitly rejects proceeding without noting an unresolved gap.
Retrying doesn't apply here — this isn't a transient technical failure, it's a policy-interpretation question that retries can never resolve regardless of attempt count.

questions.stem: Two investigation subagents mapping a legacy service each hit a permission-denied error on a locked directory. One subagent silently skips the files and continues; the other halts entirely and returns nothing. Both report to the same coordinator. Which architectural principle, if followed, prevents this kind of inconsistent handling?
questions.why: The coordinator is the hub because it centralizes error-handling decisions and information control; subagents should surface structured failures upward and let the coordinator decide consistently, rather than each subagent inventing its own handling.
ww: Hardcoding retry logic separately into each subagent's own prompt is still decentralized, probabilistic per-instance behavior — it doesn't create the coordinator-level consistency the architecture is designed to provide.
Merging the subagents sacrifices the separation of responsibilities that hub-and-spoke exists to preserve, and doesn't scale as more specialized subagents are added.
