Direct subagent-to-subagent communication is explicitly the pattern hub-and-spoke architecture prohibits — it removes the coordinator's visibility into what happened and breaks centralized error handling.

questions.stem: Your `cleanup_stale_branches` automation exposes a `dry_run: boolean` flag so engineers can preview which branches would be deleted before anything actually runs. Logs show the automation sometimes invokes it with `dry_run=false` on the very first call, skipping the preview step policy requires. Which redesign makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible?
questions.why: The two-tool token-binding pattern makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible, since the confirmation token the execute step requires only exists after a genuine preview call; a single tool with a boolean flag can always be called with the flag skipped.
ww: A prompt reminder is exactly the probabilistic fix the corpus rejects for this pattern — the agent can still call the tool with `dry_run=false` regardless of what the prompt says.
Auditing after the fact detects the problem once branches may already be deleted; it doesn't prevent the skip from happening in the first place.
A confirmation string is just another parameter the agent can supply on the same first call — it doesn't require an actual prior preview to have occurred, so it's still bypassable.

questions.stem: A documentation-generation subagent frequently needs to check the linter's current rule configuration while writing code examples, adding a full round-trip through the coordinator to the linting subagent nearly every time. Complex linting-policy questions are rare. What is the most effective tool configuration for the documentation subagent?
questions.why: A narrowly scoped cross-role tool is the sanctioned exception to strict role separation for a high-frequency simple need; it avoids constant coordinator round-trips while complex cases still route through the coordinator to the specialized subagent.
ww: Giving the documentation subagent the full linting tool set risks cross-specialization misuse — it can now attempt open-ended linting-policy work well outside its scope, the exact failure mode scoped tools are meant to prevent.

This preserves correct scoping but does nothing about the overhead problem described — the round-trip cost on a high-frequency simple need is precisely what a scoped cross-role tool exists to eliminate.

Merging the subagents collapses their distinct specializations and undermines least-privilege tool scoping for no benefit beyond avoiding round-trips, which a scoped tool already solves without merging.

questions.stem: An automation uses Bash-driven search-and-replace across the codebase for repetitive cleanup tasks. Engineers want a guarantee that any single Edit or Write operation touching more than 50 files triggers mandatory human confirmation first — not just a reminder the agent might follow. What should they configure?
questions.why: A `PreToolUse` hook is deterministic code that intercepts tool calls before execution and can block operations above a defined threshold, guaranteeing the confirmation step regardless of what the LLM decides, unlike any prompt-level instruction.
ww: A prompt instruction to pause is probabilistic — the agent may proceed with a large change without pausing, exactly the guarantee gap the engineers want closed.
A boolean parameter the automation itself sets is bypassable the same way `dry_run=false` is bypassable — nothing forces it to be set correctly before the operation proceeds.
Few-shot examples can improve consistency for ambiguous format or selection problems, but they don't guarantee threshold enforcement — the agent can still proceed without confirming.

questions.stem: Before migrating snapshot tests to a new format, an engineer asks Claude Code to enumerate every snapshot test file across a mixed monorepo. The agent greps file contents for the word 'snapshot' and misses dozens of snapshot files that never contain that literal word, while also matching unrelated files that mention it in a comment. What tool should it use instead?
questions.why: This is a file-path pattern-matching task, not a content search: Glob finds files by name/extension pattern, which is exactly what's needed to enumerate snapshot files regardless of what text, if any, they contain.
ww: This is a better Grep target than "snapshot" but is still content search — it inherits the same fundamental mismatch, since snapshot files here are identified by filename convention, not a reliably present internal string.

Reading every file in the monorepo upfront to manually classify each one is the exhaustive bulk-read anti-pattern the corpus rejects; discovery should be driven by targeted search, not exhaustive reading.
Shelling out to a custom script bypasses the built-in tool designed for exactly this job; Glob already performs efficient name-pattern matching without an ad hoc workaround.

questions.stem: Your project's CLAUDE.md now mixes two things: coding conventions every session should follow, and a lengthy checklist for scaffolding new boilerplate modules that only matters when creating one. Engineers scaffolding a new module say the checklist is essential then; engineers doing ordinary bug fixes say it's dead weight cluttering every session. How should this content be split?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md content loads in every session, so conventions everyone always needs belong there; workflow-specific guidance like a scaffolding checklist belongs in a Skill, invoked on demand only when that workflow is actually happening.
ww: Moving the always-relevant coding conventions into a Skill too means they'd require explicit invocation every session instead of loading automatically — exactly the coverage CLAUDE.md exists to guarantee for universal standards.
`.claude/rules/` loads based on file-path glob matching, not on which workflow (scaffolding vs. ordinary work) is underway — it's the wrong mechanism for workflow-scoped, not path-scoped, content.
A heading helps a human skim the file but doesn't reduce what actually loads into every session's context — the clutter problem persists regardless of navigation aids.

questions.stem: An engineer is centralizing scattered session-token-reading logic spread across 45 files into one shared helper. Locating every call site first produces a long list with surrounding context that fills most of the session's window before the design conversation about the helper's interface can even start. What is the most effective way to complete this discovery phase?
questions.why: An Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output (the full call-site listing) in its own context and returns a concise summary to the main session, preserving room for the design conversation that follows.
ww: `/compact` mid-discovery risks losing exact file and line-level details the design conversation still needs — it trades precision for space instead of isolating the verbose output.
A larger context window doesn't stop the call-site listing from crowding out the design conversation within that same session — it only delays the same problem to a bigger ceiling.
Skipping discovery risks missing call sites the engineer doesn't already remember, which is exactly the risk the discovery phase exists to eliminate before centralizing the logic.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to generate a boilerplate adapter that maps a legacy record format to a normalized schema through several conditional field transformations and unit conversions — a genuinely multi-step reasoning task. Which prompting addition most reliably improves accuracy here, and is it worth adding to a separate one-line boilerplate rename task too?
questions.why: A step-by-step reasoning cue measurably helps multi-step transformation tasks like conditional field mapping across formats, but the corpus explicitly says not to add it for single-step tasks, where it adds no value.
ww: Applying the cue "everywhere because it never hurts" ignores the corpus's explicit guidance that reasoning cues are for multi-step tasks — a single-field rename is a one-step transformation with nothing to reason through.

Few-shot examples address inconsistent format output, a different problem from reasoning depth on a multi-step transformation — the two techniques solve different failure modes and shouldn't be swapped for each other.
Temperature controls output randomness, not reasoning depth or multi-step accuracy — it doesn't address why a multi-stage transformation needs more deliberate reasoning.

questions.stem: Your support bot's agentic loop stops the moment any reply includes a `process_refund` or `escalate_to_human` tool_use block, treating those tool names as always final. Logs show cases where Claude calls `get_customer` first, expecting a follow-up `lookup_order` call, but the loop already returned a raw tool result instead of continuing. What should the loop check instead?
questions.why: The agentic loop is driven by the structured stop_reason field, not by which tool was named: execute on tool_use, append the result, call Claude again, and stop only on end_turn (D1 §1.1).
ww: This still ties continuation to specific tool names rather than the generic stop_reason signal — the same anti-pattern that caused the premature stop, just inverted (D1 §1.1).
Parsing response text for keywords instead of checking the structured stop_reason field is probabilistic and unreliable — the documented anti-pattern for loop control (D1 §1.1).
An arbitrary iteration cap can cut off a case that genuinely needs a third tool call, or waste a call when Claude already finished after one (D1 §1.1).

questions.stem: A harness defines `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, and `escalate_to_human` as tools. When a response arrives with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` naming `escalate_to_human`, the harness marks the case escalated in its own database and ends the request, without calling the handler or sending anything back to Claude. If the session continues, it repeats the same escalation attempt. What step is missing?
questions.why: The agentic loop requires the application to execute the requested tool and append a tool_result content block matched to the tool_use id before Claude can continue — skipping this leaves the loop incomplete, which is why the session re-attempts the escalation (D2 §2.1).
ww: Checking the id field matters for matching tool_use to tool_result once the tool runs — it doesn't substitute for actually executing the tool and returning a result (D2 §2.1).
tool_choice only shapes which tool Claude selects on a future request; it doesn't perform the missing execution-and-result step needed to close out this tool_use (D2 §2.1).
stop_reason is returned by Claude, not set by the application — the harness cannot manufacture end_turn to paper over a step it skipped (D2 §2.1).

questions.stem: Your `process_refund` tool's description reads only: 'Issues a refund for a given order.' It expects an order_id formatted as ORD-12345. Production logs show 9% of calls fail validation because the agent instead passes the raw digits a customer types in chat, like '12345', or the subject line of the customer's order-confirmation email. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool descriptions must specify the accepted input format, with an example and boundary cases — that's the primary lever for tool selection and input handling, and the first thing to fix before adding infrastructure (D2 §2.2).
ww: Silently reformatting non-conforming input masks the underlying description gap and risks quietly converting a genuinely wrong ID into a different, still-wrong, valid-looking one (D2 §2.2).
Renaming clarifies the tool's purpose relative to other tools, but does nothing to specify the expected format — these failures are about format, not ambiguity between similar tools (D2 §2.2).
A preprocessing classifier is infrastructure that compensates for an under-specified description rather than fixing the signal itself — fix the description first (D2 §2.2).

questions.stem: `process_refund` accepts a list of order IDs to refund several at once. Policy requires any single call refunding more than 5 orders to be routed to a human for sign-off before it executes. Today the rule lives only in the system prompt. A monthly audit finds 3% of bulk refund calls above that threshold execute anyway, mostly during high-volume shifts. Which change enforces this deterministically?
questions.why: PreToolUse hooks are deterministic code that fires before a tool executes, making threshold enforcement guaranteed regardless of LLM behavior — exactly the gap a prompt-only rule leaves open (D2 §2.7).
ww: Still a prompt instruction — probabilistic, and the exam distinguishes hooks (deterministic) from prompts (probabilistic) precisely for safety-critical thresholds (D2 §2.7).
PostToolUse fires after the tool has already executed — logging after the fact detects the violation but doesn't prevent an unauthorized bulk refund from completing (D2 §2.7).
A lower threshold in the same prompt-only mechanism doesn't change that the rule can still be skipped; it only shrinks the exposure window (D2 §2.7).

questions.stem: The support widget now lets a customer refresh the page mid-conversation while your backend keeps the same conversation ID in its own database. After a refresh, the agent has no memory of anything said before, even though the conversation ID hasn't changed. An engineer proposes fixing this with a persist_context: true field on the Claude API request so the API retains prior turns server-side.
questions.why: Claude's API is fully stateless; every call is independent, so the only way conversation 'memory' persists is the application including the complete prior messages in the request every time (D5 §5.1).
ww: persist_context is not a real parameter — the exam corpus consistently debunks fabricated flags that imply server-side memory (Key Distinction #25).
No session_id parameter exists on the Messages API; this is the exact documented misconception the corpus calls out for stateless-memory questions (Key Distinction #25).
--resume is a Claude Code CLI concept for developer sessions, not a mechanism available to a customer-facing web widget calling the Messages API directly (D5 §5.1).

questions.stem: As your support bot scales, it splits into a coordinator plus billing-disputes and returns subagents, both able to call process_refund. The returns subagent is wired to notify the billing subagent directly once it approves a refund, bypassing the coordinator. A damaged-item return and a separate double-billing dispute on the same order each independently approve a refund, and the order is refunded twice before anyone notices. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The coordinator is the hub; subagents never communicate directly, precisely so the coordinator has the visibility needed to catch a conflict like a duplicate refund before either one executes (D1 §1.2).
ww: Direct subagent-to-subagent messaging still breaks the hub-and-spoke architecture; it adds a manual check instead of restoring the coordinator's visibility (D1 §1.2).
A shared lock is infrastructure patched around the missing coordinator visibility rather than restoring the architecture that would have caught the conflict up front (D1 §1.2).
A once-daily reconciliation catches the duplicate after the fact; it doesn't prevent the customer from being refunded twice in the first place (D1 §1.2).

questions.stem: The returns subagent's AgentDefinition is configured with all four tools — get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human — though its scope is only to evaluate return eligibility and issue refunds. Over several weeks it starts unilaterally escalating billing disputes that belong to the billing subagent's scope, since nothing in its configuration stops it. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: allowed_tools is the configuration-level lever for least privilege; each subagent type should be restricted to the tools its scope needs, not given the full set 'for flexibility' (D1 §1.3).
ww: A prompt instruction is probabilistic — it doesn't structurally prevent the subagent from calling a tool it still has access to (D1 §1.3).
Merging collapses the separation of responsibilities the split was meant to create, rather than fixing the tool-restriction gap (D1 §1.3).
Expanding the billing subagent's tools the same way compounds the least-privilege violation instead of fixing it (D1 §1.3).

questions.stem: The billing subagent's coordinator prompt reads like a fixed script: call get_customer, then lookup_order, then if the discrepancy exceeds $50 call process_refund, then done. On disputes spanning three related orders with a mix of overcharges and a missing discount, the subagent follows the steps correctly but produces a shallow, incomplete resolution. Which change to the coordinator prompt is most effective?
questions.why: Goal-oriented prompts stating goals and quality criteria let the subagent adapt to what a case actually contains; procedural step-lists are brittle and break exactly when reality deviates from the fixed script (D1 §1.4).
ww: Adding more predetermined steps deepens the same rigidity that caused the shallow handling — it can't anticipate every combination (D1 §1.4).
More subagents executing the same rigid script doesn't fix the script itself (D1 §1.4).
A bolted-on review pass treats the symptom after the fact rather than fixing the coordinator prompt that produced the shallow plan (D1 §1.4).

questions.stem: The billing subagent resolves disputes by checking exactly two things: the charge amount and the discount code applied. Every check completes and reports correctly, yet disputes caused by a duplicate transaction charge keep coming back unresolved, since neither check was ever designed to look for a duplicate charge. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: When every delegated check succeeds but a whole category of cases is never covered, the root cause is the coordinator's decomposition being too narrow, not the execution quality of the checks that exist (D1 §1.6).
ww: The tool description isn't the problem — no check was ever created to look for duplicate charges, regardless of how well lookup_order is described (D1 §1.6).
This isn't a capability failure; the subagent was never assigned the subtask, so its reasoning ability is irrelevant here (D1 §1.6).
Few-shot examples would refine an existing check's accuracy, but duplicate-charge detection was never decomposed into a check to refine (D1 §1.6).

questions.stem: The team is scoping how the coordinator should investigate multi-year loyalty-point disputes, where the relevant orders, transfers, and promotions only become clear once the first lookup runs. An engineer proposes a fixed pipeline: always run get_customer, then lookup_order for every order on the account, then check point-expiration rules, in that exact order, for every case. Which decomposition strategy is actually more appropriate, and why?
questions.why: Dynamic adaptive decomposition fits open-ended investigations where the full scope isn't known up front and each step depends on what earlier findings reveal; a fixed pipeline can't react to an unexpected transfer or promotion mid-investigation (D1 §1.7).
ww: Reproducibility suits predictable, template-following tasks, but a multi-year loyalty dispute's relevant sub-issues are exactly what can't be anticipated in a fixed step list (D1 §1.7).
'High-stakes' doesn't determine which decomposition strategy fits — the deciding factor is whether the steps are predictable up front, which they aren't here (D1 §1.7).
More subagents executing the same fixed sequence doesn't add the adaptability the case needs; the fix is decomposition strategy, not subagent count (D1 §1.7).

questions.stem: The coordinator now merges the billing subagent's overcharge findings and the returns subagent's already-processed-refund findings into one free-text paragraph before building an escalation handoff summary. A human agent receiving an escalation on a case touching both subagents finds the refund amount attributed to the wrong order number, since the merge lost track of which subagent's output supplied which figure. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Structured formats separating content from source metadata preserve attribution through aggregation; merging as free text is exactly what loses the claim-to-order mapping (D1 §1.5).
ww: A prompt instruction to 'be careful' is probabilistic and gives the coordinator no structural way to recover attribution it never received (D1 §1.5).
Re-querying the tools duplicates work the subagents already did and risks reattributing to the wrong order all over again (D1 §1.5).
Picking whichever subagent reported first is arbitrary and has no bearing on which figure is actually correct for which order (D1 §1.5).

questions.stem: The team adds a close_account tool with a dry_run: boolean parameter so an engineer can preview which subscriptions and open orders would be affected before permanently closing an account. Production logs show the agent sometimes calls close_account with dry_run=false on the very first attempt, closing an account with no preview ever generated. Which redesign makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible?
questions.why: The two-tool token-binding pattern makes execution architecturally impossible without a prior preview, since the token only exists after a preview call; a single tool with a boolean parameter can always be called with the flag already set to skip the check (D2 §2.4; Key Distinction #12).
ww: A prompt instruction is probabilistic — the agent can still call close_account with dry_run=false directly, exactly as logs show happening (D2 §2.4).
A confirmation string is just another parameter the agent can supply directly on the first call — the same bypassable shape as dry_run, only renamed (D2 §2.4).
PostToolUse fires after the account is already closed; auditing after the fact doesn't prevent the unauthorized closure from happening (D2 §2.4).

questions.stem: The returns subagent frequently needs a customer's current loyalty-tier discount percentage while evaluating a return — a simple, high-frequency lookup. Today every check routes through the coordinator to a separate loyalty-program subagent, adding a full extra loop. Complex disputes, like a contested retroactive tier change, are rare but still need that subagent's deeper investigation. What is the most effective tool configuration?
questions.why: A narrowly scoped cross-role tool is the sanctioned exception to strict role scoping for a high-frequency, simple need, while complex cases still route through the coordinator to the specialist subagent (D2 §2.5).
ww: Full loyalty-program tool access invites cross-specialization misuse — the returns subagent starts handling complex loyalty questions it isn't scoped for (D2 §2.5).
Correctly scoped, but ignores that the round-trip overhead on a high-frequency simple check is exactly the cost scoped cross-role tools exist to avoid (D2 §2.5).
Merging collapses the separation of responsibilities the split was designed to create (D2 §2.5).

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md pastes the full billing-dispute and returns conventions inline, so every subagent's session loads both regardless of which it's running. The billing subagent's maintainers want their config to load only the billing conventions file, without deleting the returns content from version control or maintaining two copies by hand. Which approach best achieves this?
questions.why: @import lets each subagent's own CLAUDE.md pull in only the standards file relevant to it, keeping the content in version control and in context without every session loading the combined file (D3 §3.1).
ww: Relying on the model to ignore irrelevant loaded content still burns context tokens on both conventions files every session and isn't a configuration fix (D3 §3.1).
.claude/rules/ triggers on file-path glob matches, not on which subagent or config is active — the wrong mechanism for a content split that isn't tied to which files are being edited (D3 §3.1).
Manual deletion has to be repeated every session and isn't tracked or reliable — not a configuration solution at all (D3 §3.1).

questions.stem: A 55-turn conversation about a delayed shipment includes the customer's updated delivery address and a gate code needed for access, buried among long stretches of routine back-and-forth about tracking updates and carrier delays. The team needs to cut token cost as these threads grow without losing the address and gate-code precision. Which context management strategy is most effective?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — extract critical structured facts, summarize lower-density general discussion, keep recent exchanges verbatim — preserves an exact detail like a gate code while still controlling token growth (D5 §5.3).
ww: Uniform summarization risks compressing a specific gate code into a vague phrase like 'delivery instructions were discussed,' losing exactly the precision that matters (D5 §5.3).
If the address or gate code was mentioned earlier than the retained window, a pure sliding window drops it entirely regardless of how many messages are kept (D5 §5.3).
A bigger context window addresses cost and capacity, not precision — the address and gate code are still sitting in an unstructured pile of turns, at risk of being paraphrased away (D5 §5.3).

questions.stem: To reduce round-trips through the coordinator, the report-generation subagent was given full `web_search` access so it could 'double-check a stat while formatting the final report.' Production logs show it now independently re-researches topics the web-search and synthesis subagents already covered, tripling report latency without improving accuracy. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Least privilege requires each subagent hold only the tools its defined scope needs; removing web_search from report-generation and routing verification back through the coordinator eliminates the redundant re-research without adding infrastructure (D1 §1.11).
ww: Giving every subagent the full catalog is the documented anti-pattern — agents outside their specialization tend to misuse tools they weren't scoped for (D1 §1.11).
Batching all verification to the end is called out as blocking, since later steps may need earlier-verified facts, and it doesn't address why report-generation has web_search at all (D1 §1.11).
A prompt instruction limiting use to 'quick' checks is probabilistic, not a deterministic scope restriction — the corpus consistently rejects prompt-level fixes for tool-scope problems (D1 §1.11).

questions.stem: The web-search subagent's `extract_snippets` tool and the document-analysis subagent's `extract_excerpts` tool are both described only as 'extracts relevant text from a source.' Synthesis requests route to `extract_snippets` for downloaded PDFs 38% of the time, when `extract_excerpts` was needed. How should this misrouting be fixed?
questions.why: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses for tool selection; specifying input format and a boundary example for each tool fixes the misrouting at its root (D2 §2.2).
ww: A pre-routing classifier adds infrastructure without fixing the underlying ambiguous descriptions that caused the misrouting (D2 §2.2).
Merging the tools loses the semantic precision that lets Claude distinguish web content from local documents (D2 §2.2).
Renaming without rewriting the description leaves the actual signal — what Claude reads to decide — unchanged; the corpus's fix requires both (D2 §2.2).

questions.stem: The team connects three separate MCP servers to the web-search subagent: a news-archive server, a patent-database server, and a regulatory-filing-index server. An engineer worries the subagent will only see tools from whichever server it 'attaches to' last, and plans to write orchestration code to merge each server's tool list manually before every request. What should the engineer expect instead?
questions.why: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and made available to the agent simultaneously — no manual merging or reactivation step exists (D2 §2.6).
ww: There is no single-server-at-a-time restriction in MCP; this describes a limitation that doesn't exist (D2 §2.6).
No `list_servers` activation call is part of MCP's documented behavior — this is a fabricated mechanism (D2 §2.6).
`.mcp.json` listing order does not gate tool availability; all configured servers' tools load together (D2 §2.6).

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent processes scanned regulatory filings; roughly 40% fail: some are permanently unreadable low-resolution scans, others failed only because the file-storage endpoint briefly timed out. Every failure returns the same generic `{"status": "failed"}`, so the coordinator retries all identically, wasting cycles on scans that will never parse. What should the subagent report instead?
questions.why: Structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, and whether retry is worth it — lets the coordinator make an intelligent recovery decision instead of retrying every failure identically (D1 §1.9).
ww: A bare `retryable` boolean is better than nothing but strictly worse than handling transient failures internally and surfacing only what needs a coordinator decision (D1 §1.9).
Silently dropping failed filings hides information from the coordinator and risks synthesis proceeding on an artificially narrow set of sources (D1 §1.9).
Escalating every OCR failure, including the network-timeout subset that could simply be retried, is disproportionate given the structured-context alternative (D1 §1.9).

questions.stem: The web-search subagent returns full results for 4 of 6 requested source categories; the other two — patent filings and conference proceedings — time out entirely. The document-analysis subagent has processed everything it was given without issue. What should the synthesis subagent do with this mixed-completeness input?
questions.why: With most sources available, the correct response is to complete synthesis on what's available and annotate coverage gaps rather than block or hide them (D1 §1.10).
ww: Returning an error treats a partial-but-usable result as a total failure, which the corpus explicitly rejects (D1 §1.10).
Proceeding without noting the gap hides the limitation from anyone reading the report (D1 §1.10).
Waiting indefinitely for a manual re-run blocks the pipeline unnecessarily when synthesis can proceed now with an honest coverage annotation (D1 §1.10).

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent's `submit_report_draft` tool starts rejecting drafts that exceed the client's contracted page-limit policy. The tool currently returns the same generic `{"error": "Operation failed"}` for this as for a genuine service outage, and logs show the subagent retries the rejected submission up to three times before escalating. How should the tool's error handling be restructured?
questions.why: A business-rule rejection is a valid outcome, not a failure — returning `retriable: false` with a clear explanation stops wasted retries and tells the subagent to act on the policy outcome (D2 §2.3).
ww: Labeling a business-rule rejection as transient wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change no matter how many times it's retried (D2 §2.3).
Returning success with an empty result masks the actual failure — the corpus explicitly rejects returning success with embedded error meaning (D2 §2.3).
Escalating immediately without returning any details skips the structured-response mechanism that would let the subagent resolve this itself (D2 §2.3).

questions.stem: The research system's `archive_source_cache` operation permanently deletes a completed project's raw document cache. An architect proposes an orchestration-layer confirmation dialog that pops up before the call reaches Claude, requiring a human click before execution. A teammate argues the two-tool preview/execute token pattern (`preview_archive_source_cache` returning a token, `execute_archive_source_cache` requiring it) is still preferable. Why?
questions.why: The two-tool token-binding pattern enforces the precondition at the interface level — architecturally, no execution can occur without a prior preview — with no orchestration-layer infrastructure required, unlike a confirmation dialog (D2 §2.4; Key Distinction #12).
ww: This inverts the entire mechanism — the pattern's whole point is that a token only exists after a genuine preview of that specific operation (D2 §2.4).
The two approaches are not equivalent: the dialog requires separate orchestration-layer infrastructure to intercept every call, which the token pattern avoids (D2 §2.4).
A prompt reminder is probabilistic — the agent can still call the execute step directly; only the token requirement makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible (D2 §2.4).

questions.stem: The web-search subagent has accreted 14 tools over eight months of piecemeal additions — separate tools for each source type, format converters, and a legacy fallback nobody removed. It now calls the wrong retrieval tool 22% of the time, while a peer synthesis subagent with 5 role-scoped tools selects correctly almost every time. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Restricting the subagent to the 4-5 tools relevant to its role directly reduces the decision space causing misrouting (D2 §2.5).
ww: Better descriptions help, but the official guide identifies tool count itself as the root cause once it climbs toward numbers like 14-18 instead of 4-5 (D2 §2.5).
Giving synthesis the same 14 tools risks the same cross-role misuse the corpus warns against — tools outside a subagent's specialization tend to be misapplied (D2 §2.5).
A routing layer adds infrastructure to compensate for an oversized tool set instead of shrinking the tool set itself (D2 §2.5).

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent calls `format_report` and then `attach_citations` in two separate sequential turns, even though every report needs both together. This adds a full extra API loop to every research task the system completes. What is the most effective way to reduce this overhead?
questions.why: The corpus's preferred fix for tools habitually called together is a prompt instruction to bundle them into one turn, not a composite tool (D2 §2.8).
ww: A composite tool is explicitly the 'not preferred' approach — it hides the composition rather than letting Claude naturally request both tools together (D2 §2.8).
Having the coordinator call subagent-scoped tools directly on the subagent's behalf breaks the hub-and-spoke separation of responsibilities (D2 §2.8).
Extra `max_tokens` addresses response length, not why the two calls are split across separate turns — it misdiagnoses the cause (D2 §2.8).

questions.stem: The coordinator has already re-delegated targeted queries and re-invoked synthesis twice because the draft kept omitting implementation-timeline details the document-analysis subagent had actually logged earlier. A third synthesis pass still lacks the timelines. Should the coordinator re-delegate a fourth time?
questions.why: The refinement loop needs a defined sufficiency criterion to know when to stop — the coordinator should keep re-delegating only until its quality criteria are actually met, not loop or stop on an arbitrary count (D1 §1.8).
ww: Looping again automatically with no upper bound or criterion is exactly the failure mode the corpus warns against — the loop needs a defined stopping condition (D1 §1.8).
Shipping with a generic 'further research needed' note is for unrecoverable gaps, not a substitute for the re-delegation loop when re-delegation is still available (D1 §1.8).
Having synthesis search for the missing information itself breaks the least-privilege separation of responsibilities between synthesis and the research subagents (D1 §1.8).

questions.stem: A client's research brief is silent on whether a report about current grid-storage incentives should include regulations that were superseded last year — omitting them could miss important historical context, but including them could make the report read as describing rules that no longer apply. Nothing in the brief or house style guide resolves this. What should the coordinator do?
questions.why: When the brief is silent on a genuine policy question and either choice risks being wrong, the coordinator should escalate rather than invent an interpretation (D1 §1.12).
ww: Choosing 'include by default' invents a policy the brief never stated, the same error as unilaterally interpreting an undefined rule (D1 §1.12).
Excluding by default has the identical flaw as including by default — both invent a resolution to a genuine policy gap (D1 §1.12).
Delegating the decision to a citation-frequency heuristic substitutes an arbitrary proxy for an actual policy answer (D1 §1.12).

questions.stem: The coordinator's citation-formatting checks have grown into a `/cite-check` command that every research subagent's output should pass before a report ships. One team member built it locally and now wants it invoked identically by all six teammates the moment they pull the latest repo changes, with zero manual setup on each machine. Where should the command file live?
questions.why: Project-scoped commands under `.claude/commands/` are version-controlled and become available to every teammate automatically the moment they pull, with no manual per-machine setup (D3 §3.4).
ww: Personal-scope commands under the author's own home directory aren't shared via version control, so nobody else receives the command at all (D3 §3.4).
Manual per-teammate copying isn't automatic and drifts out of sync the next time the command file changes (D3 §3.4).
CLAUDE.md documents conventions as instructions the model reads; it can't reproduce an invocable `/cite-check` command's actual behavior (D3 §3.4).

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent finds two credible sources disagreeing on a grid-storage rollout timeline: a government energy agency projects full deployment by 2030, while an industry consortium report projects 2035. Both sources pass the subagent's credibility checks. What should it do?
questions.why: The corpus's rule for conflicting credible sources is to preserve both values with attribution and let the coordinator (or a human) reconcile — never resolve the conflict autonomously (D5 §5.10).
ww: Averaging invents a third figure neither source actually reported, manufacturing false precision (D5 §5.10).
Preferring the government figure by default is a heuristic selection the corpus explicitly rejects — it abandons a decision above the subagent's scope (D5 §5.10).
Stopping the entire analysis to ask before completing it blocks the pipeline unnecessarily; the subagent can finish and flag the conflict instead (D5 §5.10).

questions.stem: The coordinator's citation schema marks `publication_year` as required and non-nullable for every source, reasoning that every citation needs a year for the report's timeline section. An audit of 5,000 citations finds 9% carry a plausible-looking year that traces to no actual publication date — many are working papers and preprints that never listed one. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: Marking a field required and non-nullable when the source data is sometimes genuinely absent pushes the model to fabricate values; making `publication_year` nullable lets it return `null` honestly instead (D4 §4.5).
ww: A plausibility range check doesn't stop fabrication of an in-range but nonexistent year — it only catches obviously implausible ones (D4 §4.5).
Requiring a separate search for a missing date is expensive and error-prone when a nullable field already solves the fabrication problem (D4 §4.5).
Removing the field entirely discards genuinely available publication years along with the fabricated ones — nullable preserves the real data (D4 §4.5).

questions.stem: Across 14 months and dozens of completed research projects for a recurring client, a researcher wants to know whether the team has ever covered a specific niche subtopic — floating offshore wind subsidy structures — without manually rereading every past report. What is the most effective way to support this kind of recall?
questions.why: Semantic retrieval over the full archive surfaces specifically relevant past reports on demand, which is the corpus's answer for precise recall across a large, multi-month history (D5 §5.7).
ww: A rolling window of only the 10 most recent projects discards most of the 14-month history, including whatever might be relevant (D5 §5.7).
Progressive summarization compresses specific, rarely-mentioned details into abstractions — a niche subtopic like this could vanish from a single running summary (D5 §5.7).
Manually scanning every tagged report in order doesn't scale across dozens of reports and 14 months of history (D5 §5.7).

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline must, on every document, render dates as ISO-8601, return null instead of fabricating any missing field, and never wrap the JSON payload in explanatory prose. An engineer needs these three rules to hold for every document processed in a session, not just the first one. Where should the rules be defined?
questions.why: Persistent behavioral constraints that must hold for the entire conversation belong in the system prompt, which is included in every request — D4 §4.3.
ww: Restating rules in each user message loses authority as the session accumulates documents and other content.
Environment variables have no effect on model behavior — the model never reads them.
Constraining only the first assistant message doesn't bind later documents; the model can deviate from its own earlier statement.

questions.stem: The pipeline must call `extract_metadata` before any of its three type-specific extraction tools run, since downstream steps depend on knowing a document's source and page count first. A prompt instruction saying 'always call `extract_metadata` first' is followed only about 85% of the time. Which `tool_choice` configuration reliably guarantees the metadata step runs first?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool on the first request guarantees that exact call, then relaxing tool_choice back to auto lets later steps proceed normally — D4 §4.6.
ww: A prompt instruction, however strongly worded, remains probabilistic — exactly the 85% compliance already observed.
`{"type": "any"}` guarantees some tool call but not that specific one first; forced on every turn it would also block later type-specific calls.
Few-shot examples improve format and style consistency, not a hard, guaranteed execution order.

questions.stem: The pipeline's enrichment step needs to validate vendor tax IDs against a national business registry. A well-maintained community MCP server already wraps this exact registry, but a colleague proposes building a custom, in-house MCP server from scratch instead, arguing it gives the team full control. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: For standard integrations, prefer existing community MCP servers; build custom servers only for workflows unique to the team — D2 §2.6.
ww: Reinvents a maintained standard integration the corpus explicitly rejects building from scratch 'for control.'
`~/.claude.json` is personal, unshared configuration; the team needs one shared, version-controlled setup, not a per-engineer personal one.
Resources are read-only content catalogs the agent browses; a per-document validation lookup that returns a result is an action — a tool, not a resource.

questions.stem: The extraction team hand-writes the JSON schema used in the tool definition, while a different engineer separately maintains a validation module checking rules like `sum(line_items) == total`. Twice this quarter, a field was added to one but not the other, and validation failures slipped through undetected until traced. What change most directly prevents this drift?
questions.why: A typed model (e.g., Pydantic) can generate the JSON Schema used in the tool definition, so one definition drives both the tool_use contract and the validator — D4 §4.8.
ww: A checklist item is a process patch for an architecture problem — still two artifacts someone must remember to update.
Misconception — tool_use enforces structure at generation time, but code should still validate business rules like sum(line_items) == total that no JSON schema expresses.
Still two hand-maintained representations in spirit; 'whoever touches it most recently' doesn't establish one source of truth generating the other.

questions.stem: A new extraction field requires computing an invoice's effective tax rate: summing several line-item tax codes, applying jurisdiction exemptions, and cross-checking the result against the stated total. The current prompt states only the target field name, with no other guidance. Which prompting addition most reliably improves accuracy here?
questions.why: A step-by-step reasoning cue improves accuracy on multi-step mathematical reasoning and stepwise transformations like this one — D4 §4.2.
ww: Token budget isn't the failure mode; the model isn't running out of room, it's making a reasoning error.
Exhaustive per-jurisdiction coverage targets breadth; the corpus favors a small, targeted example set for ambiguous cases, not bulk volume, and doesn't add reasoning structure.
Temperature governs sampling randomness, not whether a multi-step derivation is calculated correctly.

questions.stem: During an interactive review session, a specialist corrects a misread vendor name on document 14. That correction must be available to the model when it processes document 15 moments later, without restructuring the system prompt or restarting the session. What is the most effective way to make the correction available?
questions.why: Prefilling/injecting real-time context as a prefix to the next user message makes new information available immediately without rebuilding the system prompt — D4 §4.4.
ww: Rebuilding the system prompt requires reconstructing session context — heavier and unnecessary compared to a message prefix.
A synthetic user message unrelated to the actual submission breaks the natural flow of the review session.
Batching corrections to the end delays a correction past the point where it's actually needed — the very next document.

questions.stem: The extraction team is building internal tooling: a nightly `claude -p` job reviewing the day's failed extractions that must hand a ticketing script exactly four fields per failure — `document_id`, `failure_category`, `suggested_fix`, `retry_count`. Which CLI configuration most reliably produces output the ticketing script can parse every night?
questions.why: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` produces reliable, schema-valid structured output parseable by downstream tools — D3 §3.9.
ww: Documenting the format in `CLAUDE.md` is not guaranteed consistent — it's guidance the model may or may not follow precisely every run.
A prompt instruction alone has variable compliance across runs, with no guarantee of a stable, parseable shape.
Brittle — a regex parser breaks whenever wording or phrasing shifts, exactly the failure mode structured output is meant to eliminate.

questions.stem: To catch cross-document inconsistencies, the pipeline validates a bundle of 8 related vendor statements for account reconciliation in one prompt call. QA finds detailed, accurate flags on the first two or three statements, but a duplicate-line-item pattern is caught in statement 2 and missed in statement 6 of the same bundle. How should this review be restructured?
questions.why: Focused per-item passes plus a separate integration pass fix the attention dilution that produces inconsistent depth across many items — D4 §4.12.
ww: A larger context window doesn't fix attention quality; the dilution problem exists regardless of window size.
Shifts work onto humans instead of restructuring the review, and doesn't scale as bundle sizes grow.
Repeating an instruction doesn't address attention dilution; the same root cause remains structurally unaddressed.

questions.stem: For documents flagged low-confidence, the workflow re-asks the same model instance, in the same conversation, to 'double-check this extraction carefully' before routing to a human. An audit later finds several of these self-confirmed extractions were still wrong on the exact fields the model claimed to have re-checked. What most directly addresses this?
questions.why: True independence requires a fresh request with only the artifact and review criteria, not the generation conversation, so the reviewer isn't anchored to the original reasoning — D4 §4.13.
ww: A same-conversation pass still carries the full reasoning in context and tends to reconfirm it; a third pass inherits the identical anchoring.
Extended thinking gives the same anchored instance more reasoning, not independent scrutiny from a fresh perspective.
Self-review inside the same context inherits the same blind spots that produced the original result.

questions.stem: Onboarding a new vendor's document template, a schema-suggestion step proposes 9 new field-mapping rules. Developers find 6 of them duplicate mappings already defined in the existing vendor-mapping config, because the prompt generating suggestions doesn't include that config. What change most effectively reduces duplicate mapping suggestions?
questions.why: Claude can only avoid duplicates if it knows what already exists; including the existing config in context is the direct fix — D4 §4.18.
ww: Assumes the first few suggestions are the most valuable; doesn't address why duplicates were suggested at all.
Fragile keyword matching misses semantically equivalent mappings phrased differently.
Neither independent instance has visibility into the existing config; the same duplication risk persists in both lists.

questions.stem: The pipeline escalates straightforward duplicate-invoice matches to human review while attempting genuinely ambiguous multi-currency reconciliations autonomously. Auto-resolution sits at 58% against an 80% target, and no written criteria distinguish which cases should route where. What is the most effective way to improve this calibration?
questions.why: Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing 'escalate this / don't escalate this' directly fixes miscalibrated routing — D4 §4.15.
ww: Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is poorly correlated with actual difficulty; the model can be confidently wrong.
Adds infrastructure without addressing the root cause — unclear decision boundaries in the existing prompt.
Currency count is a blunt proxy for complexity, not the real criterion; it floods review with resolvable cases.

questions.stem: The system prompt requires ISO-8601 dates and two-decimal currency on every extraction. During an interactive correction session reprocessing flagged documents one by one, this holds for about 20 documents; by document 22 the model reverts to source-document date formats and single-decimal currency, though the session is only 2,800 tokens. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: As assistant responses accumulate, system prompt influence dilutes relative to that growing body of content; the model pattern-matches its own prior outputs, not a context limit — D4 §4.20.
ww: 2,800 tokens is nowhere near a realistic context limit — overflow is ruled out.
False — the system prompt is included in every request, not applied once.
No such overwrite mechanism exists; this misattributes drift to document content rather than accumulated conversation history.

questions.stem: The pipeline extracts clauses from a 300-page agreement, page by page, across many sequential tool calls in one long session. By page 200, the model gives inconsistent answers about clauses found on early pages, referencing 'typical contract language' instead of the specific text extracted earlier. What sustains accuracy across a task this long?
questions.why: Writing intermediate state to a scratchpad file and reading it back at the start of each continuation lets a long task survive without degrading into generic patterns — D5 §5.12.
ww: `/compact` risks losing exact clause text and specific detail needed for precise contract extraction.
Splitting into unconnected sessions discards continuity; later pages need what was already found, not a clean break.
A larger response budget doesn't address why the model is losing track of prior specific findings.

questions.stem: The interactive correction session for flagged documents keeps only the last 15 exchanges verbatim, dropping everything earlier. An early correction about how to round multi-currency line items falls outside that window by exchange 30, and the model reintroduces the original rounding error on a later document. What is the most effective restructuring?
questions.why: The hybrid window (recent verbatim + running summary + a structured facts block that's never dropped) fixes the sliding-window problem of losing early, still-relevant corrections — D5 §5.13.
ww: A bigger fixed window just delays the same problem — an even earlier correction eventually falls outside it.
Uniform summarization compresses a precise rule into something vaguer, losing exactly the precision that mattered.
Relies on the model reliably recalling and restating something it has no structural guarantee of retaining.

questions.stem: In the enrichment step, three lookup tools return dates in three different formats — Unix epoch, DD/MM/YYYY, and MM-DD-YYYY — and the model occasionally misreads a country-ambiguous date when composing the final record. What is the most maintainable way to fix this?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook centrally normalizes mismatched tool output formats deterministically, before the data ever reaches the model's context — D5 §5.14.
ww: Relies on LLM interpretation of the mismatch every time, rather than fixing it deterministically.
Fragmented maintenance — separate fixes for controlled vs. third-party tools, instead of one centralized normalization point.
Adds an extra LLM call and a tool-selection dependency; the model must remember to invoke it every time.

questions.stem: The reporting pipeline spans 85 files across three modules. To trace why a duplicate-suppression flag sometimes fails to propagate, the engineer Globs all three modules, then has the agent Read all 85 files before writing a single line of analysis. By the time it reaches the delivery module — the only place the flag is actually consumed — most of the context budget is already spent on files that never reference the flag. What investigation strategy should the engineer have used instead?
questions.why: Incremental investigation means Grep locates entry points by content first, then Read follows only the files that actually reference the flag — spending context only on relevant material (D2 §2.9; Key Distinction #28).
ww: A bigger window doesn't fix the anti-pattern of reading everything upfront; the problem is that most of the 85 files are irrelevant to the flag, not that they don't fit.

Glob matches file paths/names, not file content; a flag referenced inside a file's code wouldn't necessarily appear in that file's name, so this Glob-first approach can miss the real consumers entirely.
Manual pre-triage outside the tool isn't the sanctioned strategy and doesn't scale as the pipeline changes — the corpus prescribes a Grep-then-Read loop, not human pre-filtering.

questions.stem: Standardizing error handling, the engineer has Claude Code call Edit on `transform-utils.js` with the anchor `wrapError(err)`. Edit fails: that exact snippet appears in 15 places in the file, so Edit cannot determine which occurrence to change. A teammate suggests shortening the anchor to just `wrapError(` to make the match more specific. What should happen instead?
questions.why: When Edit's anchor is non-unique, the sanctioned fallback is Read the full file, modify the content, then Write it back — a reliable full-file modification (D2 §2.9; Key Distinction #27).
ww: Shortening the anchor makes it more likely to match in even more places, not fewer — the exact opposite of what's needed.
Bypasses the tool designed for the job; forcing the change with a shell command discards the review/safety properties Edit and the Read+Write fallback provide.
Edit still requires a unique anchor per call; there is no mechanism to address 'half' of 15 identical occurrences, so splitting doesn't create the uniqueness Edit needs.

questions.stem: The team wires in an MCP server that returns typed caller/callee call-graph relationships, distinct from plain text matching. Its description reads only "Finds references in the codebase." When tracing how a config key propagates across module boundaries, the agent still reaches for built-in Grep roughly 70% of the time, even on queries the call-graph server answers more precisely. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions; enhancing the MCP tool's description to spell out its unique, superior capability is the fix — not removing or renaming the built-in alternative (D2 §2.9; Key Distinction #29).
ww: Removing Grep breaks legitimate plain-text search cases; the root cause is an under-specified description, not Grep's existence.
A blunt 'always prefer' system-prompt rule is keyword-sensitive and can misroute cases where Grep genuinely is the better tool.
Renaming or duplicating the server under a new name doesn't change the underlying problem — the description is still what drives selection.

questions.stem: The engineer wants the ingestion module's Python files to follow a type-hints convention, the transformation module's Go files to follow a specific error-wrapping pattern, and the delivery module's TypeScript files to follow a strict-lint convention — plus a shared testing convention for test files, which sit scattered next to the code they cover across all three modules. Which configuration applies the right convention automatically regardless of which module is being worked on?
questions.why: Path-scoped rules under `.claude/rules/` solve exactly this multi-convention, multi-location problem, including the scattered test-file convention (D3 §3.2).
ww: Relies on model inference from headings rather than deterministic file-path matching; doesn't guarantee the correct convention loads only where relevant.
Doesn't work for the test convention since test files are scattered next to code across all three modules, not confined to one directory.
Workflow-specific, on-demand skills are for invoked procedures (deploy, PR review), not for conventions that should apply automatically based on file path.

questions.stem: The engineer builds a `/purge-orphan-configs` skill meant only to identify orphaned config files for review. Its SKILL.md frontmatter sets no tool restrictions, and during a run the skill unexpectedly deletes two files it was only supposed to flag. What frontmatter change most directly prevents this kind of destructive action?
questions.why: Per the official exam framing, allowed-tools restricts tool access during skill execution — scoping to a safe, non-destructive whitelist prevents the skill from writing or deleting (D3 §3.3).
ww: context: fork isolates a skill's output from the main session; it does not restrict which tools the skill can call, so a destructive call could still fire inside the fork.
argument-hint only affects what's displayed when invoking the command; it has no bearing on which tools the skill can actually execute.
A clearer name doesn't change tool access — the skill remains just as capable of destructive operations regardless of what it's called.

questions.stem: A developer wants to customize the shared `/format-report` skill — adding a personal pre-commit formatting pass — without changing what the rest of the eight-person team sees when they run the same command after cloning the repo. What should they do?
questions.why: A personal skill overrides a project skill of the same name, giving individual customization without affecting the shared, version-controlled command (D3 §3.5).
ww: Modifying the shared, version-controlled skill changes behavior for the whole team — the opposite of what's wanted.
A differently-named skill creates a new `/format-report-personal` command, losing the familiar `/format-report` invocation the developer wants to keep using.
CLAUDE.md content loads every session as instructions, not as an executable skill override; it can't reproduce a skill's actual behavior.

questions.stem: The engineer is asked to restructure the ingestion module to support streaming ingestion instead of batch files — a change touching all 32 ingestion files and requiring decisions about how partial records should be buffered and replayed. Multiple valid designs exist. Which execution approach should the engineer use?
questions.why: Large scope, architectural decisions, and multiple valid approaches call for planning mode before any side effects (D3 §3.6).
ww: The buffering/replay design isn't settled — direct execution is for well-defined, routine changes, not open architectural questions.
Reactive switching after the fact is exactly the expensive trap the corpus warns against; plan upfront when the task demands it.
Planning mode and direct execution are sequential phases for one task, not something applied file-by-file to a subset of the work.

questions.stem: A currency-conversion bug in the transformation module mishandles null exchange-rate values on certain lookups. The engineer describes the bug in prose to Claude Code three times, each time getting a fix that handles only the specific null case just described, leaving other null-rate scenarios unfixed. What is the most effective next step?
questions.why: Test-driven iteration anchors the fix to a concrete, machine-checkable failure — an objective definition of 'done' that prose descriptions of edge cases can't provide (D3 §3.7).
ww: Prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently — this repeats the same failed approach, just with more emphasis.
Writing tests after generation is verification, not test-driven iteration — it doesn't anchor generation to a concrete failure signal beforehand.
A bigger context window doesn't resolve ambiguous prose requirements; the fix is a concrete test case, not more reasoning capacity.

questions.stem: A nightly CI job invokes Claude Code to generate tests for changed files in the delivery module. Generated tests consistently invent their own fixtures and ad-hoc mocks instead of using the team's existing fixture helpers and shared HTTP-client mock already used throughout the suite. The job's prompt is just the changed diff and a short instruction. What most reliably makes generated tests follow the team's conventions?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude project context (testing standards, fixture conventions); including existing test files avoids inventing conventions from scratch (D3 §3.8).
ww: More output tokens don't tell Claude Code what the team's actual fixture conventions are; it can still generate a longer version of the wrong pattern.
Manual post-hoc rewriting treats the symptom on every single run instead of fixing what context the generation step receives.
Retrying without providing the conventions is a matter of chance — nothing anchors any attempt to house style.

questions.stem: Three candidate workloads: a pre-deploy compatibility check blocking the release pipeline until it completes, a nightly job regenerating yesterday's failed reports, and a one-time backfill of 500,000 legacy reports with no one waiting. Which assignment of API approach is correct?
questions.why: A blocking workload needs synchronous calls; latency-tolerant, non-blocking workloads (nightly regeneration, one-time bulk backfill) belong on the Batches API for the discount (D3 §3.10).
ww: The pre-deploy check blocks the release pipeline — a process is waiting, so up to 24 hours with no SLA is unacceptable there.
Forgoing batch savings on the nightly job and the one-time backfill wastes the 50% discount on exactly the two workloads that can tolerate the delay.
Puts the blocking pre-deploy check on the one API with no latency guarantee, while wastefully keeping the flexible nightly job on the pricier synchronous path.

questions.stem: The pipeline's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 350+ lines: universal formatting and error-handling conventions, plus a lengthy delivery-outage escalation checklist used only a handful of times a year. Every session loads the full file, and engineers say the checklist adds irrelevant bulk to routine work. Which restructuring keeps the universal conventions always available while loading the rare checklist only when needed?
questions.why: Universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md, which loads every session; workflow-specific, rarely-invoked guidance becomes a skill invoked on demand (D3 §3.11).
ww: Deleting the checklist removes documented incident guidance instead of relocating it — a real capability loss.
.claude/rules/ is path-scoped, not workflow-scoped; an escalation checklist isn't tied to a file-path pattern, so a glob can't gate it the way an on-demand skill invocation can.
Two files both loaded every session doesn't reduce routine-session bulk at all — the rare checklist still loads on every ordinary task.

questions.stem: After Claude Code completes a full analysis of the delivery module's retry behavior, the team wants to evaluate two competing designs for safer retries: exponential backoff with a shared circuit breaker, versus a per-request idempotency key. Both should start from the same completed analysis, without re-running the expensive analysis twice or letting either evaluation bias the other. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: fork_session branches inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently — exactly the use case of comparing two approaches from one shared, expensive baseline (D3 §3.12).
ww: The second evaluation in the same session is biased by the first's reasoning and conclusions.
Two brand-new sessions would each have to redo the expensive retry analysis, exactly the duplicated cost the team wants to avoid.
/compact risks losing exact details from the analysis (specific findings, numeric values) that both evaluations need intact.

questions.stem: A dependency-upgrade automation hits a version conflict it cannot resolve — two teams pin incompatible major versions of the same library — and escalates with only a generic 'needs manual review' flag. The on-call engineer has no access to the automation's session and must re-discover which packages were touched, what versions were tried, and where the conflict lives. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: A self-contained structured handoff summary with root cause, attempted actions, and a recommended resolution replaces a generic flag, since the receiving human has no transcript access (D1 §1.13).
ww: The human lacks transcript access by design in this pattern, and a raw transcript would force re-reading the entire run instead of getting a concise summary.
Re-running the automation's tools to rebuild context duplicates work and slows resolution — the point is to avoid the human re-deriving what's already known.
Escalating earlier means less context has accumulated, which degrades autonomous resolution and doesn't fix the information-loss problem at escalation time.

questions.stem: The release automation must confirm a prior deploy's lock file has cleared before starting a new deploy, since deploying while the lock is held corrupts the release. Today this rule exists only as a prompt comment. During a high-traffic release window, the automation deployed while the previous lock was still present, corrupting that release. What change most reliably prevents a recurrence?
questions.why: For safety-critical sequencing, enforce at the code level with a programmatic precondition rather than relying on probabilistic prompt compliance (D1 §1.14).
ww: Stronger wording is still a prompt instruction — probabilistic, and the incident already shows prompt compliance isn't reliable under load.
A few-shot example is also probabilistic guidance; it can reduce but not guarantee compliance the way a code-level block does.
After-the-fact alerting documents the failure but does nothing to prevent it — the deploy still corrupts the release in the moment.

questions.stem: The dependency-upgrade automation's summary reports `stated_packages_updated: 47` after each run, self-counted as it works. Engineers now suspect this self-reported figure sometimes diverges from the actual number of package-manifest diffs produced, but nobody notices until a much later audit. What extraction design change most directly catches this at the time of the run?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern builds re-derivation into the output schema — stated vs. independently calculated value plus a conflict flag — so every run produces a machine-readable signal (D4 §4.10).
ww: A vague 'be careful' instruction gives no detection mechanism — exactly the kind of prompt-only fix this pattern is meant to replace.
A monthly reconciliation report only surfaces the mismatch weeks later — the whole point is to move detection to run time.
Asking the model to confirm its own answer conversationally after the fact isn't the structural pattern; re-derivation belongs in the schema on every run, not as an optional follow-up.

questions.stem: Weeks ago, your coordinator's investigation into two customer accounts suspected of being duplicates stalled pending legal sign-off, and that session was set aside. Sign-off finally arrives, but order histories and refund policy have both changed since then. Rather than resuming the old session, an engineer starts a brand-new one and pastes in a three-sentence summary of the original findings. Which named pattern does this exemplify?
questions.why: A resumed session reasons over old tool results as current; since policy and order data changed, starting fresh and injecting a structured summary of conclusions carries the findings forward without the stale evidence.
ww: Session forking branches two approaches from a shared, still-valid baseline to compare them — it doesn't address stale evidence in a single stalled session.
The iterative refinement loop is the coordinator re-delegating to close synthesis coverage gaps within an active investigation, not a way to handle a stale resumed session.
Coverage annotation marks well-supported versus data-gap conclusions within one synthesis pass; it doesn't resolve whether a session's underlying evidence is still current.

questions.stem: Separately, a fraud-review subagent and a billing subagent are wired to message each other directly on suspected-stolen-card cases, skipping the coordinator, to place holds faster. When a customer disputes a hold, the escalation handoff is missing the fraud subagent's original reasoning, because the coordinator's own logs never captured the exchange. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Hub-and-spoke requires all inter-agent communication to flow through the coordinator, giving it visibility and centralized, uniform error handling — the missing reasoning is a direct symptom of bypassing that hub.
ww: Still bypasses the coordinator entirely, and granting full transcript access also breaks the context isolation subagents are meant to have.
Still a direct inter-agent channel, just routed through a database instead of a message — the coordinator remains blind to the exchange.
Patches the symptom by adding a field while leaving the direct communication path — and the visibility gap it causes — untouched.

questions.stem: Engineers notice the coordinator never delegates account-merge verification work, even though billing and verification subagent types are fully described in its system prompt with clear scopes. Instead it tries to resolve every merge case itself in one long response. Inspecting its AgentDefinition, the only tool listed is get_customer. What most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: A coordinator's allowed_tools must include Task or it cannot spawn subagents at all, no matter how the prompt is worded — the tool grant is the structural gate.
ww: A prompt instruction cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds; this is a probabilistic fix aimed at a structural gap.
Descriptions don't enable spawning subagents — only the Task tool in allowed_tools does; the prompt already describes them in detail.
Doesn't address why the coordinator never delegates in the first place, and weakens the least-privilege scoping the subagent was given.

questions.stem: The verification subagent's findings return, and the coordinator's synthesis recommends the merge is safe to proceed. Reviewing the draft, the coordinator itself notices it never checked whether either account has an active subscription that a merge would silently double-bill. What should the coordinator do next?
questions.why: The coordinator owns gap evaluation and loop termination: it re-delegates a targeted query aimed at the specific gap, then re-invokes synthesis with the enriched findings.
ww: Coverage annotation is for gaps that are unrecoverable, not a substitute for re-delegation when a targeted follow-up is available.
Gives the synthesis step direct tool access, breaking separation of responsibilities and the least-privilege tooling each stage should keep.
Wastes the already-completed, still-valid findings; only the missed subscription check needs re-delegating, not the whole investigation.

questions.stem: Drafting a structured JSON handoff summary for a complex escalation, one API call hits the token limit partway through the payload, returning a max_tokens stop reason. The loop's current logic treats any stop reason other than tool_use as done, so it forwards the truncated, half-written JSON straight to the human queue. What should the loop check instead?
questions.why: Each stop_reason value demands its own handling; max_tokens signals a truncated response needing explicit continuation or retry, not silent pass-through as if finished.
ww: end_turn means Claude finished; conflating it with max_tokens is exactly the bug — a truncated response is not a finished one.
Iteration count is irrelevant here; the loop already stopped correctly per its own condition, the condition itself is wrong.
Inspecting text content to infer completeness is the anti-pattern the loop should avoid — decide from stop_reason, not from parsing output.

questions.stem: With the merge complete, a customer asks for the two accounts' loyalty-tier progress to be combined retroactively into one higher tier. Policy defines tier calculation only for a single continuous account history and says nothing about merged accounts. The agent has already confirmed both accounts and their order histories. What should it do?
questions.why: A genuine policy gap on a high-stakes calculation is a defined escalation trigger — the agent cannot determine the correct action within stated policy and must not invent one.
ww: Applies an existing rule to a case it was never written to cover — this invents an interpretation the policy doesn't state.
Refuses based on a prohibition that isn't actually stated; policy is silent on merged accounts, not prohibitive.
Picks a plausible-sounding default without authorization — the same invented-policy problem as applying the standard formula, just more generous.

questions.stem: Your new merge_duplicate_accounts tool accepts a dry_run: boolean so engineers can preview which subscriptions and order histories would combine before committing. Production logs show the agent sometimes calls it with dry_run=false on the very first attempt, merging accounts with no preview ever generated. Which redesign makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible?
questions.why: Two-tool token-binding makes execution impossible without a prior preview call — the confirmation token only exists after preview_merge_accounts runs, a code-level guarantee rather than a prompt-level hope.
ww: A timing heuristic is fragile: a fast legitimate call gets blocked while a deliberately delayed bypass still slips through untouched.
Adds orchestration-layer infrastructure, but the underlying tool can still be called directly from another integration path, bypassing the prompt entirely.
Prompt-level compliance is probabilistic — production logs already show the agent skipping the preview despite instructions, the exact pattern Key Distinction #12 warns against.

questions.stem: Verifying identity for a merge case, the agent calls get_customer and lookup_order in the same turn. When get_customer needs a retry after a transient failure, the harness appends the retried result before the original lookup_order result, and Claude's next response attributes order details to the wrong customer. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The id field is what binds a tool_result to its originating tool_use call — matching by id, not by the order results are appended, is the correct mechanism.
ww: Forces sequential calls, losing the latency benefit of the parallel execution without actually fixing the underlying attribution bug.
Backoff timing doesn't address the root cause — a result appended out of order is still identifiable by its id if the harness checked it.
Re-sending both calls on any single retry duplicates work and still doesn't fix how results get matched back to their calls.

questions.stem: The fraud case in the loyalty-tier dispute needs `escalate_to_human` for a live handoff, but a newer `flag_for_review` tool — which only queues the case for later, asynchronous review — keeps getting called instead when the customer explicitly asks for a person right now. Both descriptions read only a one-line purpose. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Expanding descriptions with what each tool does, when to use it, and when not to is the primary lever for fixing tool selection — check descriptions before adding infrastructure.
ww: Merging into one parameterized tool loses the semantic precision that made the original distinction meaningful.
Adds a classifier layer to compensate for a bad signal instead of fixing the signal — infrastructure without fixing the root cause.
A rename alone doesn't add the missing boundary information the descriptions still lack — the ambiguity in purpose remains.

questions.stem: Your reissue_shipping_label tool fails two ways: some accounts have hit their monthly reissue cap, others fail because the carrier API credential expired. Both currently return an identical generic error, and the agent retries both the same way — wasting attempts on the cap case and never refreshing credentials on the other. How should the tool's error handling be restructured?
questions.why: Business-rule and permission errors are both non-retryable but demand different agent responses — explain the policy outcome versus escalate or refresh credentials — so they need distinct categories.
ww: A single retryable flag can't distinguish two failure types that both need different, non-retry handling from the agent.
Retrying a permission failure without refreshing the credential fails identically every time — wasted effort with no path to success.
