Keeps the agent guessing from undifferentiated error text; the whole point is giving it enough signal to act correctly.

questions.stem: A new reliability mechanism retries any support message that times out by resending it through a background queue, but the retry payload carries only that single message, not the conversation so far. The agent treats the merge case as brand new, though the case ID is unchanged. An engineer proposes adding a session_id field so the API can look up prior turns itself. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.why: The API is fully stateless: whatever process sends the request — including a retry queue — must include the complete prior messages array. No session_id capability exists to look up history server-side.
ww: No such session_id capability exists; this is the classic fabricated-feature misconception the API's statelessness rules out entirely.
A single retried message can't exceed the context window; the omission here is an architectural gap in what the queue resends, not a size problem.
A vector database is for retrieval over long histories spanning months, not for restoring a message that was simply never resent.

questions.stem: The merged account's loyalty-tier dispute runs long. Early on, the customer states a corrected tier level, but the team's sliding window keeps only the last 20 message pairs — 25 turns later, the correction has dropped out, and the agent quotes the original, wrong tier again. Which restructuring is most effective?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — recent verbatim, a running summary of general discussion, and a never-dropped structured facts block — preserves precise corrected values no matter how long the conversation runs.
ww: A bigger fixed window only delays the same problem; a long enough dispute will still eventually push the correction out.
Pure summarization loses precision — a corrected tier level becomes a vague paraphrase rather than a preserved, exact fact.
Raising the threshold buys some time, but the correction still eventually gets compressed away once the threshold is crossed.

questions.stem: To route merge-dispute cases, a team proposes having the agent self-rate its confidence 1–10 and auto-escalate anything below 7. Early testing shows several confidently-scored cases were resolved incorrectly, while some cases scored below the threshold turned out to be straightforward. What is the most effective way to design this routing decision instead?
questions.why: Self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and poorly correlated with actual case difficulty; reliable escalation triggers are structural signals, not the model's own confidence estimate.
ww: Adjusting the threshold still relies on the same unreliable signal, just applied at a different cutoff point.
A second self-rating is still self-rated confidence, just duplicated — it doesn't fix the underlying miscalibration.
A coarser label doesn't fix the core problem; confidence itself, however it's expressed, isn't a reliable complexity proxy.

questions.stem: In the support bot's own repository, the billing subagent's Python files follow one validation pattern, the returns subagent's TypeScript files follow another, and both subagents' test files sit scattered next to the code they cover. Engineers want the right convention applied automatically based on which files are being touched. Which configuration best achieves this?
questions.why: Path-scoped rules with glob patterns load automatically only when working on matching files, applying the correct convention deterministically regardless of directory.
ww: Relies on the model inferring the right heading to follow rather than deterministic file-path matching.
Doesn't scale once test files are scattered across many directories rather than cleanly separated by convention.
Asks the model to infer the convention from context instead of loading the correct rule deterministically.

questions.stem: A customer writes only "the merge thing still isn't right" — it could mean the loyalty tier, the combined order history display, or a duplicate charge from before the accounts merged. Asking which of the three they mean, plus follow-up details for each, would take several more messages. What should the agent do?
questions.why: Stating an explicit assumption and proceeding, while inviting correction, avoids the abandonment that clarifying questions cause on vague requests.
ww: A compound message of three questions still demands upfront effort from the customer before any progress is made.
Picks silently without stating the assumption — the customer has no way to know what was guessed or to correct it.
Sequential one-at-a-time questioning adds several round-trips, the exact abandonment risk the proceed-with-assumption pattern is meant to avoid.

questions.stem: Your coding agent applies a required commit-message convention during some Claude Code sessions but skips it in others, even though every developer's repo checkout is identical and up to date. Two developers working on the same branch see opposite behavior in the same afternoon. What is the most effective first diagnostic step?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md files are concatenated from a discovered set, not injected by magic — when behavior is inconsistent across otherwise-identical sessions, `/memory` shows exactly which memory files loaded in that session, turning a guess into a fact.
ww: Duplicating the file into a personal location doesn't explain why the existing hierarchy is loading inconsistently — it papers over the symptom without diagnosing which file is missing where.
Restating the instruction in-prompt is a probabilistic workaround that doesn't explain why the convention was already present in some sessions and absent in others.
Converting an always-required convention into an on-demand skill makes it opt-in by design — guaranteeing future inconsistency rather than diagnosing the current one.

questions.stem: Your team's `/cleanup-artifacts` skill deletes stale build outputs after each release. A typo in one invocation modified source files outside the build directory. The team wants the skill hard-restricted to file-write operations only — no shell access, no reads elsewhere. Which configuration change is most effective?
questions.why: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter is the mechanism for scoping what tools a skill may use during execution — the official exam framing treats it as a restriction, exactly fitting a request to limit a skill to safe file-write operations.
ww: `context: fork` isolates the skill's output from polluting the main session's context — it has nothing to do with which tools the skill is permitted to call.
A glob-scoped rules file loads guidance text when matching files are touched; it's advisory prose, not an enforced tool restriction, and it isn't tied to a specific skill's execution.
A CLAUDE.md bullet point is a probabilistic instruction the model may or may not follow — it provides no architectural guarantee against a repeat of the same typo-driven mistake.

questions.stem: A developer on your team wants a personal `/tidy-imports` slash command for their own pre-commit habit. Teammates haven't asked for it and shouldn't see it appear automatically after cloning the repo. Where should the developer create the command file so it stays personal to them?
questions.why: Personal commands live in `~/.claude/commands/` — outside the repo, so they're never version-controlled and never surface for teammates who clone or pull.
ww: `.claude/commands/` inside the repo is exactly the project-wide, version-controlled location — the opposite of what a personal-only command needs.
Committing anything to a branch inside the repo still surfaces it to teammates once the branch merges or is inspected; skills committed in-repo are not private by default.
A wiki description doesn't create an invokable `/tidy-imports` command at all — it's documentation, not configuration.

questions.stem: A stack trace pinpoints a missing null check in exactly one function, in one file, with a clear one-line fix already identified. Before asking Claude Code to make the change, an engineer debates opening plan mode first to review the surrounding file. Which approach is most effective?
questions.why: A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace and an already-identified fix is the textbook case for direct execution — the scope and approach are settled, so planning overhead adds nothing.
ww: Planning mode exists for large-scope or architecturally ambiguous changes; reviewing a whole file for a pinpointed one-line fix is unnecessary overhead.
Reactive switching — starting direct and only planning if it breaks — is explicitly the wrong pattern; it doesn't apply here anyway since there's no ambiguity to trigger a switch.
There is no genuine alternative approach to weigh — inventing a planning step for a single well-defined fix is disproportionate to the task.

questions.stem: You asked Claude Code to fix a date-parsing helper that mishandles daylight-saving transitions. Prompted only with 'make sure daylight saving is handled correctly,' each of two attempts fixes the specific transition date you mentioned but breaks a different one you didn't mention. What is the most effective approach for the next iteration?
questions.why: A concrete failing test case with a sample input and exact expected output is the fastest way to converge on a genuine edge-case fix — it replaces guesswork with an objective, machine-checkable target.
ww: Adding emphasis to prose that's already failing to communicate the requirement doesn't fix inconsistent interpretation — the model is already trying to satisfy the vague instruction.
Without a concrete case to anchor it, the model's own test suite is likely to test the same set of assumptions that already produced two incomplete fixes.
Abandoning the fix avoids the bug rather than converging on a correct one, and leaves the original defect unresolved.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline already invokes the coding assistant with `--output-format json` so a downstream dashboard can ingest findings automatically. Roughly one run in twenty returns a valid JSON object that's simply missing the `severity` field, and the ingestion job crashes whenever that happens. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: `--output-format json` alone doesn't enforce which fields are present; pairing it with `--json-schema` and marking `severity` required guarantees schema-conformant output on every run.
ww: A CLAUDE.md instruction is not guaranteed consistent — the corpus explicitly rejects prompt-level format requests as a substitute for enforced schema output.
Silently substituting a default severity masks the gap instead of fixing it — the dashboard would show a fabricated value with no signal that it was ever missing.
Reverting to plain text reintroduces exactly the parsing fragility structured output was adopted to eliminate.

questions.stem: Your project CLAUDE.md holds two things: general coding conventions every session should follow, and a lengthy checklist for the recurring security-review pass that only a fraction of sessions ever run. Engineers doing routine feature work say the security checklist clutters every session's context for no benefit. Which restructuring is most effective?
questions.why: Universal, always-needed conventions belong in CLAUDE.md, which loads every session; workflow-specific guidance like a periodic security-review checklist belongs in a skill invoked only when that workflow actually runs.
ww: Deleting the checklist discards real, needed guidance rather than reorganizing it to load only when relevant.
Per-directory duplication doesn't map onto a workflow boundary and isn't how project-scoped instruction content is organized.
Forcing the always-needed general conventions behind an on-demand skill defeats the purpose of always-loaded configuration — the exact opposite of what should stay in CLAUDE.md.

questions.stem: A pairing session redesigning a search endpoint's caching layer reaches 60,000 tokens. It contains an agreed cache TTL value, the chosen invalidation-key format, several long tangents comparing caching libraries, and the last few exchanges finalizing the implementation. You need to cut tokens while keeping the session useful. Which context management strategy is most effective?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — extract precise agreed values into a structured block, compress the lower-density discussion, and keep the current exchanges verbatim — preserves exact configuration while cutting overall tokens.
ww: Pure summarization is exactly the pattern that turns a precise TTL value or key format into a vague paraphrase, risking a wrong configuration downstream.
A sliding window risks dropping the TTL and key-format decisions entirely if they were agreed earlier than the retained window.
Delaying when summarization triggers only postpones the same precision-loss problem rather than solving it.

questions.stem: Your team wants to retire a deprecated authentication middleware used across roughly 90 API route handlers. Mapping every route that imports it produces a long list of file paths and call context, and running that discovery in the main session threatens to fill the context window before the replacement design conversation starts. What is the most effective way to proceed?
questions.why: An Explore subagent isolates the verbose discovery output in its own context and returns only a concise summary, preserving the main session's context for the design and implementation phases that follow.
ww: Mid-task compaction risks losing precise details — such as exact file paths and call sites — that the implementation phase still needs.
Splitting across multiple resumed sessions adds coordination overhead and consistency risk without the isolation benefit a subagent provides.
Inferring affected routes from general knowledge instead of grounding in the actual codebase risks an incomplete or fabricated inventory.

questions.stem: Your coding assistant runs three separate static-analysis tools during review, and each reports severity differently: one uses `1`/`2`/`3`, another uses `low`/`medium`/`high`, and a third uses `info`/`warn`/`error`. Findings from all three accumulate in the session, and the assistant's own severity summaries have started contradicting each other. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook centrally normalizes divergent output formats from tools you don't control at the point they enter context — deterministic, and it fixes the inconsistency at its source.
ww: Relying on the model to reconcile three scales via instruction is probabilistic, and the tokens for all three raw formats still accumulate in context regardless.
Re-deriving a ranking on every summarization adds repeated LLM effort and repeats the same ambiguity each time instead of resolving it once.
Discarding two tools to sidestep a formatting mismatch throws away real detection coverage — disproportionate to what is fundamentally a normalization problem.

questions.stem: A Claude Code investigation into a legacy billing module ran three weeks ago and is saved as a named session. Since then, a different team has substantially rewritten the module across dozens of files, and the original investigation's tool results no longer reflect the current code at all. What is the most effective way to continue the work?
questions.why: When prior tool results are so stale they no longer reflect the current code, a fresh session with an injected structured summary carries the conclusions forward without the invalid evidence — better than resuming a session that reasons over stale results as if they were current.
ww: A resumed session treats its old tool results as still valid unless told otherwise — exactly the failure mode that produces wrong conclusions from a substantially rewritten module.
Resuming still carries the old session's stale reasoning even while re-reading files, and re-reading the whole module is wasteful compared to a clean summary-based restart.
`fork_session` is for branching two approaches off one still-valid shared baseline, not for handling a baseline that's already known to be stale.

questions.stem: Claude Code writes a CSV-export function and, in its own reasoning, confirms it streams rows instead of loading the full result set into memory. Asked in that same conversation to review its own change, it reports the approach is sound. Weeks later, a memory spike in production traces back to this function silently buffering the entire result set. What most directly addresses why the same-session check missed this?
questions.why: A second, independent instance without access to the generator's justification evaluates the code fresh, catching blind spots the original session rationalized away — same-session self-checks inherit the same anchoring bias.
ww: More reasoning by the same already-anchored instance is not independent scrutiny — it still confirms its own prior conclusion.
A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context; the model re-reads and reaffirms its own justification rather than evaluating independently.
A stronger instruction at generation time is probabilistic and doesn't address the structural self-check limitation that let the bug through in the first place.

questions.stem: Your team wires an internal component-library MCP server into Claude Code so it can scaffold new UI components from existing design-system pieces. Before scaffolding, the assistant burns several tool calls issuing guessed `search_components` queries just to discover what components and props even exist. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: MCP resources expose content catalogs so the agent has an immediate map of what exists without exploratory tool calls — exactly the fix for guessed queries burned on plain discovery.
ww: A `list_all_components` tool is still an LLM call the agent must remember to make; a resource provides the map as readable context without relying on the model to think to use it.
A static dump in CLAUDE.md bloats every session's context regardless of need and goes stale as the design system evolves.
Better example queries still leave the assistant guessing at what exists rather than fixing the underlying lack of visibility.

questions.stem: Before renaming a widely-used validation helper, `sanitizeInput`, across the codebase, the coding assistant runs `Glob("**/sanitizeInput*")` and reports two matches, both inside the helper's own module. A manual check turns up a dozen more files that call the helper but don't have that string in their file name. What should the assistant have used instead?
questions.why: The target is what a file's content calls, not what a file is named — Grep searches inside file content, which is exactly what finding every caller of a function requires.
ww: Widening the file-name pattern is still a path match, not a content search — files that call the helper without having 'sanitize' in their own name are still missed.
Reading every file upfront is the anti-pattern the corpus rejects — discovery should be driven by content search first, then targeted reads, not exhaustive bulk reading.
A find-based command still matches on file paths, the same category error as Glob — it does not search file contents.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline extracts structured findings from static-analysis output using a retry-with-feedback loop against a JSON schema. A `cve_id` field is marked required, and extraction retries up to five times whenever it's missing. Investigation shows 30% of findings are genuinely novel issues with no CVE assigned yet. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: When the information is genuinely absent from the source, no amount of retrying can produce it — making the field nullable lets the model return `null` and stops retries from burning tokens on an unrecoverable case.
ww: More retry attempts cannot conjure a CVE that was never assigned — absent information stays absent regardless of attempt count.
No feedback message, however specific, can supply data that doesn't exist in the source.
Forcing a placeholder value guarantees fabrication — exactly the outcome nullable fields exist to prevent.

questions.stem: The coordinator's prompt for the drone-delivery project is a fixed checklist: search three trade-press sites, open the top six results from each, summarize each in 80 words. Shipped reports keep excluding a newly announced airspace-corridor rule the subagents' own searches already surfaced, since nothing in the checklist calls for pursuing it. Which change to the coordinator's prompt is most effective?
questions.why: Goal-oriented prompts specifying goals and quality criteria let subagents adapt their approach as findings emerge, rather than executing a brittle fixed checklist that can't react to a discovery it wasn't scripted for.
ww: Still procedural — one more checklist item doesn't remove the rigidity that caused the miss; the next unanticipated discovery hits the same wall.
More results per site doesn't fix a fixed checklist's inability to adapt; it only delays the same kind of miss.
Adds infrastructure to patch a symptom instead of fixing the coordinator prompt itself, which is the actual root cause.

questions.stem: After the coordinator's prompt is rewritten to be goal-oriented, the web-search and document-analysis subagents each hand back long write-ups, which the coordinator stitches into one block before passing it to synthesis. A fact-check later finds the shipped report's "340% pilot-volume growth" claim can't be traced to either subagent's notes. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Structured formats that separate content from source metadata preserve attribution through the pipeline; stitching findings into free text is exactly what loses claim-to-source mappings during aggregation.
ww: Probabilistic instruction — the synthesis subagent cannot cite metadata it was never given in structured form, no matter how it's reminded.
Duplicated, expensive work that risks attributing the claim to the wrong source, rather than fixing the upstream data-passing format.
Arbitrarily discards one subagent's findings instead of preserving structured attribution for both, losing information rather than recovering it.

questions.stem: Every subagent completes successfully on the drone-delivery project: web-search finds relevant articles, document-analysis summarizes filings correctly, synthesis produces coherent text. Yet the report covers only airspace rules and omits noise-ordinance disputes, insurance-liability questions, and neighborhood-acceptance surveys. The coordinator's logs show it decomposed the topic into three airspace-only subtasks. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: The coordinator's decomposition is its most critical responsibility; every subagent executed correctly on the (too-narrow) scope it was actually assigned, so the root cause sits upstream at decomposition.
ww: Blames a subagent that performed correctly on the narrow scope it was assigned — the query wording wasn't the constraint, the assigned subtopic was.
Same misattribution — the subagent had no non-airspace documents to filter because none were ever assigned to it.
Synthesis correctly reflects the one-dimensional input it received; detecting a decomposition gap isn't its responsibility.

questions.stem: For the drone-delivery project's exploratory phase, nobody yet knows whether regulation, cost, or public acceptance will be the binding constraint on adoption — that only becomes clear once initial findings arrive. An engineer proposes a fixed pipeline with steps set up front: search, extract, validate, format. Which decomposition strategy actually fits better, and why?
questions.why: Dynamic adaptive decomposition fits open-ended investigations where full scope is unknown up front and each step depends on the previous step's discoveries — exactly this case.
ww: A fixed pipeline suits predictable, template-following tasks; it can't react when the actual binding constraint is genuinely unknown in advance.
An unmotivated, unsupported hybrid that adds complexity without addressing why the constraint is unknown at the outset.
An unscoped single pass risks attention dilution and lacks the explicit partitioning that prevents missed coverage.

questions.stem: Investigating insurance-liability precedents in one state, the web-search subagent's query gets rate-limited mid-search and returns nothing further. It reports back only `{"status": "failed"}`, leaving the coordinator no way to judge whether to retry, switch source category, or move on with what it has. What should the failure report include instead?
questions.why: Structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and alternatives — is what the coordinator needs to make an intelligent recovery decision rather than guessing.
ww: Forces retry regardless of whether the failure is transient or permanent, without giving the coordinator the context to decide.
Masks the failure as success, hiding the rate limit entirely from the coordinator — a silent failure the exam corpus treats as an anti-pattern.
Wildly disproportionate — never terminate the whole workflow for one subagent failure when recovery options exist.

questions.stem: Two of the five drone-delivery source categories assigned to the web-search subagent — municipal-ordinance archives and insurance bulletins — are down for scheduled maintenance and return nothing; the other three come back complete. Document-analysis processes everything it was handed without trouble. What should the synthesis subagent do given this gap?
questions.why: Graceful degradation means completing synthesis on available data while annotating coverage gaps, so uncertainty is visible upstream rather than hidden or blocking the pipeline.
ww: Incomplete input isn't the same as invalid input; erroring out discards usable partial data unnecessarily.
Silently proceeding hides real coverage gaps from anyone reading the report.
Blocks the pipeline on a maintenance window that may slip, when annotated partial synthesis is available now.

questions.stem: While drafting the drone-delivery report, the synthesis subagent keeps needing to confirm isolated details — a statistic, a named regulator, a date — before finishing a paragraph. An audit finds roughly 78% of these are one-off lookups; the remaining 22% require tracing a claim across several filings. Which tool configuration handles this most effectively?
questions.why: A narrowly scoped cross-role tool for the high-frequency simple case avoids constant coordinator round-trips, while complex cases still route through the coordinator — exactly the sanctioned exception to strict role scoping.
ww: Full web-search access breaks separation of responsibilities — the synthesis subagent starts doing open-ended research instead of synthesizing.
Batching blocks progress, since later drafting steps may depend on facts that were already confirmed earlier in the pass.
Shifts the responsibility to an agent with less context on the draft's specific claims, rather than fixing the scoping problem directly.

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent's citation-retraction action permanently deletes an excerpt and unlinks it from every section citing it — irreversible. The team built two tools: `preview_retract_citation`, returning a single-use token, and `execute_retract_citation`, which requires it. A teammate argues one tool with a strengthened prompt and few-shot examples would be simpler. Why is the two-tool design still preferable?
questions.why: Token-binding makes the mandatory sequence a code-level guarantee, not a prompt-level hope — no token exists until a preview call produces one, so execution without preview is architecturally impossible.
ww: This is exactly the misconception the pattern is designed to defeat: prompt instructions and examples remain probabilistic, no matter how well-written, and an agent can still call execute directly.
Both designs still require two calls to complete a retraction properly; call count isn't the actual benefit being traded off here.
Audit logging is a minor side effect, not the reason the design is architecturally superior — it misidentifies the actual enforcement mechanism.

questions.stem: Every filing the document-analysis subagent processes needs its jurisdiction, date, and source type extracted before any deeper analysis tool runs. A prompt instruction saying "always call `extract_source_metadata` first" still lets the subagent skip straight to analysis on roughly one run in ten. Which configuration most reliably guarantees the metadata step runs first?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool on the first turn guarantees the required first step, then relaxing to `auto` afterward lets the subagent proceed normally through the rest of its analysis.
ww: Guarantees a tool call happens but not which one — `any` doesn't guarantee metadata extraction specifically runs first.
Still a probabilistic prompt instruction; repetition doesn't turn it into a guarantee.
Forcing the same tool every turn prevents the subagent from ever calling its deeper analysis tools at all.

questions.stem: The web-search subagent's ranking tool returns reliability as a 0-1 float, the document-analysis subagent's tool returns a 1-100 integer, and a third-party fact-checking MCP server you cannot modify returns a letter grade A-F. Synthesis occasionally misreads these mismatched scales when choosing which findings to feature. What is the most maintainable fix?
questions.why: A `PostToolUse` hook centrally normalizes output scales deterministically, working even for third-party tools the team cannot modify, without adding LLM call overhead or relying on interpretation.
ww: Adds an extra LLM-driven tool call and still depends on the model remembering to invoke it every time.
Relies on LLM interpretation of documented scales rather than deterministic normalization — probabilistic, not guaranteed.
Fragments maintenance across many hand-written wrappers instead of centralizing normalization in one place.

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent calls `compile_report_body`, then in a separate turn calls `append_source_index` — though every finished report always needs both, one right after the other. This doubles the API calls needed per deliverable. What is the most effective way to cut down on this back-and-forth?
questions.why: The preferred approach is prompting the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn rather than hiding the composition inside a composite tool.
ww: A composite tool hides the composition and is explicitly not the preferred approach when the agent can naturally request both tools in one turn.
A wider tool set doesn't address the sequencing problem and risks the exact tool-selection issues a scoped tool set avoids.
Hooks run deterministic code around a tool call; they aren't the mechanism for triggering a second tool call in the agentic loop.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent now outputs a field-level confidence score for every extracted regulatory fact. Aggregate accuracy across the drone-delivery project sits at 91%, and the team proposes ending human review for every extraction above the confidence threshold. What should the team do before making that change?
questions.why: An aggregate figure can hide a much higher failure rate on a rare document type; validating accuracy by segment plus ongoing stratified sampling catches novel error patterns before they compound.
ww: The aggregate-accuracy masking trap — a rare segment could be failing far more often than the overall number suggests.
Self-reported confidence is uncalibrated and unreliable until tuned against a labeled validation set.
Unstratified random sampling wastes reviewer capacity on easy, common segments and undersamples the rare, problem-prone ones.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent pulls two credible readings on drone-corridor safety: a municipal aviation-safety office logs 2.4 near-misses per 10,000 flights; an industry safety consortium puts the same corridor at 0.6 per 10,000. Both pass credibility checks, and the gap could change the report's safety conclusion. What should the subagent do?
questions.why: The subagent should not resolve conflicts autonomously; preserving both readings with source attribution and escalating the reconciliation decision keeps it within its scope.
ww: Abandons a reconciliation decision that belongs above the subagent's scope by picking a value on an unstated heuristic.
Blocks the pipeline unnecessarily instead of completing the analysis and flagging the conflict for the coordinator.
Fabricates a blended figure neither source actually reported, destroying the transparency the annotation approach preserves.

questions.stem: Two figures in the drone-delivery report seem to clash: one filing reports a 22% delivery-window reduction, another reports 31%. The synthesis subagent's structured input carries each filing's collection date — the numbers actually come from filings gathered fourteen months apart. Which provenance practice most effectively prevents this from reading as a contradiction while keeping every claim traceable?
questions.why: Preserving claim-to-source mappings with collection dates through synthesis, and rendering tabular data as a table, correctly reveals the two figures as sequential data points rather than a contradiction.
ww: A general bibliography breaks the claim-to-source mapping — individual figures are no longer traceable to a specific entry.
Without weighing the collection dates already available, this misreports normal temporal change as a genuine contradiction.
Expensive and error-prone; the mapping should be preserved through the pipeline rather than reconstructed after the fact.

questions.stem: The team's shared `/source-audit` skill at project scope loads automatically for every researcher. One researcher wants to pilot a stricter citation-format rule in her own sessions for a week before proposing it team-wide, without changing what the other five see after pulling the same repo. Where should she place the modified skill file, and why does it take effect automatically?
questions.why: Personal skills override project skills of the same name automatically; placing the pilot version at the personal skills path achieves an isolated trial with no extra configuration.
ww: A new command name creates `/source-audit-pilot` instead, losing the familiar `/source-audit` invocation the eventual team-wide rollout needs to test.
Editing the shared project file directly changes behavior for all six teammates immediately, not just her own sessions.
Fabricates a required registration step — personal-over-project precedence is automatic and needs no additional settings change.

questions.stem: The CI job invokes Claude Code fresh on every PR with only the diff and a generic 'review this code' prompt, no other project context. It repeatedly flags the team's deliberate module-level mutable-state pattern as a bug, even though it is an established, documented convention. What single change would most reduce this recurring false positive?
questions.why: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude project context — testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria — which reduces low-value output like a false positive on an established convention.
ww: A longer per-call prompt instruction is the same probabilistic approach already failing; CLAUDE.md is the corpus-sanctioned persistent context mechanism, not a bigger inline reminder.
Blunt, uniform strictness reduction damages accurate categories too and doesn't address the specific misunderstanding about this convention.
Forcing a tool call controls whether output is structured, not what the model believes about the codebase's conventions.

questions.stem: The team wants to move an iterative review workload to the Message Batches API for the 50% discount: for each file, the review bot fetches related files via tool calls mid-analysis before writing its finding. Is this workload a good fit for the Batches API, and why?
questions.why: Batch is fire-and-forget: it cannot execute a tool mid-request and return results to Claude within that request, which is exactly what iterative file-fetching review needs.
ww: False — this is precisely the limitation the corpus flags; batch cannot pause mid-request for a tool result.
No such pause-and-resume mechanism exists for a single batch request; this is a fabricated capability.
Overgeneralized — batch requests can include tool definitions; the specific limitation is mid-request multi-turn tool execution, not tool definitions generally.

questions.stem: A named pipeline session mapped a service's dependency graph yesterday. Overnight, a separate merge rewrote several files inside that service. This morning's run needs to continue the investigation without reasoning over now-incorrect tool results. What should it do?
questions.why: A resumed session reasons over old tool results as if current; a fresh session with an injected summary carries forward conclusions without the stale evidence — and naming the changed files enables targeted re-analysis.
ww: Resuming trusts stale tool results as current — exactly the risk the corpus flags for resumed sessions after file changes.
Compact risks losing exact details in summarization and doesn't specifically address that the underlying tool results are now stale.
fork_session is for diverging into two comparable approaches from one shared baseline, not for handling stale tool results.

questions.stem: The team wants the review bot's terse tone, its requirement to always cite a specific line number, and its finding format to hold consistently across an entire CI run, not just the first response. Where should these constraints be defined?
questions.why: The system prompt is the correct location for tone, persona constraints, and response-format requirements that must apply for the entire conversation.
ww: A first user message loses authority as the conversation continues, unlike a system prompt.
Environment variables have no effect on model behavior.
That describes prefilling, a mechanism for continuing a specific response, not for setting a persistent behavioral rule.

questions.stem: Developers complain that every PR comment the review bot posts opens with a variant of 'Sure, happy to review this!' before the actual finding. The team wants the filler gone without touching what findings get flagged. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Prefilling — appending a direct opening partial response for Claude to continue from — reliably suppresses filler phrases like this.
ww: Temperature controls randomness, not a specific recurring phrase.
A fragile workaround that treats the symptom rather than preventing the filler from being generated.
A system prompt instruction is less reliable than prefilling for suppressing one specific opening pattern.

questions.stem: The pipeline must always receive a schema-valid finding object — file, line, severity, fix — even when a PR has no issues, so the ingestion script never parses free text. Two tools are defined: `flag_finding` and `report_no_issues`. Which configuration guarantees structured output on every run?
questions.why: `{"type": "any"}` forces a tool call while letting the model pick the best-fitting one of several schemas, guaranteeing structured output whether or not issues exist.
ww: Auto lets the model answer in free text instead of calling a tool — no structure guarantee.
A prompt instruction is not enforced; the model can still return prose despite it.
Forces the wrong tool on clean PRs, since `report_no_issues` also needs to be callable.

questions.stem: After the review bot moved to `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema, malformed-JSON failures in the pipeline's ingestion step dropped to zero. Developers still occasionally see a finding that cites the wrong line number for the file it's attached to. What is the most accurate way to interpret this?
questions.why: Strict schemas eliminate the syntax-error class but do nothing for semantic errors like a wrong line number; those need business-rule validation and retry feedback.
ww: No schema field-type constraint can verify a line number is semantically correct for the finding.
Reverting would reintroduce the syntax-error class the tool use eliminated, on top of the unsolved semantic one.
Switching to auto removes the structure guarantee entirely and does nothing to fix content correctness.

questions.stem: The pipeline hand-maintains the finding tool's JSON schema in one config file and a separate Pydantic class validates results afterward. When the team added a new `blocking` severity level, they updated the tool schema but forgot the Pydantic class — every `blocking` finding silently failed validation and was dropped from the PR status for two weeks. What most directly prevents this?
questions.why: Generating the tool's JSON schema from the Pydantic model gives a single source of truth, so the tool contract and validator can never drift apart.
ww: Still two independently maintained files that can drift; this detects the problem after the fact instead of eliminating it.
Tool use enforces structure at generation time only; the Pydantic layer still checks semantic and business rules a schema can't express.
A process control that doesn't fix the underlying architecture-level duplication causing the drift.

questions.stem: A CI run reviews an 11-file PR in one pass. The bot's comments run long and specific for the first three files, then shrink to one-line 'no issues found' notes for the remaining eight — including a file that actually has an unguarded array index. An engineer proposes moving to a model with a much larger context window. What should the team do instead?
questions.why: The front-loaded thoroughness that fades across files is attention dilution, not a window-size problem; focused per-file passes plus an integration pass restore consistent depth.
ww: A larger context window does not fix attention quality — the exam-flagged wrong fix for attention dilution.
Papers over the underlying review-depth problem rather than fixing it for PRs of realistic size.
An abstract instruction is unlikely to reliably reverse a pattern already showing up in production behavior.

questions.stem: The review bot is asked, within the same conversation that generated a proposed fix, to 'review this change carefully for bugs before finishing.' It reports the fix is safe. A subtle race condition ships anyway and is caught only when a person reviews the diff cold days later. What most directly addresses this?
questions.why: True independence requires a separate instance or request without the generator's reasoning context; only that catches the blind spots the generator rationalized away.
ww: More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny.
A same-conversation second pass still carries the full generation reasoning in context and tends to reaffirm it.
A self-review instruction inherits the same anchoring that produced the missed bug in the first place.

questions.stem: The review bot should auto-resolve routine flaky-test findings but escalate genuinely ambiguous ones. Logs show it escalates obvious, single-assertion flakiness while trying to resolve complex multi-service timing issues on its own. Auto-resolution sits at 52%, target 80%. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing simple from complex cases directly fixes the unclear decision boundary causing the misrouting.
ww: Adds routing infrastructure without addressing the root cause of an unclear decision boundary in the prompt.
Overkill given the root cause is prompt-level ambiguity, not a need for a separate model.
Reduces coverage of findings rather than fixing the routing decision itself.

questions.stem: On a PR's third review round, the bot re-flags the exact same 'extract this into a helper' suggestion on a line a developer already replied to, explaining why the duplication is intentional here. Each round's prompt receives only the current diff. What change most effectively stops the bot from re-raising an already-addressed suggestion?
questions.why: The bot can only avoid re-raising an addressed suggestion if it can see what was already discussed; including prior findings and replies in context makes that possible.
ww: Reduces overall coverage instead of fixing the specific redundancy problem.
Fragile keyword matching misses semantic acknowledgments like 'this duplication is intentional.'
Without the prior context in the prompt, the instruction has nothing concrete to check the new suggestion against.

questions.stem: The review bot's 2,600-token system prompt states clear severity-calibration rules. On a long overnight run reviewing PR after PR in one continuous session, by the 12th PR it assigns severities that ignore those rules, drifting toward whatever pattern its own recent comments established. The session is nowhere near a context-window limit. What is the root cause?
questions.why: As assistant responses accumulate, system prompt influence dilutes relative to the growing body of the model's own prior outputs, which it increasingly pattern-matches instead.
ww: Explicitly ruled out — the session is nowhere near any context-window limit.
A misconception the corpus explicitly rejects; the system prompt applies throughout, just with diluting influence.
A fabricated mechanism; no such hidden token cap on system prompts is documented.

questions.stem: Pipeline policy requires a finding only auto-post as a blocking status via `post_blocking_status` after the classification tool has confirmed it as a real defect. Today this rule lives only in the system prompt: 'always classify before blocking.' Audit logs show 11% of blocking statuses were posted without classification ever running. What most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: For security- or correctness-critical sequencing, a programmatic precondition enforces the order at code level, unlike prompt-based instructions which remain probabilistic.
ww: Still probabilistic — the same class of fix that already failed 11% of the time.
Few-shot examples are also probabilistic guidance, not a guarantee the sequence is followed.
Changes where the instruction sits, not the enforcement mechanism, so the failure mode persists.

questions.stem: A finding flags a possible unhandled null case in a function inside a 40-file service. Before commenting, the review bot needs to confirm whether the same unguarded pattern shows up elsewhere in the service. What is the most effective way for it to investigate?
questions.why: Incremental investigation starts with Grep to locate entry points matching the pattern, then Read only the files that actually match — never reading everything upfront.
ww: Bulk upfront reading is the exam's flagged anti-pattern; it burns context on files that don't contain the pattern.
Glob matches file paths and names, not file contents — it can't locate the pattern itself.
Bypasses the tool designed for content search; Grep, not a shell workaround, is the sanctioned approach.

questions.stem: Your onboarding coordinator spawns a mapping subagent to chart a legacy monolith's structure with Grep, Glob, and Read, and a separate test-generation subagent to draft tests for whatever it finds. The test-generation subagent never learns what the mapping subagent discovered unless the coordinator copies those findings into its prompt. Which named architecture pattern does this reflect?
questions.why: The test-generation subagent has no visibility into the mapping subagent's findings unless the coordinator explicitly forwards them — this is context isolation, the defining trait of how information flows in a hub-and-spoke architecture.
ww: Least-privilege tooling is about scoping each subagent's *tool* access to its role, not about how *information* flows between subagents — nothing here is about tool permissions.
Structured handoff describes the self-contained summary built for a human reviewer during escalation — there is no human escalation in this scenario, only a subagent-to-subagent information gap.
Iterative refinement describes the coordinator re-delegating after evaluating a synthesis draft for gaps — nothing here involves evaluating or re-running a synthesis pass.

questions.stem: The migration subagent runs a standard agentic loop: it calls Bash to run a codemod script against the legacy monolith, inspects the result, and either continues or stops. On one turn, the response carries no `tool_use` block, only prose summarizing the change just made. What should the orchestrator check to decide whether to stop?
questions.why: stop_reason is the deterministic signal for loop control: tool_use means continue and execute the requested tools; end_turn means Claude has finished and the loop should stop.
ww: Counting tool calls treats an arbitrary iteration limit as the stopping signal instead of checking whether Claude actually finished.
Scanning response text for phrases like "done" relies on text content instead of the structured stop_reason field.
A fixed post-result delay is a timing heuristic, not a check of the API's own completion signal — fragile and unrelated to whether Claude finished.

questions.stem: The mapping subagent discovers that the legacy monolith's checkout flow depends on an undocumented internal pricing service, then times out before finishing the rest of its scan. The coordinator tells the test-generation subagent only to 'write tests for the checkout module.' The generated tests never mock the undocumented dependency. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: Subagents have isolated context — they see only what the coordinator explicitly includes in their prompt. The coordinator's instruction dropped the mapping subagent's dependency finding, so the generated tests had no way to know about it.
ww: The test-generation subagent's tooling isn't the issue — the mapping subagent already found the dependency; the finding simply never reached the test-generation subagent's prompt.
Hub-and-spoke architecture keeps inter-subagent communication flowing through the coordinator; subagents messaging each other directly isn't how this architecture is designed to propagate findings.
This isn't random variation — it's a specific, traceable context-passing gap between two turns, with a clear architectural fix.

questions.stem: The coordinator's prompt to the mapping subagents reads like a fixed script: 'Step 1: Grep for exported functions. Step 2: open the first 10 matches. Step 3: summarize each in 50 words.' The resulting map consistently misses modules exporting functions through a non-standard pattern the script never anticipated. Which change to the prompt is most effective?
questions.why: Goal-oriented prompts state the objective and quality bar and let the subagent adapt its approach as it discovers non-standard cases; procedural, step-locked prompts break the moment reality deviates from the script.
ww: Adding more steps to cover this one discovered case deepens the rigidity that caused the problem — the next non-standard pattern will break the script again.
More subagents executing the same fixed, incomplete script produces the same gap in parallel — it doesn't fix the script itself.
The mapping subagents already have the tools needed to find exports; the failure is in what the prompt tells them to do, not a missing tool.

questions.stem: Asked to map every way the legacy monolith's checkout flow reads and writes data, the coordinator splits the work into subtasks covering only direct SQL queries. All three subagents complete their subtasks correctly. The final map never mentions the caching layer or the billing API the checkout flow also uses. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: Every subagent executed its assigned subtask correctly — the gap traces to the coordinator's own decomposition, which never carved out subtasks for the caching layer or the billing API in the first place.
ww: Query quality inside each subtask isn't the issue — the subagents were never assigned the caching or billing subtopics to begin with.
There is no synthesis step failing to notice a gap here; the root cause is upstream, in how the coordinator partitioned the investigation before any subagent started.
A bigger context window doesn't expand the scope a subagent was assigned — the subagents were simply never told to look at caching or billing.

questions.stem: Tracing call sites across module boundaries, the dependency-tracing subagent's connection to an internal metadata service times out after it has confirmed 6 of 9 call sites. Per the architecture's error-propagation design, what should its failure report to the coordinator include?
questions.why: The required error payload is failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — this gives the coordinator what it needs to decide whether to retry, narrow scope, or continue with partial coverage.
ww: A generic flag with no detail forces the coordinator to re-run everything blind, discarding the 6 already-confirmed call sites.
Silently marking an incomplete branch as done masks a real failure as a success — the coordinator would believe the trace finished when 3 call sites were never checked.
Presenting an unfinished, timed-out branch identically to a branch that legitimately ran out of call sites erases the distinction between a valid result and an unresolved failure.

questions.stem: During an automated migration, the coordinator finds 12 modules marked deprecated in code comments but never scheduled for removal, several still with live callers elsewhere in the monolith. Team conventions say nothing about whether deprecated-but-referenced modules should be deleted, archived, or left alone during a migration. What should the coordinator do?
questions.why: No documented convention tells the coordinator whether to delete, archive, or leave these modules — this is a policy gap, one of the defined triggers for escalating to a human rather than inventing an interpretation.
ww: Treating a deprecated comment as unambiguous removal authority invents a policy nobody actually wrote — exactly the kind of guess escalation exists to avoid.
Silently leaving the ambiguous modules alone and reporting completion drops part of the task instead of surfacing the actual gap to someone who can resolve it.
This isn't a technical failure a different query can resolve — the ambiguity is about policy, not about finding more information in the codebase.

questions.stem: Production logs show the onboarding coordinator's `lookup_symbol` tool (source-code definitions) gets called for roughly 38% of requests that actually needed `lookup_reference` (internal documentation). Both tools are described only as 'looks up information for a given name.' What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses to select between tools — renaming away from the near-identical name and adding purpose, input, and boundary detail to both descriptions fixes the actual ambiguity.
ww: Merging the two into one parameterized tool loses the semantic precision that let Claude distinguish a code-definition request from a documentation request.
A pre-routing classifier adds a whole new component to work around descriptions that could simply be fixed directly.
A blunt 'always prefer' instruction doesn't teach the coordinator when each tool actually applies, and misroutes the genuine documentation-lookup cases entirely.

questions.stem: The `generate_migration_script` tool starts rejecting requests for one legacy module because it exceeds the team's file-size limit for automatic migration — a policy limit, not a service problem. The tool returns a bare `{"error": "failed"}`, and the migration subagent retries the identical call three times before giving up. How should its error handling be restructured?
questions.why: A file-size policy limit is a business-rule outcome, not a failure of the tool — marking it non-retryable with a clear explanation lets the subagent stop wasting retries and report the actual reason.
ww: Labeling a policy rejection as transient and retryable wastes attempts on an outcome that will never change no matter how many times it's retried.
A generic failure message gives the subagent no way to distinguish a policy rejection from a real outage, which is exactly why it keeps retrying instead of stopping.
Reporting the rejection as an empty success conflates a policy denial with a module that genuinely had nothing to migrate, hiding the real reason from anyone reading the result.

questions.stem: The mapping subagent pulls each module's owner from three sources: a wiki export returning a full name string, a build-metadata service returning a numeric team ID, and a ticketing system returning an email address. Its onboarding report has started grouping the same team under three different labels. What is the most maintainable fix?
questions.why: A PostToolUse hook intercepts tool output deterministically regardless of which of the three sources produced it — normalizing centrally, once, instead of depending on the model to reconcile formats.
ww: Modifying tools directly plus hand-writing a wrapper for the one the team can't change fragments maintenance across three code paths instead of one central fix.
A callable normalization tool depends on the subagent remembering to invoke it every time — an extra LLM decision point instead of a guaranteed step.
Documenting the three formats in CLAUDE.md relies on the model correctly interpreting and converting them on every single call — probabilistic, not guaranteed.

questions.stem: The mapping subagent calls `get_module_metadata` and, in a separate later turn, `get_test_coverage` — even on requests where the onboarding report always needs both together. This adds a full extra API round-trip to nearly every module the subagent covers. What is the most effective way to reduce this overhead?
questions.why: Claude can naturally request multiple tools in a single turn when the prompt makes that expectation clear — prompting the subagent to bundle the habitually-paired calls is the preferred fix over building new tooling.
ww: A composite tool works, but it hides the two-step composition behind a new interface instead of using the simpler fix of prompting Claude to bundle its existing calls.
Hooks fire around individual tool calls after the model has already committed to them — they aren't the mechanism for getting two independent calls issued together in one turn.
A larger context window doesn't change what the prompt asks the subagent to do on a given turn — it still has no instruction to request both calls together.

questions.stem: An engineer's Claude Code sessions investigating the legacy monolith reliably flagged undocumented external dependencies throughout last month's onboarding sprint. Picking the same investigation back up this week, on the same machine and repository checkout, Claude no longer mentions dependency risk at all, even on modules it flagged before. What is the most effective first step?
questions.why: Discovered CLAUDE.md files load as a concatenated set, not a single guaranteed file — when behavior changes with nothing else different, /memory shows exactly which files are actually loaded now, turning a guess into a fact.
ww: CLAUDE.md files concatenate into context rather than overriding one another — there is no documented mechanism by which a lower-level file silently replaces a higher-level instruction, so deleting one on that theory is as likely to remove something needed as to fix anything.
Re-typing the instruction treats the symptom for one session at a time instead of finding out why the file holding it stopped being discovered.
/compact compresses an existing session's conversation history to save tokens — it has nothing to do with which CLAUDE.md or memory files get loaded at session start.

questions.stem: The mapping subagent's dependency scan flags exactly one call site — a single line in the notifications module — still using a helper the team deprecated last quarter, and confirms no other file references it. The team's migration notes give the exact one-line replacement call. Before making the change, should the engineer open planning mode first?
questions.why: Scope, root cause, and the exact fix are already fully defined by the scan and the migration notes — a single-file, fully-scoped change with a known solution is the textbook case for direct execution, not planning mode.
ww: The scan has already confirmed this is the only reference — reopening that question in planning mode re-explores something already established, adding process the task doesn't need.
fork_session compares genuinely competing designs from a shared analysis baseline — there is only one documented replacement here, not alternatives to evaluate against each other.
Re-scanning the entire monolith to re-verify a result the scan already reported adds redundant work instead of just making the already-confirmed change.

questions.stem: The team's `/map-legacy-module` skill runs a deep dependency and coverage scan of one module at a time. After it runs mid-investigation, the coordinator's replies slow down and re-explain basics of the onboarding task the engineer already established, as if earlier context had been pushed out. Which fix keeps the skill's full depth while preventing this?
questions.why: context: fork runs the skill's large, exploratory output in an isolated subagent context, so the deep scan's bulk never floods the main session — only a summary comes back, preserving both scan depth and the original task's context.
ww: A faster model processes the same bloated context more quickly but doesn't stop that context from crowding out the original task.
Forcing the skill itself to compress to two sentences discards scan depth the team wants to keep, trading away capability instead of isolating where it runs.
Splitting into two skills run sequentially doesn't stop either skill's output from still landing directly in the main session.

questions.stem: The migration subagent has been converting the legacy monolith's data-layer modules to a new schema one at a time across a multi-day run — 40 of 120 modules done — when the coordinator's host process crashes and restarts. The migration plan itself hasn't changed. What should the architecture do to avoid re-converting the 40 completed modules?
questions.why: Each unit of work exporting structured state to a known location, with the coordinator loading a manifest on restart, lets the architecture resume from the checkpoint instead of losing or re-doing completed work.
ww: The API is stateless and the process itself crashed — there is no conversation history left to reconstruct progress from once the host restarts.
Re-converting all 120 modules from scratch discards the 40 already done, wasting real, completed work that a checkpoint could have preserved.
State that lives only inside a subagent's own context window disappears the moment the process holding that context crashes — nothing survives for the coordinator to resume from.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline sends any document that doesn't fit its three extraction tools to an on-call queue with a free-text status note. Every note opens with 'I apologize for the inconvenience, but...' before the actual problem, and the queue's ticket list truncates each note at 80 characters, so the real detail rarely shows. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Prefilling the response with a direct opening bypasses the model's own generated preamble — the documented fix for suppressing one specific recurring opening phrase; the model continues from the supplied text instead of generating filler first.
ww: Temperature controls sampling randomness, not the presence of a specific recurring phrase; a low-temperature model can still consistently choose the same apology opening.
A system-prompt instruction to avoid a phrase relies on probabilistic compliance, documented as less reliable than prefilling for suppressing one specific recurring opening.
Stripping the phrase after generation is a fragile downstream workaround that treats the symptom on every note instead of preventing the preamble at the source.

questions.stem: Before any of the three extraction tools can run, the pipeline must call `redact_sensitive_fields` on every document, since downstream storage may never hold unredacted PII. With `tool_choice` left at its default, logs show the model sometimes calls an extraction tool directly on raw text, skipping redaction. Which `tool_choice` configuration most reliably closes this gap?
questions.why: Forcing the specific tool guarantees that particular tool runs. The documented distinction is that 'any' guarantees a tool call, not that specific one — a mandatory first step needs the named-tool form.
ww: 'any' guarantees some tool is called but lets the model pick which one, so an extraction tool can still run before the mandatory redaction step — it doesn't force this specific tool first.
A prompt instruction is followed with probabilistic compliance; the documented fix for a mandatory sequencing requirement is deterministic enforcement through tool_choice, not an added instruction.
Temperature controls sampling randomness in phrasing, not which tool gets selected under the default auto mode; it doesn't address tool selection at all.

questions.stem: `extract_invoice`'s `payment_terms` field must normalize wildly varied source phrasing — 'net thirty days,' '30D,' 'due within 30 days of invoice date,' 'COD' — into a fixed enum. Prose instructions alone leave these phrasings inconsistent, though already-standard phrasing like 'Net 30' normalizes correctly every time. How should the team select few-shot examples to fix this?
questions.why: Few-shot examples work best targeted at the 4-6 specific ambiguous cases where the model currently gets it wrong, not padded with cases that already normalize correctly.
ww: Adding 10-15 examples that include already-correct phrasing doesn't help the specific ambiguous cases that fail; the corpus explicitly warns against padding with clear cases.
The prose instruction is already failing to produce consistent output; further refining it with more explicit written rules doesn't fix what targeted examples fix.
Temperature controls output randomness, not which canonical value a given phrasing maps to; it doesn't address the mapping ambiguity itself.

questions.stem: `extract_invoice` must also flag duplicate line items — same SKU, matching or near-matching unit price, listed more than once on the same document. Prompted with only the target field name, duplicate detection misses roughly a third of true duplicates once an invoice has more than eight line items. Which prompting addition most reliably improves accuracy here?
questions.why: Comparison across N items is one of the documented triggers for a step-by-step reasoning cue; instructing the model to work through every pairwise comparison explicitly improves accuracy on exactly this kind of multi-step task.
ww: Few-shot examples target ambiguous categorization and format consistency; the corpus lists comparison across N items as a chain-of-thought trigger, not a few-shot one.
Temperature controls sampling randomness, not whether the model actually performs the comparison; it adds no reasoning structure at all.
A self-reported count with no supporting instruction gives the model no mechanism to actually perform the comparison — it just asks for a number without structuring how to derive it.

questions.stem: `extract_invoice`'s schema marks `vat_registration_number` as required and non-nullable, reasoning that every business-to-business invoice needs one for tax filing. An audit of 4,000 extracted invoices finds 13% carry a plausible-looking VAT number that traces to no real registration — those vendors were below the VAT threshold and never had one. What schema change most directly stops this?
questions.why: A required, non-nullable field pushes the model to fabricate a value when the source data is genuinely absent; making it nullable lets the model honestly return null instead.
ww: Prompt instructions rely on probabilistic compliance; the documented fix for fabrication pressure from a required field is a schema change, not an instruction competing against the schema's own constraint.
A confidence field doesn't relieve the pressure a required, non-nullable field creates — the model still must supply some value, confidently wrong or not.
Discarding the structured field for free text abandons the schema's shape entirely; the fix is to make the specific field nullable, not to give up structure.

questions.stem: Since `extract_invoice` moved to `tool_use` with a strict schema, every response parses cleanly and every field passes its type check — zero validation failures for three straight weeks. Auditors still occasionally find invoices where `invoice_date` and `due_date` are swapped: both are valid dates, just in the wrong field. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: tool_use with a strict schema eliminates the syntax-error class entirely but does nothing for semantic errors — a value in the wrong field is valid JSON with wrong content, exactly the documented split between the two error classes.
ww: No JSON Schema constraint can verify a date belongs in one field versus another when both are syntactically valid dates; tightening the schema further cannot catch a semantic field swap.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the syntax-error class tool_use just eliminated, stacked on top of the semantic errors the switch never touched.
A vague self-check instruction gives the model no structural mechanism to catch a field swap; the documented answer to this error class is structured cross-field validation or self-correction fields.

questions.stem: The retry loop resubmits failed extractions with the document, prior output, and validation error. On a batch of `extract_delivery_confirmation` documents, `carrier_tracking_number` keeps failing every retry; investigation shows the number only appears on the shipping label, a separate document the pipeline never receives. An engineer wants to raise max retries to 8. What should the team do instead?
questions.why: When the required information lives in a document the pipeline never receives, no amount of retrying against the document actually provided can produce it; the documented fix is a nullable field plus a stop to retrying.
ww: Retrying more times cannot supply information the source document never contained; more attempts against the same incomplete input just burns tokens.
A more specific feedback message can guide the model to reformat data it has — it cannot invent a tracking number never present in the document supplied.
Keeping the field required for reporting completeness pressures the model to fabricate a plausible tracking number rather than honestly reporting it's absent from the source.

questions.stem: The pipeline also processes vendor contracts alongside invoices. A contract's cover page states 'This agreement includes 8 exhibits,' and extraction separately lists each exhibit heading found in the body. Weeks later, a compliance review finds a contract with only 6 actual exhibit headings — the stated count was simply wrong. What design change most directly catches this?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern generalizes beyond financial totals: extract both the document's own claimed value and an independently re-derived value, with a boolean flag when they disagree, surfacing the conflict as structured data at extraction time.
ww: A periodic manual audit only catches the mismatch weeks later on a sample; the documented pattern moves detection to extraction time, on every document.

A vague 'double-check carefully' instruction is not a structural mechanism and produces no machine-readable signal when the model is wrong; the pattern requires building re-derivation into the schema itself.
Dropping the stated count discards the exact information needed to detect a mismatch; the fix keeps both values and compares them.

questions.stem: During a long correction session, an analyst states early on: 'Documents from this vendor should always route to `extract_receipt`, never `extract_invoice`.' Sixty exchanges later, after several rounds of summarization, the pipeline routes a new document from that same vendor to `extract_invoice` again — the summarized history now reads only 'a vendor-specific routing exception was discussed.' What fix is most effective?
questions.why: A persistent case-facts block carried in every prompt, outside the summarized history, survives context compression — the documented fix for a precise rule getting vagued away by summarization.
ww: Raising the threshold delays compression but doesn't prevent it; the rule eventually gets summarized away regardless.
This still relies on the summarizer perfectly preserving every specific rule every time; a dedicated persistent block removes that dependency entirely.
External storage and retrieval is overkill for a session-level fact; the documented fix is a simple persistent block carried in every prompt.

questions.stem: Before documents reach the three extraction tools, `run_ocr_pass` returns page-level bounding boxes, per-character confidence scores, and font metadata — 60+ fields per page — when only the plain text and overall page confidence matter downstream. On multi-page scans, this bulk accumulates in context and later pages' extractions start drifting. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: A PostToolUse hook that filters a tool's result to only the relevant fields before it enters context is the documented fix for a tool returning far more fields than the task needs.
ww: Asking the model to ignore fields in the system prompt doesn't reduce token consumption — the tokens are still there and attention cost remains.
More aggressive summarization treats the symptom; the verbose OCR output keeps flooding in on every subsequent page regardless.
A larger context window raises cost and still leaves the noise problem itself unaddressed.

questions.stem: A submission bundle includes an invoice and its matching delivery confirmation for the same order. `extract_invoice` reports 500 units of a line item; `extract_delivery_confirmation` reports 480 units for the identical item. Both documents are legible and internally consistent. How should the pipeline handle this discrepancy?
questions.why: When two credible sources within the same extraction genuinely disagree, the documented pattern completes the extraction with both values, explicitly annotates the conflict with source attribution, and lets downstream reconciliation decide — not resolving it autonomously.
ww: Picking one document's value by a precedence heuristic abandons a decision above the extraction step's scope — the documented misconception of resolving a genuine conflict autonomously.
Pausing the entire bundle before completing extraction blocks the pipeline unnecessarily; the documented pattern completes the analysis with both values annotated rather than stopping first.
Silently dropping the delivery confirmation's figure loses information the downstream reconciliation step needs; neither source is discarded in the documented pattern.

questions.stem: The pipeline's monthly reconciliation report merges extracted due dates, amounts, and payment references from dozens of vendor statements into one continuous narrative paragraph per vendor, done for a more uniform reading style. Auditors say the report is now hard to scan and cross-check line by line against the source statements. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Financial and tabular data should render as tables in synthesis output, not be flattened into uniform narrative prose — the documented content-type-aware rendering guidance exists because prose makes precise figures harder to scan and verify.
ww: A general bibliography at the end loses the mapping from each individual claim to its specific source — the documented failure of dropping per-claim attribution.
Flagging every month-over-month change as a conflict without accounting for the fact that amounts are simply expected to differ over time is the documented false-contradiction pattern.
Re-deriving attributions after the fact by re-searching is expensive and error-prone; the documented fix preserves the mapping through the pipeline as it runs.

questions.stem: The pipeline needs jurisdiction-code validation for cross-border shipments. A well-maintained community MCP server already wraps the international registry this requires, but an engineer proposes building a custom in-house server instead, arguing it gives the team full control over the validation logic. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: For standard integrations a well-maintained community server already covers, prefer it over a custom build; reserve custom-server effort for workflows unique to the team that no existing server addresses.
ww: "Full control" does not justify reinventing a maintained standard integration — this is the documented anti-pattern for exactly this situation.
Running both in parallel adds ongoing maintenance burden for two overlapping integrations instead of simply choosing the one that already meets the need.
A manual spreadsheet workaround reintroduces the unreliable, non-scalable process MCP integration exists to replace, and still leaves the actual build-vs-buy decision unresolved.

questions.stem: A nightly `claude -p` job writes one JSON record per batch — `batch_id`, `exceptions_found`, `flagged_document_ids` — to a ledger file a compliance script parses. On batches with zero exceptions, the job sometimes replies with a line like 'No exceptions were found' instead of the record, and the parser throws. What is the most reliable fix?
questions.why: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` forces and enforces schema-valid JSON on every invocation, including the zero-exception case — eliminating the gap where a clean result tips the model into free text.
ww: A CLAUDE.md format section is documentation the model may or may not consistently follow; it is not a guaranteed enforcement mechanism the way the CLI flags are.
A prompt instruction is followed with variable compliance — exactly the gap already showing up on the zero-exception case; it doesn't guarantee format the way schema enforcement does.
Treating any non-JSON line as an implicit zero-exception result is a fragile workaround that could just as easily mask a genuine error as a clean batch.

questions.stem: The pipeline's nightly run submits 3,000 document-extraction requests through the Message Batches API. An engineer's first implementation leaves every request's `custom_id` set to the same placeholder value. Results return the next morning in a different order than submitted, and the pipeline can't tell which record belongs to which document. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: `custom_id` is the batch API's per-request identifier for matching outputs back to inputs; giving every request a unique, meaningful custom_id works regardless of what order results return in.
