ww: Moving to synchronous processing abandons the batch discount for a problem the API's own custom_id mechanism already solves; nothing in this workload needs synchronous latency.
Smaller chunks don't fix a placeholder custom_id shared across every request — the matching problem persists at any batch size until each request gets its own identifier.
A timestamp doesn't reconstruct the specific input-to-output mapping the way a unique custom_id does; it's an unnecessary workaround for a problem custom_id already solves directly.

questions.stem: Your coordinator's subagent roster lists a `returns_agent` and a `billing_agent`, both with the `description` field set to the same generic text: 'Handles customer requests.' Both subagents already have correctly scoped `allowed_tools` and accurate system prompts for their roles. Logs show the coordinator routes billing-dispute cases to `returns_agent` roughly a third of the time. What change most effectively fixes the routing?
questions.why: The `description` field is what the orchestration layer reads to decide which subagent type to invoke; two subagent types sharing a generic description give the coordinator no reliable signal to route on, regardless of how well-scoped their tools or system prompts are.
ww: The system prompt governs behavior after a subagent type is already selected — it has no influence on the coordinator's initial choice of which subagent type to invoke, so this doesn't touch the actual routing decision.
Broadening both subagents' tool access doesn't change which one gets picked, and it breaks least-privilege scoping without addressing the root cause, which is indistinguishable descriptions.

`Task` is the coordinator's tool for spawning subagents, not a channel for subagents to hand cases to each other — giving subagents `Task` doesn't change how the coordinator itself routes an incoming case, and direct subagent-to-subagent handoff breaks the hub-and-spoke model.

questions.stem: Investigating a loyalty-tier dispute, two subagents return conflicting data: the account-history subagent reports Gold tier reached March 3, while the billing subagent's audit log shows the upgrade posting March 18. Both cite their own tool calls confidently, and the discrepancy changes which perks apply. What should the coordinator do?
questions.why: On conflicting statistics between sources, the rule is to preserve both values with attribution and annotate the conflict rather than arbitrarily resolving it during the merge — the coordinator, which has visibility across both subagents, is where the decision belongs.
ww: Silently picking one subagent's value and dropping the other is exactly the arbitrary-pick failure the rule exists to prevent — it discards a legitimate, differently-sourced data point instead of preserving it.

Re-running both subagents doesn't resolve a genuine conflict between two real source systems — it will most likely reproduce the same two dates, since each subagent is accurately reporting what its own source says.

Averaging two conflicting source values manufactures a third, fabricated date that neither source actually reported — worse than either original value, and it hides the discrepancy instead of surfacing it.

questions.stem: Every standard refund case follows the same sequence: verify identity, confirm eligibility, check the return window, then process the refund — identical steps across roughly 40,000 cases last quarter. An engineer proposes replacing this scripted flow with dynamic decomposition that re-plans the investigation from scratch on every case. What is the most effective decomposition strategy?
questions.why: When task structure is predictable and every step is known up front, a fixed sequential pipeline gives stability and reproducibility without paying the overhead of re-planning on every case — exactly the profile this refund flow fits.
ww: Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended tasks whose scope isn't known up front; applying it to an already-predictable, template-following flow is unnecessary complexity, not a safety net.
Dropping defined steps in favor of one open-ended instruction sacrifices the reproducibility a fixed pipeline is chosen for, without matching either named decomposition pattern.

These four steps have a required order — identity must be verified before a refund is processed — so treating them as independent, parallelizable work misapplies a different concept to a case that actually calls for a fixed, ordered pipeline.

questions.stem: Your coordinator delegates a three-charge billing dispute to the billing subagent, which returns a resolution draft addressing two of the three disputed charges and says nothing about the third. This is the coordinator's first evaluation of the draft. What should the coordinator do?
questions.why: Gap evaluation and re-delegation belong to the coordinator: it should send a targeted query aimed at the specific gap back to the subagent best suited to it, then re-invoke synthesis with the enriched findings — the refinement loop working as designed.
ww: Letting the subagent chase the gap on its own bypasses the coordinator's ownership of gap evaluation and re-delegation, and risks the subagent operating outside its defined scope.

A coverage annotation is for gaps that can't be recovered through further delegation — here, re-delegation is available and hasn't even been tried yet, so shipping with a caveat skips the refinement loop prematurely.

The coordinator investigating the charge itself, rather than routing back to the subagent that owns billing-dispute investigation, blurs the coordinator's delegating role and duplicates work the billing subagent is already positioned to do.

questions.stem: A refund-eligibility check on a disputed high-value order runs three verification calls in parallel: payment-method match, shipping-address match, and prior-dispute-history lookup. The prior-dispute-history call times out; the other two return clean results confirming legitimacy. The agent must produce a recommendation for the human reviewer queue. How should this output be structured?
questions.why: Graceful degradation means completing synthesis with the data actually available while annotating which parts are well-supported and where gaps remain, so uncertainty is propagated upward instead of hidden or used to block everything.
ww: Refusing outright because one of three checks is incomplete discards two clean, usable results — the rule explicitly rejects returning an error just because an input is incomplete.
Presenting the recommendation as fully verified when a check never returned silently drops the gap from the reviewer's view — the rule explicitly rejects proceeding without noting what's missing.

Holding the recommendation until every check eventually returns defeats the purpose of graceful degradation, which is to proceed with available data rather than stall the case on a slow or failing dependency.

questions.stem: Your `update_shipping_address` tool was built as a general-purpose order-modification endpoint: beyond address fields, it also accepts optional `refund_amount` and `cancel_order` parameters 'for convenience.' The returns subagent, scoped only to handle address corrections, has started passing `refund_amount` through this same tool to issue refunds directly. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Replacing an over-broad tool with a constrained alternative enforces the boundary at the interface level — the returns subagent physically cannot pass a refund amount through a tool that no longer accepts one, which removes the capability rather than just discouraging its use.
ww: Granting the full tool set moves further from least privilege, not toward it — it hands a subagent scoped to address corrections direct refund authority instead of removing the accidental capability it already has.
A prompt instruction not to use a parameter the tool still accepts is probabilistic — nothing stops a future call, whether by model error or a later prompt change, from passing a refund amount again.

Blocking on a specific parameter value is a fragile, pattern-based patch — it only catches the exact misuse already observed, leaves the underlying capability in place, and won't generalize to a differently-shaped bypass.

questions.stem: Your escalation handoff payload already includes `customer_id`, `order_id`, and `issue_summary`, so human agents no longer re-ask customers for basic details. Agents still report spending several minutes per case re-reading raw tool outputs to figure out what the bot already tried and what it thinks should happen next. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The core handoff fields the exam names include actions already taken and a recommended action, alongside customer ID and root cause — without them, the human still has to reconstruct the bot's work from raw outputs even once identity and order fields are present.
ww: Human agents don't have transcript or raw tool-output access by design, and granting it re-creates the problem the structured summary exists to solve — forcing a slow read-through instead of a compact record.
A priority field helps decide which case to open first; it does nothing for the time cost once an agent is already inside a case, which is what the complaint describes.

Escalating earlier hands humans less investigation, not more context — it removes the bot's own conclusions from the payload entirely and pushes more raw work onto the human, the opposite of the fix needed here.

questions.stem: Once `escalate_to_human` fires on a case, a human takes over review — but your support bot's loop has no way to know that and keeps running. Logs show 8% of escalated cases get an automatic `process_refund` call from the same session minutes later, occasionally issuing a refund the human was still reviewing for denial. What change most reliably prevents this?
questions.why: For sequencing that must hold reliably — here, no further action after a case is escalated — the fix is a programmatic precondition enforced at the code/orchestration level, not a rule the model is merely asked to follow.
ww: A strengthened prompt instruction is still probabilistic compliance for this exact class of problem, since nothing stops the model from calling the tool anyway on a given turn.
Few-shot examples shape behavior probabilistically, the same category of fix rejected for critical sequencing — they make the correct behavior more likely, not guaranteed.

Reversing a wrongly-issued refund after the fact addresses the symptom once damage is already done — including a refund a human was actively reviewing for denial — instead of preventing the disallowed call from happening at all.

questions.stem: A customer's message raises three independent issues: a shipping delay on one order, an unrelated loyalty-tier question, and a request to update the email on file. Your coordinator emits one `Task` call, waits for the result, then emits the next `Task` call in a following response — tripling wall-clock latency versus a similar single-issue case. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Multiple `Task` calls run in parallel only when emitted together in a single coordinator response; issuing them one per turn, as the current implementation does, runs them sequentially no matter how independent the underlying issues are.
ww: Combining three unrelated issues into one subagent call cuts coordinator round-trips but keeps the actual work sequential inside that one call, and mixes scopes a specialized subagent shouldn't need to hold at once.
More subagent types is a specialization change, not an execution-timing change — the three `Task` calls would still be issued one response at a time, so latency is unaffected.

Caching only helps on an exact repeat of the same combination of issues; this is a first-time combination for this customer, so there is nothing to cache yet and it does nothing for this case's latency.

questions.stem: A first implementation of your support bot's tool-calling harness gets a response with `stop_reason: 'tool_use'` naming `lookup_order`, executes the tool, then sends a new user-role text message describing the result instead of a proper tool result. Claude's next reply is confused and sometimes repeats the call. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The tool-use flow requires the application to append a `tool_result` content block, matched by `id` to the original `tool_use` call, before continuing the conversation — a free-text user message is not a substitute for that structured continuation step.
ww: `tool_choice` governs whether and which tool Claude calls on its next turn — it has no bearing on how the harness itself is supposed to report a completed tool's result back into the conversation.

The system prompt is for durable instructions, not turn-specific data; stuffing a single tool result into it doesn't fix the missing `tool_result` block and won't scale to later tool calls in the same conversation.

The tool executed successfully — the failure is in how its result was returned to Claude, a harness-level protocol gap. Retrying an already-successful call misdiagnoses a continuation-format bug as a tool-reliability problem.

questions.stem: Your `cancel_subscription` action is irreversible once it runs, so it was split into `preview_cancel_subscription` (returns impact details plus a single-use confirmation token) and `execute_cancel_subscription` (requires that token). A teammate calls this over-engineered and proposes one `cancel_subscription` tool with a `confirmed: boolean` parameter, backed by a strengthened prompt and worked examples. Why keep the two-tool design?
questions.why: The two-tool split makes the bypass architecturally impossible: the single-use token that `execute_cancel_subscription` requires simply does not exist until `preview_cancel_subscription` has been called, whereas a `confirmed: boolean` parameter can always be set directly regardless of how the prompt is worded.
ww: This restates the exact failure mode the token-binding pattern exists to eliminate — prompt instructions and examples are probabilistic, not guaranteed, so `confirmed=true` can still be called on the first attempt.

An orchestration-layer confirmation dialog can work, but it requires extra infrastructure outside the API request itself — ranked below the two-tool split, which achieves the same guarantee inside the tool design alone.

This confuses the two-tool pattern with a different lesson — reducing an agent's total tool count for selection reliability. The token-binding split actually adds a tool; its benefit is architectural enforcement, not a smaller tool catalog.

questions.stem: Your returns subagent currently selects correctly among its 5 role-scoped tools nearly every time. A product manager wants to fold in 13 more tools — order-modification variants, loyalty adjustments, and shipping overrides — so the same subagent can handle anything a customer might ask in one place. What is the most effective response to this proposal?
questions.why: The official guidance's own numbers show that 18 tools instead of 4-5 degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity — each additional near-miss tool is another candidate the model must discriminate between on every turn, independent of how good any individual description is.
ww: This is the corpus's own rejected fix: better descriptions help, but they don't address tool count, which is the root cause of degraded selection once a subagent's catalog grows this large.
Extending the same bloated catalog to a second, currently well-scoped subagent spreads the reliability problem instead of avoiding it — it moves a working subagent in the wrong direction.
A preprocessing classifier is infrastructure overkill layered on top of the actual problem; it doesn't remove the oversized tool catalog, it just adds a new component to compensate for it.

questions.stem: An engineer investigating why `process_refund` sometimes computes the wrong discount wants to find every file in the codebase that references a deprecated `legacyDiscountRate` variable, regardless of what the containing file happens to be named. Which built-in tool should they reach for first?
questions.why: The target is content inside files — every place the variable is referenced — not files named after it, which is exactly the Grep-vs-Glob distinction: Grep searches file contents, Glob matches file paths.
ww: Glob matches file paths and names, not what's inside a file's contents — this would only surface files literally named `legacyDiscountRate`, missing every file that merely references the variable in code.
Reading every file under a module upfront before searching is the anti-pattern called out directly — it burns context on irrelevant files instead of letting content search drive discovery first.
Manually scanning files via Bash bypasses the tool actually built for content search and doesn't scale reliably across a codebase-wide reference the way a direct Grep does.

questions.stem: Your coordinator burns 4-6 tool calls per session issuing guessed `search_policies` queries just to discover what refund-policy categories even exist, before it can search productively for the one relevant to a case. The policy-lookup MCP server could expose a category index without requiring a tool call. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: MCP resources expose content catalogs the agent can read directly for an immediate map of what exists, without spending exploratory tool calls to discover it — exactly the guessed-query overhead described here.
ww: A resource provides the map as readable context with no extra model turn required; a tool still costs an LLM call and depends on the agent remembering to call it first, which doesn't remove the exploratory-call problem.

Resources are requested on demand; pasting the full catalog into the system prompt bloats context permanently and goes stale the moment policies change, unlike a resource the agent reads when it actually needs it.
Building a predictive classification model is infrastructure overkill for a discovery problem that exposing an existing MCP resource solves directly, with no new component to train or maintain.

questions.stem: Your support bot's system prompt states a firm rule: never promise a specific refund timeline beyond 'within our standard processing window.' This holds reliably in short conversations. In extended, multi-issue conversations running 30+ turns — still well within the token limit throughout — logs show the agent increasingly gives specific day-counts instead. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: System-prompt authority diminishes relative to accumulated assistant responses as a conversation lengthens; the preventive patterns are reinforcement at breakpoints and replacing abstract rules with concrete few-shot examples, since examples hold up longer than abstract instructions.
ww: The rule is already stated once at the top; the problem is drift across accumulated turns, not weak initial emphasis — repeating it louder in the same static spot doesn't address turns well into the conversation.

The case states the conversation stays well within token limits throughout — this is instruction drift, not a context-budget problem, so a larger window doesn't touch the actual mechanism causing the rule to erode.

Summarizing addresses token cost, a different problem the case explicitly rules out; it does nothing to reinforce the system prompt's authority against accumulating assistant responses, which is what's actually drifting here.

questions.stem: The pipeline's review bot must apply stricter conventions to files under services/payments/, relaxed conventions to services/notifications/, and a shared testing convention to test files scattered next to the code they cover. What configuration makes the right convention load automatically based on which files are in a PR's diff?
questions.why: Path-scoped `.claude/rules/` files with glob frontmatter load automatically only for matching files, giving payments, notifications, and tests their own conventions without relying on model inference.
ww: Headings inside one CLAUDE.md rely on the model correctly inferring which section applies to the current diff — not deterministic path matching.
Per-directory CLAUDE.md files don't scale well once matching files (like the scattered test files here) are spread across many directories.
A manually invoked command depends on someone remembering to run it every time; it isn't automatic the way path-scoped rules are.

questions.stem: The pipeline's `/triage-failure` command should take a CI job's failure category as an argument, invoked as `/triage-failure flaky-test`. Inside the command file, an engineer references the typed text as `$INPUT`. Every invocation instead produces a note containing the literal string `$INPUT`, never the category actually typed. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The text typed after a command name is available inside the command file as `$ARGUMENTS`; referencing any other variable name never receives the substitution.
ww: Renaming the file doesn't create the missing substitution; the command's filename and the argument-variable name are unrelated to each other.
`argument-hint` only displays a hint when the command is invoked — it doesn't create or rename the substitution variable itself.
`context: fork` isolates a skill's output into a separate subagent context; it has no effect on argument substitution.

questions.stem: An engineer copies the shared `/review-checklist` skill into `~/.claude/skills/review-checklist/` on their laptop to trial a stricter severity rule before proposing it to the team. The same `/review-checklist` skill also runs inside the CI job on every pull request. What happens when the review bot runs inside the CI job?
questions.why: Personal skills live outside version control in the user's home directory; CI checks out only the repository, so it always runs the project-scoped skill.
ww: No such sync mechanism exists — a non-version-controlled personal skill never propagates to CI.
A same-name personal and project skill don't collide into a startup failure; the personal copy simply overrides locally for that one user.
Personal overrides don't merge with the project version — precedence means one applies, not a blend of both.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to fix a bug in the pipeline's finding-formatter script: PR titles containing an ampersand or embedded quote break the JSON payload the ingestion API expects. Each prose re-description ('handle special characters') fixes only the character just mentioned, leaving others broken. What converges on a complete fix?
questions.why: A specific failing test case with example input and expected output is the fastest way to converge on an edge-case fix — each iteration gets a concrete, checkable target.
ww: Silently swallowing the error hides the bug instead of fixing the escaping logic — a symptom patch, not a fix.
Prose re-description, even emphatic, is interpreted inconsistently turn to turn — the exact pattern that produced only partial fixes so far.
Stripping all non-alphanumeric characters changes legitimate title content instead of fixing the escaping logic, and sidesteps validating the actual expected output.

questions.stem: The pipeline re-runs the review bot from a blank prompt on every commit pushed to an open PR. A PR with five findings on push one gets, after push two fixes three, a review reporting only two new nits — the two unaddressed findings go unmentioned. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Feeding prior findings into the re-run prompt keeps the reviewer consistent across runs and lets it explicitly report unresolved items instead of silently dropping them.
ww: More output room doesn't give the model memory of a run it never saw; token budget isn't the missing input.
A separate tracking system bypasses the actual problem — the review bot's own prompt still starts blank each run — and adds infrastructure instead of fixing the input.
Consensus voting across duplicate runs suppresses real signal; a genuinely unresolved finding could fail to reappear in either run.

questions.stem: The pipeline's shared CLAUDE.md has grown past 600 lines covering linting, commit-message format, security-review criteria, and release-notes formatting in one file. Because every engineer edits the same file for unrelated changes, PRs touching it now collide in merge conflicts weekly. Which restructuring most reduces these conflicts while keeping all content available every session?
questions.why: Separate single-topic files under `.claude/rules/` is the supported modularization approach — engineers editing different topics touch different files, and every session still loads all the content.
ww: Bundling everything into one skill still keeps it as a single file competing for edits, and universal standards would now need explicit invocation instead of loading automatically.
Manual coordination doesn't change the underlying single-file structure causing the collisions; it's a process workaround, not a fix.
A partial split still leaves two topics sharing one file, so engineers editing security-review and release-notes together still collide.

questions.stem: Reviewing twelve PRs in one long session, an engineer runs `/compact` as the context nears its limit. Afterward, the review bot describes test coverage as 'roughly a third' — the tool output with the exact figure, 34.2%, was part of what got compressed away. What does this show about `/compact`, and what should the team do for sessions where exact figures matter?
questions.why: `/compact` compresses context while preserving essential information, but exact numeric values can be lost in the summary — the documented risk of this feature.
ww: `/compact` summarizes the session's content broadly, including tool-output-derived detail; the scenario shows precisely that the exact figure was lost.
`fork_session` branches the current session but doesn't solve a token-budget problem forcing compaction in the first place — both branches still need managing.
Dismissing the precision loss as a non-issue ignores that the exact figure genuinely existed in the tool output; rounding discards real information instead of preserving it.

questions.stem: A nightly job feeds the pipeline's PR-description generator one merged PR after another in a single long-running session. It reliably writes the required three-part format for the first several PRs, then by the ninth PR, in a session still under 4,000 tokens, drops the 'Risk' section and writes one free-flowing paragraph instead. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.why: As assistant-generated content accumulates, system-prompt influence dilutes relative to the growing body of the model's own prior outputs — the documented mechanism behind this drift.
ww: Context-window overflow is impossible at under 4,000 tokens on a modern context window; the symptom appears far too early for this explanation.
The system prompt is included in every request, not just the first — this is a documented misconception, not how the API works.
Nothing in the scenario supports a silently-dropped system prompt; this is a plausible-sounding but unsupported explanation competing with the real, documented mechanism.

questions.stem: The team wants to move the pipeline's nightly dependency-vulnerability scan, which processes roughly 8,000 files, onto the Message Batches API for the 50% discount. An engineer proposes submitting all 8,000 files in one batch tonight and refining the extraction prompt based on tomorrow's results if needed. What is the most effective way to de-risk this rollout?
questions.why: Validating on a synchronous sample before committing a large batch maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying for, and waiting up to 24 hours on, a prompt defect replicated across the whole run.
ww: Each wasted iteration still costs a full batch and up to a 24-hour wait; the discount doesn't make blind full-scale iteration cheap.
Splitting into two untested batches still commits the unvalidated prompt at scale twice, without ever checking correctness on a small sample first.
This is a non-blocking, latency-tolerant nightly workload — exactly what the Batches API fits; abandoning it doesn't address the actual risk, which is prompt correctness.

questions.stem: The pipeline's nightly test-generation step uses one prompt that both decides which scenarios a function needs and writes the test code for each in the same pass. Only the two or three most obvious scenarios get real depth; the rest get a one-line test or are skipped. What restructuring gives scenario identification its own full attention?
questions.why: Breaking the task into sequential focused prompts — enumerate, then implement — gives each step the model's full attention and lets the second step build directly on the first's output.
ww: A reasoning-cue addition doesn't structurally separate the two concerns; scenario identification still shares the same crowded pass as code-writing.
More worked examples don't change that both concerns are still decided in one rushed pass; it doesn't add focused attention to enumeration specifically.
More output room doesn't fix a rushed, single-pass reasoning problem; the model is still doing both jobs at once.

questions.stem: The pipeline's cross-service impact check is instructed only to 'flag changes that might affect other services.' Reviewing a shared authentication helper, it flags a same-file variable rename as cross-service risk while missing an actual signature change to a function three other services call directly. What change would most reliably fix this inconsistent flagging?
questions.why: Replacing a vague instruction with explicit, testable criteria is the documented fix for inconsistent flagging — the model now has a concrete rule to apply rather than a judgment call.
ww: Temperature affects randomness, not what counts as a flaggable change; the inconsistency here is about undefined criteria, not run-to-run variance.
A new severity tier doesn't address what triggers a flag in the first place — the vague trigger stays vague.
Erring toward flagging shifts the threshold without adding precision, and would likely increase false positives rather than fix the underlying inconsistency.

questions.stem: The review bot's response returns `stop_reason: 'tool_use'` requesting a `fetch_file_contents` call. The harness runs the tool, then sends only a new message with the `tool_result` block back — omitting the original conversation and the `tool_use` block. The next response comes back confused, as if it never asked for the file. What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Each API call is stateless and must carry the full conversation so far; the application appends the `tool_result` to that history rather than sending it alone.
ww: Dismisses `id`-matching as irrelevant and points at an unrelated parameter; the actual defect is the missing conversation history, not output length.
No such expiry exists for `tool_use` blocks — a fabricated mechanic.
`tool_choice` controls whether and which tool Claude calls next; it doesn't restore missing prior conversation context.

questions.stem: The review bot ingests one consolidated 60,000-token diff bundle for a large PR in a single pass. Its summary covers the diff's opening version bumps and closing test updates, but never mentions a breaking return-type change sitting in the bundle's middle third — exactly what downstream callers need to know. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Placing key findings at the start (primacy) and adding navigable section headings are the documented mitigations for reliable attention on beginning-and-end content missing the middle.
ww: Trimming toward a smaller bundle risks cutting exactly the finding that matters, without addressing why mid-content gets missed in the first place.
Rotating file order doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern — content still lands in a reliably-worse middle position regardless of which content it is.
More output room doesn't improve attention to input content; the limiting factor is what gets noticed while reading, not how much can be written back.

questions.stem: A Claude Code session debugging a flaky nightly pipeline job runs long, reaching 70,000 tokens. Early on, the failing test's name, the commit SHA that introduced the flake, and a config value already ruled out get established; most of the rest is exploratory back-and-forth chasing false leads. Which context management strategy best cuts token cost from here?
questions.why: The hybrid approach — structured facts kept verbatim, general discussion summarized, recent exchanges kept verbatim — preserves precision on identifiers while cutting token cost.
ww: Pure summarization risks paraphrasing or truncating exact identifiers like a commit SHA into a vague reference, losing the precision that matters.
A fixed recent-token window drops the test name, SHA, and ruled-out value established early, exactly the detail the team needs to keep.
Restarting discards real investigative progress instead of preserving it; this isn't a stale-results problem, just a cost-management one.

questions.stem: Before generating tests for a legacy billing module with almost no coverage, the pipeline's test-generation step first surveys all 90 functions directly in its own session, reading each one and cataloging dependencies. By the time the survey finishes, the session's context is nearly full, leaving little room to write the new tests. What is the most effective restructuring?
questions.why: Delegating verbose discovery to a subagent that returns only a concise summary isolates the exploration output from the main session, preserving context for the design-and-implementation phase.
ww: `/compact` mid-task risks losing precision needed for the implementation phase that follows.
Multiple sessions handed off via `--resume` add coordination overhead and consistency risk compared to a single subagent-isolated summary.
A larger context window doesn't fix the structural problem of verbose discovery crowding out implementation work; it only delays the same problem at greater cost.

questions.stem: Your team splits standards per package. `services/booking/CLAUDE.md` contains the line `Booking conventions: @standards/booking-conventions.md`, and that file sits at the repository root under `standards/`. Sessions in that package never apply the booking conventions, and `/memory` lists the package CLAUDE.md as loaded but not the standards file. What is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.why: §3.1 states that relative `@path` imports resolve relative to the file containing the import. Written inside `services/booking/CLAUDE.md`, `@standards/...` resolves to `services/booking/standards/`, which does not exist, so nothing is imported — exactly what `/memory` shows. Rewriting the path relative to the importing file resolves it.
ww: Encodes the real depth-5 import limit but misapplies it. §3.1 caps import nesting at 5 levels; this configuration has a single import from a single file, so the limit cannot explain a one-level failure.

Encodes the override-precedence misconception §3.1 explicitly rejects: discovered CLAUDE.md files are concatenated in load order, not overridden, so no directory-level file replaces a project-level one. It also abandons the modular per-package standards pattern §3.1 recommends.
Contradicts §3.1, which states that `@path` supports both relative and absolute paths. Relative paths are not skipped — they resolve against the importing file, which is the actual defect here.

questions.stem: Your `/scaffold-module` skill takes the new module's name as its argument and uses it to name every generated file. Developers frequently invoke it bare, producing placeholder-named files, and the slash-command menu gives no sign that an argument is expected. Which SKILL.md frontmatter key addresses this?
questions.why: §3.3's frontmatter table assigns `argument-hint` exactly this job: it is displayed when the command is invoked and prompts for required args. That addresses both symptoms — the bare invocations and the menu entry that signals nothing.
ww: §3.3 documents `description` as the text shown in the slash-command menu. It can mention the argument but does not prompt for one at invocation time, so bare invocations and placeholder-named files continue.

§3.3 scopes `allowed-tools` to which tools the skill may use during execution. It has no bearing on whether an argument was supplied — the skill still runs with a placeholder name, just with fewer tools available.
§3.3 documents `context: fork` as running the skill in an isolated subagent context to keep large output from polluting the main session. It solves context pollution, not a missing argument.

questions.stem: An engineer objects that planning mode is limited: on a cross-module change it explored with Read, Grep, and Glob but would not run the test suite or make a scratch edit to check an assumption. The proposal is to drop planning mode and start every task in direct execution. How should the team respond?
questions.why: §3.6 defines planning mode as deliberately side-effect-free — Read/Grep/Glob only — so Claude explores, understands, and designs before anything executes, and prescribes the combined approach: planning mode for investigation and design, user approval, then direct execution to implement. The read-only constraint is what prevents expensive rework, not a defect to route around.
ww: This is the trap §3.6 names explicitly: start in direct execution and switch to planning when it gets hard. Reactive switching is expensive because work already executed has to be unwound — the rework the section exists to prevent.

Inverts §3.6's mapping. Direct execution applies when scope is clear, the approach is defined, and changes are routine; a multi-module change with an unsettled design is the textbook planning-mode case.
Over-applies planning mode. §3.6 lists a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace as a direct-execution case; routing it through planning adds overhead when there is no ambiguity to resolve.

questions.stem: The availability-rules module has a written spec that names its edge cases precisely: overlapping windows, bookings straddling a timezone change, and blackout dates. Your workflow generates the module first, then writes tests against what was produced. Each round surfaces another spec case the code misses, and fixing one regresses another. Which change converges fastest?
questions.why: §3.7.2 defines test-driven iteration: write the test suite first covering expected behavior, edge cases and performance requirements, then iterate by sharing the failures until everything is green. Tests are an objective, machine-checkable definition of done, so each iteration gets a concrete failure signal and a regression on a previously-passing case surfaces immediately.
ww: Encodes the misconception §3.7.2 names: writing tests after generation is verification, not test-driven iteration. §3.7.1 adds that prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently — which is why each round misses a different case.
§3.7.1 rejects iterating on generated code one missed requirement at a time: it is slow, and each fix can disturb the last — precisely the regression pattern already observed.

Concrete input/output pairs are §3.7.3's remedy for a transformation described ambiguously in prose. Here the spec already names the edge cases unambiguously, and examples still leave no machine-checkable definition of done across the full edge-case surface.

questions.stem: A wrapper around `claude -p` scaffolds modules and must hand the module registry four fields per artifact: file path, module type, exported symbols, and follow-up TODOs. An engineer proposes documenting the required shape in CLAUDE.md. Registry ingestion currently fails on roughly one run in twelve. Which change is most reliable?
questions.why: §3.9 pairs `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` for exactly this case — a downstream consumer that needs named fields. The schema enforces the shape, guaranteeing well-formed output parseable by the tool that consumes it rather than leaving the format to model compliance.
ww: §3.9 rejects an Output Format section in CLAUDE.md for this purpose: it is not guaranteed consistent. That is precisely the one-run-in-twelve failure already being observed.
§3.9 lists a format instruction in the prompt as producing variable compliance. Moving it to the end of the prompt changes its position, not the probabilistic nature of instruction-following.
A symptom-level fix: it hardens the parser against wordings seen so far while the generator remains free to produce new ones. §3.9's mechanism removes the variability at the source instead.

questions.stem: Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to roughly 380 lines: naming and error-handling conventions every session must follow, plus a release-cut checklist and a data-backfill procedure each used a few times a quarter. An engineer proposes converting the entire file into Skills so nothing loads unless invoked. How should the team evaluate this proposal?
questions.why: §3.11 prescribes exactly this split: universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md because that content loads in every session, while workflow-specific guidance — PR review, deploy, migration and similar procedures — becomes Skills invoked on demand with trigger keywords.
ww: §3.11 names moving everything to Skills as not preferred: the universal standards would then need explicit invocation each session, so conventions that must always apply stop being unconditional.

§3.11 rejects splitting this content into `.claude/rules/` because rules are path-scoped, not workflow-scoped. Applied to universal conventions the mismatch is worse — any session touching files outside the glob patterns loses them entirely.

Leaves the whole file loading in every session, which §3.11 identifies as the cost driver, and substitutes model inference for a deterministic mechanism — the same flaw §3.2 flags when conventions are left to headings rather than file-path matching.

questions.stem: Long modernization sessions now run past 80,000 tokens. They hold exact values the work depends on — the agreed migration batch size, two schema column names, a retry budget in milliseconds — plus long exploratory stretches that led nowhere and recent implementation exchanges. An engineer proposes summarizing everything before the last ten exchanges. Which approach is most effective?
questions.why: This is §5.3's hybrid approach: extract critical structured data into a compact block preserved verbatim, summarize the lower-information-density general discussion, and keep recent exchanges verbatim for conversational coherence. It is the only option that cuts tokens without putting the exact values at risk.
ww: §5.3 rejects pure summarization because precision is lost — exact values degrade into vague references, the way a stated percentage becomes 'pricing was discussed'. The batch size and column names are exactly what summarization blurs.
§5.3 rejects keeping only the most recent tokens: anything agreed early falls outside the window and is gone. The retry budget and column names were settled long before the last exchanges.
§5.3's objection to summarization applies whenever compression finally runs; a higher threshold only delays it, and the same precise values are blurred when it does.

questions.stem: Auditing which nightly jobs still write to the legacy availability table means enumerating every job definition and its queries — output that fills the main session before the team can discuss the replacement write path. An engineer proposes splitting the audit across several sessions joined with `--continue`. How should the team evaluate this?
questions.why: §5.6 treats context isolation as a feature: run the verbose discovery phase in an Explore subagent, have it return a concise summary, and preserve the main session's context for the design and implementation phases. That is the documented fix for discovery output flooding the window.
ww: §5.6 rejects splitting the work across multiple sessions with `--continue`: it introduces coordination overhead and consistency risk between the phases, without actually isolating the verbose output.
§5.6 rejects `/compact` mid-task because it loses precision the later phases need — here, the specific job definitions the replacement write path has to cover.
The bigger-context response the corpus dismisses: a larger window raises cost while the verbose output keeps accumulating and competing for attention. Isolation, not capacity, is the documented fix.

questions.stem: Dozens of Claude Code session transcripts from this quarter total well past 100,000 tokens. An engineer needs the tradeoff the team accepted when it chose between two locking strategies for the booking module in week three. A teammate proposes tagging every future decision so it can be found later. What is most effective?
questions.why: §5.7 prescribes semantic retrieval over the full history for conversations spanning many sessions: it retrieves the specifically relevant past exchange on demand, which is exactly what a question about one week-three decision requires.
ww: §5.7 lists XML tags marking discussion conclusions as not solving retrieval at this scale. Tagging also does nothing for the quarter of transcripts already written, which is where the answer lives.
§5.7 rejects a rolling window because it discards early sessions — the week-three decision is precisely what would be dropped.
§5.7 rejects progressive summarization: it compresses specific quoted conclusions into abstractions, so the particular tradeoff that was accepted is no longer recoverable.

questions.stem: Converting the reminders module off a deprecated notification client spans several days and many tool calls, with a different engineer picking it up each morning. Each day starts by re-running the same call-site discovery, because the prior day's findings lived only in that session. What is most effective?
questions.why: §5.12 prescribes exactly this for tasks needing state across many tool calls: write intermediate state and key findings to a scratchpad file rather than holding them in context, and read from the scratchpad at the start of each continuation, so the task survives context limits and session boundaries.
ww: §5.12 rejects re-running work from scratch after an interruption — it wastes effort that could have been persisted, which is exactly the cost the team pays every morning.
§5.12 rejects relying on conversation history to survive: the API is stateless and an ended session's context is gone, so nothing carries into the next morning's session regardless of intent.
§5.12 rejects keeping all findings in the agent's own context window — the window fills, and nothing survives the session boundary no matter how little is compressed.

questions.stem: After an expensive analysis of the booking module, the team used `fork_session` to evaluate two migration approaches from that shared baseline. The branch evaluating the first approach then discovers an undocumented dependency on an internal pricing call. An engineer assumes the other branch already knows. What actually happens, and what should the team do?
questions.why: §1.16 states that both forks inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently — that independence is what keeps the two explorations from contaminating each other. A discovery made after the fork therefore exists in one branch only and must be passed into the other explicitly.
ww: This is the misconception the section corrects: forks do not share a live context past the branch point. Believing they do means the second evaluation silently proceeds without a constraint that could change its verdict.
§1.16 rejects two brand-new sessions here — each would have to redo the expensive shared baseline analysis that forking exists to reuse.
§1.16 rejects running both strategies sequentially in one session: the second evaluation is biased by the first's reasoning and conclusions, which is the exact failure forking prevents.

questions.stem: Your team added a second Claude Code instance to review generated changes before human review, and passes it the generating session's full reasoning transcript along with the diff. Across 40 reviews it has concurred with the generator every time, including on a change a human later flagged as unsafe. What is most effective?
questions.why: §1.17 requires the second instance to run with no access to the first instance's reasoning — that is what makes it independent and lets it mirror human peer review, catching what the author rationalized away. Feeding it the transcript reimports the very rationalizations the review exists to challenge.
ww: An instruction cannot undo the contamination: the reviewer is still reasoning from the generator's own justification for the change. §1.17 locates the fix in withholding that context, not in prompting against it.
§1.17 rejects extended thinking on the generation stage — it does not address the self-check limitation, because the same instance is still evaluating conclusions it just reached.
§1.17 rejects self-review by the generating instance: same instance, same confirmation bias, which is exactly the unbroken concurrence the logs show.

questions.stem: Two workloads run against the scheduling service. New modules are always scaffolded by the same five steps: generate, wire routes, add fixtures, run the suite, update the registry. Separately, a dead-code sweep must find and remove unused helpers whose scope nobody knows until the search runs. Which assignment is correct?
questions.why: §1.7 maps each pattern to a task shape: a fixed sequential pipeline where the structure is predictable and stability and reproducibility matter, and dynamic adaptive decomposition where scope is unknown up front and each step depends on the previous step's findings. The two workloads sit on opposite sides of that line.
ww: §1.7 rejects a fixed pipeline for open-ended work: the scope is unknown up front and a predetermined script cannot react to what the search discovers as it proceeds.
§1.7 rejects dynamic decomposition where the structure is already predictable — it is unnecessary complexity, and it costs the reproducibility the fixed scaffolding steps exist to provide.
§1.7 rejects one giant single-pass prompt covering everything: attention dilutes across the work, giving deep treatment to some parts and shallow treatment to others.

questions.stem: Standardizing an error wrapper, the assistant's `Edit` call fails: the anchor `catch (err) {` appears in fourteen places, so `Edit` cannot tell which occurrence to change. The engineer runs a Bash `sed` substitution instead, which rewrites all fourteen — including two that should have been left alone. What is the sanctioned approach?
questions.why: §2.9 states that Edit works by unique text matching and fails when the anchor appears more than once. The documented fallback is Read the full file, modify the content, then Write the updated version — a reliable full-file modification that does not depend on any anchor being unique.
ww: §2.9 rejects this explicitly: shorter anchors are more likely to be non-unique, not less. `catch (` would match at least the same fourteen sites and Edit would fail again for the same reason.

§2.9 rejects using Bash `sed` to force the replacement — it bypasses the tool designed for the job, and the two collateral edits already show the cost. Scoping the same bypass does not make it the sanctioned fallback.

Misapplies the tool semantics §2.9 documents: Write creates a file or fully replaces its contents, so writing only the corrected block discards the rest of the file. Read must load the full content first, which is why the fallback is Read plus Write.

questions.stem: Your codegen MCP server exposes `fetch_template`, returning the empty house boilerplate for a module type, and `fetch_reference_module`, returning a production module as a worked example. Both are described only as "Returns example code for a module type." When an engineer asks for a real working example, logs show `fetch_template` is called 40% of the time. What is most effective?
questions.why: §2.2 makes tool descriptions the primary input Claude uses to decide which tool to call, and requires each description to state what it does, what input it accepts, when to use it versus similar tools, and when not to use it. Two tools sharing one generic line give the model nothing to select on; expanding both is the root-cause fix and the section's instruction to check descriptions first.
ww: §2.2 rejects combining near-duplicate tools into a single one: it loses the semantic precision that lets the model distinguish the two cases, and relocates the same ambiguity into a parameter value.
§2.2 rejects a pre-routing classifier — it adds infrastructure on top of the bad signal without fixing the root cause, and the under-specified descriptions remain in place.

A blunt prompt-level layer over the same defective signal. §2.2's rule is to check and fix the descriptions first; a rule enumerating tool-to-request mappings is keyword-sensitive and degrades as tools are added.

questions.stem: The coordinator's prompt for the antimicrobial-resistance report has grown to forty numbered steps — one added after each incident review, naming exact databases to query and how many results to open. Shipped reports now read as checklists and consistently miss findings the subagents' own searches surfaced. Which change to the coordinator's prompt is most effective?
questions.why: Coordinator prompts should state research goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedure. Goal-oriented prompts let subagents adapt their approach as findings emerge; a procedural prompt locks the system into a fixed script that breaks whenever reality deviates from it — producing exactly the checklist-shaped output that drops findings the script never anticipated.
ww: Encodes the belief that a script fails because it is insufficiently detailed. Adding detail deepens the rigidity that caused the problem; §1.4 names more detailed step-by-step instructions as the wrong response to shallow, checklist-like results.
More agents executing a bad script does not fix the script. §1.4 lists increasing the number of subagents as a documented wrong answer — the defect is in the prompt's form, not in throughput.

A formalized pipeline is still a predetermined script. §1.4's point is that the procedural form itself prevents adaptation; adding validation stages between fixed steps does not let the coordinator pursue a finding the steps never named.

questions.stem: Findings now reach the synthesis subagent as JSON, but each finding is a single string with the source folded into the sentence: 'Carbapenem resistance rose 18% (hospital-network bulletin).' Synthesis rewrites and merges those sentences, and a spot check finds 1 in 5 shipped citations attached to the wrong document. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Context passed between agents must use a structured format that separates content from metadata (source URL, document name, page number, retrieved date). That separation is what preserves the claim-to-source mapping through aggregation and summarization; a source folded into the sentence survives only until something rewrites the sentence.
ww: This is the documented 'remind the agent to cite sources' fix. The subagent cannot reliably preserve attribution it only ever received as prose inside a sentence it has been asked to rewrite and merge — the metadata was never structurally distinct.

§1.5 names re-searching to find a source for each claim as the wrong answer: it duplicates work already completed and can attribute claims to the wrong source, which is the very failure being reported.
Merging into narrative is precisely where attribution is lost in §1.5's root-cause analysis. Deduplicating into fewer sentences before synthesis compounds the loss rather than reducing it.

questions.stem: The coordinator reviews a synthesis draft and finds it never covers pediatric wards, though the document-analysis subagent logged relevant records earlier. It re-invokes the synthesis subagent with the same findings plus 'also cover pediatric wards.' The redraft adds two hedged sentences and no new evidence. What should the coordinator do instead?
questions.why: The refinement loop runs: coordinator evaluates the synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries aimed at the specific gap to the search and analysis subagents, then re-invokes synthesis with the enriched findings. Re-invoking synthesis alone cannot produce evidence that was never gathered — hence the hedged filler.
ww: §1.8 explicitly rejects shipping with a 'further research needed' note when re-delegation is still available. Coverage annotation is reserved for unrecoverable gaps, and this gap is recoverable — the records already exist.
§1.8 names having the synthesis agent search for itself as the wrong fix: it breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling, turning the synthesizer into a second researcher.

This loops on the wrong stage and without a sufficiency criterion. §1.8 requires re-delegation to the research subagents between passes, and requires defined quality criteria so the coordinator knows when to stop.

questions.stem: Two of six source categories — a national surveillance archive and a hospital-network bulletin series — are offline for the whole project window and will return nothing this cycle. The synthesis subagent completes a draft from the other four and presents every conclusion with equal confidence. What should its output do instead?
questions.why: When upstream inputs are incomplete, the synthesis agent completes synthesis using available data, annotates coverage so well-supported conclusions are distinguishable from those resting on gaps, and propagates that uncertainty upward. Graceful degradation preserves both the deliverable and an honest picture of its limits.
ww: §1.10 names returning an error because the input is incomplete as the wrong response. Four of six categories returned usable data; refusing to synthesize discards work that is genuinely informative.

Retrying retrieval is outside the synthesis agent's scope, and the categories are unavailable for the entire project window — the loop blocks the pipeline indefinitely without changing the outcome §1.10 already prescribes a response for.

This is the documented 'proceed without noting the gaps' failure in a subtractive form. Silently removing affected conclusions leaves the reader unable to tell that the report's scope was reduced or where.

questions.stem: The report-generation subagent has a general-purpose `fetch_resource` tool for pulling excerpts from the project store. Because it accepts any record identifier, the subagent has started quoting raw source material the document-analysis subagent never reviewed. Roughly 7% of shipped paragraphs contain such material. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Least privilege is enforced at the interface, not by instruction: replace the over-broad general-purpose tool with a constrained alternative that validates what it will accept. This fixes the root cause — the tool's own contract now makes the out-of-scope behavior impossible rather than merely discouraged.
ww: §1.11 names prompt instructions as probabilistic rather than deterministic. The tool still accepts exactly the identifiers the instruction forbids, so compliance depends on the model getting it right every time.

A denylist patches symptoms downstream of the real problem — the interface is still permissive. Every newly ingested unreviewed record is absent from the list until someone adds it, so the boundary is never actually enforced.

This is the inverse of least privilege. §1.11 requires each subagent to hold only the tools its defined scope needs; broadening access across subagents produces exactly the scope creep described here.

questions.stem: The research pipeline's MCP server for a licensed surveillance database is configured in each researcher's own `~/.claude.json`, since every researcher holds a personal access credential. New team members routinely have no working database access for days, and two researchers are pointed at a stale endpoint nobody noticed. What is the most effective configuration?
questions.why: A shared team MCP server belongs in the project-root `.mcp.json`, which is version-controlled so every teammate gets identical configuration on clone. Per-developer credentials are handled by `${VAR}` environment-variable substitution, which keeps the config shareable while the secret stays out of the repository — solving both the onboarding delay and the endpoint drift at once.
ww: This keeps the server in user scope, which §2.6 names as the wrong answer for a shared team server precisely because it produces inconsistent tooling. A pasteable reference block is a manual process that drifts exactly the way the stale endpoint already has.

§2.6 flags committing a credential alongside project config as a security risk, and it also discards the per-researcher access the licensed database requires. Environment-variable substitution exists to avoid this trade-off entirely.

A runtime warning detects drift after the fact rather than preventing it, and it still leaves every researcher hand-maintaining their own entry — the configuration remains inconsistent, only now with an alert attached.

questions.stem: Every retrieval call must carry a date-range parameter bounded to the project's approved study window; records outside it contaminate the trend analysis. A system-prompt rule states this, and an audit finds 6% of calls omit the parameter. An engineer proposes a `PostToolUse` hook that discards results from non-compliant calls. What is the most effective enforcement?
questions.why: `PreToolUse` fires before the tool executes and is the hook for validating, blocking, or modifying parameters. It is deterministic — it fires regardless of what the model does — and it is the only point at which a non-compliant retrieval can be prevented rather than cleaned up after the fact.
ww: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool returns, so the out-of-window retrieval has already happened by the time the hook sees it. §2.7 scopes PostToolUse to transforming, logging, and normalizing output — not to preventing a call.
§2.7's core distinction: hooks are deterministic, system-prompt instructions are probabilistic. Strengthening the wording leaves the 6% gap as a matter of model compliance rather than enforcement.
An after-the-fact review by another agent inherits both weaknesses §2.7 says hooks exist to remove: it is probabilistic, and it runs after the call has already executed.

questions.stem: `fetch_surveillance_record` returns `isError: true` with a prose `description` only. The coordinator reads that text to decide retries: it spends the full retry budget on records permanently retracted from the archive — a state no retry can change — while abandoning genuine index timeouts after one attempt. How should the tool's error response be restructured?
questions.why: A structured error carrying an explicit category plus a retryability flag is what lets the agent separate a transient failure a retry can resolve from a permanent one that never will. §2.3 states the principle directly: returning a retryable boolean is better than forcing the agent to guess retryability from error text.
ww: A blanket retry policy spends the budget on permanently-failing calls whose outcome can never change. §2.3's transient-versus-permanent split exists precisely so retry effort is not wasted on errors that will fail identically every time.

This is still guessing from error text, merely relocated into the coordinator. §2.3 identifies inferring retryability from the description as the inferior design that an explicit retryable flag replaces — and keyword matching breaks the moment the wording changes.

§2.3 forbids signalling a failed retrieval as a successful empty result. The coordinator then reports that no data was found when the underlying record simply could not be retrieved — a false statement produced by masking the failure.

questions.stem: To guarantee `extract_study_metadata` runs before any analysis tool, the team set `tool_choice` to that specific tool. It now stays forced on every turn of the document-analysis subagent's loop, and production logs show the subagent calls the metadata tool repeatedly and never reaches its analysis tools. What is the correct configuration?
questions.why: This is the forced-first-step pattern: force the specific tool on the first request to guarantee execution order, then process subsequent steps in follow-up turns with `tool_choice` relaxed back to `"auto"`. §2.5 names leaving it forced on every turn as the documented failure — the model can then never call any other tool.
ww: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees that some tool is called but not which one — with several tools available the model still picks whichever it judges best, so the ordering guarantee the team needed is lost.
§2.5 names a prompt instruction here as probabilistic, not guaranteed. Removing the configuration reintroduces exactly the skipping that forcing `tool_choice` was added to eliminate.

§2.5 answers execution-order requirements with `tool_choice`, not by collapsing tools. A composite tool also removes the subagent's ability to select the right analysis tool per document, which is what its role-scoped tool set exists for.

questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent now emits field-level confidence per extracted fact. After per-segment validation, high-confidence facts are auto-accepted and only low-confidence ones reach a reviewer. Six months on, a reviewer stumbles on a systematic error in an auto-accepted field class nobody had been checking. What should the oversight design add?
questions.why: Even high-confidence extractions need a regularly audited random sample, stratified across document types and field categories rather than drawn only from the top of the review queue. That is what measures the automated path's true error rate and surfaces novel error patterns before they compound — the exact failure described.
ww: §5.9 names a fixed, unstratified random slice as the wrong design: it spends limited reviewer capacity on easy segments while under-sampling the problem segments where errors actually cluster.

Enlarging the low-confidence queue still never inspects the auto-accepted stream, which is where the undetected error lives. §5.9 also requires thresholds to be tuned against a labeled validation set rather than moved by intuition.

§5.9 rejects universal human re-review — it defeats the automation that calibration exists to enable and does not scale. The point of calibrated confidence is targeted oversight, not blanket inspection.

questions.stem: A house rule tells the document-analysis subagent that when two credible sources disagree it should keep the figure from the official agency and drop the other. Audit shows 11% of reports now carry a single figure where the pipeline held two, and reviewers cannot see what was discarded. What is the most effective change?
questions.why: An agent processing conflicting sources should not resolve the conflict autonomously. §5.10 prescribes completing the analysis with both conflicting values, explicitly annotating the conflict with source attribution, and leaving reconciliation to the coordinator or a human — a decision above the subagent's scope.
ww: The subagent is still resolving the conflict on its own; only the evidence trail changes. §5.10 requires the conflict to be visible in the analysis output where the reconciliation decision is actually made, not buried in a side channel.

§5.10 names stopping to ask the coordinator before completing the analysis as the wrong response — it blocks the pipeline unnecessarily when the subagent can finish its work and annotate the disagreement.

Swapping one heuristic for a more sophisticated one still picks a most-likely-correct value autonomously, which §5.10 identifies as abandoning responsibility for a decision above the subagent's scope.

questions.stem: For a consistent house voice, the report-generation subagent renders every finding as narrative prose — including per-ward resistance rates for twelve hospitals and a five-year trend series. Reviewers say they can no longer cross-check figures against the sources and the chronology is hard to follow. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: §5.11 requires rendering by content type rather than flattening everything to uniform prose: financial and tabular data belong in tables, time series in chronological ordering, technical findings in structured lists. Converting all findings to narrative for consistency makes tabular data imprecise and harder to verify — exactly the reviewers' complaint.
ww: §5.11 names an end-of-report bibliography as the wrong answer: individual claims stop being traceable to specific sources. It also does nothing about a rate table dissolved into sentences.

§5.11 rejects re-deriving attributions at the end by searching the sources again — expensive and error-prone. The claim-to-source mapping should be preserved through the pipeline, not reconstructed at compile time.
A symptom-level edit. §5.11's point is that tabular and time-series data expressed as prose is imprecise and harder to verify regardless of how tightly the prose is written.

questions.stem: The team's shared `/draft-lint` skill lives at `.claude/skills/draft-lint/SKILL.md`. A researcher built a stricter personal version at `~/.claude/skills/my-draft-lint/SKILL.md`, but typing `/draft-lint` out of habit still runs the team's checks. She wants her own version on that command, with teammates unaffected when they pull. What is the cause and fix?
questions.why: Personal skills override project skills with the same name. A differently-named personal folder simply creates a second, differently-named command and loses the familiar invocation — §3.5's documented mistake. Renaming the personal folder to match makes `/draft-lint` resolve to her version in her sessions, with nothing in the repository changing for teammates.
ww: No such opt-in field exists. §3.5 determines precedence by name and scope alone; inventing a frontmatter flag is the classic right-concept, wrong-mechanism error.

The whole point of §3.5's precedence rule is that the personal skill wins while the project skill stays in place. Deleting the project folder locally is unnecessary and leaves her checkout diverged from the team's.
This inverts the documented precedence. §3.5 exists so a developer can customize a shared command for themselves without affecting teammates — personal beats project on a name collision.

questions.stem: The synthesis subagent drafts the report, then in the same request is asked to re-read its draft and flag any claim the findings do not fully support. It reports none. A human reviewer later finds three claims that overreach what the underlying records actually said. What most directly addresses this?
questions.why: A model that generated an output retains its generation reasoning and stays anchored to its own decisions. True independence requires a fresh request containing only the artifact plus review criteria — without the generator's justifications in context, the reviewer evaluates the claims on their own merits and catches what the generator rationalized away.
ww: Self-review inside the same context inherits the same anchoring that produced the overreach, however precisely the instruction is worded. §4.13 names strengthened self-review instructions as the wrong fix.
§4.13 rejects this directly: more reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny. The blind spots that produced the claims survive additional thinking within the same session.

§4.13's stated misconception. A second pass in the same conversation still carries the full generation reasoning in context, so the model re-reads its own justifications and confirms them — same-conversation second pass is not independent review.

questions.stem: The coordinator escalates to a human research lead. The lead's queue shows 62% of escalations are routine calls she simply hands back — which citation form fits a preprint, for instance — while two of the last five genuinely ambiguous scope decisions were made autonomously and had to be redone. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The pattern — escalating the simple cases while attempting the complex ones autonomously — is the signature of an unclear decision boundary in the prompt. §4.15's fix is explicit escalation criteria paired with few-shot examples showing 'escalate when' versus 'resolve autonomously when', which corrects the boundary itself.
ww: §4.15 names self-confidence rating plus an automatic routing threshold as infrastructure built around the problem without addressing its root cause — and self-reported confidence is uncalibrated, so the threshold routes on an unreliable signal.

§4.15 calls a separate classifier model overkill here. The defect is unclear decision boundaries in the prompt, not insufficient classification capacity, so the classifier inherits the same ambiguity.
Defaulting to escalation floods the human queue with cases the coordinator could resolve — worsening the 62% figure it is meant to fix — and still never states the boundary §4.15 requires.

questions.stem: Your team's chore-automation assistant runs a coordinator plus specialist workers. To save a hop, engineers wired the scaffold worker to write results into a shared file the flag-cleanup worker reads directly. Since then the coordinator's run summary no longer reflects what actually happened, and one worker silently consumed a malformed handoff. What should the team change?
questions.why: Hub-and-spoke requires that subagents never communicate directly with each other — all inter-agent communication flows through the coordinator. That is what buys visibility (the coordinator observes all interactions), uniform error handling, and information control (the coordinator decides what context each subagent receives). The shared-file side channel removes all three at once, which is exactly the symptom pair reported.
ww: Encodes the misconception that a bad handoff is a data-quality problem rather than an architecture problem. Schema validation at the consumer may catch a malformed payload, but the coordinator still observes nothing and still cannot make the retry-vs-skip-vs-escalate decision that hub-and-spoke assigns to it.

Inverts the context-passing principle: subagents have isolated context by design and see only what the coordinator explicitly includes in their prompt. Broadcasting the coordinator's full history to every worker destroys information control and floods each worker with context irrelevant to its narrow scope.

Sacrifices separation of responsibilities, one of the stated reasons for hub-and-spoke — each subagent should have a narrow, well-defined scope. Collapsing two workers into one removes the handoff by removing the specialization, and leaves the coordinator no better able to observe the work.

questions.stem: The scaffold worker's AgentDefinition sets allowed_tools to Read, Write, and Grep, and its system prompt ends with 'always run the module's test suite before reporting completion.' Across three weeks of runs it has never run the suite once, though it scaffolds files correctly. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: allowed_tools is a whitelist, and it is the configuration — not the prompt — that determines what an agent can touch. Running a shell command such as a test suite is the Bash tool's job, and Bash is absent from this worker's whitelist, so the instruction is unexecutable no matter how it is worded. This is the same structural principle the exam applies to a coordinator missing Task.
ww: This is the documented anti-pattern of rewriting the system prompt to obtain a behavior the configuration forbids. The corpus is explicit that the prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds; a more emphatic instruction changes nothing about which tools are available at execution time.

Encodes the misconception that descriptions enable capability. Descriptions tell the orchestration layer what an agent type is for; they do not add a tool to any whitelist. The corpus rejects the parallel move of adding subagent descriptions to a coordinator's prompt to make it spawn subagents.

This is the 'give each subagent the full tool set for flexibility' misconception, which the corpus rejects outright: per-subagent tool restrictions ARE the mechanism for separation of responsibilities and least privilege. Granting one specific missing tool is the fix; abandoning the whitelist is not.

questions.stem: The coordinator hands two cleanup workers the same instruction — 'retire the stale feature flags in this repo' — without dividing the flag list. Logs show both workers opened edits on the same three files, one flag was removed twice, and the run took twice as long with no additional flags retired. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The coordinator must explicitly partition the work space before delegating — assigning distinct subtopics or scopes to each agent — which is what prevents both duplication and missed coverage. The exam pattern is precise: when two agents investigate the same ground, the fix is partitioning before delegation, not deduplication after.
ww: This is the documented wrong answer for exactly this symptom: deduplicating or reconciling after the fact. The duplicated effort and doubled run time have already been spent by the time a merge step runs, and the reconciliation does nothing to widen coverage.

Serializing removes the parallelism without addressing the cause, which is an unpartitioned delegation. It also assumes the second worker can infer scope from the first worker's changes, which subagent context isolation does not support.

Pushes a coordinator responsibility onto the workers as a probabilistic instruction. A worker has no visibility into what its sibling was assigned, since subagents receive only what the coordinator passes them, so it cannot reliably decide what to skip.

questions.stem: A nightly chore run covers 30 repositories. On repository 4, the scaffold worker's template render fails and returns a bare failed status. The coordinator ends the entire run there, so the remaining 26 repositories go untouched and no one learns what the render was attempting. How should the failure be handled?
questions.why: A failing subagent must return structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and potential alternatives — so the coordinator can make an intelligent recovery decision. The corpus is equally explicit on the other half: never terminate the entire workflow for one subagent failure. Both halves are needed here, since a bare status on one repository is currently costing 26 others.
ww: This is the silent-failure anti-pattern the corpus names directly: never catch an error and silently return success. It would complete the run while masking a real failure, leaving the team believing repository 4 was scaffolded when it was not.
