Treats every failure as if it were transient. The corpus separates transient failures, which are worth retrying, from permanent ones such as syntax or access errors, which should not be retried at all — an unbounded retry on a permanent failure never terminates and still yields no context.

Inverts the documented level of handling. Transient failures a subagent can resolve belong at the subagent level; only errors it cannot resolve should escalate, carrying full context and partial progress. Forwarding everything drags the coordinator into routine error handling.

questions.stem: For three consecutive nightly runs the cleanup worker has failed the same chore on one module: the repo's pre-commit hook rejects its change with a message the worker cannot interpret, and it has exhausted every remedy its instructions describe. Nothing in the team's runbook covers this hook. What is the most appropriate next behavior?
questions.why: Escalation is warranted when the agent is unable to make progress — multiple retries have failed and it cannot resolve the task. That trigger is met here three runs over, and it is reinforced by a second listed trigger: the runbook is silent on this hook, so a policy interpretation is required that the agent must not invent for itself.
ww: Encodes the misconception that repeated failure is a retry signal rather than an escalation signal. The corpus lists exhausted retries as a positive escalation criterion; continuing to retry with no new information neither resolves the chore nor surfaces it to anyone who can.

Has the agent invent an exception no policy grants it — the same error as applying own-site pricing rules to a competitor price-match request. Where the documented rules are silent, the agent must escalate for interpretation, not create a workaround.

Silently narrows the chore's scope and suppresses an unresolved problem, so no human ever learns the module is being skipped. This both dodges the escalation trigger and repeats the never-silently-succeed failure mode.

questions.stem: When the assistant escalates a blocked chore, the on-call engineer's queue entry carries only the chore name and a one-line note, and the engineer cannot open the assistant's session. Surveys show engineers routinely re-run the same searches the assistant already ran before they can act. What change most effectively fixes this?
questions.why: Escalating is not merely firing an escalation call — the agent must compile a structured handoff summary, because the human receiving it has no access to the conversation and the summary is everything they see. The corpus names the core fields: an identifier, root-cause analysis, the relevant amount or scope, actions already taken, and a recommended action.
ww: The corpus rejects transcript access on two counts: humans lack it by design, and a raw transcript would force the engineer to re-read an entire session to extract what a structured summary states directly. It converts a missing-information problem into a reading-burden problem.

This is the named wrong answer for this exact symptom. Escalating earlier does not fix the information loss — the same generic note arrives, just sooner — and it degrades the assistant's autonomous resolution rate by handing off work it could have finished.

The corpus rejects having the human re-run the agent's tools to rebuild context: it duplicates work already done and slows resolution. It also describes the current failing behavior rather than changing it.

questions.stem: The assistant's client-regeneration chore always runs the same four steps in the same order: fetch the API spec, regenerate the client, run the codegen linter, then open a pull request. Nothing about the sequence depends on what any step discovers. Which named architecture pattern does this design exemplify?
questions.why: Prompt chaining is defined in the named-pattern table as a fixed sequential pipeline for predictable multi-step or multi-aspect workflows. Every distinguishing feature is present: four steps, fixed order, and no dependence on intermediate findings.
ww: Dynamic adaptive decomposition is the real pattern where subtasks are generated from intermediate findings and the plan adapts as discoveries emerge. It is the direct contrast to this chore, whose stem states the sequence depends on nothing any step discovers.

The iterative refinement loop is a real pattern in which the coordinator evaluates a synthesis for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient. This pipeline contains no gap evaluation and no re-delegation cycle.

Evaluator-optimizer is a real two-stage pattern pairing a generator with an independent critic or reviewer. The codegen linter is a fixed step in the chain, not an independent review instance evaluating the generator's output, so the defining second stage is absent.

questions.stem: You are building the assistant's own API loop by hand. Claude returns a response with stop_reason 'tool_use' and a tool_use block naming the template renderer. Your code runs the renderer and now holds its output. What must the next request to Claude contain?
questions.why: The documented tool-use cycle is: Claude returns stop_reason tool_use with a tool_use block, the application executes the tool, the application appends a tool_result content block, and Claude continues from the result. The tool_use block's id is the field that matches a result back to the call that requested it, so it must be carried on the returned result.
ww: Substitutes prose for the documented mechanism. Step 4 of the cycle specifies a tool_result content block, and a free-text user message carries no id, so nothing binds the output to the originating tool_use block.

Misapplies tool_choice, which controls whether Claude must use a tool — auto, any, or a named tool — not how an executed tool's output is returned. Forcing another tool call re-requests work already done instead of feeding back its result.

Inverts the loop's control flow. A tool_use stop reason is the signal to execute the tool and continue; end_turn is the signal to stop. Terminating on tool_use ends the loop precisely when Claude is waiting on a result.

questions.stem: The team is designing the flag-retirement tool before rollout. Retiring a flag deletes its code paths across dozens of files and cannot be undone from the assistant's side, so policy requires an impact preview the engineer sees first. A reviewer notes that the assistant chooses its own call sequence. Which design guarantees the preview always precedes execution?
questions.why: For operations that must always be preceded by a preview, the corpus prescribes splitting one tool into two: a preview call that returns impact details plus a single-use confirmation token, and an execute call that requires that token as a parameter. Because the token only exists after a preview, skipping the preview becomes architecturally impossible — a code-level guarantee rather than a prompt-level hope.
ww: This is the documented problem the pattern exists to solve. A dry_run boolean on a single tool leaves the agent free to call with dry_run=false directly, and the accompanying instruction is probabilistic prompt compliance, not enforcement.

This is the server-side timing heuristic the corpus names and rejects as fragile to timing conditions. A legitimate preview followed by slow deliberation fails the window, while nothing structurally prevents an execute call that the heuristic happens to accept.

This is the orchestration-layer confirmation prompt the corpus names as an inferior alternative because it requires extra infrastructure outside the tool contract. The tool itself remains skippable by design; the guarantee lives in a separate layer that must be built and maintained.

questions.stem: Scaffolding a module always needs both the template manifest and the team's lint profile, yet the assistant requests the manifest in one turn and the lint profile in the next, adding a round-trip to nearly every scaffold. An engineer proposes building a single combined tool that returns both. How should the team evaluate this proposal?
questions.why: The corpus states the preference directly: when an agent calls multiple tools in sequence for the same operation, prompt it to bundle the tool requests into one turn rather than creating a composite tool, since the agent can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously. Creating a combined tool is explicitly marked as not preferred because it hides the composition.
ww: Rests on a false premise. Requesting several tools in a single turn is exactly the behavior the corpus recommends prompting for, so the stated reason for adopting the composite does not hold.

Compounds the dispreferred option by also destroying semantic precision, the same reason the corpus rejects merging two distinct lookup tools into one generic tool. Scaffolding is not the only use of either tool, and retiring both removes legitimate single-purpose calls.

Accepts the avoidable round-trip and justifies it with a risk the corpus does not attach to bundling. Parameter mixing is documented for multi-issue user requests, not for an agent issuing two well-scoped tool calls in one turn.

questions.stem: An MCP server exposes a tool that maps a changed file to the exact tests covering it from a maintained index. Logs show the assistant instead shells out through `Bash` to run the whole suite on roughly 70% of chores. The MCP tool's description reads only 'Returns test information.' What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Tool selection runs on descriptions, so an agent falls back to a familiar built-in whenever a more capable MCP tool's description fails to make its superior capability explicit. 'Returns test information' says nothing about mapping a changed file to its covering tests, so the fix is to spell out the unique capability, the inputs and outputs, and what built-in tools cannot provide. Fix the signal before adding a layer or removing a tool to compensate for it.
ww: This is the named wrong answer: removing or disabling the built-in so the agent has no alternative. It breaks legitimate uses of Bash — running the suite is sometimes exactly right — and it leaves the actual root cause, an under-specified description, untouched.

The corpus rejects a blanket 'always prefer MCP tools' rule as blunt and keyword-sensitive. It misroutes the cases where a built-in genuinely is the right tool, and it still gives the model no information about what this particular MCP tool does.

Adds infrastructure to compensate for a bad signal instead of fixing the signal — the same reason a pre-routing classifier is rejected for near-duplicate tool descriptions. It also cements the wrong description in place, so any tool added later inherits the same problem.

questions.stem: The flag-retirement tool fails two ways, neither of which a repeat call can change: some flags are locked pending a compliance review, and some repositories sit outside the assistant's write scope. Both return the same generic 'unable to retire flag' error, so the assistant treats them identically and never surfaces the second for credential escalation. How should the tool's error responses be restructured?
questions.why: The corpus separates business errors from permission errors as distinct categories that demand different agent responses: a business-rule violation is a valid answer that the action is disallowed, so the agent should explain the policy outcome in customer-friendly terms, while a permission failure calls for escalation or different credentials. A structured errorCategory plus a plain-language explanation gives the agent exactly the signal it needs to choose between those two responses.
ww: Forces the agent to guess the category from error text. The corpus is explicit that a structured signal is better than making the agent infer from wording, and a generic failure leaves it unable to tell a policy denial from an access problem — which is the current behavior, only wordier.

Masks a real outcome as success. The corpus forbids returning success with embedded error metadata, and reserves the empty-result signal for a query that ran and found zero matches — not for an action the policy actively disallowed.

Collapses two categories the corpus deliberately keeps apart. A compliance lock is a business-rule outcome to be explained to the requester; treating it as a permission failure sends the assistant chasing credential escalation for a decision no credential can change.

questions.stem: Files the assistant generates under a generated/ path must carry a do-not-edit header and must never be reformatted by the team's usual style pass. That instruction currently sits in root CLAUDE.md, so it loads into every session, and the assistant has begun applying the do-not-edit rule to hand-written files that merely resemble generated ones. Which configuration applies it only where it belongs?
questions.why: Conventions scoped to a file type or directory belong in .claude/rules/ with glob patterns. Rules declare their paths in YAML frontmatter and load automatically only when Claude works on matching files, which both keeps irrelevant rules out of context and makes the scoping deterministic rather than inferred — exactly what stops the rule leaking onto lookalike hand-written files.
ww: This is the named wrong answer for path-scoped conventions: root CLAUDE.md under headings relies on model inference rather than deterministic file-path matching. It is the current configuration and the direct cause of the misapplication described.

The corpus rejects a separate CLAUDE.md per subdirectory as a poor fit when the affected files are spread across many directories, which is the case for generated output. It also multiplies the number of places the single convention must be kept in sync.

Misassigns the content type. The corpus reserves skills for workflow-specific guidance such as PR review or deploy; a convention that must apply automatically whenever matching files are touched cannot depend on an engineer remembering to invoke it first.

questions.stem: The team ships a `/retire-flag` command from `.claude/commands/` so everyone gets it on clone. Engineers type the command followed by a flag name, but the command file has no placeholder for that name, so the assistant asks which flag is meant on nearly every invocation. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: The text typed after a command name is available inside the command file as the $ARGUMENTS variable. The flag name is already being typed; the command file simply never reads it, so referencing $ARGUMENTS closes the gap with no change to how engineers invoke the command or where the file lives.
ww: Shifts the burden back onto engineers to supply by hand what the command mechanism already passes automatically, preserving the extra round-trip the question asks to remove.

Encodes the misconception that commands cannot be parameterized, so variation must be expressed as separate files. $ARGUMENTS exists precisely so one command file serves every flag; a file per flag is unmaintainable and stale the moment a new flag appears.

Confuses scope with parameterization and reverses a deliberate choice. Personal commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are not shared through version control, so the team would lose the on-clone availability the stem establishes — and hard-coding still cannot serve an engineer working on two flags.

questions.stem: An interactive chore session that began at roughly two seconds per assistant turn is noticeably slower and several times more expensive per turn by exchange 60. The assistant's replies are the same length as at the start, and the session is still well within the context window. What is the primary cause?
questions.why: The API is fully stateless, so every request must include the complete conversation history in the messages array. The corpus names this as the root cause of exactly this symptom: as turns accumulate, more tokens are sent with each request, and more tokens mean more cost and more latency.
ww: The corpus explicitly rules out progressively longer model responses as the cause of growing cost and latency, and the stem forecloses it directly by stating reply length is unchanged from the start of the session.

Attributes the growth to a limit the session has not reached — the stem states it is well within the window. The corpus dismisses the same 'context window exceeded' reasoning for a conversation nowhere near the limit; the cost curve rises from turn one, long before any window boundary.
The corpus rules out slowing database operations as the cause of this pattern. The growth is in the input token count sent to the API each turn, not in the application's own storage layer.

questions.stem: The review bot gets its behavior rules — stay terse, never speculate beyond the diff, one finding per comment — in the first user message of each CI run; the system prompt is one generic line. Early comments obey all three; late in a long run the bot writes multi-issue paragraphs and speculates freely. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Persistent behavioral constraints — tone, response format, and rules meant to hold for the whole conversation — belong in the system prompt, the one location that keeps its authority from the first turn to the last. The rules here are exactly that class, so the fix is placement, not reinforcement.
ww: Encodes the idea that a rule stated in a user turn can be kept alive by repetition. It cannot: each reminder is just another user message that later content dilutes again, which is why the rules already decay. Repetition patches the symptom and leaves the constraint outside the only position that holds for an entire run.

Environment variables configure the process, not the model. Nothing in an exported variable reaches Claude's context, so the rules would stop being followed at all rather than being followed inconsistently.

A commitment placed in the assistant's own first message is something the model can deviate from later — it is prior output, not a governing instruction. It carries strictly less authority over a long run than the system prompt does.

questions.stem: Each finding carries a `category` field constrained to the enum `correctness`, `security`, `performance`, `style`. A quarterly audit finds that findings fitting none of the four — an expired license header, a banned transitive dependency — are filed confidently as `style`, where triage buries them. What schema change most directly fixes this?
questions.why: This is the documented schema shape for a field whose values are mostly known but occasionally new: an enum with an `other` member plus a companion detail field. The finding stops being forced into a wrong category, and the detail field preserves what it actually is so triage can route it.
ww: A process patch for a schema problem. Every genuinely novel finding type still gets mis-filed once before anyone can add its member, and the audit that catches it runs quarterly. The schema needs a designed escape hatch, not a maintenance ritual.

Nullable is the right tool when information is genuinely absent from the source. Here the finding exists and is describable — only the category vocabulary is short. An unset category carries no routing signal and no description of what was found, which is worse than a wrong label.

Per-field confidence is a routing aid for uncertain values, not a fix for a vocabulary gap. The bot is confident and wrong, so a high score is exactly what these findings would carry, and the wrong category is still what gets recorded.

questions.stem: Since findings moved to `tool_use` with a strict schema, the ingestion step has not failed to parse a response in six weeks. Reviewers still report that roughly 5% of findings carry a `suggested_fix` patch that edits a line the pull request never touched. An engineer concludes the schema must still be too loose. How should the team interpret this?
questions.why: A strict schema eliminates the entire syntax class — malformed JSON, wrong types, missing required fields — and does nothing for the semantic class. A patch that edits an untouched line is perfectly schema-shaped and simply wrong in content, which is the expected residue once the syntax class is gone.
ww: No JSON Schema constraint can express "this patch must apply to a line the diff changed" — the schema governs shape, not the relationship between a value and the document it came from. Tightening it further cannot reach this defect class.

Reverting reintroduces the syntax class — prose preambles, markdown fences, malformed JSON — on top of the semantic errors that would remain untouched. The team would trade zero parse failures for two failure classes instead of one.

This is the documented misconception that a passing validator means a correct extraction. Semantic errors clear schema validation by definition: the JSON is valid and the content is wrong. The ingestion step is applying exactly what it was handed.

questions.stem: The pipeline validates every finding in code after receiving it — types, enum membership, and rules such as `line` falling inside a changed hunk. An engineer proposes deleting that layer, arguing the tool's JSON schema already guarantees the shape and a second check is dead weight. How should the team respond?
questions.why: The validation layer sits in code, after the model's output, and does work the schema cannot: business rules like a line falling inside a changed hunk, cross-field consistency, and defense-in-depth for everything downstream consumes. Tool use enforces structure at generation time; the validators check meaning.
ww: Encodes the documented misconception that tool use makes code-side validation redundant, and compounds it by discarding failures silently. Business-rule violations would reach the pull request unchallenged, and the ones that did not would vanish without a signal anyone can act on.
A parse check is the one part tool use genuinely does make redundant. Keeping only that discards exactly the semantic and business-rule checks no JSON schema can express — the layer's actual value.

Sampling detects a fraction of violations after they have already been posted, instead of validating every finding before it is. It also gives the retry loop nothing to work with, since a weekly audit produces no per-item error to feed back.

questions.stem: Validation rejects a finding when its `line` falls outside the pull request's changed hunks. On rejection the pipeline resends the diff and prompt with one sentence appended: "The previous output was invalid. Try again." Roughly half of retries fail again, and logs show the bot rewrites the description while leaving the line untouched. What change most improves retry success?
questions.why: A retry request needs three things: the original input, the previous failed output, and the specific validation error. Generic "try again" feedback leaves the bot guessing which field failed, so it edits the wrong one. Naming the rejected value and the constraint it violated is what makes this class of error correctable.
ww: Loop tuning without changing the information the loop carries. Each of the ten attempts receives the same uninformative feedback, so the bot keeps guessing which field to change and simply burns more tokens doing it.

Removes the previous failed extraction, one of the three ingredients a retry needs. Without seeing what it produced last time, the bot has no way to know which value to change and can reproduce the same out-of-range line.

Nullable is the documented fix when information is genuinely absent from the source. The correct line is present in the diff, so making the field optional silently discards recoverable data and hides a defect the retry loop can actually fix.

questions.stem: The bot's dependency-upgrade check emits `breaking_changes_found: false` plus a free-text notes field. A post-incident review finds a pull request that merged green while that same finding's notes described a public method the upgrade had removed. The verdict and the evidence contradicted each other and nothing caught it. What design change most directly catches this?
questions.why: The self-correction pattern is structural: have the model emit both the claimed value and an independently re-derived one, plus a boolean when they disagree. Building the re-derivation into the output schema makes the contradiction machine-readable at check time and lets the pipeline route conflicts instead of merging green.
ww: This is the documented misconception that self-correction means asking the model whether it is sure. It adds no detection mechanism and produces no signal the pipeline can act on — the same contradictory finding still merges green, just after a vaguer instruction.

Post-hoc reconciliation surfaces the conflict weeks after the pull request merged, which is exactly the failure the incident review already demonstrated. The pattern's point is moving detection to the moment the finding is produced.

Adds a human bottleneck on every upgrade rather than making the internal contradiction visible. Reviewers would still be reading the same verdict and the same prose notes, with nothing flagging that the two disagree.

questions.stem: After the review was split into one focused pass per changed file, per-file feedback became uniformly detailed. One defect class still survives: a helper's return type changes in one file and three callers in other files go unflagged, because no pass sees beyond its own file. What should the team add?
questions.why: The documented architecture is two-part: per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass examining cross-file data flows. The per-file split already fixed attention dilution; the surviving defect is inherently cross-file, so it needs the pass designed to look there.
ww: The bigger-context trap. A larger window does not improve attention quality, so merging the passes back would reinstate the shallow, inconsistent single-pass feedback the split just cured, while still not guaranteeing cross-file reasoning.

Reintroduces the many-items-at-once condition that caused attention dilution in the first place. Each pass would carry the whole diff again, diluting the focus that made per-file feedback uniform, without a pass dedicated to cross-file relationships.

A post-processing patch stitched onto passes that never reasoned across files. Cross-file breakage shows up in data flow, not in assumptions a single-file pass happens to write down, so the script can only correlate what was already noticed.

questions.stem: The bot's unused-code check is instructed to "report code that is no longer used." On one pull request it flags a new helper that has no caller yet; on another it says nothing about a function whose last caller that same diff deleted. Developers say they cannot predict what it will flag. What change most reliably fixes this?
questions.why: Inconsistent output from a vague instruction is fixed by moving from abstract intent to a concrete, testable criterion. "No longer used" leaves the bot to invent a definition per pull request; "the diff removes its last remaining caller" is checkable and produces the same verdict on both examples every time.
ww: Treats an undefined criterion as an information shortage. The bot already sees the diff and the symbol in both failing cases — it just has no rule telling it which situation counts as unused, and a larger window supplies no rule.

Consensus filtering hides a symptom instead of defining the criterion. Both failures are systematic rather than random, so a second run against the same vague instruction reproduces them — and the filter suppresses genuine findings along the way.

Adds a scoring mechanism on top of the ambiguity rather than removing it. A confidently-applied wrong definition scores high, so the unpredictable flags survive the threshold while the criterion stays undefined.

questions.stem: Measured precision across the bot's four finding categories: security 92%, correctness 88%, style 46%, documentation 44%. Developers now resolve every bot comment without opening it, security findings included. The team needs security findings taken seriously again within this sprint, while the weak categories get fixed. What is the most effective approach?
questions.why: Two noisy categories have taught developers that the bot as a whole is noise, so accurate categories are being discarded with them. Temporarily disabling the high-false-positive categories stops the trust bleed immediately and leaves only high-precision findings in front of developers while the noisy prompts are repaired.
ww: Uniform relaxation damages the two categories that are already accurate, suppressing real security and correctness findings to compensate for problems in style and documentation. The precision spread is category-specific, so the response must be too.

Every low-precision finding still appears on the pull request. Developers who have stopped opening comments at all do not start reading them because a number was added, so the noise keeps eroding trust in the accurate categories.

The right long-term repair on the wrong timeline. Improving prompts takes weeks during which the noisy categories keep posting, trust keeps eroding, and the sprint deadline for security findings passes with nothing changed.

questions.stem: Developers request a deep-dive review by labelling a pull request and adding a one-line note. On ambiguous notes — "look at the concurrency work" on a diff touching three concurrent paths — the bot asks a clarifying question and waits. Telemetry shows 40% of authors never reply; the job then times out after six hours, holding the merge queue. How should it handle these instead?
questions.why: The documented strategy for vague requests is to state assumptions explicitly and proceed, inviting correction — rather than blocking on questions, which drives high abandonment. The author gets a real review immediately, sees precisely what was assumed, and can redirect it, while the merge queue keeps moving.
ww: Bundling the questions into one comment still puts the burden on the author before any work happens. The 40% who never reply are no likelier to answer a longer question, so the job keeps stalling — the compound form is explicitly not the fix.

A hidden default. The author never learns which of the three paths was reviewed, so a review that skipped the path they cared about reads like a clean bill of health. Assumptions must be stated, not silently applied.

Keeps the blocking question that causes the abandonment and adds a shorter fuse. On the 40% of pull requests where nobody replies, the author now receives no review at all — the queue is freed by producing nothing.

questions.stem: A second CI job is added to generate tests for changed modules. Its step invokes Claude Code with the prompt as a positional argument and no flags; the step never returns, and the nightly window closes with no tests generated. Teammates propose four ways to make it run unattended. Which is the documented approach?
questions.why: `-p` (`--print`) is the documented non-interactive mode: Claude Code processes the prompt, writes to stdout, and exits, which is exactly what a pipeline step needs. Without it Claude Code waits for interactive input, which is why the step never returns and the job produces nothing.
ww: `--batch` is not a Claude Code flag — a plausible-sounding invention. The step would fail on an unrecognized argument rather than run unattended, and the batching idea it borrows belongs to a different API entirely.
`CLAUDE_HEADLESS` is not a recognized environment variable. Exporting it changes nothing about how the CLI behaves, so the step would still sit waiting for input until the nightly window closed.

A Unix workaround rather than the documented approach. Closing standard input stops the process waiting, but it is not how Claude Code is meant to be driven non-interactively, and it leaves the pipeline depending on shell plumbing instead of a supported mode.

questions.stem: Finance asks the team to capture the Message Batches API's 50% discount on its most expensive job: the pre-merge review that blocks a pull request from merging until it posts a status. An engineer notes that in testing every batch came back in under an hour. What should the team do?
questions.why: Batch has no latency SLA — the processing window runs up to 24 hours — so anything a developer or pipeline is blocking on must stay synchronous. The discount belongs on the latency-tolerant work: the nightly test-generation run and the weekly audit, which nobody is waiting on.
ww: Treats batch as a cheaper synchronous API with a delay that faster polling can manage. Polling frequency has no effect on when a batch completes, and the one batch that takes many hours blocks a merge for exactly that long.

There is no latency guarantee to build a timeout against. A fifteen-minute deadline converts a cost saving into a merge gate that fails whenever the batch is slower than the observed typical case, which the 24-hour window explicitly permits.

Batch turnaround is a property of the processing window, not of request size, so smaller requests carry no timing promise. `custom_id` correctly joins results back to inputs but does nothing to make a blocking check safe on batch.

questions.stem: To compare two test-generation strategies against one expensive repository-wide analysis, the pipeline resumed the analysis session, ran the first strategy, then continued that same session with the second. Reviewers note the second write-up echoes the first's conclusions and reuses its ordering almost verbatim. What should the pipeline have done?
questions.why: Forking creates two branches that inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently. Each strategy is evaluated against the same expensive baseline, paid for once, with none of the other strategy's reasoning in view — exactly what the echoed second write-up was missing.
ww: Independence is a property of session structure, not of instructions. The first strategy's reasoning is still in context and still gets reasoned over, so the second evaluation stays anchored to it however the prompt is worded.

Buys independence by paying for the expensive repository-wide analysis twice — the cost the fork pattern exists to avoid. It also risks the two baselines differing, which makes the comparison less trustworthy rather than more.

Compaction compresses context rather than partitioning it: the first strategy's conclusions survive in summarized form while exact values and specific details from the analysis can be lost. Both problems get worse.

questions.stem: An audit of last quarter's pull requests finds that 9% of the bot's own blocking findings were dismissed without the file ever being re-read — several on lines no later commit had touched. The requirement to re-read and confirm the lines changed before dismissing exists only as a sentence in the system prompt. What most reliably closes this gap?
questions.why: When correct sequencing is mandatory, the precondition belongs in code, not in the prompt. Blocking the dismissal until the required read has returned makes the out-of-order case impossible rather than unlikely — the deterministic enforcement the 9% gap calls for.
ww: Prompt compliance is probabilistic. A more forceful instruction lowers the violation rate without eliminating it, which is the same failure mode as the current rule — and it is already a system-prompt rule the bot ignores 9% of the time.

Few-shot examples also work by influencing the model's behavior rather than constraining it. They make the correct order more likely, but nothing prevents a dismissal that skips the read, so a residual violation rate survives.

A self-report is a claim, not an enforced precondition — the bot can assert a read it never performed. It also moves detection to a weekly audit, well after the finding was dismissed and the pull request merged.

questions.stem: Before writing tests, the nightly job calls a coverage tool returning per-line hit counts for every file in the repository plus ninety days of trend history — when only the current module's uncovered ranges matter. Twelve modules in, the window is nearly full and the last modules get one-line placeholder tests. What is the most effective fix?
questions.why: Trimming verbose tool output to the relevant fields before it enters context is the documented fix — a PostToolUse hook keeps only what the task needs. The irrelevant fields never consume tokens and never linger for every later module, so the run stops exhausting its window partway through.
ww: Telling the model to ignore fields does not stop those fields being paid for. The full report still enters context and still consumes tokens on every subsequent turn; only the attention cost is nominally addressed, and the window still fills.

Treats the symptom while the cause keeps recurring: each module's call floods the context again, so summarization runs harder and more often and loses precision the later tests need. The verbose results themselves are what must be trimmed.

Raises cost and leaves the noise problem intact. A larger window delays the point at which the run exhausts it, and the model still reads ninety days of irrelevant trend history alongside every module it works on.
